en: Oṃ.
The Moonlight of the Consciousness-Sky.
Composed by the illustrious great poet Kālidāsa, [this work] accompanied by the commentary composed by Agnihotra Śāstrī Śarmā, who is adorned with the title Dhanadānandanātha-dīkṣita.
It is beautifully adorned with the commentary known as the *Divyacakorikā*.

The *Lalitāśataka* and *Haṃsatārāvalī* were edited by Mr. K. R. Jogalekar, M.A., LL.B., of Bombay, a member of the Asiatic Society of Bengal in Calcutta; and by the venerable Śrī Svāmī Trivikrama Tīrtha, who was initiated by Śrī Rāmānandanātha and known as Śāstrī, residing in the city of Sikanndrābād, who had been awarded the three titles of "Vidvān" (*Vidyāvāridhi*), "Sāhityaratna," and "Rājakoṣa" for his mastery of the three languages—English and others—in accordance with the regulations of the Government College, the Nijām’s College.

Furthermore, by the venerable Saripella Viśvanātha Śāstrin, who has been honored with the title of Professor for his composition of numerous poetic works such as *Kāmavilāsa*, and who has adorned even the *Glānuvāda-ṭīkā* with its nominal stems alone, this work has been edited, printed, and brought to light in his own Śrīśāradāmudrākṣaraśālā for the benefit of the students of the Vidyārīṇa [school] residing in the village of Bhaṭnavilli, within the Āmalāpuram tālūk of the Iṣṭugodāvari district; thus it stands triumphant.
Now, in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*, with its commentary *Divyacakorikā*, this is the introductory section of the first book (*pūrvapīṭhikā*).

O noble sirs! You whose hearts are solely intent upon investigating conduct, who are marked by thousands of great titles such as "Caturmukha" (the Four-faced One) for your mastery of character, who dwell within the various regions, sub-continents, and districts of Jambūdvīpa and other islands, and who are the foremost among scholars in discerning the meaning of speech—having understood this, I offer a certain request at dawn, which is like the digit of the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight: a request that is my own, natural, and inherent, characterized by its own resonance and the emission of its own sound, and which finds its sole delight in the twilight.

I humbly submit this with a thousand prostrations and joined palms: may you favor me by looking upon me with a desire to bestow grace, even as you contemplate the aesthetic power (*kalā*) of sound, word, and meaning—which must be cultivated through the reflective awareness of nominal stems (*prātipadika-vimarśa*). Furthermore, I entreat you to turn your gaze—though it may be distracted by the contemplation of the deeds of others—from the right, from the left, or from the rear, and to cast it here with a non-leftward (right) and non-beastly (divine) focus, without any partiality.

This has indeed been understood by certain Westerners—those who do not reside in the East and hold left-handed views, as well as those who follow them—who, through critical examinations of the unity and diversity between the creator and the names of the creators in both the *Prakṛti* (the work *Cidgaganacandrikā*) and the author Kālidāsa, have investigated their respective natures and concluded with a determination of whether the work belongs to the same category as its creator or otherwise. As for this great poet, how many years old was he?

"How many great poets indeed are there who possess the name-element 'Kali'?"—with such series of questions, which seek the moon of the *kuhū* [new-moon] day, yet result merely in searching for the moon of the Kali age that remains beyond perception; and which, along with those questions, concern the etymological analysis of the word-meanings of "Kali" as a part of a name—whether belonging to him [Kālidāsa], or to one's own [the questioner], or to the meanings of words in the sky of consciousness (*cidgagana*)—for those who, due to a specific lack of understanding regarding the connection between the meaning and the great purpose of such etymological analyses of word-meanings, ask: "How many great poets are there who possess the name-element 'Kali'?"

It is a matter of great concern that, even when questioned by those who possess their own hidden intentions, the bold and leading modern critics—those preeminent scholars who, though ignorant of any individual author among the manifestations of the Moon-like Great Poet, nevertheless indulge in the playful composition of verbal disputes regarding the investigation of the vast Prākṛta universe—have run hither and thither until now without reaching a conclusion; and whether it be regarding Prākṛta itself, or having ascended to the pinnacle of indifference toward Prākṛta, alas, they still do not rest. This is truly a great matter.

This is a cause for grief for the world; and for me too, as I have heard it again and again and seen it repeatedly—according to the worldly saying, "Even a horse, though not a mule, being free from greed, acts like a donkey"—this doubt has arisen regarding the identity of form between the agent (*kṛti*) and the material cause (*prakṛti*), based on the principle that no contradiction arises [between two things] when they appear identical.

Thus, regarding this subject of dispute concerning the identity of the author, the source material, and the title of the work, the members of the Āgama-anusandhāna Committee residing in the city of Calcutta—who are both the editors and publishers of this composition based on the original source—have declared in their own preface: "It can be ascertained even by a close study of the text that the author of this work is Kālidāsa," and further proclaimed: "Popular tradition also asserts this indeed."

Having established that the oral tradition (*janaśruti*) has its root in scripture (*śrutimūlatā*) through the passage beginning with "And she is the Truth," [the author] likewise—in the root text itself—by means of the word "Kālī," which reveals the secret of the practice of the sequence of the unsurpassed Great Reality (*mahārtha*), and similarly by the name "Kālidāsa," and further by the phrases "that which was spoken by myself and whispered by the servant" and "the *pañcikā* composed by Kālidāsa"—[all of these] being included within the count of verses along with the word "Jānaśruti," with the intention of representing the form of his own self, his guru, the circle of deities, and the sequence of names.

Having settled the dispute through profound meditative absorption, those who—like words that are inherently authoritative—themselves serve as the authority for unifying their own scripture with the agent, the material cause, and the names and forms [of the world], have brought to rest this verbal contention, which was previously so clever and bold. Now, regarding the resolution of the verbal dispute over whether the Great Form (Mahākṛti) and Primordial Matter (Prakṛti) belong to Him or do not belong to Him, or whether they have an end or no end, this very [scripture] is sufficient as a means of knowledge for those desiring to know the truth.

In this context, regarding the occasion of describing the Great Meanings (*mahārthakrama*) consisting of three, four, or five currents (*vāha*), which are composed of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—namely, word and meaning—and which consist of the triads of the nine *nāda-nādānta* and the three *tripuṭīs*, [this occurs] through the state of identity with the perfected union of Kālī and Kāla via the worship of the "I-grasp" (*ahaṃgrahopāsti*), whether it be of a worldly or Vedic nature; and through the single-minded absorption (*ekarasya*) of the great poets and Vedic-Tantric practitioners into the Great Meaning-krama of the five currents. This takes place within the five Vedic sheaths (*pañcakośa*), beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

By means of the method of the middle path (*madhyamamānanyāya*), within the subtle *liṅga* composed of the vital breath, mind, and consciousness, or in the ether, [one meditates upon] the couple Kālī and Kāleśvara, whose body consists of speech, mind, breath, and the Vaiśvānara-sound; with the intention of expressing their status as the cause of the entire universe, [they are described as] "those two who have become the fruit of each other's perfection of austerity."

"We praise the primordial Parents, the Mother and Father of phenomenal expansion (prapañca), the Husband and Wife. Thus, it is precisely in this Great Sūtra-Self—the couple that is the aggregate of the great triad of the knower and so forth (the *mahā-tripuṭī*), whose nature is both engagement and cessation, which is without beginning, which contains the six paths of sound (*nāda*), and which is characterized by these definitions—that [the scriptures declare]: "From whom indeed these beings are born," "Whose breath is the Vedas, who fashioned the entire world from the Vedas," and "This Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, and Sāmaveda are indeed the breath of this Great Being."

Thus, regarding the meanings of the sounds and words found within the Tantras and Āgamas—beginning with the Śruti and ending with the Nāda—as defined above, one should apply the vowels, consonants, and *kalās* of the *mātṛkā*, through the processes of *tripuṭī* and *pañcīkaraṇa*, and by means of the integration of the adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the bliss of the Fourth State (*turya*) and that which transcends it. This is expressed in such passages as: "If you desire to perceive Śiva constantly with the eye of consciousness (*cillōcana*) within the lineage and in its true being, and to attain the state of fullness, then direct your mind toward this [practice]."

"In accordance with the principle stated in the penultimate section of the *Taittirīya Mahānārāyaṇīya Upaniṣad*: 'This very Puruṣa is fivefold, consisting of five aspects, by whom all this is woven together—the earth, the intermediate space, the heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate directions; he indeed is this entire world, including the past, the present, and the future'"; and in conjunction with the unity of the three sequences of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) within the description of the consciousness of the abodes (*dhāmasaṃvit*) that will be explained later, beginning with: "'That which bestows the abode becomes one with the Mudrā'."

For this great leader among scholars, the Moon among Poets (Kavicandra), who describes the worship of the circle of the *bṛndā*—whose very form consists of light and bliss—in all its primary and secondary limbs, his own opening benedictory verse of the *Raghuvaṃśa* Mahākāvya, beginning with "As if speech and meaning were joined together," serves as a kind of universally accepted aphorism. By means of the guise of a simile, it establishes the realization of the essential truth that word and meaning are one and the same—a fact that has entered the category of what is impossible for any disputant or opponent to refute.

Just like the verses of the *Śrīmadrāmāyaṇa-sūtra* beginning with “*mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhām tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ*,” she—having been described by such words as “*yāham ity uditavākparā ca sā*” (*she who is intent on the speech uttered as 'I am'*)—is praised with devotion for the attainment of the Great Knowledge (*mahāvidyā*) and bliss, which consists of the comprehension of all words and their meanings even in relation to her own purpose; thereafter: “O Siddha, the praise of that state [of yours] was composed at Pūrṇapīṭha with reverence.”

It is understood both from his own statement—that "Śrīvatso composed that great secret for the sake of the Vānara"—and from the body of the text ending with those words, which is as if completed by its own commentary; furthermore, it is evident here from the passage: "From the perspective of *dharma*, *mudrā*, phoneme (*varṇa*), digit (*kalā*), consciousness (*saṃvit*), and the nature of being (*bhāvasvabhāva*)."

And by the vision of the *pātāla-niketadṛṣṭi*, the eightfold *bṛndacakra* taught in the *Tantrāloka* and other texts is revealed; that is, by describing how the various types of vision for the worship of the eightfold *bṛndacakra* as stated in the *Tantrāloka* and elsewhere are included within the three sequences of the *dhāma*, *saṃvit*, and *varṇa*.

By describing the various distinctions among the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the eight cities—beginning with the verse, "The city that radiates in eight ways, through the nature of the latent impressions arising from the eight cities"—there is an identification of his own eightfold form as described in the *nāndī* verse of the drama *Abhijñānaśākuntalam*. Furthermore, in the completion of the fourth quarter of the second auspicious verse of the first *vimarśa*, there is an identification of his own eightfold form as described in the *nāndī* verse of his own drama, *Mālavikāgnimitram*.

In the first reflection (*vimarśa*), in the completion of the fourth quarter of the second auspicious verse (*maṅgalaśloka*), there is the recognition of his own eightfold form described in the *nāndī* verse of his own play, the *Mālavikāgnimitra*.

In the first investigation, regarding the completion of the fourth quarter of the second maṅgala-verse, the fact that [the author] has directly incorporated—by way of stealing its unique words, meaning, and sentiment—the very fourth quarter of the *nāndī* verse from his own play *Mālavikāgnimitra*, namely, "May the Lord remove your dark disposition for the sake of beholding the true path," constitutes many distinguishing features; thus, these factors naturally reinforce the identity of this work with that [other] one, making it almost redundant.

Furthermore, the statement composed by the Emperor of Poets (Kavicakravartin) in his *Hṛdayacandrikā*—namely, "There shines a certain moon named Kālidāsa, a treasury of the nectar of speech, by whom the moonlight of consciousness has been created within the heart-caves of the wise, and darkness has been dispelled"—also stands as a verbal authority (*śābdapramāṇa*) for this very point.

Likewise, in this very first *Vimarśa*, within the verse-sūtra that constitutes the subject matter beginning with "He who is indeed the one who... (*yaḥ kilāsa*), there occurs—by virtue of the excellence of the description of the great meaning of the supreme *Mahānirvāṇa-caraṇa* (the Great Nirvāṇa Chapter), which consists of the conduct of latent impressions mixed by the friction of the feet of the Word and its Meaning composed of the Supreme *Ahaṃ-mantra*, and which serves as a constituent part of the *Para-śāmbhava-bheda* (the Supreme Śāmbhava Division) indicated by that [sūtra]—a passage under the guise of the Yakṣa’s instruction to the cloud during the description of Gaurī’s Peak in the *Meghadūta* poem: "In which... (*yasmin*).

"Those who have seen [the truth] and whose sins have been eradicated shall, after the departure of the body, become fit for the attainment of the stable state of the Gaṇas, provided they possess faith"—by such words, the majestic power (*vibhūti*) of the feet of Mahāśambhu, though uninvoked, enters the path of memory; thus, for those who have attained the great goal of the Anuttara tradition, this is the supreme illustration of authoritative proof in this matter. Nevertheless, my doubt remains exactly as it was regarding the identity of the name and form of the original work composed by Kālidāsa.

Since there remains the possibility that some form of doubt—whether it has assumed another form or is itself formless, whether it possesses a nature like the moonlight-form of the sky of his consciousness or is like a great physical form—persists because the fifth element of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which exists even beyond the fourth state (*turyātīta*) by having its very root in unreality, has not been uprooted; therefore, disregarding even the fear of being repeatedly accused of such audacity, I am ashamed before the foremost among investigators and the preeminent heroes among scholars of the East and West who have run so far [in their pursuit of truth], for I have merely scratched the surface. May I be forgiven for this.

I shall now cease from this effort of scrutinizing the investigations of those who are not from the East—an endeavor as futile as weighing a ram’s testicles—having already declared that even the modesty of offering this report is sufficient for those who have personally examined the root text along with my commentary from beginning to end.

Furthermore, here there is something that, though irrelevant to the present subject, concerns the nature of things belonging to both the ordinary and the extraordinary time; it is concealed by the guise of a religious teacher (dharmācārya) and, through illusion (māyā), deceives the world of the non-illusory. To the great people in this world, it appears as if something real, based on the authority of the sublime words of the great poet Candrācārya—stated up to the fourth reflection (*vimarśa*)—which include "the praise of that sequence composed by Siddhanātha and the *Pañcikā* composed by Kālidāsa. This [work] is rooted in that original composition made by the primordial Siddhanātha.

Out of a desire to offer praise for the Krama system, disregarding even great hardship such as expenditure and the like, he wandered to very distant places and endured even unbearable suffering; yet, failing to attain it, all of that was as if offered into the fire and reduced to ashes.

Then, by the power of the expansion of the feet of my own true guru’s nirvāṇa, I directly attained the unimpeded movement within the streams of the three, four, and five-fold layers (*puṭī*) of the sequence of the meaning of speech—the *kalā* of the *bindu* of the supreme, unsurpassed *tvaranāda*. Thus, even though I was destitute of the treatises on the unsurpassed Siddhānta, my desire to explain them became so urgent that it gripped my throat; this will be explained immediately below in the section concerning the announcement of the root scripture in the *Uttarapīṭhikā*.

However, having crossed over the turbulent ocean of obstacles—consisting of the fivefold duties such as writing the six-fold syllables of the Viśvamaya-grantha (which are necessary for the minting of iron coins)—due to the fear of adverse winds of place, time, and direction like a village pig, and due to the loss of worldly wealth; [he has now reached] the divine female Cakora bird wandering on the shores of the Milk Ocean, who, since the beginning of the two-year period, has remained like a female Cakravāka bird amidst the dawns of the decline of Dharma during the autumnal evenings, even through such a flow of time.

Even upon seeing a worldly moonlight, one who, out of a thirst for its taste, appears like a woman separated from her lover observing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow—though she has fasted—one repeatedly recalls the wise maxim, "All undertakings have their root in a *prastha* of rice," and asks, "What is my recourse? Thus, becoming a vessel for great suffering through the loss of leaves and other items used for upward-looking [offerings], through poverty resulting from the payment required to redeem them, and through the loss of ritual implements essential for the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) intended for that purpose, he is rendered a mere pedestal filled with supreme destitution.

Until I became disenchanted—having, within this interval, directly perceived with the skill of a wise man that entire mass of most unbearable sufferings, from wandering through regions as they were being experienced to the loss of provisions such as the poverty of paper and ink, even though my four eyes were not yet exhausted—I reached the city of Śikindrābād, where the venerable Śāstrimahodayas [said]: "Grass, ground, water, and kind speech are the four requisites."

"Never indeed are [the lineages] of the virtuous cut off in the houses of the good"—having personally become the exemplar of this great Smārta dharma thus declared, and having first established his own domestic hearth (*āvasathya*), the King of Mithilā, like a royal sage, [acted] within the celestial sky of the heart of Kālidāsa regarding this commentary on the *Divyacakorikā*—namely, the *Mahāsītāsāvitrī*—in the sacrificial arena of the *Saubhika*, throughout the narrative from the plowing of the altar up to the marriage of Rāma, extending as far as the world.

While the Upānāyaka was being brought in like a *pīṭhamarda* for the purpose of carrying the weight, under the condition of pulling the *pāśupata* bow, he returned to his quarters; during those very days, a certain man named Śāṅkarāpaśada—a betrayer even of those whose dharma is merely a banner of righteousness (*dharmadhvaja*), and the establisher of a similar seat of a teacher of false semblance of dharma—like Śauṣkala, the priest of Rāvaṇa, [appeared] at some point in the dead of night, [claiming], "For the sake of suppressing the subversion of dharma in the city of Ādilābāda, I am with the Agnihotra-teacher..."

"For two months, she should be sent to the vicinity of the Jagadguru-pīṭha to perform duties such as establishing the religious order for the purpose of fasting. Thus [spoke] Nāgeśa Śāstrin of Dhārvāḍanagarī regarding the venerable Śāstri-mahodayas—those who, upon merely hearing the name "Jagadguru-pīṭha," were easily deceived due to their lack of vigilance caused by the fault of non-realization; they were mere bearers of the banner of worldly religion, possessing the dignity of the world at the end of the age (*kalyanta*), yet hostile to the true *pīṭha*-dharma, and having learned the secrets of the religious banners for the sake of acquiring wealth.

Having thoroughly deceived the great scholars Rājeśvara Śāstrin of Vārāṇasī—who were authors of excellent treatises—by means of letters and responses composed with a semblance of courtesy yet marked by signs of profound and well-concealed guile, as much as he requested, that man, though skilled in deceiving others, was himself utterly deceived regarding the burden of his own great undertaking, such as the printing of his *Divyacakorikā*, even after having announced it; for he failed to fulfill the task of printing and so forth that he had himself initiated.

Thinking that he had found a handhold as it were, and having sighed over all that which was not to be trusted, while he was still breathing out—O friend! even our own beneficial words, beginning with "The seat of Virūpākṣa is indeed Akula, solely intent on dissolution among the Kula-vidyās, and this has been experienced by me before," he disregarded; and being utterly deceived, for the sake of leveling the subversion of Dharma, he brought me into the presence of that seat along with that false follower of Śaṅkara.

They repeatedly urged me in many ways to fill the vacancy left by the late scholar. Although I had myself committed misdeeds in the past, I was bound on both sides by the dignity of the Śāstri’s office and his personal kindness—like a bird caught in a net—and thus remained in the vicinity of that seat like a jackal sluggish with the delusion of having lost its testicles.

"O King, many days have been spent here; O elder, [this is] illusion"—thus spoke a certain wise man with a well-turned aphorism. Following the maxim of the jackal weary from the delusion of seeing a falling egg, I remained right there for nearly four months. Although summoned daily by letters and other means from the city of Śikandrābād by the excellent Śāstrins, and though I was eager to depart, I was restrained by the venerable Gurus—who, despite their disdain for festivals, would say "tomorrow" or "the day after," and who were like the son of Śukra (Kubera) under the guise of being followers of Śaṅkara.

In the meantime, my own village jewel—a merchant who was like a son to me, illustrious, never swerving from his own duty, wealthy, and as dear as my own life—was on the verge of death; when I was summoned by the news of the lute-strings out of an intense desire to see him, saying, "Come quickly," I was sent away in vain, having failed even to provide him with the provisions for the journey under the pretext of being a follower of Śaṅkara. When my load of provisions fell upon the heads of the venerable Śāstris, it was already too late.

At that time, indeed, along with me, the removal of the previously mentioned delusion regarding the castration of the ram by the wretched Śaṅkara—like the release of a pearl from a pearl-oyster—was accomplished with great effort; and having thus overcome thousands of such obstacles created by the wicked Śaṅkaras through their own will, lack of will, or the will of others, as if they were obstacles brought about by divine destiny, the commentary named *Divyacakorikā* was completed amidst the joy of the marriage festival of Arāma on this earth.

It is a source of great joy that even this much has been experienced as a vessel for the bliss of the festival of the first and second sections of the *Vimarśa*; herein, the author of the root text, along with the other eminent English scholar of the Āgama-anusandhāna-samiti, having written and explained an English introduction comparable to the *Gotrapravara*, cites the poet’s final verse-pledge beginning with "pūrṇapīṭhakṛtaṃ siddhe" in the *Anuṣṭubh* meter, [revealing] that this work is also known by the name Śrīvatsa.

Furthermore, a certain excellent scholar named Coritakālidāsa Mahārthavarana appears as if he were the actual author; thus, his audacity in displaying a scholarly proficiency in writing—born of either a lack of discernment or ignorance regarding the aesthetic arts and the meaning of the words of Śrīvatsa—elicits great derision even from ancient scholars, though they be shaven-headed. Enough, then, with this pedantry in investigating the manifestations of Kali.

This will also become directly evident to those who examine the commentary on this verse by means of the analogy of the grain from the cooking pot (*sthālīpulāka-nyāya*). Thus, the pen—though not inferior—having turned away from both the marking of that [text] and its own signature as if it were new, comes to rest in its own true nature; therefore, there is no further attachment even to that. Thus ends this introductory preface. Śrī Śrī Śrī.

Now, following the channel of the lineage of gurus regarding the objects of knowledge, there is this scripture named *Saprameya* (Endowed with Objects of Knowledge), which is like the very nature of this moonlight in the sky of consciousness; it serves as the introductory preface (*upoddhāta*) and the subsequent pedestal (*uttarapīṭhikā*).

Now, while the course of this primary work—the King of Kings—was proceeding without interruption due to certain circumstances during the month of Āśvina, in the bright fortnight, in the year Bahudhanya and so forth, at Rājamahendravarapura, I approached the venerable Dr. K. R. Jogalekar, a scholar endowed with Brahmanic glory who had arrived in my vicinity by chance; and from him, for the sake of making [the work] accessible, I received a brief portion of a commentary intended as a mere beginning.

In that regard, if I were to proceed with courtesy even though I am uncourteous, it would be as if a boil had formed upon a tumor; following the worldly maxim, even against my will, I would be seized by the throat by the grand display of sealing [the texts] and so forth, just like the grand display of saṃsāra. Thinking thus, out of fear of future complications and with a hidden intention, and having twice or thrice refused with a mind striving for the hardness of the unsurpassed stream—even while becoming dispassionate—[he acted].

Whether for the sake of milking the cow of worldly wealth and desire from the sixty-four arts—which, though mastered through nearly fifty years of study, remain as if devoid of self-nature; or because they are useless for the acquisition of human riches; or out of fear of their improper employment like the desires of the poor; or perhaps out of a longing to offer handfuls of mantra-flowers in the worship of the linguistic corpus, which is inseparable from the definitions of words and meanings in the Indian tradition; or finally, out of a longing for the purificatory bath at the conclusion of the great sacrifice of literature—[these arts have been presented].

Whether by the power of the impulsion of one's own tutelary deity, or indeed by the force of destiny whose root is unknown, this engagement was undertaken as if by sheer compulsion. Consequently, having returned home like one possessed by a spirit, for six months she has been marked day and night with an unblinking gaze, as if by a great malevolent spirit (mahākṛtyā) in the form of a collyrium-stick; this is the commentary on the "female chakora bird" who is but a semblance of a chakora.

Thereafter, due to the poverty of the literature of the *anuttara-siddhānta* tantras, and out of a desire for them, [the author] was received as a *paṭṭabhadra* by the venerable Brahmaśrī Karre Subrahmaṇya Śāstrī Mahodaya—who are of our own lineage (*sagotra*), who were previously acquainted with him, who are like brothers, whose fame has been established from birth until this day, and who have adorned the city of Śrīnagara until the end of the kalpa—at Ballāriḍi and Hospeṭaḍi.

Having approached the presence of the judges at the Musaph Court, who have reached the furthest limits of the highest established doctrines, and having stayed there for a meaningful month, I intend to recite the *Ābhāsacakorikā*, marked with the seal of my own composition, up to the point where it is available within those specific relevant portions of the following works: the *Tantrāloka*, the *Tantrasāra*, the *Laghuvivṛti*, the *Mālinīvijayavārtika*, the *Hṛdayacandrikā*, the *Saubhāgyavāsanāpaddhati*, the *Mahānayaprakāśa*, and the *Ānandakalpalatikā*.

By that very means, through those [efforts] filled with the abundance of the joy of bliss, twenty-two years ago, the *Cidgaganacandrikā*—which was composed, finalized, and preserved as if it were merely the original work itself—has now become worthy of its name, complete with its ornaments and hermitages, providing rest and appearing as a true Kalpa; and thus, by the mere assistance of one who perceives no sequence from beginning to end, it has been brought forth like a sigh, with the inner self saturated by the moonlight of satisfaction.

Then, having manifested their own abundance of bliss and exultation through the medium of the letter, they departed for heaven as if feeling their purpose fulfilled. Afterwards, when my heart’s sky—marked by remorse and bound by regret for them—was about to fly up to heaven with them, out of a desire to turn them into celestial cakorī birds, like its own light, I traversed the stellar firmament via the path of the sixfold way of Vedic meaning; at that time, even those who were my sole physical relatives appeared like humble disciples.

In the three languages—Sanskrit, Telugu, and English—he was known by the English professional name "Śāstrī," having been consecrated as a Professor of Sanskrit and Telugu at the Anglo-Vernacular College named Nizam’s College in the city of Hyderabad, a position he attained by surpassing the three ranks of *paṭṭabhadra*, such as *vidvān* (scholar), in accordance with the regulations for official titles in the branches of learning; yet he was also consecrated to the sovereign state of the supreme bliss of the ultimate doctrine (*anuttarasiddhānta-mahānanda-sāmrājya*) and bore the name Rāmānandanātha-dīkṣita.

The illustrious Saripella Viśvanātha Śāstri Mahodaya, the author of numerous poetic works such as the *Lalitāśataka*, *Haṃsatārāvalī*, and *Kāmavilāsa*, has, with joyful zeal for the great benefit of the community of English scholars, personally undertaken—like the twin mountains Yugandhara—the burden of printing this divine commentary, the *Divyacakorikā*, upon the mere meaning of the verses of this work, even while translating its sentence-meanings into the English language; oh, what a great boldness!

Thus, this method of transmission (*āgama-prakāra*) proceeds through a lineage of masters (*guru-paramparā*) headed by the three primary gurus. In this context, for the sake of convincing the world, as if to complete the thirty [members] of my own *Atri* clan—which has descended from the thousand-petalled lotus of the *Kula*, bears the seal of the *karropa* (the hand-symbol), and whose sole source is the potency of *vidyā*—there exists such a state even amidst the various sequences of bringing forth three, four, or five [transmissions].

As if for the purpose of marking me with a brand, by means of the synonym *daṇḍa* used in the Prakrit Āndhra dialect for the word *kara*, and through the persistence of the sequence of *daṇḍas*, even though the sequence of *daṇḍas* was distinguished by the aforementioned varieties of three, four, or five carriers, I—having fallen into the row of the multitude of disciples, following the sequence of the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) as if drawn by fate through a desire for the great sequence for the sake of my father, like the renunciation of a triple-staff ascetic—appeared in former times as if marked with the form of ink, like a mere semblance of a female partridge (*cakorikā*).

By the very power of the thousand-petaled lotus of the *kulākula*, she was made into a celestial *cakorī* bird; and in this manner, over the course of time, the entire tradition—including its roots and its continuous transmission—was established. Just as the scripture (*āgama*) itself is connected to the sequence of the letters of the abiding consciousness through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), so too is it connected to the three wheels that are the embodiments of Light and Bliss. Furthermore, although impelled by Trivikrama Tīrtha of the Committee for the Investigation of the Scriptures of the Immortals at Kalikātā, [this work] follows the non-triple-stepped sequence (*atrivikramakrama*) in accordance with the fourth *Kula* lineage, within the joint of the staff of the lineage.

"Madīye" means "in me" or "my own. By the phrase "formed into a circle by the embodiment of the Great Bliss beyond the Fourth (turyātīta-mahānanda)," it is meant that through the intensity of the surge of the essence of the waves of Great Bliss, I have become this very thing; indeed, even the sequence of the Fourth and Beyond has been brought to completion in this creation, and I have become solely the form of the circle of the embodiment of the Bliss of the Fourth (turīyānanda). "The tonsure (muṇḍana) consists in the manifestation of knowledge, and the staff (daṇḍana) consists in the nature of action. Therefore, the sequence of the Tonsure and the Staff are considered to be of the nature of Knowledge and Action."

Thus, according to the method set forth in other Tantras cited in the *Mahārthamañjarī*, the *Parimala*, and other works, and following the direction previously established for our own sequence of the *Kriyāmayānandacakra-daṇḍa*, the venerable Śaripella Viśvanātha Śāstrin himself adopted it; consequently, in the remaining *Muṇḍakrama* alone, rest was attained by his own light within the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra*) of Akula, year after year, like the sun within the sun.

In this very interval, as previously described in the first section (*pūrvapīṭhikā*), having experienced the great deception committed by that outcaste of Śiva (*śāṅkarāpaśada*)—who, while presiding over the Virūpākṣa Pīṭha, acted in opposition to his own duty through hostility toward his own self-nature—the illustrious Śāstri Mahodaya, out of confusion regarding what ought to be done, [sought the counsel] of the eminent scholars of the Vijayanagara establishment, the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Tātā Subbarāya Śāstri Mahodaya, who was adorned with titles such as *Kalāprapūrṇa*. [The text continues: ...of the venerable... [and so forth].

I was also encouraged by the esteemed Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa Śāstrin, author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, to edit [the work]; however, I took up only the *Ābhāsa-cakorikā* from the ancient manuscript. There, that very [text] was read aloud to those two [scholars]. Upon their satisfaction from hearing it, they presented her with a certificate of appreciation; yet this was not solely on account of that divine *cakorikā*. The same applies to Harihara Śāstrin and others, as it would be redundant to state further.

Therefore, having informed the honorable readers that the divine Abhāsacakorī was created immediately after the bringing of each respective letter, I shall desist from writing further accounts of the arrival of this literary composition.

In this root treatise titled *Cidgaganacandrikā*, belonging to the Āgama Research Committee located in the city of Calcutta, five verses are not found. And those [missing verses] are as follows: "In the sky where all sequences of activity have been cast out," "O Mother! consisting of the collection of phonemes grasped from beginning to end," "O Mother! composed of the water of the ether of consciousness," "Wherever the rays meet," and "O Mother! worshiper of Your two feet."

Regarding that, although the first, third, and fourth verses were pointed out by the editors of the root text, Svāmī Trivikrama Tīrtha Pāda, through their citation in commentaries such as the *Yoginīhṛdayasetubandha*—which were accepted as authoritative by various teachers following the conclusion of the root work—they were not found in the root text as it was obtained by them. Consequently, for fear of disrupting the internal consistency or due to some other reason, they did not include them in their own printed edition of the root text, despite the daring act of inserting them from elsewhere.

It has not been omitted from the edition. The second verse was found by being cited as an authority in another work and in the *Saundaryalaharī-vyākhyāna* composed by Vandāru-āśrama-pūjyapāda; thus, the two verses beginning with "khe nirasta" appear in order in two locations marked with the number 2 in the second *vimarśa*, while the remaining two verses beginning with "amba kecit" appear in two locations in the third *vimarśa*, and the fifth [verse] likewise appears in its location in the fourth *vimarśa*.

It has been interpolated and explained solely out of a desire for association with those [other texts]. Therefore, it is also announced that these five [verses] should be understood by discerning and excellent scholars as being worthy of interpolation either within those [texts] or in other places. May there be auspiciousness!

Now, regarding the essential portion of the subject matter concerning the fourfold sequence beginning with the object, *Citgaganacandrikā*—this great work, by virtue of its body consisting of words and meanings compiled from the "Gahvara" (the Abyss) which is accompanied by the fourfold *vimarśa*, can rightly be said to be the great work of the moon among great poets, Kālidāsa himself, and not that of anyone else. In this regard, we say that the very title of the composition itself explains the answer to the questions: "What kind of great work is it? and "What is the 'Abyss' (*gahvara*) that is the king of subjects? How so? "The sky of consciousness" (*cidgagana*) is the light of knowledge, non-different from the Great Fire (*mahāhāra*). "Moonlight" (*candrikā*) is indeed the radiance of the moon.

And that [power], by means of a mental faculty (*buddhi*) differentiated by the various forms of attachment and aversion toward its own respective objects of dharma and adharma—[a faculty] which is equivalent to the threefold five-syllable mantra or the fifteen-syllable mantra; which consists of the triad of the path of meaning (*arthādhvan*) as infused with the six paths of speech and meaning (*vāgartha-ṣaḍadhvan*); which likewise consists of the threefold five-syllable mantra or the fifteen-syllable mantra formed from the triad of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*; and which, through conventional terminology (*sāṅketika-paribhāṣā*), is equivalent to the triad of the path of sound (*śabdādhvan*) within the rosaries (*akṣamālā*).

It should be understood that "in the single form of Prakṛti and Puruṣa, undivided by space and time" is the summary statement (*saṃgrahavākya*). By such [a form], through the distinctions of lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth in the bright and dark fortnights, or through the various divisions of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*) belonging to each, as will be stated in their respective places—in the first *Vimarśa* with the words beginning "That which is the interval between fullness and thinness," in the second with "The digit of the Lord of Day and the Lord of Night," and likewise in the third and fourth *Vimarśas*.

By transcending the conventional measurements of space and time—such as those pertaining to place, duration, human beings, ancestors, and so forth—and through the differentiation of the conceptualization of pure, ultimate, divine, ancestral, and final temporal measures, [it is said]: "The seven great sages of old and likewise the four Manus..."

"Those whose mental offspring are born of my own nature—these are the progeny in this world. Even within the scriptural conventions of the great Manu and the supreme sages, concerning the fourteen yugas beginning with the four yugas as described by the Teacher of the Gītā, there is a distinction based on the divisions of *chandas*, *kalā*, *kāla*, *karma*, and the *tripuṭī-kalpa*, extending from the four thousand yugas up to the day of Brahmā; and this is for the purpose of ascending the *kalās* of the form of Brahmā, which will be explained in the third *vimarśa*, in order to expand the respective accomplishments of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to those who hold office.

Through gradual increase and decrease—designated as "gradual" (*krama*) and "non-gradual" (*akrama*)—the ultimate emergence of the limbs of the Vedic Brahman-body consists precisely in the attainment of identity with the couple Kālī and Kāla, which is the essential nature of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the *Kula* and *Akula*. Whether it be Vedic or Tantric, that ascent is indeed the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*). Or rather, that Great Purpose itself is the ascent.

According to the perspective of the *Yāmala* and other Tantric scriptures, by accepting the three levels of existence (*sattātraya*) and by including the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* within the level of phenomenal existence (*vyavahārasattā*), there arises the ultimate Great Purpose (*mahārtha*). This consists of the worship through the method of "I-grasping" (*ahaṃgraha-upāsanā*), which is essentially the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the triad of the knower and so forth; it is differentiated according to the various capacities of the practitioner—whether superior, middling, or inferior—and takes the singular form of the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*) comprising the three, four, or five meanings, from the Western Tradition (*paścimāmnāya*) up to the Upper Tradition (*ūrdhvāmnāya*).

According to the Vedic perspective, however, since conventional reality is not admitted, the supreme goal of human life (*paramapuruṣārtha*) is the fourth state (*turya*), which consists of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* alone—designated as the two types of existence, the phenomenal and the ultimate—or it is the very nature of the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*). Thus, through a discernment between the Tantric and Vedic views, one must determine the ascent of Kālaśiva—the causal adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*)—or Karmaśiva—the effected adjunct (*kāryopādhi*)—to the status of the limbs (*kalā*) of the body of Brahman.

For indeed, within each single day of Brahmā, or within his kalpa consisting of ritual activity, fourteen manvantaras must be passed. Among those manvantaras, there are four decades of states; thus they are fourteen, numbering fourteen in total.

In the *Turīyavimarśa*, through various etymological analyses such as "that which [is present] in all states everywhere," etc., [the Lord is described] by means of the expansion of the universe characterized by the secret terminology (*guptibhāṣita*) to be explained hereafter. He manifests sequentially in the form of the seven Vedic meters beginning with *Gāyatrī* and ending with *Jagatī*, consisting of seven meters each increasing by four syllables; and in the Tantric form, from fifteen syllables (the *Pañcadaśākṣarī*) up to seventeen and eighteen syllables, through the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the emission (*vaisargika-daśā*) and the couple (*mithuna*).

The very potency of mantra (*māntravīrya*) consists of the form of the aggregate of vowels and consonants, as well as the form of the Great Sixteen Kalās; it has evolved into the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of speech and meaning, which constitute the body [of the universe]—an internal triad of mutual interpenetration—manifesting as the power of the six paths of the lineage of gurus from the multitude of disciples up to the supreme multitude. That this is the power of the six paths of speech and meaning, consisting of the *Mātṛkā*, has been loudly proclaimed by the great poet in this work with his own voice.

This very [reality] is Kālī as *prakṛti* within the *puruṣa* by way of the union of *kula* and *visarga*, and externally she is Kālī as *kāla-prakṛti* by way of the *puruṣa*. Thus, from the statement "the form of *puruṣa* and *kāla* internally and externally," and so forth, this has been proclaimed throughout the fivefold corpus of the Vedas, Vedāṅgas, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Kāvyas, as well as in the *Bhārata* literature and the five *kalpas*. Furthermore, it has been described as consisting of the five faces of the five Brahmans, such as Sadyojāta and the rest, characterized by the syllables of mantra, through the expansion of the universe spoken in secret, which is of the singular nature of light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*).

It is to be perceived by an extremely subtle vision. However, in this matter, due to the defect of unrefined eyesight and human error, there are those who—like those bitten by a snake at an improper time—perceive their own Brāhmī triad (consisting of direction, space, and time) along with the force of that poison as something external, through non-self-identification, as if in a creation. Consequently, even though there is no actual transformation, those who see their own radiance but possess distorted minds and disregard the Teacher will encounter various distinctions based on defects of vision; this is a universal truth.

Even there, according to the varying degrees of authority in their discernment (*vimarśa*), some fall within the scope of the discernment of wandering through various artistic forms (*kalā*) and cosmic cycles (*kalpa*) due to the blindness of non-discrimination regarding the distinctions between the followers of Manu, Bhānava, and Māna; others, even therein, through stubborn dogmatism, fall within the scope of the discernment of external objects—whether they be inert externals or external inert things. Such is the extent of this interpretation, because the word *manu* is the sole indicator of the discernment of the mantra and its meaning. In that context, the "cosmic cycle" (*kalpa*) is precisely the union of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*).

Regarding the definition of *kalpa*, there is a statement from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*: "The body emaciated by diseases is called a *kalpa*; because it indicates that [emaciation], the wise know the *Kalpasūtra* as such. In this context, [the term *kalpa*] refers to the meaning of the first sentence of the third *Vimarśa*: "O Ambikā, you are the form whose manifestation is the primordial consciousness."

In that very context, according to the eloquent statement of the great poet beginning with "brahmavigrahakalādhirohiṇī," the so-called *brāhma-kalpa* refers to any one of the five forms of the Brahmas—namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—which, according to its specific authority, possesses the state of any one of the stages of the practitioner's qualification.

In this regard, there are fourteen *manus*, who constitute the *manvantaras* according to the previously mentioned distinctions of form and etymology; or [they are so called] from the perspective of the distinction between cause and fruit regarding the *pravṛtti* (active) and *nivṛtti* (withdrawn) paths of dharma, and through their creation; or as a duality consisting of the seed and its effect along with the seven [groups]; or by means of a distinction imagined solely within pure perception (*dṛṅmātra*); or through the skillful manifestation of cause and fruit. Since the word *anu* is common to both the sense of "subsequent" and "mantra," it should be understood—according to the respective qualification and as appropriate—that there is a division of *manus* and intermediate measures, owing to their coexistence with the aggregate of body and senses.

In the same way, even within a single *kalpa*—which, though measured by seventy-one great *yugas*, is but a minute fraction of his [Brahmā’s] lifespan—one must understand, according to the appropriate method of calculation, how the *yugas* ending with the *Manvantara*, the *Saptarṣi*, the *Divya*, the *Paitrya*, the *Prājāpatya*, and the *Brāhma* correspond to the five types of months used in common practice, such as the solar and lunar.

Indeed, for all measurements of time—from the human day up to the day of Brahmā—it is only by relying on the calculation of days and *kalpas* that the duration of time, as well as the scriptural measures of lifespan such as "A person has a hundredfold measure, a hundred-year life, and a hundred faculties," becomes possible.

This being the case, whether regarding the primary meaning of words on the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*), or within the *prakṛti* itself, or among the incarnate beings (*avatārapuruṣa*) belonging to the Vaivasvata Manvantara—specifically those of the twenty-eighth Kali Yuga—there exist manifold differences of opinion concerning the great poet Kālidāsa, who is like the moon. This is indeed an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), for through the act of gambling characterized as will be described—which is like a game of dice won by those excellent scholars whose forms are the very arts and times of those respective [beings]—the games of chance known as *kṛta*, *āya*, and so forth, have been won by the vision of Kālidāsa’s poetic activity.

Whether it be by ascending his own bodily form through his specific karma, or by means of one's own respective *prakṛti*, let alone the ascent to his great form consisting of his digits (*kalā*) and time (*kāla*). For that very point was proclaimed by him himself at the conclusion of the work: "By whom the ocean of the lake of play is constantly entered, by whom Śiva [enters] me."

If it is argued that, since the ascent of the structural parts of its constituent actions is the subject at hand, one should—by means of the etymological derivation of the name and form of the composition (*prabandha*) as speech and meaning—determine the essence of the matter through the principle of their identity with the name and form of that [composition], alongside the determination of the fourfold contextual adjuncts such as the subject matter, then let the determination of the nature of the term *cidgagana* (the sky of consciousness) be made accordingly: whether it be "the sky in consciousness" or "consciousness itself is the sky," or "the sky itself is [consciousness]."

Or rather, it may be through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the non-difference between consciousness and the sky; or else, by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound with "sky" as the final member, such that "consciousness is where the sky is. In the same way, regarding the analysis of the words and their meanings in the phrase "moonlight in the sky of consciousness," it may be an *adhikaraṇa-tatpuruṣa* (locative determinative) compound, namely "moonlight in the sky of consciousness"; or perhaps it is a *śākta-karmadhāraya* (possessive appositional) analysis, meaning "that whose sky is consciousness is the 'consciousness-sky,' and she is that moonlight"; or finally, as before, it may be that the sky of consciousness itself is the moonlight, or the moonlight itself is the sky of consciousness.

Or, "the sky of consciousness" (*cidgagana*) may signify the realization of non-duality; thus, among these six types of etymological analyses (*vigraha*), when two of them result in the realization of non-duality, five remain. By which analysis, or in what manner, is the determination of the reality of the Great Nature (*mahākṛti*) or Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) established within the nature of that analysis? Or how, with its assistance, is the determination of the reality of the fourfold connection—consisting of the abyss (*gahvara*), the object (*viṣaya*), the king (*rāja*), and so forth—established? It is precisely by the Moon of the Great Poet (*mahākavicandra*) that [this] abyss (*gahvara*) serves as the excellent answer to such a multitude of questions.

The "King of Objects" (*viṣayarāja*)—whether as the nature of a continuous composition (*prabandha*) or as the composition itself—is transformed and refined by means of a single expression that brings about the aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the sixfold analysis of grammatical relations (*kāraka*), paths (*adhvan*), and syntactic structures (*vigraha*). Having thus been transformed like the sun and the moon and rendered pure, it is to be understood as "concentration" (*samādhi*) in each instance. This is how it should be explained.

If one asks how this is so: according to the definition of the opening of a literary work (*prabandha-mukha*) stated as "the benediction (*āśis*), the salutation (*namaskriyā*), or the mention of the subject matter (*vastunirdeśa*) constitutes its opening," it is indeed the established convention of the ancient great poets to indicate the fourfold preliminary connection (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*) by means of any one of these—benediction and so forth. Therefore, here, in the auspicious verse beginning with "The Ocean of Milk" (*kṣīroda*), the fact that [the work] is indeed the very nature of that Puruṣa is expressed by the words themselves, within the context of the Great Emanation (*mahāvaisargikī*) designated as the "Sixteenth."

And that [reality], from the perspective of inner vision, consists of the exertion within the heart; yet from the perspective of outer vision, it takes the singular form of the triad of direction, place, and time as employed therein. Although these two are, to those of gross vision, like a great couple of noble men—one a devoted husband and the other a chaste wife—held together by their mutual skill, they are in truth a single Vedic pair of word and meaning. Within its very essence, it flashes forth as a most subtle union of entities: as the individual soul and the Lord (Jīveśvarau), the world and the living being (Jagajjīvau), Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Pārvatī and Parameśvara, Kālī and Kāla.

By means of the Vedic speech beginning with "the teacher and the disciple," and through its various inseparable synonymous names, [the scripture]—employing the skill of conceptualization up to the level of conventional perception—distinguishes the attributes of one's own Self and awakens it. According to the capacity of the disciple, this occurs through the sequence of word and meaning known as the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), whether designated as sequential or non-sequential: the sixth and seventh [states] are bound to the two aspects of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); the eighth is bound to the aspect of the object (*prameya*), thus forming the triad of knower, means, and object; and the ninth and tenth consist solely of the nature of word and meaning.

The couple (*mithuna*). And thus, even in the determination of the names of the previously mentioned compositions, which consist of two triplets (*tripuṭī*), by means of the technical terminology of the sixfold verbal analysis (*ṣaḍvidha-śābdavigraha-paribhāṣā*)—through synonymous names such as the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and the six philosophical systems (*ṣaḍdarśana*), which are designated by the six paths of the grammatical factors (*kāraka*)—and by means of the technical terminology of the six paths of the objects to be denoted (*tattad-abhidheya-artha-ṣaḍadhva-vigraha-paribhāṣā*) within the wheel of the ten senses joined with mind and intellect, in the nature of the Person (*puruṣa*), in the attainment of the goals of man (*pumartha-sampatti*), and in the triplets of word and meaning consisting of three, four, or five vehicles (*vāha*), [these are established] through both the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*yaṣṭi*).

Because within the continuum of word and meaning, there is a single form in the six, twelve, sixteen, and beyond, within the Great Bindu; likewise, even regarding the reality of the triad of direction, space, and time, there is both a dual and a single form through the collective and individual aspects of the equinox-year, the intercalary month, either of the two seasons of winter or spring, and the various divisions of time, as well as the triad of the digits of time, speech, and meaning.

Thus, this pair or triad of *tripuṭīs* is the primordial couple of Time and Puruṣa; or else, one of these couples is the ultimate, fourth (*turya*) form itself. Having either set that aside within the sphere of the object of worship (*upāsya-koṭi*), or having introduced it into the sphere of the worshipper (*upāsaka-koṭi*), what remains in the fivefold group of *tripuṭīs*—which consists of two, four, or five currents—is the very nature of the Self, designated as the Fourth (*turya*) and the Great Reality (*mahārtha*). This is indicated both by the collective and individual aspects of the triad of orbs of Agni, Soma, and Sūrya, which sets in motion the *kalās* and Time.

[This includes] the Śaiva and Śākta Tantras and Āgamas, extending up to the Hakrama, as well as the practical application of the fivefold acts (*pañcakṛtya*). In this regard, those who follow the tradition of the Śaiva, Śākta, and other Tantras and Āgamas do so by relying on the sequence of the established doctrines of the *sṛṣṭidṛṣṭivāda* (the theory that the world is seen after it is created), which is designated as the inversion of the view of the [dualistic] physical reality (*tadatraivaṃbhūtabhautikadṛgviparyāya*). And those who worship according to the Vedic path do so by relying on the sequence of the established doctrine of the *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda* (the theory that the world is created when it is seen), which is designated as the withdrawal of the phenomenal view (*prātibhāsikadṛksaṃhāra*), following the path of non-sequentiality (*akramamārga*). This is because the nature of the ultimate, real entity (*pāramārthikasadvastusvarūpa*) is beyond verbal expression (*aśābdatva*).

Having inverted the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattā*) itself into the conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent (*prātibhāsika*), and having manifoldly expanded upon it as a further proliferation (*prapañca*), they have described that very essential nature (*svarūpa*) for the sake of awakening to reality. This the great poet himself explicitly indicated in the second verse of the second *vimarśa* with the words, "characterized by the reflection on the non-sequential and the sequential," and so forth. Let this matter rest for now.

Regarding the two aspects previously mentioned—the heart, effort, speech, and meaning—which constitute the nature of Prakṛti, and the word and meaning of the term *cidgaganacandrikā*, one may understand their essential identity (*svarūpasāmarasya*) even by means of any one of the six philosophical systems (*ṣaḍdarśana*) or through a formal definition (*vigraha*), according to the analogy of the blind men and the elephant; thus, through the internal vision of the Vedas, they are indeed the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) known by other names such as Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*).

Whether through the worldly perspective established by the Tantras and Āgamas, or through the external view where the triad of subject, object, and means of knowledge (pramātṛ-ādi-tripuṭī)—also known as fire, water, and earth—is identified with the triad of emission (visarga) consisting of Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Āṇava, or alternatively as the triad of abodes (dhāma-tripuṭī) consisting of fire, moon, and sun; one need not trouble oneself with such divisions when defining the very nature of the Fourth (turya) reality as being manifested through this threefold process.

Nevertheless, since this work is a composition in the form of a Tantric treatise (*tantra-prabandha*), it is primarily the Tantric technical terminology (*tāntrikī paribhāṣā*) that is employed for the description of its various subject matters, rather than Vedic terminology; thus, that [Tantric terminology] is generally adopted. However, even Vedic terminology is indeed explained incidentally within the respective sections for the benefit of the world of its practitioners—such is the established method of exposition.

In this context, according to the technical terminology of the Tantras, that which is called the "Śāktavisarga" (the emission of power) consists of the fivefold activities—creation, maintenance, withdrawal, the Inexplicable (Anākhyā), and manifestation (Ābhāsā)—and their reverse order. Within this pentad, the pair of activities known as the Inexplicable and Manifestation—which are otherwise termed "contradiction" and "grace"—is subsumed within the two activities of withdrawal and maintenance, or else within the great state of maintenance at the central pivot of the triad of activities beginning with creation. Thus, even within the triad of activities beginning with creation, which is itself pregnant with the Inexplicable and Manifestation, that which is designated as "successive" and "non-successive" exists through its presence at the beginning and the end.

Having internalized within the Great Abiding (mahāsthiti) of one’s own self the two functions—known as emission and withdrawal, or conversely designated as withdrawal and emission—as mere semblances of function, and having desired the full nature of the couple consisting of Śiva and Śakti (whose essence is Nature and Spirit eternally united) through the plenitude of such a Great Abiding that contains this fourfold function, or through its being the form of full power; then, in that Great Abiding or Great Power which is like a maiden in her rising youth, [one should pray]: "Bestow upon me a son in this state."

"Make me the eleventh"—this is well-known from such Śruti and Smṛti texts as "The ten forms of Nārāyaṇa produced from the nails of the fingers of his hands. Being complete with six limbs and endowed with the ten senses, [the emission] is called the eighteenfold emission of power (*śaktivisarga*). This is because, by means of the birth of a son who is the union of consciousness and unconsciousness—the one who upholds the lineage of knowledge and vigor—it brings about the fulfillment of the six-limbed state for both oneself and one's own power. Thus, like one who is complete with six limbs, it is itself attained through identity with power, and is characterized solely by the awakening of the mind.

The *śāmbhava-visarga*, however, is the ground of bliss (*ānandabhūmi*); indeed, the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) of the word *Śambhu* is the Self (*ātman*). And that [Self], although satisfied by the fullness of consciousness during the experience of external bliss within the previously mentioned five-fold cosmic acts (*pañcakṛtya*)—such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth, which follow the natural order—is nevertheless intent upon the full experience of the inward-turned bliss of its own power (*svaśāktānanda*). Thus, for those whose minds remain extroverted, it is the seed of latent impressions (*vāsanābīja*) characterized as follows: beginning with the appearance of objects already perceived (like a jar) and ending with the appearance of non-conceptual objects of knowledge.

Alternatively, through the act of withdrawal of the seeds and sprouts, by means of the internal form of the fire of consciousness, he himself becomes the offerer within his own power; because this is characterized solely by the dissolution of the mind, he is designated as the seventeenth, Śambhu.

Now, even the *āṇava* emission (*visarga*), assuming the form of an individual soul (*jīvāṇu*) that is itself incomplete, desiring either a resting in the self—which is non-knowledge—or the fullness of its own nature in the form of the *arthāṇava-bindu*, seeks between the previously mentioned *mahāsthiti* and the *śākta-śāmbhava* emissions both entry and settlement, as well as the state of being full through the recitation containing the *śākta* emission. Desiring thus the fullness of the senses and the fullness within the senses, it rests in that very [state] by means of that [emission], and not by means of the unstruck (*anāhata*) emission which is full of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*).

This fifteenth or sixteenth emission (*visarga*), characterized by the resting of the mind, should be examined in detail in works such as the *Tantrāloka*, the *Tantrasāra*, and the *Laghuvivṛtti*, where the correspondence between the characteristics and the objects of the three emissions is set forth. This very triad of emissions is also dealt with in the world through the technical terminology of the three genders—feminine, masculine, and neuter—within the "six paths" (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of speech and meaning, and as the triad of persons: first, middle, and last.

If one wishes to perceive with the eye of consciousness (*camatkāra-cakṣus*) these three emissions (*visarga*)—endowed with the characteristics thus described—by means of the Unsurpassed Act (*anuttara-kṛti*), then: at the end of the section on the vowels of the Mātṛkā, the Śākta emission is the union of the couple, consisting of the emission of Fire and Moon (*agnīṣomīya-visarga*) which is like two drops of oil and clarified butter; the Śāmbhava emission is the nature of the Sun or the Great Moon, consisting of the non-dual, full *anusvāra*; and the Āṇava emission is the objectified meaning, manifested as a gross line beginning with the letter 'A' through the Unsurpassed Form, by means of the body of the Kula composed of phonemes (*varṇamaya-kula-śarīra*).

This must be understood by those who are preeminent among investigators—whether they be knowers of the secrets of the Trika doctrine or proponents of the secrets of the Spanda doctrine—according to the boundaries of the Kaula Anuttara Siddhānta, having discerned it through the mouth of a Guru by means of the full realization of the true existence of the synthesis of the definitions of the phonemes of the Mātṛkā, speech, and their meanings.

Even in the world, having discerned and understood [the Self] through the bodies of effects characterized as mother, father, and son; through the bodies of the three activities consisting of the functions of creation and so forth; through the bodies of the great purpose consisting of the three aims of life beginning with dharma; and through the causal bodies of the three abodes beginning with Agni and Soma—one should worship, according to one's qualification, at the end of the twelve (dvādaśānta), in the ultimate fifteenth state of the Great Subject (mahāpramātṛ) and so forth, at the end of the Great Cause (mahākāraṇa) within the triad (tripuṭī), and finally at the sixteenth, at the end of the sixteen.

In this context, this *visarga* is indeed the nature of speech, the meaning, the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), and the soul within transmigratory existence, as well as the form of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). Furthermore, the two *visargas*—the Śākta and the Śāmbhava—are expressed by the three *bindus*, being clearly manifest through the ninefold division of the Śākta and Śāmbhava *nāda*s.

In the Mātṛkā, at the end of its own section, within and without the threefold enclosure (tripuṭī) and the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), there is that which is to be attended to through both the individual and the collective aspects, extending from the twelve and sixteen [ends] down to the Nāda, Vāk, Artha, and the nine Akṣas, up to Unmanī, Mahānāda, and Bindu; and by means of the ultimate division of the couple, it is indeed the form of the goal (sādhya-rūpa) itself, culminating in the attainment of the Great Accomplishment (mahārtha-siddhi).

It has been previously indicated that even during the state of manifestation through clear articulation, within the individual (āṇava) level—where the six paths consisting of sound, speech, and meaning arise as the flash of differentiation among the potencies ranging from the agent and instruments to the action and its result—the sequence of speech and meaning remains non-different from the cause, both in its individual and collective aspects, in the form of the triad of the three abodes such as Agni and Soma.

In this context, within the fourfold bond (*anubandha-catuṣṭaya*), it is the individual soul (*jīva*) alone that is the primary subject (*adhikārī*) characterized by the atomic emission (*āṇava-visarga*). Driven by the force of time, being carried along in the stream of births and deaths at whatever stage of life or point in time, he falls into the womb of the empowered emission (*śākta-visarga*) when only a slight remnant of the atomic impurity (*āṇava-mala*) remains. That very moment constitutes his final birth in the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) or his destruction by time.

And at that time, he descends into the land of action (karmabhūmi) as the son of Śakti—manifesting as Gaṇeśa—because he embodies the sixfold sacrifice (ṣaḍadhvara) which is the meaning of the speech of Gāṇāpatya derived from the Vedic mantra "O Lord of Brahmans, [lead] the Brahmans," while seated upon the couch of Mahākālasaṅkarṣiṇī, the Supreme Deity, who is free from all conceptual proliferation (prapañca). Or, if he has fallen within the emission of Śambhu (śāmbhavavisarga), he descends as the six-faced Śivakumāra. This indeed is the secret.

That which was indicated at the beginning of the work by the final quarter of the benedictory verse—"Gaṇeśa is born from Śakti"—and in the second *vimarśa* by the passage beginning with "As long as [the state] of the Person who is Ambā is peaceful," refers here to one or another of the powers such as Nāda, Vāk, Artha, and Pramātṛ mentioned previously. While remaining transcendent to the universe, He descends to the ground through His sovereignty from the womb-casket of whichever power it may be, as described in the third *vimarśa* in this verse: "By the number of the multitude of the wheels of the senses."

He is designated as Gaṇeśa because, according to the manner that will be explained, he is the sovereign lord over the groups of objects pertaining to the internal and external senses. This alone is the true nature of the qualified seeker (adhikārin); such also is his relationship [to the goal].

From the aforementioned incarnation of Gaṇeśa up to Sādāśiva on the throne, throughout the five Brahma-incarnations, there exists—in accordance with the sequence of those respective incarnations and ultimately through identity with or non-differentiation from the couple Mahākālī and Kāla—a relationship of the signified and the signifier between that [text] and the *Prabandha* (the treatise), which is another name for the *Pañcavāha-Mahārthakrama*. This relationship is established according to one's capacity as the nature of the *Gahvara*, the *Viṣaya*, and the *Rājasvarūpa*, just like the exertion of the heart of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). Furthermore, there is a relationship of the goal to be attained and the means of attainment between the *Sāvaka* (the follower) and [the text]. Thus is the connection.

The nature of the relationship and its object, as well as the purpose [of this work], are as follows: By means of the entry into the womb of power (*śaktigarbhapraveśa*) indicated by the final quarter of the opening benedictory verse of the author, and through the process of the sequential absorption of the states of Viṣṇu and Rudra, [the author aims for] the state of Śiva—expressed in another Tantra as "Īśvara is the outward expansion (*unmeṣa*), Sadāśiva is the inward contraction (*nimeṣa*)"—either through a sequence of experience over one or many births, or by transcending even the state of the fifth Brahma, so as to "constantly behold Śiva with the eye of consciousness" (*cillōcanena satataṃ śivam īkṣitum*), as stated at the beginning of the text.

Through the fulfillment of the state of perfect integration (samanvaya) and the state of plenitude (pūrṇabhāva), as promised in the fourth verse, there ultimately occurs the attainment of the nature of the supreme couple, Sadāśiva and Śakti. By this, there is also the purpose of abandoning the discordant friendship previously promised at the beginning of the work with the words "I, desiring the cave of the heart... This constitutes the definition of the nature of the purpose. Thus, at the beginning of the work, the four (or five) ancillaries (anubandha) have been indicated by the Great Poet himself through these four (or five) verses.

As for the detailed nature of that [impurity]: according to the technical terminology of the Tantras and Āgamas, the triad of impurities—known by the other names *māyīya*, *kārmaṇa*, and *āṇava*—rests respectively upon the three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies. It manifests, as if obstructing both one's ultimate liberation (*naiśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), through defects of vision such as negligence and laziness; we say this because it is experienced as having delusion alone as its sole body, which is the defining characteristic of its insentient nature (*jaḍaprakṛti*).

For instance: "That which is called *māyika* (illusory) is considered to be the impurity arising from the feminine principle (*yoṣit*) that brings about duality; or, it is the *māyīya* (pertaining to *māyā*) which manifests as duality. According to this definition, even externalists such as the Mādhyamikas admit that the manifestation of duality—which is non-existent by its own nature even in the external world, such as the body composed of the five elements—is nothing but an error (*bhrānti*). Likewise, regarding the *kārmaṇa* (karmic) [impurity]: "Whatever action a person undertakes through body, speech, and mind—whether it be righteous or its opposite—these five are its causes."

"In that very case, he who, due to a lack of instrumental understanding, perceives the self alone as the sole agent—that person of dull intellect does not see," according to such words of the Blessed One. By superimposing upon the self a purely figurative agency that is actually non-existent, one thinks, "What good have I done? What evil have I done? and so forth. This too is another form of delusion, consisting of the threefold suffering caused by the agency of good and evil actions as described in the *Brahmavallī* of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad.

Likewise, even this [statement]: "The loss of freedom for consciousness and the lack of consciousness regarding freedom—this is declared to be the twofold *āṇava* impurity, due to the forfeiture of one's own true nature"—is nothing more than the forgetting of the wealth of one's own nature, omnipresence, and so forth, caused by the delusion characterized by these two aforementioned signs; thus, there is not even a trace of doubt that this triad is indeed of the nature of delusion.

Having thus refuted each [of the three views] in this triad by means of one verse for each, in sequence beginning with the verse "akṣīroda," preceded by a benediction; then, in the fourth [verse], through the direct realization of one's own Śiva—who is the couple consisting of Īśvara and Sādāśiva—by means of the eye of stainless knowledge, or else through the desire to effect that [realization]; for the sake of the experience of full bliss consisting in transcendence of the universe, attained through the state of being filled with the true existence of that [realization] by one who has been consumed by the forest-fire of transmigratory existence; [this is done] as if for the contemplation of the treatise which is the moonlight in the sky of one's own consciousness, bestowed upon oneself.

Having established that [the Nādakārikās] constitute the primary means, among the sixfold paths (ṣaḍadhvan) of sound, word, and meaning which are to be described through a collective treatise, the second chapter describes the conventional triad of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge within the two [categories of] sound and the non-sound, which are themselves the collective form of the triad of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss. In the third [chapter], there is a description of the ultimate great triad beginning with the supreme subject; and in the fourth, regarding the nature of the two aspects—Name and Form—which consist of pure Consciousness and are designated as "succession" and "non-succession" within the resultant great fourth triad.

And by means of the reversal of the sequences of emanation and withdrawal, through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the identity between the two—the *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, which are respectively transcendent of the universe and consisting of the light of consciousness—within both sets of nine faculties (the organs of action and the organs of cognition), which are termed the triad of the empirical subject, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; for the sake of establishing the identity with one's own Self as described in the first *vimarśa* (which is like a thread), [the author] has composed eighteen aphoristic verses (*sūtraśloka*) that function almost as *sūtras*, beginning with "Desire the cave of the heart," and so forth.

In the three hundred and first verse of the commentary titled *Pañcikā*—which is a commentary on the work known by the alternative title *Kramastuti* dedicated to the Siddha Nādabhaṭṭāraka, whose name is synonymous with Ādinātha and Mahākṛti—the identity between the previously mentioned sixfold body (*ṣaḍvidhavigraha*) of the Siddha and that of the seeker (*sādhaka*) Kālidāsa is proclaimed aloud in the verse beginning with "muktameva na mayā," as evidenced by the fourfold thematic connection (*anubandhacatuṣṭaya*).

The essence of the core subject matter of this treatise, as indicated by the *Jñānavarṇava*, the *Mahānaya-prakāśa*, and other works, has been described here according to the nature of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of word and meaning, in conjunction with the unity of the lineage of the sixfold succession of Gurus (*gurvaugha-krama*), out of a desire to favor the multitude of disciples and a wish to experience one's own bliss. Let the wise discern this. This very unity is explained in detail in the fourth *vimarśa* within the verse beginning, "You [reside] in the form of the nine-syllable inner wheel" (*tvaṃ navārṇamanucakravigrahe*); that should be consulted. Thus, this is the essential portion of the subject matter of the work; such is the direction. Thus concludes the author, the one who makes this announcement.
Oṃ.
Salutation to the Supreme Deity.
The Moonlight of the Consciousness-Sky.
It is adorned by the *Divyacakorikā*, composed by Karropapadāgnihotraśāstrin, who bears the name Dhanadānandanāthadīkṣita.
The First Inquiry.
