The introductory verses of the commentary.

Oṃ, salutations to the ancestral sages who initiated the tradition of the supreme and unsurpassed Siddhānta Vidyā; salutations to the great sages beginning with Paraugha; salutations to the gurus. I am indeed Brahman—free from all afflictions, a mass of pure consciousness, the full reality of the inner self.

Salutations to the form of the Guru, for the sake of fulfilling the great manifestation of one's own self-reflection; in the vision of whom even the eye does not suddenly perceive anything as a mere object. || 1 ||

I bow to those two who are like the sound and the resonance, eternally joined together for their own perception, whose nature is perpetual bliss, and who consist of the pair of the syllables *A* and *Ka*.
To what can I compare my prostration before the divine couple Śrī Kāmākṣī and Ānandanātha?
For by their grace, the profound path of Tantra has dawned upon me.
Known by the name Ānandanātha, the other [name being] Dīkṣā, he whose full splendor was bestowed by Kāmākṣi and Bhāmā;

the venerable Acyutapūrṇasoma (the eighth Vīrarāma), the lord of teachers, whose abode is the six paths, who has closed off his own boundaries, having ascended to the palace of Parā, wanders in the Golden Grove.
I, Mānasānandanārāma, explain this work day by day. || 5 ||
Born in the lineage of Atri, bearing two names as the embodiment of Agni,
he made the subordinate title "Daṇḍakrama" flourish.

For the sake of pacifying the faults perceived by others, I am perfectly at peace while burning the body—known as the "fuel-bearer"—in the fire of the lineage using the fuel of the so-called "house. (7)
For in the northern quarter lies Kuheḍa,
from which [the city] called Dhanadānandana shines forth, graced by the presence of the Guru’s form.
"May I be impelled by force to hold the term 'knowledge-wealth' (vidyādhanam) in its literal sense;
if this great accomplishment of action were to be true," he sighed thus. (9)
I compose this commentary on the work of Kālidāsa, titled *Divyacakorikā*, for those who are intoxicated by the tasting of the moonlight [of his poetry], yet remain mad without its true essence. 10.
I bow constantly; what is that action? Why is it not told? Should one say "the husband and wife" (dampati), or rather "the husband and wife" (dampatī)? 11.

If the first [type of suggestion] is not accepted because of the impropriety of the word despite its semantic fitness, then the last [type] is certainly not accepted either, due to the very nature of the meaninglessness of the word despite its propriety. (12)
Therefore, it is impossible to describe the object of the act of salutation;
here, the attainment of that very state is intended as the third way.
In the fourth state, there is the consciousness of identity, which is not perceived in time;
therein lies the "Great Offering," which is remembered as the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
Where am I—a dull-witted child within [this world]—and where is the torrent of the great poet’s speech?
May that torrent lead me, who desires to cross that difficult-to-traverse [ocean], to the further shore, the state of the Guru. (15)
May the virtuous forgive this rashness (or the sixteenth childish caprice) of mine:
that [I have spoken of] the herbs which were born from the earth for the sake of the gods in the three ages of old. (16)
Thus, in the Oṣadhīśa-sūkta and other such texts, the Traipura Yoga is proclaimed;
as well as a fondness for the indirect and likewise a hatred for the direct.
Furthermore, because the expansion of the word prevails even among the Vedas and the gods, that very [reality] is considered the pair of the meanings of three, four, or five words. (18)
That very [reality] exists even in the unsurpassed abode, transcending both space and time;
it is revealed through that secret for the sake of favoring the practitioners. (19)
Indeed, this work was composed here by means of the unfolding of the six paths;
thus, while it is directly engaged in explaining their meaning, it proceeds incidentally as well. (20)
Worn out by debates, disputations, and discourses on the three Vedas and the six systems of philosophy, my own work too shall be a treatise on their discernment, according to my understanding. (21)
May he here show me favor, by whom I have indeed been impelled;
like a pond that has easily attained the name of the poet Kālidāsa.
Despising me for my short stature, she submerged me in the service of a slave-girl;
there, at the conclusion of the three Vedas, having emerged, I recalled the words of Trivikrama. || 23 ||
From the mountain Nāchala, having ascended the fivefold wealth of Bali consisting of the three-footed [earth],
I gave that glory of the Guru to the Teacher, the King of the Gods.
My retinue here consists of those who move upon the earth; the sequence proceeds from the staff (daṇḍa).
He whose infinite sovereignty consists of the garland of names (or forms) and the garland of phonemes (varṇa)—[to him I bow]. (25)

Abiding within that, moving at will, and governed by the conduct of one's own desire (not constrained by scripture, nor constrained by the three-fold Rāma), there liberation arises as one's own nature, possessing the unsurpassed great purpose.
In this path of auspicious and ultimate accomplishment, Vaikharī speech possesses five flows;
thus, may this fragmentary narrative be for me a complete and perfect story.
In the Kṛta age, the laws of Manu were established; in the Tretā, those of Gautama are remembered;
in the Dvāpara, those of Śaṅkha and Likhita; and in the Kali age, those of Parāśara are considered authoritative.
In the Kṛta age, Reṇukā was the Śakti; in the Tretā age, the daughter of Janaka; in the Dvāpara age, Draupadī was the Śakti; and in the Kali age, the Śakti is Kālikā.
In the Kali age, there is neither that scripture nor the capacity [to follow it] due to the conflict of the Kali time;
therefore, with every effort in the Kali age, one should worship Kālikī (or uphold the Kali).
The Vedic union at the proper time is indeed the destroyer of the accumulation of sins;
this has been heard even in the Vāmadevya Sāman, which is considered the lord of the Sāmans. || 31 ||
Otherwise, there would be the possibility of the destruction of the continuity described as being at the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta);
this is recorded in the path of yoga for the sacrifice to the messenger (dūtī-yāga) as taught in the Jñānārṇava and other texts. || 32 ||
The sequence of the closing of the flowers of the gurus is also an illustration here;
that too has been taught according to rule in the sixteenth chapter of that very [text]. (33)
Therefore, here too, it should be understood that within the sequence of sound, word, and meaning, there is necessarily a fourfold connection according to their respective functions. (34)
Just as there is an ascending and descending sequence in the study of the Vedic recitation through the *krama*, *jaṭā*, and *ghana* methods,
so too is there a fixed order of the three, six, and twelve paths (*adhvan*) on the path of sound (*nāda*).

The head [of the deity], whose form is fashioned from sapphires, which produces the sprout of consciousness through the syllable *klīṃ* at its hands and feet, which is adorned with the sun, the moon, and the aesthetic flavors as its eyes, and which bestows relief from the suffering of the two-fold embodiment of Kālikā—[I bow to that]. 36.

May Bhramarāmbā (Samarembā), whose side-glances are as delightful as a garland of flowers for the learned grammarians, and who has uttered cries of joy from the excitement of chewing the nectar of the three dots (Bindus), shine forth. 37.

He who is victorious in the science of grammar and its matrices (mātṛkā), who is firmly established in the singular essence of word and meaning, and whose sole purpose is the supreme goal transcending the triad of direction, place, and time; || 38 ||
Through the perfect realization of the Śabdabrahman, one attains the Supreme Brahman;
thus, this Great Purpose (Mahārtha) also possesses the six paths consisting of the unity of word and meaning. (39)
With its inner radiance spread forth like the orb of the autumn moon,
this work of expansive scope is composed of a network of thirty-six verses.
Let those scorched by the great heat of false teachers resort to this for a long time;
for in the world of humans, success born of ritual action is swiftly attained. 41.
This action is of two kinds: innate (sahaja) and adventitious (āgantuka).
Innate action is that which is vocal; it is so called because it is produced together with birth. (42)

But that which is adventitious would be dependent on an external object, because of its adventitious nature; in that case, the accomplishment of human worldly goals would depend upon something prior. (43)
Success in the Brahman consisting of sacred word is the attainment of the Brāhmaṇa; that of the Kṣatriya, however, is worldly.
Indeed, the success in wealth for Vaiśyas—this is the eternal path.
Now that this [work] has been completed, which indicates the objects of knowledge and so forth, let it be thoroughly reflected upon;
for [the reality of consciousness] is based solely on the reflective awareness of the state of being the Great Subject alone. 45.
In this context, it is primarily in the form of a sūtra; though it is composed of three, four, or five sections in the Mahākrama, it is here summarized and presented as a sūtra.
In the second [state], the subject—encompassing within himself the stream of power, consciousness, and action—finds his sole repose in the Nāda that is employed for worldly transaction. (47)
In the third [chapter], however, that which is established within the womb of the Mātṛkā has been investigated—
[namely] its three, four, and fivefold functions regarding the single path of word and meaning.

Through the unfolding of the authority of the sequence of the phoneme-groups within the consciousness of the abodes, and by resting solely in the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta) via the openings of the Mūlādhāra, the heart, and the forehead; || 49 ||

Established in the sequence of the sacrificial rites at the seats (pīṭha), cremation grounds (śmaśāna), meeting places (melāpaka), and fields (kṣetra), [one proceeds] by way of the abode (dhāman), mudrās, phonemes (varṇa), digits (kalā), consciousness (saṃvit), and the nature of being (bhāvasvabhāva). || 50 ||
Through the vision of the abode of Pātāla and through emanation, by means of the manifestation of the wheel of the *bṛnda*,
he is the cause for the appearance of the rosary (*akṣamālā*) of the threefold emission (*visarga*).
With the fire of his fuel within and possessing the nature of the eightfold external forms,
he is the "I" who possesses the senses within the circles of the multitude amidst the manifestations of form, bliss, and light.
Because it is established within all forms of knowledge, action, and worship, the Śāmbhava [state], endowed with the sense of "I" as the means of valid cognition, is here discerned. || 53 ||
But in the Fourth State (turiya), one who has the Fourth as his "I" rests here upon the support of the senses;
yet he is turned away from the state of "I-ness" belonging to the Great Subject (mahāpramātṛ) into his own true nature.
The investigation of the senses is of great measure and vast progression;
it is the "Lolita" [chapter], which is the universe of the sense-families, because it illuminates the sequence of the senses. (55)
Because of its identity with the universe, it possesses a nature that transcends the entire universe;
[this occurs] through the reversal of the sequences of the Śākta and Śāmbhava emanations. (56)

Because of the manifestation of the Self as the totality of the world, which is conversant with the secret [of reality], and because of the essential nature of the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) resulting from the contemplation of the *kula* and *akula*. || 57 ||
By means of the self-nature of Mahākāla, through resting in the unique state at the end of the twelve,
the moon of consciousness (cic-candra) is the great light that illuminates the reflective awareness of consciousness (cid-vimarśa).
Through the expansion of the ninefold space and the unification of the sequence of *nāda* and the phonemes (*varṇa*),
the sequence of the senses as the "I" who am the great object of knowledge has been investigated within the sacred seat (*pīṭha*).
This great sacrifice of the Mahādūtī, consisting of speech and presided over by the Lord Śambhu,
has been described here together with its limbs and sub-limbs, ending with the oblation of the Great I-consciousness (mahāhaṃtā).
Herein is worshipped the one who possesses the supreme great accomplishment;
let it be well-considered by those seeking to accomplish the Great Immeasurable-I. (61)

Through the five purposes of the unsurpassed great form, in the fivefold activity, even one who seeks only material gain [should perform] the great sacrifice according to his own specific qualification. (62)
He should be served by those seeking their welfare, for he is the preventer of one's own misfortune;
indeed, the cause for the arising of misfortune therein is simply the lack of distinction from one's own [limited] vision.
Thus, for those whose inner state is free from blemish when there is equality between the desirable and the undesirable—
since Brahman is indeed faultless and equal— they are established in Brahman.
"One should not rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant"—this is the instruction of the Gītā;
here, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, taught it to Pārtha.
This is the essence of the established conclusions of all Vedānta, the great heart;
let the doctrine of the unsurpassed Great Consciousness be seen right here as well. 66.

Furthermore, according to the instruction of the Teacher of the Gītā, even in the unsurpassed abode, the cause of suffering arises from the activity of the wicked due to a lack of recognition [of one's true nature]. (67)
This [scripture], possessing the great axle of the unity of word and meaning, is the cause of the foundation of birth; it is proclaimed in fifty regional dialects. (68)
The supreme great form exists within the six paths and the five currents;
it is the nature of the vibration of the Great Breath (Mahāprāṇa), characterized by each of the six paths individually.
Another, higher *nāda* is *śākta*, characterized by the nature of the five flows;
and that other, supreme *mahāprāṇa-nāda* is also *śāmbhava*.

Thus, by means of the ritual procedures for each sacrifice, which are endowed with the sixfold unity, and which— having been composed from the *Mārāra*— are manifested as the supreme reality through the functions of word and meaning, and are pregnant with both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).
May [she] grant us satisfaction for the Goddess who is beyond the Praṇava. || 71 ||
The index of the subjects of the verses is here written down in prose;
may it also be of assistance here, and let it be observed even in the world at large. (72)

In the exposition of the reality of the meaning of Sound and Speech, this "purification of the path" is merely the manifestation of one's own ignorance on the part of those who do not know the true reality. (73)
For this treatise appears like mere gibberish to those whose minds are indolent in perceiving its greatness, yet it does not forfeit its inherent excellence.
Just as in the case of Manu, Indra, and the others, when measured by individual time units within the sequence of Yugas, the number of Yugas is also represented by seventy-one verses. (75)

Even regarding the true nature of the Kalā, Vāk, and Artha, according to the measure of the number of Yugas, let him understand the enumeration of Manus within the Brahmakalpa across the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan).
In this manner, let the expansion of the yugas be understood through the conjunction of parts and time,
beginning from the site, its years, and its divisions, up to the eighty-one squares.
In this context, even a number exceeding the limit for the sake of another indicates the meaning of the word;
it is well-composed with the mantra beginning with "arbuda" and ending with "svāhā. (78)
In this section on the Aśvamedha sacrifice, because it is stated that "speech is the arbuda," one should likewise [offer] with "nyarbudāya" and so forth, ending each with "svāhā. (79)
That which is speech and that which is the earth is called *Nyarbuda*;
therefore, worldly accomplishment through mantras is indeed dependent upon both of these.
This worship of the Mātṛkā, which is worldly, is for the delight of the virtuous;
thus, this pavilion of the Mātṛkā-abode is the creator of the universe. (81)

Indeed, here the great poet named Kālidāsa, the ornament of the assembly of poets and supremely compassionate, desiring to uplift all his devotees—whether of dull, middling, or superior intellects—without distinction, has composed this work. Within the various forms of worship such as *pratīka* (symbolic) and others, he establishes the worship of the threefold circle (*trividhabṛndacakra*) through the names of the embodiments of Light, Consciousness, the Sequence of the Three Phonemes (*varṇakrama*), and the Manifestation of Bliss, as described below. This worship of the deities is an inseparable concomitant [of the path], according to the Lord’s own words in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*: "The form of the Person and Time, both internal and external," referring to the inner Self (*daharātman*).

It is the regulator of the entire world of moving and non-moving beings through its external form as Time; it is the essence of the unsurpassed Siddhānta-tattva known as the Mahārthakrama—the fivefold flow of Mahākālī, who is non-different from Śiva and Śakti, whose nature is the meaning of the root *kal* (to fashion/time). "Aha! We shall proclaim the secret; do not wander among the spheres of the womb!"

Desiring to manifest—under the guise of the literary work *Cidgaganacandrikā* and according to the conventions of poetry—the form of the "exertion of the Heart" (*hṛdayodyoga*), defined in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala* as "the thorough deliberation upon the Heart which is exceedingly near," he first [addresses] the lineages of Gurus within the "throne-pedestal" of the Supreme Deity (as described in the forthcoming text), ranging from the multitude of disciples up to the Great Supreme Lineage, or specifically the form beginning with the Guru-lineage of the first pedestal-foot: "Even when one has attained merely the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he who does not become heedless..."

"The Vināyakas lead one toward those impermanent enjoyments"—according to this statement from the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*, [Gaṇeśa] is to be worshipped first because he is the means for unimpeded accomplishment (*nirvighnasiddhi*), as he is the cause of vigilance (*apramāda*) through his status as the leader of the host of deities presiding over the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), and because he is known by the name "First Drop" (*prathama-pāda*) descended through the lineage of the true tradition; and furthermore, because: "The syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two were formerly created by Brahmā..."

Having pierced the throat, both have emerged; therefore, they are both auspicious. In accordance with this statement, [the author] first composes the work with intentional epithets, desiring to demonstrate his own experience, beginning with that which has the Great *Praṇava* as its voice for piercing the *brahmagranthi*, which is the single trunk for the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), the son of Śakti, whose face is that of the great king of elephants, the presiding auspicious embodiment, and the indicator of the four appendices (*anubandha*):

"He who, like the full moon over the Ocean of Milk, shines forth without waves—the pervasive resonance of the void (*cidvyoman*)—with the rows of wave-like syllables (*mālā*) of the Bindu shining from the mass of his radiance."

May this Gaṇeśa—the nature of whose primordial vibration is the manifestation of the syllable Oṃ, who possesses the trunk of the syllable Oṃ, whose mouth is the dental [letter 'da'], and who is born from Śakti—swiftly pacify your misfortunes through his power of action and vision. || 1 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with *kṣīroda* and so forth: although it was stated at the very outset that "the *ma* sound consisting of earth (*bhūmimaya*) bestows auspiciousness," according to the characteristics of the *chandogaṇa*, the *agaṇa* has Earth as its presiding deity and is thus a bringer of good fortune; nevertheless, even when the purity of the *gaṇa* is established, it is indicated that the etymological purity of the syllable is not intended here, due to the deliberate employment of the letter *kṣa*—a *kūṭārṇa* (compound syllable) formed by the conjunction of *ka* and *ṣa*.

Nevertheless, among the consonants (*sparśavarṇa*) beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, which denote the nature of the state of inert waking consciousness, one sets aside those letters from *ka* to *ma*—which, established through the *pratyāhāra* [formula], denote the gross object of human pursuit (*kāmapuruṣārtha*) residing in the bound individual soul (*pāśukajīva*). Instead, the sibilants (*ūṣmavarṇa*) *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* respectively denote the four principles (*tattva*)—or five, including the group of five—consisting of the End-of-Mouth (*antamukha*), Heart (*hṛdaya*), and Udyoga, which culminate in the pair of Paraśiva and Sādāśiva, the latter being the pure *Valli* and *Īśa* who have attained identity with the nature of Consciousness (*citprakṛti*).

Having kept in mind the intention to explain that the reality of Gaṇeśa—the Śiva-Child who consists of the first vibration (*spanda*) to be contemplated through *nididhyāsana*—is to be awakened by the *kūṭa-mantra*, [the author] takes up the letter *ka*, the first consonant which indicates contact with the waking state and so forth; and the letter *ṣa*, which denotes the Lord (*īśa*) as the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the second sibilant (*ūṣman*) among those letters that signify the reality of the fourth state (*turya*). This [Gaṇeśa] is characterized by the play of the emission of Śakti, as understood from the epithet "Born of Śakti" (*śaktijanma*), or by the play of the emission of the individual soul (*āṇava-visarga*) that has fallen upon that [Śaktic emission].

Through *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal), when the senses are turned inward within the space of the heart (*hṛdvyoman*), there arises the cognition of the meaning of words—the verbal roots and nominal stems—which are the very actions of friction. By means of the syllable *kṣa*, which is the synthesis of both [the root and the suffix] and denotes the waking state of the Lord (*īśajāgṛti*), it indicates that the principle of Gaṇeśa—who is the leader of the group presiding over the *puryaṣṭaka*—consists precisely in the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between the two conditions of activity and cessation. As it is said in the *Turyakhaṇḍa* of the *Mātṛkācakraviveka*: "The self is the bound soul (*paśu*); by that [bond], the self is indeed swallowed, yet it remains the very nature of consciousness (*citprakṛti*) in the form of cessation (*nivṛtti*)."

"In this way, the letter *kṣa*, which is the source of both nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformation (*vikrama*), is Śambhu; he exists as the supreme beyond even nature. Or else: "Here, *kṣa* is Śiva, who, due to the absence of any counter-correlate (*pratiyogibhāva*), is the very state of the Supreme Śambhu—the waking soul of consciousness (*cidātmā*). That which is the transcendence within the center of the wheel and the lordship thereof belongs to Śambhu, because of his being worthy of worship through the mere scent of his qualities. Thus it is said.

Like the full moon in the ocean of milk, Gaṇeśa—who is the nature of the manifest, primordial vibration—spreads forth the waveless expanse of consciousness all at once. The sense is that because his own self-experience is of the nature of a single, non-dual manifestation, it is a simultaneous expansion.

By this description of the similarity between Gaṇeśa—the leader of the group presiding over the *puryaṣṭaka*—and the Moon, it is also indicated that just as the moon possesses increase and decrease up to its sixteenth digit (*sādākalā*) which is indestructible, so too for Gaṇeśa, although there is an increase and decrease of the fifteen digits (*kalā*) that constitute the parts of the *puryaṣṭaka*, his increase and decrease exist only up to the sixteenth digit, just like the moon.

Alternatively, the word *sakṛt* may be construed as follows: "May [the Lord] pacify at once, with a single effort, the misfortune of you, the lay-devotees (*upāsaka*), which consists in the manifestation of illusory duality. This [word *sakṛt*] should also be applied to the qualifying attributes such as "the expansion of the radiance of the spreading resonance" (*sphāranādarucivisara*) by way of the "lamp on the threshold" maxim (*dehalī-dīpa-nyāya*), even in the case of the term *kṣīroda*. Regarding the term *kṣīroda*: it is called *kṣīra* (milk) because it emits (*īrayati*) the letter *kṣa*, which is the form of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*) within the Meru-syllable; thus, *kṣīra* refers to the internal space (*daharākāśa*). Alternatively, it is so called because it flows forth (*kṣarati*) from the functions of the senses.

The term *kṣīroda* (the milk-ocean) is an epithet of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), derived either from the sense "that in which [all things] arise" (*tad udayate 'tra*) or "from which [all things] arise" (*udīyate asmāt*). The secret meaning is that it was first a salt-ocean (*kṣāroda*) and subsequently became a milk-ocean (*kṣīroda*). Furthermore, the form *kṣīrodadhi* serves as the substantive. In both cases, the word functions to indicate the exertion of the Heart (*hṛdaya*). Regarding the phrase "of the nature of the primordial vibration" (*ādyaspandasvarūpa*): in the sequence of emanation, at the very beginning—from the form of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and so forth—it is of the nature of non-vibration, being the immovable essence of both speech and its object.

In the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), however, [the deity] is of the nature of vibration (*spanda*) during the initial withdrawal of the senses (*akṣapratyāhāra*). Since this very withdrawal of the senses marks the commencement of the process of withdrawal, this is an epithet of Gaṇeśa. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those waves (*ūrmimālā*) whose drops (*bindu*) shine forth in profusion upon their faces. Thus, he is the one in whom those wave-crests exist.

In the *Cidvyomapañca*, however, the analysis is as follows: the "drops of Brahman" known as *tālu* (palate) are the drops of the essence of speech that manifest at the time of vocal utterance—whether through the expansion of one's own inclination (*rucivisara*) or through the contemplation of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the word-meanings and poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) belonging to that [speech]. These drops exist within the "successions of waves" (*ūrmmimālā*) of the activity of speech in the mouth; the compound is thus analyzed as "that [succession of speech] which exists in the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), the space of the heart (*daharākāśa*) consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya*)."

Alternatively, there is a difference in syntactic connection (*anvayabheda*) due to a difference in meaning: [the Lord] whose body is either "bound" by the triple impurity—consisting of the *āṇava* and so forth, whose characteristics will be described later—whether that impurity remains as a slight residue or has been superimposed upon the waves of the faces of the drops (*bindu*) shining through the expansion of light in the form of external phonemes (*vaisvarī*), even though the internal resonance (*nāda*) is expanding; or [the Lord] whose body is bound by that [impurity] which is superimposed by the slight remainder of the three impurities characterized as *āṇava* and so forth, [upon those waves].

*Oṃkāraśuṇḍa*, *Kriyādṛk*, *Dantyāsya*, and *Śaktijanman*—these are the four epithets of Gaṇeśa. Among them, *Oṃkāraśuṇḍa* refers to him whose trunk (*śuṇḍā*) is the phonetic principle of the *puruṣa* denoted by the syllable *oṃ*. Thus says the Śruti: "Making the self the lower fire-drill and the *praṇava* the upper fire-drill, the wise man burns away the fetter through the practice of churning with meditation."

For this very reason, by means of the three qualifiers *kriyādṛk* (the vision of action), *dantyāsya* (the tooth-mouth), and *śaktijanma* (born of power), its nature as the *kāryabrahman* (the Brahma of the effect), consisting of knowledge, will, and action, is also indicated. In that regard, *kriyādṛk* refers to the reflective awareness of mere outward-turned action; *dantyāsya* refers to the specific face endowed with the state of youth, which illuminates the will characterized by the desire to enjoy the fruit of that [action]; and *śaktijanma* illuminates the birthplace of the body composed of action—according to the saying: "Viṣṇu is the effect, Brahmā is action, and Maheśvara is the cause."

Thus, the fact that [the deity] consists of the three forms (trimūrti) as stated in the *Brahmavaivarta Purāṇa* is also indicated. The poetic figure is *pūrṇopamā* (complete simile). The meter is *sragdharā*. Its definition is as follows: "That which consists of the sequence ma, na, bha, ra, ya, na, with pauses at the third, seventh, and eleventh syllables, is celebrated as *sragdharā*. || 1 ||

Thus, following the auspicious invocation in the form of a hymn to Gaṇeśa—which results in the removal of the *māyīya* impurity for practitioners—he now also refers to the Śiva-tattva, whose body is space (*ākāśa-śarīra*), which serves as the cause for removing the *kārmaṇa* impurity necessary for the intended *Cidgaganacandrikā* hymn:

"The gross, the subtle, and the supreme—this threefold world is here joined with the accomplishment of the penetration of its manifestation; its existence shines forth from beyond, yet its sole nature is self-manifestation."

May that Lord, whose form is consciousness and into whom the activity of reflective awareness has entered— by whom the worldly course of existence is perceived for the sake of beholding the true path— dispel from you the state of darkness.

"Stūlam" (the gross): This refers to that which is known by the names gross (*sthūla*), subtle (*sūkṣma*), and supreme (*para*), which is the substratum of the three levels of existence—empirical (*vyāvahārika*), apparent (*prātibhāsika*), and ultimate (*pāramārthika*). Alternatively, it is that whose nature consists of speech, meaning, and sound; specifically, the gross form is *vaikharī* (articulate speech), the subtle is *madhyamā* (intermediate speech), and the supreme is *paśyantī* (visionary speech) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). All three constitute the "world" (*jagat*). By the etymology "that which moves is the world" (*gacchatīti jagat*), and through either the transposition of letters or the addition of letters as established in the recitation of the *siṃhādi* group, the meaning is that it consists of the threefold power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*).

That Supreme Śiva, whose very Being flashes forth as endowed with the accomplishment of *vyāpti*—a term synonymous with *pṛthūbhāva* (expansion)—which is the realization of the penetration of His own manifestation; for this reason, He is the cause of the flashing forth of the mere difference of names. His own nature consists solely in self-manifestation, and His essential nature is His own primary pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, His existence—which belongs to that reality whose essence is Supreme Śiva—shines forth even from the world, which appears as if existing through difference from Him.

By this, it is also indicated that for us non-dualists (*abheda-vādin*), the circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) consisting in the fact that one’s own establishment is dependent on the establishment of the other—which is like a mere ornament—is not a defect, as it is for the proponents of the Veda (*veda-vādin*). By that, it is also largely explained that the creation of duality (*bheda-sṛṣṭi*) is merely a conceptual and verbal body. Likewise, He whose form is action that is nothing but pure reflective awareness (*vimarśa-mātra*), whose body is light alone; and thus says the Śruti: "The sun does not shine there," and so forth. Having followed such a One—*anu* meaning having pursued Him.

The worldly course (*lokavṛtti*)—meaning even the livelihood of the world—is observed. That Lord (*īśaḥ*) [is for] you practitioners (*sādhakānām*): for the beholding of the true path (*sanmārgālokanāya*). The "true path" (*sanmārgaḥ*) is the path to the direct realization of ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*). Alternatively, it is called a "path" (*mārga*) because one searches (*mṛgyate*) for it, or because by means of it one searches for the reality; thus, according to the sequence, its meaning should be understood as either the essential nature itself or the path to its direct realization, as appropriate. It is for the beholding—that is, the direct realization—of that [path].

May he remove that tamasic state—which consists of the impurity of performing actions that are both auspicious and inauspicious, or which takes the form of the delusion that action is a means for realizing one's true nature. The sense is that, as stated in such passages as, "Śiva does not shine by means of [external] means; rather, these [means] shine by His grace," and "The latent impression of non-duality arises in persons only through the grace of the Lord," the destruction of ignorance results from the grace of the Lord, whether it be established as being without end or established as being without means.

In the view that it is the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*): may that Lord, whose body consists of space, time, and ether, destroy the path of the existing stars for the sake of their observation—that is, the activity of darkness (*tāmasī vṛtti*), such as the blinding gloom occurring during the night of *tamisrā*, or the obstruction caused by clouds and the like. By this, it should be understood that the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of darkness in the system of the logicians (*tārkika*), as well as the substantiality or reality (*vastutva*) of false ignorance (*mithyājñāna*) in the system of the Vedāntins, are refuted.

The point is this: just as there is the conventional designation of "false ignorance" for one whose form of knowledge is obscured by darkness, so it is for one whose splendor is obscured; furthermore, it is experienced that even during nights of deep gloom, the manifestation of stars occurs solely through the light of the sky. || 2 ||

Thus, having contemplated the Śiva-principle through the method of double entendre (*śleṣa*) and by means of a variation in reading, he prays for the removal of the *āṇava* impurity—which consists of the incomplete *visarga* of Śambhu—for himself and his disciples, as it is the destroyer of the empire of bliss consisting of both knowledge and ignorance; and he also reveals his own name and that of his work:

"May this *Cidgaganacandrikā*, born of the moon Kālidāsa, which brings delight to the face, through the pretext of praise, extinguish for you (*naḥ*) the forest fire of worldly existence from the ocean of the moon of the sky of consciousness. (3)

With the words "iha" and so forth: here, in this intended composition, there is one named Kālidāsa; that very moon is the source (*prasūti*)—the place of origin—of this praise, which is thus described. This praise, titled *Ānandinī-cidgaganacandrikā*, consists of the operation of word and meaning bound by the rules of meter, feet, and so on; it is either an external or internal creation of word and meaning. "Under the guise of the ocean" means by way of the delusive ocean of saṃsāra. "Of you"—meaning of you, the readers—and "of me," the author.

The meaning is: "the forest-fire of saṃsāra" refers to the heat of the fire of saṃsāra, which consists of the threefold affliction (tāpa) caused by the impurity of limited knowledge (*kiñcijjñatva-āṇava-mala*). The word "blazing" (*sphurantaṃ*) is to be supplied as the object. The intention is: "May he not merely calm this ocean of saṃsāra, but rather [transform it into] an ocean of bliss"; that is, may he gladden us by bestowing the knowledge of the true nature of the path of Śaṅkara. In the reading *stutivyājāt*, the meaning is "under the pretext of praise."

When examined closely, this so-called "praise" is merely a negation; the sense is that this is not praise at all, but rather the very moonlight of the sky of consciousness (cidgaganacandrikā) directed toward the nature of the Absolute (anuttara). Therefore, just as the ocean of truth (satyābdhi) extinguishes for you (yuṣmākam) and for us (naḥ)—that is, for those of us who possess only limited knowledge—the heat of the submarine fire (bāḍabānala) in the form of the impurity of finitude (āṇavamala), so too does this moonlight of the sky of consciousness, having first expanded the ocean of saṃsāra through the synthesis of the words and meanings to be explained, extinguish the forest fire of that very saṃsāra.

The intention is that this is a benediction, meaning "may [it] pacify. In the *kṛti* (poetic) interpretation, *Kālī* is used as a vocative. O Kālī! This empirical moon situated in the sky, which is currently perceived, is born from the moon-like servant [of yours]; by virtue of its nature as a digit of the moon—the imperishable *sādākhya-puruṣa*—it exists solely as your servant, being subordinate to you.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as her progeny, Candrikā, was a source of delight, so too this *Cidgaganacandrikā*, being likewise a source of delight, may—by bestowing the path of Śiva—quench the scorching heat of the fire of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of the impurity of finitude (*āṇavamala*), for us who have become your servants and for my disciples. This has been stated in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*: "Where even sorrows turn into happiness, even poison turns into nectar, and transmigratory existence itself becomes liberation—that is the path of Śiva."

Alternatively, "here" refers to this vast expanse of knowledge consisting of the Vedas, Śāstras, and so forth; it is from the work titled *Citgaganacandrikā*, which is like an ocean. The sense is that the work is comparable to an ocean because it serves as a mine for the five jewels—the five incarnations—which are non-different from the five cosmic functions beginning with creation and ending with dissolution. "Born from the moon of Kālidāsa" means originating from the poet-moon named Kālidāsa; this is a punning metaphor (*śliṣṭarūpaka*).

The consciousness that is the true nature of the deities and so forth, which are non-different from the fivefold group of duties (*kṛtyapañcaka*), is a state of consciousness that brings joy like the moonlight in the sky. By means of the repetition of the word "being" (*satī*) under the guise of praise—that is, under the pretext of the act of praising—may it extinguish for you, the listeners, and for us, the readers, the forest-fire of *saṃsāra*; that is, may it pacify the scorching heat of the fire of the phenomenal world born of ignorance (*āvidyaka*). In this interpretation, it should be understood as the speech of the reader.

In this regard, through the reading *va* in the two preceding verses and the variant reading *na* for *vaḥ* in this verse, there is a fourfold distinction of authority among practitioners (*sādhaka*)—namely, the *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, *sakala*, and *niṣkala*—according to their respective capacities, based on the persistence of the triad of impurities beginning with the *āṇava* (or the dyad), or by the persistence of only the nearly destroyed *āṇava* impurity; and for himself, there is the distinction of authority for the worship of the *niṣkala*, as set forth in his own work.

The fact that he possesses the authority over the four castes including women, or alternatively, the authority over the five classes of beings including the Niṣādas as the fifth, as well as his own nature as an incarnation of the union of Mahākālī and Kālaśiva, is indicated through subtle observation; such is the secret of the three auspicious syllables. || 3 ||

Thus, for the sake of the four kinds of practitioners and devotees mentioned above, in the manner described in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*: "Come! We shall speak the secret; do not wander within the spheres of the womb (*garbhagola*). Examine the heart that is exceedingly near, and its exertion," there is a praise of the composition of the work he intends to write, which consists of the exertion of the practitioner’s heart: "Like the currents of rivers, [these works] are insignificant at first, but become increasingly vast as they proceed."

In accordance with the principle of the *Kāvyamīmāṃsā* which states, "Those undertakings of treatises that arise for the sake of the world are worthy of veneration," [the author] first provides a work in the form of aphorisms (*sūtra*), followed by increasingly extensive expositions according to the respective qualifications [of the students], which bestow the fruit of investigation. To worship—with full deliberation—the Fourth Moonlight of the Sky of Consciousness (*turīyacidgaganacandrikā*)—which, like the moonlight of the third sky of consciousness, is the object of the triad of one's own words and bestows the fruit of inquiry—he presents himself as a mirror through the device of *śleṣa* (punning wordplay):
"In order to constantly behold Śiva with your own eye, and to perceive true existence within the lineage..."
And if you would attain full perfection, then apply your minds to this [instruction]. || 4 ||

Regarding the phrase *cillocanena*: "Consciousness itself is the eye" means the eye of knowledge (*jñānanetra*). By means of that, one is to constantly behold Śiva. In the reading *tvallocanena*, the meaning is "by your eye," referring to the practitioner. One is to realize [Śiva] through direct perception (*aparokṣavṛtti*), like an uninterrupted stream of oil, in order to attain existence within the lineage (*anvaya*) and the state of fullness (*pūrṇabhāva*).

The meaning is: "In order to attain, by way of this composition, the coherent connection of words and their meanings—which have as their purport the identity of the Self with Supreme Śiva—along with the state of fullness of the Self, through the easy path. The phrase "if the mind has been set in motion" is to be supplied. "Then, contemplate this hymn," meaning reflect upon it by correctly determining its purport. Here, the *loṭ* suffix is used either in the sense of an injunction or a request. In our own school's view, [this is done] with the eye of consciousness (*cillocana*), that is, the eye of knowledge.

In the reading *tvad-locanena*, the meaning is: "by that eye," which is the very knowledge of the reality of the referent of the word *yuṣmad* (the second person), serving as the third eye that reveals the true nature of the referent of the word *asmad* (the first person). "To behold Śiva constantly" means to perceive directly the Śiva that is the Self, distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The analysis of the compound is: *anu*, *aye*, *ca*, *sadbhāvam*. And [the purpose is] "to attain fullness" by following—that is, by conforming to—that very eye which is the referent of *yuṣmad*, or to that Śiva who is the Self which is the referent of *asmad*.

The word *ca* here also serves as a conjunction for both "the state of being real" (*sadbhāva*) and "fullness" (*pūrṇabhāva*). By saying, "O friend, this Kālidāsa is a virtuous man and is full," I have attained that which is universally recognized in worldly convention—the state of being real. By implication, it is suggested that you too should attain such a state of reality.

The sense is this: although one possesses the eye of knowledge for the direct realization of Śiva and, through that, the attainment of full being (*pūrṇabhāva*), as well as learning, wealth, and so forth—even while possessing that full being—it is necessary for everyone to attain the status of a "good person" (*satpuruṣa*) in the conventional sense. This is indicated by the collection of passages in the *Brāhmaṇa Upaniṣads* and elsewhere, which teach the acquisition of the wealth of the twice-born (*dvijāma-sampat*) through the means of knowledge, ritual action, and so on, stating: "Therefore, the Brāhmaṇa who is true to his purpose is 'twice-named' (*dvināmā*)."

"He should approach the Guru with fuel in his hand," and "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas," and so forth. Alternatively, having first abandoned the two types of existence—the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent (*prātibhāsika*)—I have attained the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sadbhāva*), namely, "I am the conscious Self, uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. You too should attain that state accordingly; thus, the objection should be understood according to the respective qualifications (*adhikāra*).

If, due to the consequence of universal existence and so forth, or even due to the consequence of ultimate reality, the attainment of the realization of the state of fullness is not achieved, then one should properly contemplate this "Moonlight of the Sky of Consciousness" as being of the nature of the play of one's own mind; thus he says, "If [this]... That is to say, "If [this] Moonlight of the Sky of Consciousness"—namely, "consciousness" (cet). One should contemplate that the very play of one's own mind has been composed by the poet in the form of a hymn to the Moonlight of the Sky of Consciousness.

The sense is: "In that case, you shall attain the direct realization of Śiva through your own eyes, and through that, the state of fullness. Regarding the reading *cetassamupādyam*, the meaning is: "If there is an inclination to behold Śiva and to obtain the state of fullness, then one must 'attain a mind' (*cetassamupādyam*) for this hymn; that is, a mind capable of reflecting upon the hymn must be cultivated."

Alternatively, it may mean: "By means of the root *ad* (to eat), [the Lord] says: 'Eat'—that is, consume as food the Self which has the three impurities (*malatraya*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and likewise this hymn; [thereby] you shall properly benefit yourselves. Even when the direct realization of the Self as distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*) has arisen through the eye of knowledge consisting of inquiry (*vimarśa*), the realization of the essential nature of the Puruṣa described in the Upaniṣads cannot be attained without the peace of heart produced by the inquiry into the moonlight of the sky of consciousness (*cidgaganacandrikā-vimarśa*). Without that peace of heart born from the inquiry into the moonlight of the sky of consciousness, there is no attainment of the direct realization of the essential nature of the Upaniṣadic Puruṣa.
However, the attainment of the state of fullness—which is synonymous with the realization of the universal self—is not attained even further than that; such is the secret meaning. || 4 ||

Thus, having introduced the four verses consisting of the fourfold connection (*anubandha*) and having described the attainment of the three primary qualifications (*adhikāra*) bound by the three impurities (*mala*), [the text] explains the meaning of the Great Virāj Gāyatrī—which serves as the purifier of those [qualifications]—in its form as the powers (*śakti*) of one, two, three, four, and five feet: "The earth is a foot; the intermediate space is a foot; the sky is a foot; the directions are a foot."

It is that which brings about the fruit of establishment in Virāj as declared by the Taittirīya Śruti—"The foot beyond the dust (parorajāḥ) is established in Virāj"—and it exists in the form of the three castes and the four castes, having transformed into the supreme gross form as the Mahākālī-pañcavāha-krama, which is another name for the sequence of the five objects; it consists of the threefold sequence of the great human goals (trivarga, caturvarga, and pañcavarga), pertaining to the life-forces (jīva-śakti) of the five classes of men (pañcajana), including the Niṣādas as the fifth.

Based on the perspective that the first, fourth, and fifth human goals (puruṣārthas) consist of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of this-worldly and other-worldly intellect, and by viewing the pairs of the second and third goals—dharma and kāma—as pertaining to the other world, one may also rely upon their reversal within the sequence of worship. Furthermore, within the fivefold expansion of the *vibhūti* (manifestations), there is a distinction in the worship of the sixth through the ninth stages according to the Sāṅkhya sequence, based on the internal-external *sāmarasya* of the numbers six and seven.

[This refers to] those forms consisting of the Śākta-sampat—such as the bee and so forth—which are fashioned in accordance with the respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the six seasons, the six-faced [Kārttikeya], the seven planets, the islands, the oceans, and so on; and likewise those forms consisting of the Śaiva-cakra and so forth, which exist through the gradations of the three aims of life (*trivarga*), the four aims (*caturvarga*), the five aims (*pañcavarga*), and the distinctions of individual and collective worship (*vyaṣṭi-samaṣṭi-upāsti*), as well as the seven and eight *mātṛkās*, the nine *nanādhans*, the nine *yonis*, time, and the numberless *nādas* within the Śaiva and Śākta portions, and within the aspects of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), and the portions of name and form.

Desiring to explain in full detail, by means of a comprehensive expansion, the non-dual correspondence between the fivefold activities of the Five Brahmas—which are synonymous with the human states beginning with waking and ending with that which transcends the fourth (turiyātīta)—and the fivefold Kālīs known as Sṛṣṭi, Stiti, Saṃhāra, Anākhyā, and Bhāsā; [the author] proceeds, within the previously mentioned quarters of the Gāyatrī extending from Earth to the end of Parorajas, to show how Ego (ahaṅkāra), Vital Breath (prāṇa), Mind (manas), Intellect (buddhi), and the Senses (indriya) are, in their respective order, subject to control through an inward movement, and how, by the constant increase of the wealth of the Self that is the range of the Vedas, one may exclaim "Bṛhi! Bṛṃhi! (Grow! Prosper!).

The status of *brahman* is etymologically significant (*anvarthaka*) due to the verbal derivation from the root *vṛdh*, signifying the nourishment of the perfection of word, etymology, and self. The status of *kṣatra* consists in protection from injury (*kṣatāt-trāṇa*). The status of *vaiśya* consists in the abiding within the distinction between dharma and adharma, or the abiding within the distinction between the self and the non-self. Thus, when one possesses the primary verbal body of the *trayī*—composed of knowledge and action, consisting of the Vedic *sac-cid-ānanda*, and synonymous with the three social orders (*traivarṇika*)—it is said: "A body worn out by diseases is called 'kalpa'."

By the definition in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, "Through the indication of that [Kalpa], its status as a *kalpasūtra* is also intended," and so forth, [the Kalpa] possesses the nature of a *kalpa* consisting of the union of Kālī and Kāla-Paraśiva, who have the primary Veda—composed of the three *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—as their body through the integration of the meanings of the terms *bhautika* (material) and *abhautika* (immaterial). Furthermore, insofar as it has the six ancillaries (*ṣaḍaṅga*)—which are synonymous with the Vedic *ṣaḍadhvan*—as its verbal body, it primarily consists of the triad of the *śabdādhvan* (the path of sound) in the form of *Śikṣā*, *Vyākaraṇa*, and *Chandas*. It has the knowledge of the Vedic ancillaries as its verbal body, and takes the form of the triad of cognitions of the union of Kāla and Kālī.

It is primarily the path of the three—consisting of etymology (*nirukta*), light (*jyotis*), and ritual procedure (*kalpa*)—and takes the form of the *kalās*, *tattvas*, and *bhuvanas*. It consists of the triad of action (*kriyā*) and has the Vedāṅgas as its primary body; thus it is the primary [path]. The Śrīcakra, which comprises the threefold Veda, the Vedāṅgas, the three social classes (*varṇas*), and the nine wheels (*cakras*), is the Siddhacakra, which possesses the primary authority of the Veda.

However, in the case of one who lacks qualification (*anadhikārin*), by means of the previously mentioned five-fold *viraṭ* *gāyatrī* feet taken out of order, there occurs a state of mere *brahman* in the form of *viraṭ* through the subordination of the limbs of the self—beginning with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) and ending with the senses—by way of an outward movement; this occurs even though there is qualification only for Vedic rites as prescribed in such scriptural injunctions as: "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the *Bṛhaspatisava*, a King with the *Rājasūya*, a Vaiśya with the *Vaiśyastoma*, a *Rathakāra* should establish the sacred fires in the rainy season, and one should cause a *Niṣāda* chieftain to sacrifice with this [rite]."

Because it does not concern the intended meaning of the Vedas, but is merely devoted to the activity of *vaikharī* speech which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyaka*), it constitutes a circle of practitioners who possess the status of the three higher castes by bearing only the name—referring to that which was said: "The triple Veda is not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the degraded twice-born; therefore, the sage composed the narrative of the *Bhārata* out of compassion. This is the circle of the *sādhakas*.

In the absence of even the established limits (*maryādā*), there is the state of the five classes of people (*pañcajanatā*) and so forth, characterized by their respective mixed modes of conduct; according to the conformity with the multitude of disciples to be described, it takes the form of the *sādhya-śrīcakra*; and as the worldly assembly-circle seat (*jāgata-bṛndacakrapīṭha*), it is the wealth of the triple-folded Great Virāj (*trivṛt-triṇamahāvirāṭ-sampad*). Through the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) with the previously mentioned wealth of the *svarāṅga-gāyatrī*, [it is said]: "The ten fingers of the hands, the ten toes of the feet, and the self as the twenty-first."

By means of the non-dual identity with the plenitude of the Time-Person (*kālapuruṣa*) as declared in the Śruti—"Twelve months, five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun is the twenty-first"—and by way of the path of the concordance (*samanvaya*) of the *Bhārata* as the Fifth Veda, [one should worship] with the seed-syllables (*bīja*), clusters (*piṇḍa*), and mantras numbering five, seven, nine, and so forth, such as *krīm*, *krūm*, *khphrem*, *hsauḥ*, *shauḥ*, *hraskhphrem*, and others belonging to the *Kālī-prāsāda*, *Parā-prāsāda*, and other such mantras.

The essential meaning of all the scriptures, tantras, and treatises is precisely the state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) between the ninefold manifestation of the Sound (*nāda*)—which consists of both consciousness and insentience—of the Great Goddess Mahākālī and Kāla, who are the essence of the five traditions (*pañcāmnāya*). Desiring to favor those practitioners, whether followers of Vedic or non-Vedic paths, by awakening the vision of the Self which is the exertion of the heart, [the author] first establishes his own nature as the body consisting of vision and action, and then establishes that the body of the Supreme Woman (Artha-Nārī), who is the union of Mahākālī and Kāla, transcends that very state. This is the secret of the sequence of worship of Kālī, beginning with the origin of the Unmanifest Seat (*avyākṛta-pīṭha*), as praised in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*. It is the unfolding of the vision of the Self, which takes the form of the spiritual effort within the hearts of practitioners, both Vedic and non-Vedic. First, he demonstrates his own embodiment of vision and action; then, he demonstrates that the body of the Supreme Woman, whose nature is the couple Mahākālī and Kāla, is a state beyond that.

Demonstrating this, [the author] shows that for the sake of attaining the fruit of abandoning the friendship described as contradictory in the mantra—"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree; one of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating"—one must, through the great resonance (*mahānāda*) of the fullness of *Ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness), first traverse the path of longing within the cave of the heart. Then, by entering into that [state], he demonstrates his own state of being the full subject (*pramātṛ-pūrṇabhāva*), saying: "The triple Veda (*trayī*) is not within the range of hearing for women, Śūdras, and the degraded twice-born."

Thus addressed, he— who out of grace toward women, Śūdras, and others, reveals the *Bhārata* within his own family-dharma as the very form of the Great Kula-dharma, which constitutes the essential subject matter (*prameya*) of all Tantras, Āgamas, Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and so forth; and who, by enacting it through the meaning of the *Mahāvirāj* and *Gāyatrī*, demonstrates the Great Kaulika Lord Nārīśvara through both the body of the words and their meaning— himself enters into that [Lord] while desiring the cave of the heart through the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*), [his own] body of vision and action becoming the station of non-vision and non-action.
I honor the Jina who possesses a state of equanimity;
for by him, peace is proclaimed through the abandonment of all conceptual enumeration. || 5 ||

By the passage beginning with *hṛdguhām* (the cave of the heart), the meaning is as follows: having abandoned the secondary ego (*gauṇāhaṃtā*)—which is the locus of the sense of "mine"—and the false, limited ego (*mithyāhaṃtā*), one should abide by means of the threefold primary ego (*mukhyāhaṃtā*). This consists of: (1) the primary ego in the form of the sound of the word "I" (*ahaṃśabda-nāda*) through the *pratyāhāra* of the *mātṛkā*; (2) the primary ego in the sense of being the Supreme Father, the eldest of all, as stated in such scriptural passages as "The triad is indeed the eldest: mother, father, and son"; and (3) the primary ego in the form of the full state of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*), which is the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of the aforementioned word and its meaning. Thus, it is by this threefold ego that [one should abide] in the cave of the heart.

The root *guh* means "to conceal"; thus, the meaning is "the cave of the heart (*hṛdaya-guhā*) which is the concealed totality of word and meaning. "Desiring" (*abhilaṣan*) means wishing to face toward that cave of the heart of word and meaning. "Having the form of vision and action" (*dṛkkriyāvapuḥ*): by the etymologies "that in which vision and action are deposited" or "by means of which [they are deposited]," I am, in the state of extroversion, one whose body consists of the activity of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*). "The state beyond vision and action" (*adṛkkriyāpadaṃ*): it is a state not reached by the two—knowledge and action consisting of mental modifications; the meaning is that it is devoid of the triad (*tripuṭī*) consisting of agent, object, and action.

And it is in verse form by virtue of the vision and action directed toward the object of the unsurpassed aspect (*anuttarākāra*). It is also suggested that [it is so] because its body consists of both word and meaning. For this very reason, it is also in the form of the Great Sound (*mahānāda*), composed of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, according to the principle of resonance (*anuraṇana*). "Existing" (*santam*) means having the nature of ultimate reality. Alternatively, [the phrase] "desiring the cave of the heart" (*hṛdguhāmabhilaṣan*) may mean [desiring] by means of that very cave of the heart. Or, [it may mean] "having the body of vision and action" (*dṛkkriyāvapuḥ*) while being "the state beyond vision and action" (*adṛkkriyāpadaṃ santam*). For this very reason, it bestows equanimity (*samabhāvada*). It is *śiva*, having the nature of auspiciousness.

According to such scriptural passages as, "One becomes Brahman through the knowledge of Brahman; being Brahman, one attains Brahman; that Brahman is the supreme auspiciousness," and because the verbal root *vaś* means "to desire," the sense is also that [the Lord] is the bestower of forms such as *sārūpya* (likeness) according to one's qualification or according to one's wish. Alternatively, with the intention of qualifying either "the existent" (*santam*) or "Śiva," the meaning is "Śiva, who is the Sādākhya Puruṣa and the digit of the moon. *Emi* means "I go"; the sense is "I enter."

Alternatively, *samabhāva* is a correct (*samīcīna*) absence (*abhāva*). It is either of the nature of a locus (*adhikaraṇātmaka*) or of the nature of another positive entity (*bhāvāntararūpa*). That which gives this is *samabhāvada*. The significance of the prefix *sam-* here should be inferred as being intended to indicate the incorrectness of the "absence" (*abhāva*) as the seventh category (*padārtha*) accepted by the Logicians (*Tārkikas*). As it is stated in the *Vārttika*: "But absence is indeed another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*), depending on a certain point of view."

The venerable Bhaṭṭapāda has also stated: "Non-existence is of the nature of its locus. In the reading *santanomi samabhāvadaṅginam*, by means of these two actions, even that which is in the form of a verse possesses a common manifestation. Therefore, I thoroughly extend (*santanomi*) and expand (*tanomi*) myself as the substrate (*aṅgin*). The meaning is: having expanded it, I describe it through the definition of the transcendental state (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) regarding creation and so forth, for the sake of understanding from the perspective of the ritual injunction (*vidhi*).

Now, raising the objection as to what the fruit of such an entry—consisting in the attainment of the state of Śiva, which is the expansion of the Self—is, [the author] shows that the abandonment of hostile friendship is the fruit, stating: "the abandonment of friendship" (*sakhyahāni*). For (*hi*), by means of this Śiva, there occurs the abandonment of hostility—that is, the abandonment of the hostile friendship mentioned in the Vedic scripture, *dvā suparṇā*. The meaning is that [friendship] is produced or bestowed. The sense is that the unity of the two "I-senses" is attained; therefore, "I go to him" is the presentation of the fruit.

Therefore, it should be understood that in all three systems (*mata-traya*), the result of the abandonment of friendship (*sakhya-hāni*) is the same: in the state of the direct realization of the non-dual Self (*advitīyātma-abheda-sākṣātkāra*), and in the state of the meditation on the "I-grasp" (*ahaṃgraha-upāsanā*) of that kind, [the seeker remains] as his own essential nature; in the state of qualified non-duality (*viśiṣṭādvaita-bheda-avasthā*), [he remains] as a subordinate (*śeṣatayā*); and in the state of meditative worship through symbols (*pratīka-upāsanā*) characterized by the relationship of the served and the server, [he remains] as a servant (*sevakatayā*). Thus, due to the equality [of the seeker's status] until the abandonment of ignorance (*āvidyaka-sakhyahāni*), the fruit of the abandonment of friendship is identical across the three views.

Alternatively, based on the root list (*dhātupāṭha*) which states "√han [is used] in the senses of injury and going," it may mean that the loss of friendship and the attainment of the state of friendship through knowledge are granted; or, from the perspective of the practitioner (*upāsaka*), the consistency of this view with those seekers of knowledge who are attached to worldly objects should be understood. Therefore, the intended meaning in the present context is that Śiva alone is the agent of the action, and not "I."

This has been stated by the authors of the *Mantrarāmāyaṇa*: "The Blessed Śiva, the ground of both the particular creation and destruction, is the speaker here; I am his echo in the mountain caves. Whether there be fault or merit in this, it is certainly not within my own power. This being the case, let the great ones rejoice in envy, or let their affection overflow. In this [verse], the *rathoddhatā* meter is employed throughout. Its definition is: "The *rathoddhatā* consists of *ra*, *na*, *ra*, *vi*, *la*, and *ga*. (That is: *ra-ra-na-ra-vi-la-ga*).

In this way, even under the guise of poetic composition, by identifying the body of the Virāṭ Śiva—described in the passage, "Know the Self as the rider, and the body as the chariot itself"—as being essentially the work titled *Cidgaganacandrikā* (The Moonlight of the Consciousness-Sky) through its elevated *rathoddhatā* meter, and by making known the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that it consists of the play of word and meaning, his identity with his own body is indicated; such is the summary. || 5 ||

Thus, indicating that for Paraśiva—who is filled with the state of plenitude through the practitioner’s entry into the principle of Paraśiva—the nature consists of both *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), which is another synonym for the union of Speech (*vāk*) and Meaning (*artha*), and so forth, [the text] points to the form of Artha-Nārīśvara. Furthermore, it indicates the distinction between the *vaikharī* and *parā* speech, along with the corresponding distinctions in the perception of meaning, as established in the worldly transactions of the *avidyā*-bound realm through the differentiation of the states of the uttered (*udita*) and the unuttered (*anudita*)—referring to the Speech of one's own true nature as described in the concluding mantra of the Śukriya-kāṇḍa: "Obeisance to Speech, whether it has been uttered or not uttered; to that Speech... may the ancestors rejoice."

Reversing [the conventional order], he declares that the nature of the six paths consisting of speech and meaning is the cause of the auspiciousness and so forth [of the world], by virtue of its utility for the Great Sequence (*mahārthakrama*)—which consists of two, three, four, five, and five unsurpassed meanings—as it exists in the state of the supreme *vaikharī* speech whose essence is non-dual knowledge regarding the meanings of speech that have arisen and those yet to arise:
"That which is 'I' is the supreme speech that has arisen; and that which is the one whose body is the Self, stirred by Light..."
I take refuge in those two auspicious Śivas, the parents of the six paths, who are mutually delighted and ever intent on the upward ascent.

By the words "That which is 'I'," etc.: that speech which is "I"—meaning the word "I" consisting of the internal power of action (*abhyantara-kriyā-śakti*) through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the contraction (*pratyāhāra*) of the letters of the Mātṛkā—is "udita-vāk. It is called *udita-vāk* because it speaks of the Self (*ātman*) as having arisen, being in the state of arising. "She herself becomes the other (*parā*)"—this is the connection. Likewise, that which is the object of "I" (*ahamartha*), whose form is the Self stirred by Light (*prakāśa*)—that is, by the manifestation of the object non-different from the Word (*śabda*), meaning non-different from the speaker of the word "I"—is likewise so described.

This has been stated by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "A word or its cognition can be conceived [to apply] to an object within the range of perception, but not otherwise; yet neither [the word nor the cognition] can be conceived [to apply] to that [Self], because it is of the nature of that [Self], and the same applies to the agent of the 'I'. "Lulitaḥ" means one who has entered into words—that is, one whose specific knowledge of his own true nature has been obscured. He too is indeed the Supreme (para), whether this be understood as a change of gender (*liṅgapariṇāma*) or as a remainder (*śeṣa*). This is because of the constant syntactic connection between "yat" and "tat," and because of the natural force of the conjunction "ca" in the phrase "parā ca."

Now, one might object: "If both [the Father and Mother] are supreme, would this not lead to the consequence of duality, thereby contradicting your own established doctrine? Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that, for the sake of the sequence of the five-fold functions—beginning with the creation of speech and meaning, which will be described later—the two are mutually related as the fruit of each other's ascetic power: "We praise the ancient couple, the parents of the universe, who are mutually the fruit of each other's excellence in austerity."

He offers a rebuttal—stating that the description of their distinction according to the analogy of the elephant and the bull (in the *Gajavṛṣabha-citra*) is merely a verbal artifice—in order to illuminate the fact that they consist of a pair of word and meaning mutually interpenetrated, as expressed by the words "those two which [are] mutually": "Those two which are of the nature of word and meaning, being joined together mutually and possessing natures that are mutually interpenetrated in the manner described, [they alone exist] here in the creation of the world, which is the locus of the play consisting of the abandonment of the illusory duality mentioned in the preceding verse."

With their faces turned upward, they have abandoned the sequential conceptualization of gender (*liṅga*) and so forth—which is employed in the operations of injunction and prohibition regarding the meaning of words such as the optative suffix (*liṅ*)—in favor of the innate, non-reflective flash of the gender and other signs of word and meaning, as stated in: "Since the progeny are neither marked by the lotus nor by the thunderbolt, but are marked by the *liṅga* and the *bhaga*, therefore the progeny belong to Maheśvara. For this very reason, they are the parents of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhva*). The Mother consists of the three paths of sound (*śabdādhvan*), which are the reflectively perceived nature of phonemes, words, and mantras.

From the verbal root *māṅ* in the sense of "measuring" (*māne*): he who measures his own unconditioned nature is the *mātā* (the measurer). Thus, Śiva is the knower of His own nature, the *svarūpapramātā*. He is the *pitā* (father) because He protects (*pāti*) and sustains the true essence of His own nature through the three paths of meaning (*arthādhvan*), which consist of the categories of *kalā*, *tattva*, and *bhuvana*, as well as the objects to be manifested. Thus, Śiva is the protector of His own nature, and Śakti is the one who protects. Therefore, the mother (*mātā*) and the father (*pitā*) together are the parents (*pitarau*). They are the parents of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvapitarau*). They are the two auspicious ones (*śivau*). Both Śivā and Śiva are the two auspicious ones (*śivau*).

From the verbal root *vaś* in the sense of "desire," [Kālī and Kāla] consist of mutual desires conforming to the relationship of signifier and signified. I take refuge in Kālī and Kāla, who are expert in the creation and protection of the entire universe through the delimitation and preservation of names, and through the delimitation and preservation of forms. The meaning is: "I contemplate them as non-different from my own essential nature."

Thus, the sixfold path of direction, space, time, and the temporal (kāla) and spatial (adhvan) dimensions of the forward and backward sequences has been described in the *Saubhāgyahṛdayāmarśastava*: "O Goddess! O Daughter of Śiva! The sixfold path—consisting of phoneme, energy, word, principle, mantra, and world—shines within you, the conscious Self."

By this [explanation], even regarding the indirect and direct experiences of the meanings of the words contained in the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), just as in the creation of speech and meaning, the mere thorough knowledge of the root—the fourfold caste system consisting of Brahmins and so forth, which constitutes the letters, words, and meanings—is merely a fraction (*kalā*) of the knowledge of the referent of the word *tat* (the *tvaṃpadārtha*), which is an object of cognition conditioned by ignorance; and the thorough knowledge of the duties of one's own respective caste, caused by the conceptualization of those letters and so forth, is called a "foot" (*pada*), according to the etymology "that by which one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-tattva*) is reached," just like the knowledge of the referent of the word *tat*, which exists in the past (indirectly).

Just as the knowledge of the fruit—the intended meaning of all the Vedas, Śāstras, and so forth—which consists of the essential nature of that very *tatpadārtha* (the referent of "That") which is otherwise beyond perception, is non-different from one's own true nature (*svarūpa*); likewise, according to the method of this [present] scripture, the knowledge of the reality of the referents consisting of the collection of syllables occurs precisely through the medium of the knowledge of *kalā*—which is synonymous with the knowledge of the meaning of the syllables composed of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*—and it occurs only through such knowledge of the reality of the referents of words.

It should be understood that this also includes the knowledge of identity with the nature of the world, which constitutes the meaning of the mantra—a term synonymous with the meaning of the sentence composed of a collection of words. And as it is stated in the *Kārikāvalī*: "The cognition of the word is the instrument (*karaṇa*); therein, the cognition of the word-meaning is the intermediate step (*dvāra*); verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) is the fruit; and therein, the cognition of the expressive power (*śakti*) is the auxiliary cause (*sahakāriṇī*). By this, it should also be understood that the meaning of the sūtras propounded in the Trika system—such as those in the *Paraśurāmakalpasūtra* stating, "Words consist of phonemes and are eternal; the efficacy of mantras is of an incomparable kind"—has been restated here with full intent.

Now, one might object: "What is this contradiction that is being asserted? For here, the logicians (tārkikas) maintain that because words, cognitions, and actions persist for two moments, they perish in the third moment; whereas the venerable Paraśurāma maintains the eternity of words consisting of phonemes (varṇas). How can this be reconciled? We reply: there is no contradiction here, because both positions—eternity and non-eternity—are relative, depending on whether one considers the three functions characterized by creation and so forth, or the fivefold [process], as delimited by the specific moments marking the beginning of the ocean of mātṛkā-letters and their dissolution. Thus, we declare there is no contradiction.

This has been stated by the venerable Śrī Vidyāraṇya, the sovereign among teachers, in his *Vedāntapañcadaśī*: "The logicians say that even when the material cause has perished, the effect waits for a moment; why should that not be possible for us as well? While they have described such a moment as lasting for a number of days of threads, let a moment here be accepted as suitable for an illusion spanning countless kalpas," and so forth. (6)

Thus, for the Self, which consists of the knower, speech, and the object, in the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): "The nature of being a knower is indeed the manifestation of the true nature of the object of knowledge; and the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the means of knowledge is the state of being both the object and the subject (*nārīśatā*) of the Self."

Having thus contemplated the state of being composed of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness)—which is another synonym for the identity (*sāmarasya*) of the subject and the means of knowledge—one must consider that even for the *jīva-sādhaka-rudra*, who reflects upon the objects of knowledge belonging to those qualified for the path of smoke and flame (*dhūmārcirmārga*), the attainment of that [identity] occurs through the object of knowledge (*prameya*) whose nature is non-different from speech and meaning. Therefore, among the seven types of sacrifice taught in the *Bhagavadgītā* beginning with "Sacrificers of substances, sacrificers of austerity," it is specifically the sacrifice of substances (*dravyayajña*) which serves as the primary means, appearing as the very head of the threefold activity within the nature of both *ahantā-vidyā* and *avidyā*.

Illuminating [this], [he speaks of] the Pravargya and other rites—consisting of the joining of the head characterized by hot potency, as stated in the Vedic scripture regarding specific Vedic Soma sacrifices: "This Agni is indeed Rudra"—which are performed day after day.

Just as the Agnihotra, Darśapūrṇamāsa, and other rites—which take the place of those [Vedic sacrifices] mentioned in the Śruti such as "every month, every month, one should renounce"—possess primacy due to their obligatory nature, so too, in order to express the primacy of the specific worship consisting of the five constituent elements (pañcapadārtha) characterized by the joining of the head of Rudra with the cool potency (*śītavīrya*), [the text describes] the aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth, composed of the five elements, which stands in the position of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the Great Manthānabhairava, who is the living Rudra (*jīvarudra*) that is the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

He offers praise and salutation by identifying [the Lord] with the churning-stick used for the churning of the ocean of the fivefold cosmic acts— such as the creation and maintenance of the life-process— through non-difference from the subject: "Seated upon Śakti as His eye,
He churns the ocean of full splendor."
O Goddess! I clearly worship Rudra, who is the Mandara mountain that serves as the support for the digit of the nectar of libation. || 7 ||

By the words "O Śaktinetra," and so forth: O Goddess, whose nature is light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [the universe] is bound by the eye of power (*śaktinetra*). In the context of the fivefold activity of *vidyā* (*vidyākṛtyapañcaka*): *śakti* itself is the eye (*netra*), the organ of sight; it is bound by that. In the context of the threefold activity pertaining to *avidyā* (*āvidyakakṛtyatraya*): *śaktinetā* means the leader (*nāyaka*) or the self (*ātman*) of power; it is bound by that. In the context of the essential nature (*svarūpa*): *śakti* itself is the eye, the churning-rope (*mantharajju*); it is bound by that. Thus, it undergoes the state of being churned within the ocean of the fullness of Being (*pūrṇabhāmayapayodhi*).

Consisting of full splendor, possessing the tranquility of every mode; let him churn that ocean. Let him assume the state of Mount Mandara and the state of the churning-stick.
