Regarding the reading *āsthitam śaktinetrapariṇaddham*: in the sense of the suffix *kvip* being intended, *śaktinetrapariṇad* means "that by which a spear resembling an eye is led around"—thus the small ether (*daharākāśa*) is the one who leads around the spear resembling an eye. He vomits forth, or extends, that [ether], and thus he is *śaktinetrapariṇaddhamaḥ*.

The aggregate of the body and senses composed of the five elements, which is the expansion of all powers; "residing in that" means residing in that which is encircled by the eye of power (śaktinetra), meaning it is endowed with the body, senses, and so forth, together with all powers. In the reading *pūrṇabhāvam apayodhimanthatām*—that is, *apayodhimanthatām*—it refers to the ocean of the essential nature of the letter *A*, because everything to be known has been known.

"A is the name of the eighteen"—according to this principle of grammatical instruction (*śabdānuśāsana*), through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the *mātṛkā-kuṇḍalinī* consisting of the vowel 'A' situated in the *mūlādhāra*, [there is the attainment] of the Siddhas who are of the nature of Manthānabhairava, or of those who are devoid of activity during the churning of the ocean of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).

Therefore, in the sixth section of the fourth chapter of the second book of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, the Śruti itself—by means of the indicative power (*liṅga*) of a Vedic mantra—declares that the former gods themselves attained the form of Manthānabhairava through the principle of the "secret movement of the linga" within the wheel of the Vaiśvānara-form, whose body is encircled by the Eye of the Power of Light and Bliss, and which is characterized by the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of sound, speech, and meaning as will be described. The Śruti says: "Indeed, they did not find any other guide than this Vaiśvānara, the Agni who goes before."

"Then the undeluded gods churned this nectar, Vaiśvānara, for the sake of victory over the field," and so forth. Alternatively, it means "one who has attained a state of fullness. The meaning is: "one whose state (bhāva) is full (pūrṇa)," i.e., *pūrṇabhāva*. Or else, one who vomits (*vamati*) full splendor (*pūrṇabhā*) is *pūrṇabhāvamah*; he is also the ocean of milk (*payodhi*). Those who churn that ocean of milk are the *pūrṇabhāvamapayodhimanthānaḥ*. Among them, the construction is: "bound by the eye of Śakti" (*śaktinetrapariṇaddham*).

By this, it should be understood that in the creation of the universe consisting of Agni and Soma—where Agni is of the nature of *śakti* (power) and Soma is of the nature of the *śaktimat* (the possessor of power)—it is stated that only the *śaktimat* substance serves as the churning-stick (*manthadaṇḍa*). Consequently, substances lacking power are rendered ineffective in the fivefold functions, ritual acts, and sacrifices. Thus, the Mīmāṃsā principle that "there is no substitute for the sacrificial offering or the sacrificer when they are of the nature of Soma" is implicitly supported by this truth. This is how it should be known.

Likewise, O Goddess! The Goddess is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*). She is called *devitarpaṇā* because she is satisfied by this [nectar]. There is a masculine form in the compound for the sake of the name. And that is *sudhā*, consisting of nectar, the power of life (*jīvaśakti*). That itself is the *kalā*, which is knowledge (*vidyā*). It has that as its support. Alternatively, it is *devitarpaṇa* because the Goddess is satisfied by this; and that is the *sudhākala*, the moon. The sense is that even the nectar of Brāhmī and Lakṣmī—who are non-different from the power of consciousness—and even the wine (*vāruṇī*), are sisters of the moon.

"Or rather, it means that He whose support is that [support], namely, the support of the digits of the nectar of libation (*tarpaṇasudhākalāśrayaḥ*). Even though He possesses the splendor of the moon (*dvijarāja*), which is not praised by the darkness (*tamas*), He is nevertheless designated by the term 'king of the twice-born' (*dvijarāja*) even through a dual designation. Or else, *devi* is a vocative: "O Goddess! You who are the support of the digits of the nectar for the purpose of libation. O Goddess! those digits of the nectar intended for the purpose of your libation are the sixteen lunar digits mentioned in the Tantras, beginning with *Amṛtā* and ending with *Amṛtā*, used for the consecration of the offering materials (*arghyadravya*)."

Regarding the view of consecrating with ninety-four *kalās*: there are thirty-eight *kalās* of Agni, Sūrya, and Soma; ten each for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; four for Īśvara—namely yellow, white, reddish-brown, and black; sixteen *kalās* for Sadāśiva, beginning with Nivṛtti and ending with Vyomarūpā; and five mantras beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣat" for the purpose of consecrating the substance. Together with the root mantra and the *mūrtikalā*, these amount to ninety-four, and so forth. [The term refers to] that which has such *kalās* as its support, or the support of the *kalās*.

The *Rudramandara* [states]: It is clearly perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) by way of its form as *sphoṭa*, and by way of being a substance perceivable by the physical eye (*carmacakṣus*). It also possesses the nature of having sharp faculties (*paṭukaraṇendriya*). This is also stated in the *Rudraprapāṭhaka*: through the passage beginning with "Salutation to the Rudras who are on the earth," etc., there is a description of the weapons belonging to the hosts of Rudras residing in the three worlds starting with the earth—namely, the gross substances consisting of wind, rain, and so forth. By this, it is shown that the hosts of Rudras themselves possess the nature of being eternally perceptible and have sharp faculties.

I worship such Rudramandara. The sense is this: just as in the case of the Vaitānika Soma sacrifice—which employs the five categories (*pañcapadārtha*) as its instruments and materials—there is the performance of the *pravargya* and other rites consisting of the rejoining of the severed head of Rudra; likewise, through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that the Great Abiding (*mahāsthiti*), which consists of the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*), is essentially the rejoining of the severed head of Rudra, I continuously contemplate that it is directly a primary constituent part (*sākṣāt-pradhānāṅga*) of that [sacrifice].

This has been stated even in the *Āruṇaprapāṭhaka*, within the section on the Brahma-vidyā concerning the *Aruṇaketuka* fire, which is the primary deity for one's desired goal: "One end of the celestial bow rests upon heaven; the other is supported by the earth. Indra himself cut its bowstring in the form of a wasp (*vamri*). That [bow] is called the 'Indra-bow' (*indradhanus*), which is unstrung. Among those with the color of clouds, they call it this very thing. This is indeed the bow of Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya; this is the bow of Rudra. Indeed, the end of Rudra’s bow crushed his own head. He became the *pravargya* [offering]."

"Therefore, he who performs the Pravargya sacrifice with this [rite] restores the head of Rudra; Rudra does not afflict him who knows thus. The manner in which the five-fold ritual action consisting of worship—characterized by the materials of a "sacrifice of substances"—attains identity (*sāmarasya*) with the *cityagni* (the piled fire-altar) and so forth in the Pravargya, Aruṇaketuka, Soma sacrifices, and others, must be understood from the mouth of the Guru alone. For fear of excessive prolixity, it is not elaborated here. || 7 ||

Thus, by means of these three verses, having reflected upon how even the sacrifice consisting of material substances (*dravyamaya-yajña*) serves as the primary means through the manifestation of one's own universal nature (*sārvātmya*) in the form of the triad of subject and so forth (*pramātrādi-tripuṭī*), it is stated therein: "By whatever action living beings surely fall into hell..."

And by that very [means], they fly upward and become knowers of the three times. According to this method stated in the *Kālikāmata*, those very substances, words, actions, and so forth which are sins, are heard in scripture as being liberating depending on the difference in intention (*abhisandhi*). Thus, by means of the threefold nature of the practitioner’s intention—consisting of disposition, word, action, and substance—it makes manifest the state of universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*), while simultaneously making known that even the downward fall of the tamasic [practitioner] occurs.
[This is expressed in the verse: "The person who existed, who exists, and likewise the other who will exist, whose sequence of actions is distinct..."
There, for the sake of the greatness of the three worlds, I have entered through a single aperture in the heart that is otherwise completely dark.

By the words "yobhavat" and so forth: he who is the practitioner (*sādhaka*), namely Manthānabhairava Rudra. He is called "one whose actions are distinct" (*pṛthakkriyaḥ*) because his actions are separate, unique, and extraordinary compared to those of the world. For this very reason, he "became" (*abhavat*). The meaning is that previously, in the state of ignorance or in a former birth, he was as if devoid of existence in the form of the unsurpassed *nāda*.

In the view of Rudra as the subject (*pramātṛ*), [it is said]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed non-existent" (*asadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). According to this Śruti, although [the world] possesses name, form, and so forth whose existence was unmanifest, it came to possess existence itself; thus it "comes to be. The sense is that by the use of the present tense (*laṭ*) in the word *bhavati*, it exists in the form of the universe. And "the other" (*itaro 'pi*) likewise comes to be in the same way. Here, by the power of the word "other," it is also suggested that in the cycle of birth and death—which is eternal by way of its stream—one neither came into being nor does one come into being.

In the case of the practitioner (*sādhaka*): "Just as in a previous birth, even in the present life, because his actions are extraordinary compared to the world, or because he possesses a deficiency in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for human goals such as knowledge and action, he does not even possess existence as a mere nominal member of the count [of men]"—this is the implied meaning (*dhvanyartha*). Also in the case of Rudra: "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; if he knows 'Brahman exists'... [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6.1].

The meaning is this: because the fear of the emptiness of the self—which is censured by the Śruti as being [merely] "existent"—does not manifest for such a qualified seeker, and because it is impossible for that which is neither real nor material to appear, it simply does not shine forth. This too has been stated in the *Alātaśānti-prakaraṇa* of the Gauḍapāda-kārikās regarding the manifestation of the fourfold alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the conceit of the self: "I am," "I am not," "I both am and am not," or again, "I neither am nor am not"—these are the four alternatives. Now, as for that which is subject to differentiation...

Some actions lead to the state of the "believer" (*āstikya*) and bestow the status of superior beings, while others lead to the state of the "non-believer" (*nāstikya*) and bestow the status of inferior beings; he whose actions are thus distinguished by the operation of merit and demerit is *pṛthakkriyaḥ*. In the reading *pṛthakkramaḥ*, the meaning is that the process of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārakrama*) is distinct with respect to the aforementioned superior and inferior beings. The sense is that the *ahaṃ* (the ego-principle), which consists of the three currents—horizontal, upward, and downward—is composed of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and the three functions (*kṛtyatraya*) of the resonance of sound (*nādavāk*).

By this, the third type of transmigratory existence of the *sādhaka* soul—distinct from both the transmigratory existence of the supreme Śiva and that of the base animal—is indicated. Therefore, the meaning is that the person (*jana*) remains "one who possesses birth" (*janimān*) even in a future birth, because of his nature as a subject of doubt. Alternatively, in the case of Rudra, the word division may also be *a-janaḥ*. This means that since his activity is unique to both the world and the scriptures throughout the three periods of time, he will remain entirely devoid of connection to birth even across the three births.

Alternatively, the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "The practitioner who was previously possessed of actions distinct from the world, who is so now, and who will be so in the future"—the "belly of those three" means that which has become the belly of those three. By means of a single *ahaṃtā* (I-consciousness)—in one case, by the *ahaṃtā* of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), and in another, by that whose nature is full existence (*pūrṇasattā*). I bow to the cavity existing within the heart.

Regarding the reading *ahaṃ tathaikayā*: either it means that just as [the Self] is the belly of the three, so too by means of the single "I-ness" (*ahantā*) I am in the heart; or the meaning is that toward the Holy One (*santaṃ prati*), I am in the heart according to the measure of the cavity (*randhrapramāṇataḥ*). || 8 ||

Thus, having established the non-difference between one's own self as Śiva and the three types of practitioners (*sādhaka*), for the purpose of setting forth the path of the tradition of the True Knowledge (*sadvidyā-sampradāya*), and to illuminate how that very [Self] assumes various forms through the divisions of the lineage of Gurus (*guruparamparā*), [the author] states the root source of the collective lineages of Gurus (*gurupaṃkti*)—which removes the three impurities of speech, mind, and body through the distinct systems known as *Śābdika*, *Yoga*, and *Vaidya*—with the verse: "By Yoga, the impurity of the mind; by the Path (*pada*), that of speech; and by Medicine (*vaidyaka*), that of the body."

"I bow with joined palms to Patañjali, the foremost of sages, who composed that [work]. By thus stating this, he reveals that Patañjali—who is a manifestation of Śiva as described in the *Uktaśeṣa*—is also an incarnation of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*). He then pays homage to the lineage of gurus, beginning from Para and ending with the multitude of disciples, as follows:
"In the Lord, the Self of all, the abode of the universe, who has attained the state of Puruṣa through the act of filling..."
We pay homage to those great sages, headed by Patañjali, who have fixed their minds [upon this]. || 9 ||

By the words "in the abode of the universe," and so forth: the meaning is that [He resides] in Him whose very abode is the universe, or alternatively, in the gathering-place (*samanī*) of the universe; in both cases, it refers to the Self (*ātman*) which is eternally present. The sense is that, although the supreme and non-supreme speech and their objects possess forms conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), His own nature remains unimpeded throughout the three periods of time. For this very reason, with respect to the Lord, there is the *Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa*: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, and controls the earth from within," as well as the words of the Blessed One: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings."

In Him, the controller of all beings and their constituent elements, who exists in the form of both word and meaning; who has attained the state of *puruṣatva* (personhood) through the filling (*pūraṇa*) of the conscious and insentient portions and the unification of them into a universal oneness; and although there are many etymologies such as "because He dwells in the city (*puri śayanāt*)," "He steals the cities (*puramoṣati*)," or "He lies before the cities (*puraiva śete*)," it should be understood that in this context the etymology based on "filling" (*pūraṇāt*) is adopted because the state of being full of both word and meaning is what is intended.

Regarding the reading ending in the dative case, *puruṣatām upeyuṣe*: it should be understood that the dative is used in the sense of purpose (*tādarthye*), meaning that the *Śabdabrahman*—which has attained the state of being a person (*puruṣabhāva*) through both Word and Meaning in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), or in the forms of teacher, disciple, woman, man, and so forth—acts for the sake of the mutual welfare of all by means of preserving the tradition of the path of knowledge.

And he will say further on: "He who causes the dull-witted to stumble also delivers the wise. Thus, through their mutual stumbling and delivering one another, the teacher and the disciple possess a longing for the highest good. Therefore, [the word is used] for the Puruṣa who has attained manhood; the meaning is: for the Puruṣa whose essence is either speech or its object, or whose essence is his own six paths (ṣaḍadhvan). Those great sages...

The meaning is: those great seers (*maharṣis*) who are incarnations of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara—consisting of the streams of the *para*, *aughama*, and *divya* [traditions]—and who are the forms of the Gurus of both word and meaning, appearing as the incarnations of the lives of the hosts of perfected beings (*siddha*), humans, and disciples; they "fixed their minds" (*manaḥ praṇidadhuḥ*), that is, they directed their minds toward one another. In the phrase "we pay homage to them, headed by Patañjali," the plural number indicates the inclusion of the practitioner-lives (*sādhakajīva*) within the act of worship (*upasanā*). || 9 ||

Thus, following the salutation to the lineage of gurus beginning with Patañjali— who consist of the totality of all lineages— he contemplates his own chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), who is the cause of the origin and dissolution of the universe and consists of the fivefold vehicle that is the totality of both word and meaning, and who takes the form of the three divine lineages, as the very expanse of consciousness (cidvyoma):
"Those who always take refuge in the body of the Power of Space (vyomaśakti), which is the mass of rays emanating from the face of Khecarī..."
Wherein Śambhu desires to imitate the entire universe by means of the splendor of his son Dakṣa. || 10 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "the face of Khecarī" (*khecarīmukha*): it refers to the "network of rays" (*marīcijālaka*) of those rays to be described—namely Khecarī, Bhūcarī, Dṛkcarī, Dikcarī, and Gocarī—which have their origin (*mukha*) or commencement in *khecarī*. For the Siddhas, this network takes the form of a collection of window-lattices within the palace of the body and senses; for practitioners (*sādhakas*), who possess the spheres of the senses fashioned by the magician-like living beings and fishermen, it takes the form of the openings in the net. That void (*vyoman*) wherein this occurs is the "network of rays from the face of Khecarī."

According to Amarasimha, the word *jāla* is used in both senses of "window" and "net. *Śaktitanu*: because the Siddhas possess the power of realizing their intentions (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), [the space] has the form of Śakti’s body; or, *śaktitanu* means that whose body or physical form is Śakti herself; or, *śaktitanu* refers to that wherein Śakti is extended, spread out, or manifested according to the varying capacities of practitioners. That void which is synonymous with the *dahara*, the sky of consciousness—that I always take refuge in.

I contemplate [the Self] as my own essential nature through never-forgetting it at all times. Regarding the reading *śaktitanusaṃśrayam*: in the sense of the established position (*siddhapakṣa*), it means "that which has recourse to both Śakti and the body"; and in the sense of the practitioner's position (*sādhakapakṣa*), it means "that for which there is recourse to Śakti and the body. Through these different grammatical analyses (*vigraha*), this should be understood as an adjective qualifying *vyoman* (the void) itself. In this reading, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "there exists such a void. In that void, by the manifestation of the two bodies of Śambhu and Dakṣa...

By the manifestation—meaning by way of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—of Śambhu, who is the Self whose nature is the bliss that is the ultimate limit of joy; and of the daughter of Dakṣa (the *puryaṣṭaka*), whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) constitutes the true human effort (*satpuruṣakāra*) consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, which are non-different from Himself and capable of performing their respective functions. Alternatively, in the reading where "Śambhudakṣatanujāvabhāsana" ends in the nominative case: Śambhu is the Self whose nature is the ground of bliss; and the "daughter of Dakṣa" is the body capable of knowledge or action.

She who is born from those two, or by means of those two, is the daughter of Śambhu and Dakṣa; and she is that very manifestation—the manifestation of the daughters of Śambhu and Dakṣa. Alternatively, within the garland of letters of the Mātṛkā, which consists of the *kāmakalā* of the beginning and the end, the syllable *ahaṃ* (I) is formed through the synthesis of the initial and final phonemes. Or rather, having divided the synthesis of the letters of the Mātṛkā according to the convention of word and meaning, it takes the form of the word *atha*, which signifies the discourse on the emission (*visarga*) of the Self—beginning with *aḥ* and ending with *ka*. As it is said: "The syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two were formerly [born] from Brahmā."

Having pierced through the wood, both auspicious ones have emerged; thus, in the form of the auspicious speech and meaning as set forth in the Smṛti, within the triple-layered three-lined diagram consisting of sixteen syllables such as *akatha* and so on, there is the pair of lines representing the couple Kālī and Kāla established by the pratyāhāra of thirty-three phonemes. Within the lines and syllables of the triangle, there is the word *atha*, which signifies the subsequent rites to be performed, such as birth and so forth, as the object of worship. Following its accomplishment, [one proceeds] within the garland of letters from *a* to *kṣa*, including Mount Meru.

Since the word-form *dakṣa* is produced through the inclusion (*pratyāhāra*) of the letters beginning with *da* immediately following *tha* and ending with *kṣa*, the capacity (*dakṣatva*) of the internal notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which is the referent of the word *akṣa*, is likewise established. At that time, the very *akṣa* must also be *dakṣa*, possessing a single essence with the referent of the word, just like the notion of "I."

And thus, the meaning is as follows: she is called "the daughter of Śambhu and Dakṣa" because she is the manifestation (*avabhāsanā*) arising from Śambhu—who has severed [the bonds of] Jīva-Śiva—and from Dakṣa, who possesses capable senses, and from *tanu*, which means the body. She is that very manifestation. The sense is that she acts as if desiring (*īhate*) to imitate the real world—the empirical universe—just as word and meaning imitate each other by taking on each other's forms. She exists as if resting in that void (*tadvyoma*); or rather, the word "exists" (*asti*) connects with what precedes.

This very same meaning—the reality of the nature of Kālī and Kāla, consisting of the aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) of sound and sense—was taught by the venerable Lord Bhairava to the Supreme Goddess Śrī-Bhairavī, beginning with the words "Now, all the initial lunar days" (*athādyāstithayaḥ sarve*). Regarding this, the word *atha* was employed by the venerable Lord Bhairava at the commencement of the *Śrītrikaśāstra*. This has been explained with logical justification in the *Tantrasāra-laghuvivṛti* by the illustrious teacher Abhinavaguptapāda; it should be consulted therein.

As for the discourse on the *akathādi* [mantra], consisting of sixteen groups of sixteen syllables, the three-layered lines, the *pratyāhāra*, and so forth—this is merely a marvelous tale fashioned from the imagination of our own cheeks for the sake of instructing children who are devoted solely to ritual procedures (*prakriyā*). Enough, then, with this proliferation of logical elaborations. || 10 ||

Thus, having contemplated that which consists of the vibration of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā), which is synonymous with the "small" (dahara), and whose essential nature is the existence of the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma), he distinguishes therein the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator— the Śiva and Śakti who are of the nature of light and reflective awareness (prakāśa-vimarśa), and the Siddha and Mānava lineages who are of the nature of the undivided and the divided, respectively, as well as the Śākta and Āṇava emissions (visarga): "That [reality] which is characterized by a fullness of radiance— a vibrating existence containing within it the expansion of the divided [manifestation]..."
I bow to you, Ambika, the indivisible sovereign reality, the mistress of all principles, who has made me her very life-breath.

By the words beginning with "khaṇḍa" [it is meant]: by her who contains within her womb the expansion of the sixty-three *tattvas* which, though consisting of parts (*khaṇḍātman*), are of the nature of reality (*sad-rūpa*). Therefore, by that Mother (*ambikā*)—who, through her fullness of being (*sphuraṇa-pūrṇa-sattā*), possesses a partless nature in the form of manifestation (*sphuraṇākāra*) even while having a fragmented nature in the form of the *tattvas*—the partless Lordly *tattva* (*akhaṇḍamaiśvaraṃ tattvam*) [is established].

In the form of the unbroken *akāra* vowel-syllable—which, by way of its nature as sound and its nature as meaning, consists of the state of equilibrium between *nāda* (sound) and *nāda* (the source of sound), and is distinct from fragmented forms—it is that which is characterized as the reality (*tattva*) consisting of its own meaning. This is the sense: it becomes "indicated" (*lakṣita*), meaning it is conveyed through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) or demonstrated by its defining characteristic. [I bow] to you, the mistress of all principles (*akhilatattvanāyikā*), who, in the manner described, are the mistress of all thirty-six principles, as well as of speech and the principle of meaning—such as you, I offer my salutation.

The sense is that by the name "Prakṛti" (Nature), there is the perception of the inclusion of all principles (*tattvas*). Alternatively, by that Ambikā who contains within her the expansion of the fragmented [manifestations] (*khaṇḍasatprasaragarbhā*), that which is characterized as the fullness of manifestation (*sphuraṇapūrṇasat*)—that is, indicated through secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*)—by her, even the indivisible divine principle (*akhaṇḍamaiśvaraṃ tattvam*) is indicated. Therefore, the meaning is: "the mistress of all principles, both fragmented and indivisible. Consequently, the syntactical connection is: "I bow to you, O Ambikā. || 11 ||

Having thus analyzed the relationship between Śiva and Śakti as the illuminator and the illuminated, and although the reality is established as the nature of the supreme *Prāsāda* mantra, [the author], by means of the device of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), brings about a sense of obscurity for the multitude of disciples. Just as one might see grey hair on the head due to old age, he likewise analyzes even the conventional relationship of support and supported within that which has grey hair in the form of knowledge—that is, within the pair of word and meaning that transcends the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*).
He who is indeed "asa" (non-being) is indeed "asa" (leprosy); He is the Lord (*Īśvara*), whose true being is celebrated, and who is stirred upward at the top of the head.
O Mother! I am truly that very one who dwells where you abide—the mountain whose body consists of pure essence.

Regarding the passage beginning with *yaḥ kilāsa* and so forth: "He who is indeed Āsa"—that is, the Lord who is Āsa. In both instances, whether in the position of the injunction (*vidhi*) or the restatement (*anuvāda*), the word *kila* denotes indirectness (*pārokṣya*). The sense is that he exists in an indirect manner within the city named Alakā for the sake of those who are ignorant. Alternatively, "he who is Āsa" means he who is on the mountain named Sakilāsa, or he who is in Āsakila. O Mother! he is this very Lord.

Regarding the phrase "in the uppermost part of the head, which is agitated by the well-known *sattva*": although it is called "agitated by the well-known *sattva*" (*khyātasattvalulita*), this refers to the upper portion—the region of the head at the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*)—which consists of pure *sattva*. This is because even when *sattva* is divided into three parts—namely, that *sattva* predominant over *sattva*, that *sattva* mixed with *rajas* (where *rajas* is subordinate to *sattva*), and that *sattva* mixed with both *rajas* and *tamas*—in each division *sattva* alone remains predominant. Thus, the uppermost part is characterized as pure *sattva*.

Thus, for one whose head is turned upward (*ūrdhvamūrdhan*)—having shaken off the well-known *satva* (*khyātasatvalulita*)—and who occupies the station of Kailāsa at the level of the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), there is this state of having the head turned upward. Regarding the reading *khyātasatvalulitodhvamūrdhani*: [it means] "one who has shaken off the well-known *satva* at the 'head of the path' (*adhvamūrdhani*), that is, in the upper portion of the six paths of word and meaning (*vāgartha-ṣaḍadhvan*). "Shaken off by the well-known *satva*" (*khyātasatvalulitaḥ*) means made subordinate by the aforementioned *satva* which has been divided into three parts; this is an epithet of Īśvara.

Thus, regarding the reading *uditordhvamūrdhani*: "on the summit of the path" (*adhvamūrdhani*) means on the crest of the twelvefold end (*dvādaśānta-śikhā*), which is the meaning of speech (*vāgartha*). "Uditaḥ" means having arisen, having become manifest. Even with the reading *uditordhvamūrdhani*, it means: on the upper part of the head of that which has become manifest, there is the "renowned being" (*khyātasattva*); or rather, in the "renowned being" itself, which is like a white leprosy (*kilāsa*). "The Lord abides" (*īśvaraḥ pratitiṣṭhati*) is either an epithet of the Lord or an epithet of the white leprosy. This is where that Lord abides.

Regarding the reading *pratyaham*: the explicit meaning is "that [place] where [He] always, day after day, abides. Of this Lord who is firmly established, the mountain—which is Mount Kailāsa, His dwelling place—is *satvavapuḥ*, meaning its body consists of pure *sattva* divided into three parts as previously described. You alone are that; the meaning is that you alone are in the form of Mount Kailāsa. Thus, regarding the reading *evaṃ tvaṃ sa tattvavapuradrikaḥ*: the suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of "small," so *adrikaḥ* means a small mountain (*alpaḥ adriḥ*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: you are the true essence of Mount Kailāsa, which consists of limited categories (*parimita-tattva*); yet you alone are also that body which is joined with the limited categories. The intended meaning is that for the enjoyment of the Lord (*īśvara*), you are of the nature of a body that conforms to His will.

Thus, following the indirect (parokṣa) union of Śiva and Śakti for the ignorant, there is the position of direct (aparokṣa) union as an established reality for the wise. In this regard, just as there is a conceptual division of parts within the Virāṭ-body—which serves as the cause for the origin of the four castes as stated in such Vedic texts as "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth"—so too, even within the limited body from the feet to the head, there is a conceptual division of the fourfold aspects of form, speech, and meaning; by this, the head is characterized as the portion consisting of Parāvāk and the meaning of Paramaśiva.

Even with respect to the portions of the body, having superimposed the identity of Śiva upon the meaninglessness [of physical decay], [it is said]: "That which is leprosy (kilāsa) and graying hair"—[this refers to] the leprosy born of the bones; and that which is on the skin, born of the body, produced by the *kṛtyā* of Brahmā.

Just as the white hair (*palita*) and other marks caused by time, such as those mentioned in the *Mantra* [of the *Atharvaveda*] regarding the disease of premature aging, can be remedied through treatments like the *Kāyakalpa* section of the *Āyurveda* and the use of medicinal herbs, yet the white hair on the head that has ripened with time—such as that of a hundred-year-old—is incurable and can only be removed through direct experience; likewise is the power of the Lord of Time (*Kāla*), which is the referent of the word *Kālī*, and the majesty of His worship.

Having determined that the poet intends the very head—non-different from the pair of *nāda* and *nāda* established as the word and meaning of the speech that has attained growth through knowledge derived from the experience of hundreds of previous births—to be expressed in the form of the word and meaning of the term *kilāsa*, which signifies Kailāsa, it is now explained as follows: And thus: *yaḥ kilāsaḥ* (he who is *kilāsa*) refers to that which has the form of the pair of *nāda* and *nāda* established as the word and meaning of speech. *Saḥ sa eva kila* (he is indeed that very one). *Āsaḥ* is the pratyāhāra beginning with the Absolute (*anuttara*) and ending with *sa*; it is of the nature of the Śākta *visarga*. And *kilāsa* [is also that].

And Mount Kailāsa, as described in the corpus of Vedic, Smṛti, Purāṇa, Āgama, and other scriptures—whether of Ṛṣis or non-Ṛṣis. If one asks why, it is because it is "agitated by the renowned *sat*. It means it is agitated (*lulita*) by the quality of being the seed-syllable *sa* (sakāra-bījatva) known everywhere, which is pregnant with the supreme Śāmbhava emission (*visarga*). By such a quality of the Śākta emission, the meaning is that it has become restless (*lola*) through the form of the syllable *āsa*. "Agitated" (*lulita*) or "risen" (*udita*). At the head of the path—that is, at the summit of the six paths of speech and meaning.

Where, by means of the Śāmbhava-anuttara-bindu-dharma or the Śākta-anuttara-nāda-dharma, [the consciousness] is agitated both internally and externally—in sequence, internally as *aṃ* by the nature of *nāda*, and externally as *aḥ*; and where it is agitated in the form of the Śāmbhava-bindu conjoined with the Śākta-nāda which is the meaning of the word "I" (*aham*)—that [consciousness] abides as a representative of the supreme Śākta-nāda and bindu in the form of the letter *ā*. This is the meaning. It remains.

In the same way, if [the reality] is awakened externally and internally by means of the Śākta-anuttara through the seed-syllable *sakāra* and its dharma, and by means of the Śāmbhava-anuttara through the seed-syllable *sakāra* and its dharma consisting of the *bindu*, then it is [awakened] externally at the very head of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of speech and meaning. Thus, [it is awakened] internally by means of the form of the supreme Śākta-nāda—which consists of the sixfold reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose characteristics will be described later, namely the "unstruck" (*anuttara*), bliss (*ānanda*), will (*icchā*), Īśana, and the waves of unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—and which takes the form of the word expressing the multiplicity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the "severed" (*vicchinna*) nāda, such as "it was" (*āsa*). And [it is awakened] internally.

Regarding the three points (*bindu*) of the supreme *śāmbhava* triad—manifesting as the "I" (*aham*), which is a unified mass of the supreme witness, appearing through the form of the letter *A* and so forth, along with the lower *śāmbhava* point and its own essential nature—it remains as a representative of these three points. And it stands, as described by the phrase "with its head agitated by the well-known *sattva*" (*khyātasatvalulitordhvamūrdhanī*), or alternatively, "with its upward-pointing head arisen" (*uditordhvamūrdhanī*). In both alternative readings, the word "agitated" (*lulita*) refers to the extreme upper portion. [As stated: "The Bindu, Artha, Candra, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, and Śakti."

The meaning is that [she] abides within the form of the Great Bindu (mahābindu), which consists of the tenth nāda as taught in the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures, located above the aforementioned nine nādas—namely, Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā. Within the nature of the internal nāda, she abides either as the primordial nāda (ādināda)—the collective totality (samasthi) of the nine nādas beginning with the first—or as that which is designated by it, namely "I" (aham) or "this one" (asau). Thus she is established.

When [the breath] has arisen in the upper portion, it comes to rest in the Great Bindu (mahābindu) located at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta), the End of the Sixteen (ṣoḍaśānta), and so forth, as well as in the place of the twelve-fold cessation (dvādaśaśānta) and other such locations that have been manifested. This occurs through the sixfold contemplation (*parāmarśa*) of the previously mentioned triad of Śāmbhava bindus and nādas, or through the ninefold nāda consisting of the triad of Śākta nādas and so on, by counting either the individual nādas or their collective totality. Furthermore, externally, it comes to rest in the form of "I am [Name] Ānandanātha" or "I am [Name] Ambā," or in the form of "Svarakhaṇḍanāda. This is the meaning.

Thus, it is established internally and externally either as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) in the form "I am facing this," or as the substratum (*anuyogin*) in the form "this is facing me. O Mother! This refers to that which consists of the meaning of supreme speech (*parāvāk*). It is also implied to be the vowel-element (*ākārāṃśa*) present within both the self-mantra in the form of "I" (*aham*) and the supreme mantra in the form of "this" (*asau*). That mountain is the ground for the arising of the *nāda*, consisting either of the aforementioned sense of "I" or of the objective referent (*artha*).

The meaning is that Mount Kailāsa is not merely a place of residence for the poor; rather, it is the body of reality (*satattvavapuḥ*), the essence of the seed-syllable *sa* within the previously mentioned supreme mantra (*parāmantra*). You are the embodiment of the *visarga* of Śakti; the meaning is that you alone are the nature of the vibration of vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) expressed as *s au*. In the reading *adrikasya yaḥ*, the connection is made by adopting the second reading, *satattvavapuḥ*.

The meaning is: of the letter *a*, which—according to the principles of the science of light (*jyotiḥśāstra*)—consists of a single *drekkāṇa* (one-third part of a zodiacal sign), and which represents the principal portion within the aggregate of the three portions to be described hereafter. Alternatively, it refers to the letter *a* as it is being extracted from the sound *nāda*, which is the form of the remote word *adas*. By implication, this is understood to mean that its form is distinct from the *sakāra* (the letter *s*), the *visarga* (the emission), and the *bindu* (the point) of Śakti, or from *nāda* itself.

Of such a mountain-like one—whether it be a portion of the Śākta emission (*visarga*) or a portion of the supreme mantra—the "body of pure being" (*sattvavapuḥ*) is the embodiment of the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) with the Lord of the Supreme Sound (*anuttaranādanātha*), who is the Śāmbhava principle characterized by pure being (*sattva*). He is "I. The meaning is that he becomes the embodiment of the referent of the word "that" (*tacchabda*), which was previously beyond perception, and simultaneously the embodiment of the referent of the word "I," which is directly perceived. The intended sense is that, through the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) "This is I," or through the form of recognition "I am He," he attains the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the bliss of his own true nature (*svarūpānanda*).

The meaning that "I am that very one whose form is the sentient being" (satvavapuḥ) is also suggested for the wise, according to the view of immediate realization regarding the established reality. For this very reason, there is no dispute among anyone concerning the fact that Kālidāsa—being the form of the primordial Guru (kūṭasthādiguru) within the triad of lineages of Gurus consisting of the descent of the Lord (Īśvarāvatāra) such as Patañjali and others, spanning from the lineage of the Supreme (paraudha) to the lineage of the Divine (divyaudha)—is the form of the primordial Sound (gurunāda) within the triad of lineages of Gurus consisting of the manifestation of the individual soul (jīvāvacāra) such as Kālidāsa and others, spanning from the lineage of the Siddhas (siddhaudha) to the lineage of disciples (śiṣyaudha). Thus, everything is clarified. || 12 ||

Thus, by means of the non-difference from one's own self, and through the body of the triad of speech, object, and time—namely speech, object, and sound—the Guru reveals the relationship of support and supported residing within the sixfold group (*ṣaṭka*). Then, declaring its ineffability due to its being beyond the senses, he also reveals its state of plenitude:
"That which is beyond conceptualization and beyond the senses, which the outward-turned [consciousness] abandons in three ways, that is the goal (*lakṣya*)."
I bow to that which refutes the existence and non-existence of an intermediate state. || 13 ||

By the words "beyond conceptualization" (*kalpanātiga*) and so forth: that body, which is of the nature of Mount Kailāsa as described in the preceding verse in the form of self-recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), is beyond the senses because it is the locus of the dissolution of the resonance of Word and Meaning (*vāgarthanāda*) in the form of the *dvādaśānta* and other points; this is the sense. For this very reason, it is also "beyond conceptualization. Since it is the locus of the dissolution even of the *Kuleśvara*, who is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) that fashions Word and Meaning, there is an absence of any fashioner (*kalpaka*) therein, and thus even conceptualization is impossible; this is the sense. In that same way, it abandons the external object of perception (*lakṣya*).

The meaning is that, by virtue of its nature as the reality of the knowledge of Adhokṣaja, it even abandons being perceivable by the outward-turned functions of the senses. This has been stated in the Śruti: "The Self-existent pierced the openings toward the outside; therefore, one looks outward, not at the inner self. Regarding the reading *tridhā* (in three ways): [it means] in the form of the Śākta triad consisting of the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) and the accomplishments (*siddhi*) belonging to the three lineages—the divine, the perfected, and the human; or else, in the form of the Śāmbhava triad consisting of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth. The meaning is that it abandons the external object of perception.

The sense is that, since even for one's own triad of sound, meaning, and resonance (nāda)—which consists of the six paths—there would result an infinite regress if it were required to depend on another object to be indicated, it must be its very self, in the form of the fourth witness-consciousness, that serves as the mutual indicator. Therefore, it exists in the interval between the state of being and the state of becoming.

The meaning is that [the Self] exists as its own essence: in the case of existent things such as jars, in the form of the word and object that signify existence; and in the case of non-existent things—even the void ones such as the son of a barren woman—in the form of a third, void category of word and object that is distinct from both being and non-being and which signifies them, or else as the Fourth Witness-Self (turīyasākṣyātman). As it has been said in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*: "For existents joined with being and non-being, there is a twofold state; transcending that, salutations to the wondrous Śambhu, who is the third."

Therefore, just as there is the negation [of the unreal], so too is the negation of everything other than the Self. I am that Reality; I bow to that Mount Kailāsa which is the form of the ultimate meaning of the word "I. This very reality of the Self, which is the form of the ultimate meaning of the words "Being" and "I," was also stated by the venerable Guru Śaṅkarācārya in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "A word or a cognition can be conceived when there is an object within its range, and not otherwise. But neither [the word nor the cognition] can be conceived [in relation to the Self], because of the identity of the 'I-maker' (ahaṃkartṛ) with That (the Self)."

Regarding the reading *nirākṛtim*—the word *tam* is an adjective qualifying the mountain Kailāsa. Now, one should not raise the doubt: "How can there be the state of being both the object of salutation and the agent of salutation for one's own self alone? This is possible because of the conceptualization of the aspects of speech and meaning within oneself. Thus it has been said: "Salutations again and again to Me alone, whose form is pure, infinite consciousness unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, and whose nature consists of both the knower and the known. (13)
He also describes the very nature of that [Reality] as Brahman, by way of its pervasive aspects of knowledge, ignorance, and the worlds:
"O Mother! Whatever comes into being, it does so through its own nature, never abandoning its emergence as non-dual."
I worship that Brahman, your state, which has manifested its sequence [of creation], and which is heard in the Vedas as "Tat Sat."

By the words beginning with *amba* and so forth: O *amba*! [This is] because of the Nirukta etymology, "She is called *Ambā* because she causes the members [of the body] to grow," found in the Śāntiparva, chapter 266 of the Bhārata; or else, because she is the embodiment of the Great Vitality (*mahāprāṇa*) and the nature of Being (*sattva*), as stated in the mantra of the Aśvamedha section: "O *Ambe*, *Ambāli*, *Ambike*"; or she is *Ambā* because she breathes (*vāti*) that which is denoted by the word whose form consists of the previously mentioned vowel-sound *a* (the *nāda*), with the intention of expressing the non-difference between *ba* and *va*; her vocative is *amba*, meaning "O Thou whose essence is the *dahara*."

That which is Your state (*pada*), consisting of Mount Kailāsa as mentioned in the preceding verse, or consisting of the body of speech and meaning—that becomes [everything] through that very nature, namely through the nature of space, time, objects, and so forth. As it is said in the *Saubhāgyahṛdaya*: "Whatever object exists in whatever manner as the essence of space, time, and objects, I take refuge in that digit (*kalā*) of the All-pervasive Lord which shines in that very form. And in the *Śrīsaṃvitstotra*: "'Stability' (*sthiti*) is the maintenance of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) in the form of this or that [manifestation]."

Furthermore, of what nature is it? It does not abandon speech that is supreme (*parā*) and impelled by its own nature through non-difference from its own essence. For this very reason, it is the arising of non-duality (*advayodaya*), consisting of a manifestation that emerges as non-dual. As it is said in the *Śivasamhitā*: "The letter *A* is the foremost of all letters, the supreme light, Śiva himself. The letter *Ha* is the last, having the form of *kalā*, and is proclaimed as 'reflective awareness' (*vimarśa*). That which is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between these two is the stainless 'I' (*aham*). The object of manifestation, illumined by this 'I'-ness, is called 'this-ness' (*idantā*), yet it is composed of that [very same essence]."

"The harmony (*sāmarasya*) of these two is considered the Supreme Fullness of Consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). For this very reason, even the etymological derivation (*nirukti*) of the word *vāk* (Speech) at the time of its manifestation as *āpāduka* is shown in this same way: "Those who have served the highest Guru call You the Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*), which is undivided from the universe; established in the etymology, they declare that You speak [the word] 'vām' (the dual form of 'you'), consisting of self-luminous reflective awareness (*vimarśana*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is "that in which sequence has been removed" (*apākṛtakrama*). That in which sequence—namely, the sequence of the creation and so forth belonging to the realm of ignorance (*āvidyaka*)—has been removed (*apākṛta*), i.e., abandoned, either by itself or by that [Supreme Speech].

Regarding the reading *upākṛtakramam*—the meaning is "a sequence consisting of the commencement of transcendence. And that sequence is shown as follows in the *Śrīsaṃvitstotra*: "When those [objects] are dissolved into mental states (*bhāva*), mental states into the mind (*citta*), the mind into consciousness (*saṃvit*), and that [consciousness] into the Supreme; when it has been cast into the Sky where it reaches its cessation—therein lies the sequence consisting of transcendence."

In the *Mātṛkāstavarāja*, Kālidāsa has also shown this: "Having placed the universe within his body, and that [body] within the heart, and the person within that, and that person situated in the *bindu*, and even that in the profound [space] called ether (*viyat*), and all this in what is called knowledge (*jñāna*), and that too in the profoundness of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*)—he who is devoted to the experience of You triumphs in the form of the Great Void (*mahāvyoman*). Such is Your state; it is Brahman, well-awakened, fully expanded, or the nature of great bliss. Regarding the word "that" (*tat*): it means "beyond direct perception" (*parokṣa*).

It is indeed heard that "Sat" is of the nature of ultimate perception; the sense is that this is a well-known teaching of the Śruti. Or, in the reading "tatsaditi vā śrutam"—the word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative; the meaning is "by way of being devoid of the portions consisting of name and form. The syntactical connection is: "I worship that which is heard as 'Brahman' and so forth, that which is taught by the Śruti. || 14 ||

Having thus described the nature of Brahman, [the author] now demonstrates— through the verse beginning with "deśakāla" and so forth— that its manifestation as something external for one's own benefit occurs even by way of the paths of injunctions and prohibitions regarding the causes of action, in order to make known its true nature through both superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), using a different reading of the same text. "That which you have become, due to the specific distinctions of the calculation of space and time, is said to be enjoined or prohibited."
Your external manifestation, which is beneficial, follows a sequence based on individuals, species, and bodies. || 15 ||

O Bhavānī! O Consort of Bhava—the word *bhava* denoting Śiva, who bestows the knowledge of the universal categories such as *bhū* (the root-meaning), *jāti* (genus), *sattā* (existence), and *sāmānya* (generality); or, she who protects (*pālayantī*). This vocative is intended with specific purpose. [This is especially so] regarding the distinctions of space and time. For example, regarding the determination of space: "One should sacrifice with the Vaiśvadeva at a place sloping toward the east," or "One should perform penance on the banks of the Revā, and meet death on the banks of the Jāhnavī"; or likewise, [regarding time].

And there are [injunctions] regarding the determination of time, such as: "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma every spring," "Rites should be performed during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on auspicious days," "He releases his speech when the sun is over a tree," and "One should bathe when [the sun] is eclipsed."

Alternatively, since the aforementioned space and time are subsumed within the three paths of objects—consisting of *kalā*, *tattva*, and *bhuvana* for space—and the three paths of words—consisting of *varṇa*, *pada*, and *mantra* for time—the term "calculations" (*kalanā*) refers to the activities and cognitions of those two, space and time, which take the form of the meanings of the word "calculation" as stated [in the scripture]: "Projection, cognition, enumeration, movement, and resonance, in that order."

Alternatively, *kalanā* refers to the knowledge of specific sequences, such as "having made the *veda*, he makes the *vedi*" or "having known [the rules], one should perform the rituals. Specifically, this refers to the distinction between the paths of injunction and prohibition regarding differentiation, meaning the distinction between the paths of injunction and prohibition concerning the sequence of the speaker's own words and their functional efficacy (*arthakriyā*). The sequence based on the individual (*vyakti*) is that which relies upon the individual, such as "one desiring heaven, one desiring a son, or one desiring prosperity should sacrifice," and so forth. This sequence pertains to the body (*tanu*) that is dependent upon both the individual and the genus (*jāti*).

The sequence based on caste (*jāti*) is, for example: "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava," and so forth. The sequence based on caste is further illustrated by: "A Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava; a King (Kṣatriya) with the Rājasūya; a Vaiśya with the Vaiśyastoma; a Rathakāra should establish the sacred fires in the rainy season; with this [rite] one should cause a Niṣāda chieftain to sacrifice," and so forth. The sequence based on the body (*tanu*) is, however: "One with black hair should establish the sacred fires"; "One should immolate a white [animal]," and so forth. Thus [there is] the sequence based on the individual, the caste, and the body.

That which is called "enjoined" (*vihita*) refers to that which has arisen through the operation of the process of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), as if stated with one's own voice. In the reading "is negated" (*niṣidhyate*), it means that what was established by the process of superimposition is negated by such statements as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), [negating] spatial distinctions such as "the Self is in front" (*ātmā purastāt*); by temporal distinctions such as "all that has been, will be, and is, is indeed the Self" (*bhūtaṃ bhavyaṃ bhavacca sarvamātmaiva*); and by distinctions of conceptualization such as "He whose [Self] is unknown, by him it is known" (*yasyāmataṃ tasya matam*).

Likewise, that which is negated is done so by way of negating the sequence based on individuals, through such statements as: "Desire is never stilled by the enjoyment of objects," "free from hunger, thirst, and the like," "the father becomes no father," "the gods become non-gods," and "the Vedas become non-Vedas"; by way of negating the sequence based on classes (*jāti*), through such statements as "devoid of distinctions such as Brahmin and Kṣatriya"; and by way of negating the sequence based on bodies, through such statements as "formless and intangible," "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth.

By means of prohibitive statements whose essence is the cognition of the oneness of the Self, [the world] is negated through the exclusion of what it is not (*atad-vyāvṛtti*). This is Your external manifestation; the meaning is that it is a shining forth externally, whether by way of affirmation or by way of negation. "Beneficial" means that it is indeed wholesome for practitioners (*sādhaka*) and for those who have attained perfection (*siddha*) respectively. The point is that since a negation is necessarily preceded by a prior apprehension (*prasakti*), it is established as a rule that a negation whose instrument is knowledge must be preceded by the attainment of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, what is the point of your excessive expansion here regarding both the positive and negative aspects of the word and its meaning? It is understood that [the deity] is simply the *taddhita* suffix itself, insofar as it takes the form of the word and its meaning characterized by a *taddhita* suffix whose deity is the primordial self (*prākṛtātma-daivatyataddhita-pratyaya*). Moreover, within the nature of the deity, because the operation of the word and its meaning—consisting of the *taddhita* suffix—is more powerful than the two components of injunction and prohibition, it is understood that [the deity] is indeed the form of the word and its meaning consisting of the *taddhita* suffix.

And so it has been stated in the Vārttika as well: "Whether by means of a secondary derivative suffix (taddhita), or by the dative case, or again by the wording of a mantra—the injunction regarding the deity [is established]; among these, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding."

The meaning [of this] is as follows, according to the analogy of the resonance of a sound: in the state of *vidyā* (knowledge), as the process of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) residing in the individual is gradually discarded by the wise and perfected ones (*siddhas*) who are turned inward, by virtue of the progressive increase of knowledge for the sake of attaining the fruit of that knowledge, so too, in the state of *avidyā* (ignorance), that very same process of superimposition is respectfully practiced and maintained by the practitioners (*sādhakas*) who are unwise and turned outward, by virtue of the gradual increase of ignorance for the sake of attaining the fruit of ignorance, since it is not in opposition [to their goal]. This is the sense conveyed through the analogy of the resonance of a sound.

It is established [by the following]: "At the end of many births, the man of knowledge takes refuge in Me, realizing that Vāsudeva is everything; such a great-souled one is very rare. Those whose knowledge has been stolen away by various desires resort to other deities, adhering to their respective rules, constrained by their own natures. Such are the words of the Blessed One. Furthermore: "Let there be those in this world who know policy, who know destiny, and who know the scriptures..."

"May they be knowers of Brahman and knowers of the Vedas, yet those who truly know their own ignorance are rare. This statement by the great Mahāmahopādhyāya Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita, among others, culminates in this very same sense; such is the direction of the argument. 15.

Thus, with eleven verses beginning with "evaṃ hṛdguhām" that are composed in the manner of aphorisms (*sūtra*), [the author] presents the sequence of creation and withdrawal—which are synonymous with injunction and prohibition—along with their reverse order, as being ultimately void, regarding the reality of one's own self consisting of speech and meaning mentioned in the first verse. Then, for the sake of awakening those who are stained by the doubt that the substratum of these two might not manifest, he explains that very same reality by turning back from both sequence and non-sequence, through the final series of expansions beginning with the "triplicity" (*tripuṭī*) and ending at the "sixteenth."

In order to also express the nature of the Great Sequence (*mahārthakrama*) consisting of three, four, and five vehicles, he declares that it possesses the form of the manifestation of the threefold cosmic activity— creation and so forth— as the essence of the three *guṇas*, by way of the gross and subtle forms of the three elements (fire, water, and earth) as described in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* through the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*):
"O Mother, the body of the object established within you is that which has its arising and setting graced by Him."
And there would be darkness, which is what is being negated here;
for duality consists of the two—existence and non-existence—as well as that which has a form other than these. (16)

By the words "satvabhava" and so forth: "O Mother" (*amba*) is an address as before. Of that entity (*vastu*)—which has given rise to the operation of the threefold suffixes of injunction (*vidhi*) as something to be adopted, rejected, or performed; which, by the etymology "that in which the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*) resides," consists of a perfected substance (*siddhadravya*) or a goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*); and which is of a single form with speech and its meaning—the dawning of the Day-maker (the Sun) has been propitiated by that. "Propitiated by that" (*tatprasādita*) means made gracious by that entity.

That body (*vapuḥ*) in which there is the arising (*udaya*), that is, the birth, of compassion (*dayā*)—namely, compassion for all beings—is such a body. Alternatively, through a different etymological derivation, it is a body consisting of compassion, whether internal or external, by means of this seed of compassion (*dayā-bīja*). Sattva is indeed a quality (*guṇa*). This is the intended meaning, similar to the injunctions such as: "Food that is savory, unctuous, substantial, and pleasing to the heart is dear to those of *sattva*."

Whatever object is enjoined as something to be cultivated or practiced in the form of either speech or meaning, the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) that arises from compassion toward all beings—rendered gracious by the cultivation of that object—is a body consisting of that [object], which is called *sattva*, another synonym for the previously mentioned Kailāsa. In the reading *tat-prasāditatayodayam*, the meaning is: "the body arising by virtue of being rendered gracious by that object. Likewise, whatever is prohibited here would be *tamas*.

The sense is that this very [notion] is negated by virtue of being the gross form of the quality of *tamas*. By this, it is established that within one's own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*), which consists of both word and meaning, only the cognitions of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) are the objects of injunction and prohibition, not the reality of the essential nature itself. This has also been stated by the venerable Guru Vidyāraṇya in the *Cittadīpa* of the *Vedāntapañcadaśī*: having considered the states of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world as being [identical with] word and meaning—"When the states of being a soul and being the world are sublated, only one's own Self remains."

"There is no sublation (bādha) of those two due to non-apprehension, but rather due to the certainty of their falsity. Thus, "by way of being other than existent and non-existent" means by way of being different from the previously mentioned notions of "I-ness" (ahantā) and "this-ness" (idantā). This refers to the distinction between the forms [of the two], namely: "I am existent," whereas "this" is not within the range of the notion of "I"; and "this is non-existent," whereas it cannot be within the range of the notion of "I. The meaning is that there is a distinction between the verbal and conceptual content and their own essential natures. When these two—*ahantā* and *idantā*—are combined, they become what is called *rajas*.

Regarding the reading *dvai rajaḥ*: the term *dvairajasi* refers to the combination (*samāhāra*) of two *rajas* particles, namely the atoms of speech (*vāk*) and meaning (*artha*). The analysis (*vigraha*) is as follows: from the state of being "neither existent nor non-existent" (*sadasad-anyarūpataḥ*), there arises what is called *rajas*, due to the differentiation of speech and meaning into the forms of the paired (*mithunīkṛta*) real and unreal. By this it is shown that when the atoms of speech and meaning—namely the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*)—are mixed through their formal distinction, there arises the quality named *rajas*, which is endowed with the name *kalā*, a synonym for *niyati*.

It should be understood that non-difference (*abheda*), which is the unity of one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpaikya*), is said to be the state of being Brahman as the Self (*brahmātmatā*), which has the synonym "abiding in one's essential nature" (*svarūpasthiti*). For this very reason, having intended that the mind, vital breath, and speech alone constitute the body composed of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) in this context, it is stated in the first chapter of the *Bhāvaprakāśa*: "That substance which undergoes transformation as *sattva* is called the mind (*manas*). For the Lord and for the liberated ones, it will become their volition (*saṅkalpa*). For those subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), it proceeds by transforming into the ego-sense (*ahantā*)."

Because it is transformed into that sattva, it is called *sattva* by the wise. That substance which is the transformation of *rajas* is called *prāṇa*; it is the cause of activity for the Lord and the liberated ones, as well as for those in the flow [of existence]. Furthermore, among those in the cycle of rebirth, this [rajas] exists in the form of *prāṇa*. That substance which is the transformation of *tamas* is declared to be *vāk* (speech). For the Lord and the liberated ones, that *vāk* is auspicious; however, for those in the cycle of rebirth, it transforms again into the form of sound.

"That speech which arises from the words of the Liberated Lord (mukteśvara), accompanied by states such as anger and so forth, and which is invariably linked to their fruits, is called *vāṇī* by the wise. The Sun, the Moon, and Fire are its presiding deities respectively; this is the arrangement established by the yogis. Thus [it is said]. And regarding the nature of Pure Knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) in the verse "of the two cognitions, 'the True Reality' and 'this'," there is another Tantra: 16.

Having thus distinguished the subtle form of the three *guṇas* in speech and meaning, he describes the gross form of the three elements as consisting of the three *guṇas*: "That which is darkness (*tamas*) here is the body of the earth; that which is other than this is light (*tejas*), and that which is other than light here is sattva in Śiva."
The other dust arises from their mixture; thus, from those two and from sattva, the triad of qualities is born. || 17 ||

Regarding the passage beginning with "yat": O Śivā! O you whose nature is auspicious (*maṅgalarūpā*), or whose form is desire (*icchārūpā*)—derived from the verbal root *vaś* meaning "to desire" through the transposition of syllables (*varṇavyatyaya*)—this is the vocative. Alternatively, the locative case is used to indicate that Śivā is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). "That which is other than darkness"—meaning another form distinct from the previously mentioned subtle form, namely the gross form produced by the tripartition (*trivṛtkṛta*) of the elements, which is darkness (*tamas*). The same applies to what follows. That becomes your body of earth (*kṣitivarpuḥ*). In the reading *kṣitir vapuḥ*, the meaning is: "Earth itself is your other form; darkness is your body."

In this way, another gross form of *sattva*, which is the essence of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), becomes the body of fire (*tejas*). The meaning is that the other gross *rajas*, arising from the mixture of *sattva* and *tamas*, becomes the body of that which has become both watery and non-watery. By this, it is meant that the other gross *rajas*, arising from the mixture of *tamas* and *sattva*—the latter being of the nature of earth and fire, and fire and moon—becomes the body of that which has become both watery and non-watery.

By this, it should be understood that the intermediate dimension (*madhyama-parimāṇa*) of *rajas*—which arises from the mixture of the earthly and fiery, as well as the lunar and solar, *tamas* and *sattva*, and is produced by the conjunction of elemental waters and non-aqueous elements—is likewise established for that [body] characterized by hunger and thirst, which consists of the atoms of the seminal vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the sun; for it is produced by the conjunction of two triads (*tryaṇuka*). Thus, according to your own doctrine, because you are composed of speech and meaning, you possess the quality of *sattva* and the attribute of tranquility.

The remainder [of the sense] is that the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) become the cause of the operation of indifference toward the previously mentioned injunctions and prohibitions. In the reading *tvatsattvajam*, the meaning is that it is produced solely from your pure *sattva* quality; it consists of the three qualities and is caused by the three signs (*liṅga*) of mixed nature which are to be described hereafter. Here, this should be reflected upon:

by thus defining the triad of elements as the gross effects of the three qualities, the element of water—situated in the central pivot between its own effects (earth) and its causes (fire)—exists in the form of the essence of the equilibrium of the pure and impure, consisting of the juices of the body, the feet, the non-feet, the sacrificial offerings, and the impure.

Just as the air and space possess the state of being gross adjuncts, so too does the quality of *rajas*—which is synonymous with the sense of "mine-ness"—reside within the aggregate of the three sheaths consisting of the intellect (*vijñānamaya*), the mind (*manomaya*), and the vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). This aggregate, which is designated by the term "subtle body" (*liṅga*), stands between the two gross forms of *tamas* and *sattva*, namely the sheath of food (*annamaya*) and the sheath of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and is composed of the eightfold collection of the paths of both words and meanings, consisting of knowledge and ignorance. Furthermore, it takes its support from the pair of royal swans residing in the middle of the lake of the mind.

It should be inferred that [the vowels] possess a nature characterized by extremely subtle adjuncts (*upādhi*). For this very reason, even though the section of vowels (*svarakhaṇḍa*) within the *mātṛkā* syllabary—which makes known the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—indicates the state of inert, deep sleep according to the method explained in the *Mātṛkācakraviveka*, it is nonetheless to be defined as having the properties of being self-luminous and gentle due to its indication of the sixteen lunar digits (*kalā*) consisting of consciousness, and thus possesses the qualities of being its own sound (*svasvara*), being a section (*khaṇḍatva*), and being a phoneme (*akṣaratva*).

Likewise, although the [five] touches (sparśa) indicate the waking state born of the five sense organs and characterized by insentience, they also indicate the fourth waking state of the Sun—the primary vital breath—which consists of consciousness; thus, because they indicate touches that are essentially consciousness, they possess the nature of being "touch-sections" (sparśakhaṇḍa) and so forth.

Likewise, the nature of the "internal-heat-pervasive" (antasthoṣmāparaparyāya-vyāpakavarṇa) phoneme-segment—just as the elemental fire [digests] food, so too does this [phoneme] digest the consumed food and drink; and because it burns the empirical transmigratory existence consisting of mental constructs imagined within by the mind, it possesses the status of being an internal-heat-pervasive phoneme-segment primarily through the fire of inward-turned reflective awareness (vimarśa). All such matters are to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru.

The fact that speech, breath, and mind are composed of fire, water, and food is described with supporting arguments in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad—beginning with the passage, "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire"—and should be consulted therein. By this, it is indicated that the primary breath and fire themselves take the form of the three mandalas, and that the sun and moon are produced from their constituent parts; this serves as a corroboration for the subsequent description of the essential nature of the deities of speech and meaning, who consist of the wheels of light, bliss, and form.

This has also been stated by the Śruti in such passages as: "The moon was born from the mind; the sun was born from the eye," and so forth. Furthermore, the moon possesses the nature of the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*), which is the cause of the entire universe, as declared in mantras such as: "There is none other higher than he from whom [all] is born; he who entered into all beings, Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny—he accompanies the three lights as the sixteenth."

In the same way, according to the *Jyotiṣa-śāstra*, the moon—which is described as having an aqueous sphere (*āpyagola*)—is characterized by its nature as an effect through the description of its being an orb of the earth. Likewise, regarding the sun as well, by reflecting upon Vedic mantra and Brāhmaṇa passages such as, "The waters indeed are the essence; they have been gathered together in the rising sun; these worlds are indeed the essence of the waters; they were gathered together in that Āditya," and "The waters, indeed, are all this," [it is understood that] just as a palace appears repeatedly within each individual mirror by means of internal reflections, [so too does the universe appear within the solar orb].

Thus, the world is seen among the gods as being composed of other deities; therefore, all deities are individually the sources of the universe, as well as the sources of one another, according to what was declared by Yāska and the sages. This concludes that, by virtue of the self-nature of the Self which is the essence of all beings—as thus described—all deities possess the status of being the cause of the entire world. This is the general direction [of the argument]. || 17 ||

Thus, having revealed how she who consists of the three *guṇas* is the cause of the creation of differentiation between speech and its meaning, he now manifests her very nature as supreme sovereignty even in the form of transmigratory existence:
"O Ambikā, you are the reality whose form is imperishable sovereignty, belonging to you, the Lord, my Master!"
His knowledge, his pure action, or the fruit thereof—your perfection consists of detachment from these fruits. 18.

Regarding the phrase beginning with *īśvarasya*: O Ambike! You are the essence of limited speech, meaning, and form (*prādeśika-vāg-artha-śarīrātmikā*), by virtue of being a partial mixture of the aforementioned Sattva, Tamas, and Īśa. Thus, the vocative "O Ambike! is used with the intention of referring to this limited speech, meaning, and form. Furthermore, it is stated in the section on the Aśvamedha within the Anuvāka "Ambe! Ambāli! Ambike! that Śakti possesses a threefold body of speech and meaning; this should be examined in that very place. Therefore, [it refers to] your husband, Īśvara.

The term *bhartā* (the sustainer) is derived from the verbal root *bhṛ* (to sustain); thus, it means "of the Self who is your nourisher. The phrase "you" (*tvam*) means that you are the one whose forms consist of the gross and subtle aspects of the three aforementioned qualities (*guṇas*). [This] is in the body composed of speech, which is of the nature of imperishable sovereignty.

Furthermore, by counting from *a* to *kṣa* and again by counting in reverse order from *kṣa* to *a*, one obtains the sixty rays of the wheel of the multitude known as the Jñāna-mantra-yoga-śākta rays; because these are obtained—excluding the four types of Śāmbhava rays among the Śāmbhava phoneme-rays which will be described as "either sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are considered [in] the doctrine of Śambhu"—they possess the nature of imperishable sovereignty.

Furthermore, he will state this very intention later on, during the description of the *khaṇḍacakra*, with the words beginning, "by the rosary of senses characterized by forbearance (*kṣānti*) and so forth. Regarding the body consisting of meaning (*arthamaya-śarīra*), however, the distinction is to be understood as follows: its nature consists of inexhaustible sovereignty (*akṣayaiśvaryarūpatva*), intended to express the non-difference between the universal sovereignty over the rays and other components of time—such as the sixty-fold divisions of time comprising day and night, the *ghaṭikā*s, *vighaṭikā*s, lunar days (*tithi*), years, and so forth—which are calculated according to the ninefold measures of time of the *Svāyambhuva* [Kalpa]. Thus, the form of sovereignty belongs to both kinds of speech and meaning.

That [the Absolute] is to be treated as being beyond perception (*parokṣa*), whereas you are to be treated as being directly perceived (*aparokṣa*) and as the referent of the linguistic usage of the pronoun *yuṣmad*. Thus, the essence (*tattvam*) is indeed you. The intended meaning is that [you are so] by virtue of being the self of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of the fivefold set of activities such as the creation of speech and its objects. As it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "This is the essence of everything: that the inert world has consciousness as its essence; because its stability depends upon that, the Great Heart is the cycle of existence."

Now, one might object: if even this transmigratory world of words and meanings, consisting of the creation of differentiation, possesses the nature of supreme sovereignty, then its fruit must also be stated—just as, according to the maxim "wealth has the abandonment and enjoyment [of objects] as its fruit," human wealth such as grain, cattle, gems, gold, and silver has its own results. Anticipating this doubt, he shows the fruit as well: "jñānamasya" (knowledge belongs to this). This refers to the sovereignty consisting of the world of words and meanings. Pure and perfectly cleansed knowledge, or action, becomes its fruit.

The purity of knowledge consists in its nature as study and understanding; that of action, however, consists in the absence of desire for the fruits of practice and propagation. He states the fruit of these two as well: "Those [two] consist of detachment... Those two—namely, purified knowledge and action—have as their fruit the state of fullness consisting of detachment (*virāgamaya-pūrṇatā-phale*). "Consisting of detachment" means abundant in detachment. That which is "fullness" is the state of being complete; it is, in other words, the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in which speech and meaning are of one form, due to the absence of the perception of difference between consciousness and the insentient. It should be understood that they must become such that this very [equilibrium] is their fruit. || 18 ||

Thus, having generally revealed that speech and meaning possess the nature of inexhaustible sovereignty, he now indicates—by means of subtle observation—that even therein, it is only those two belonging to the Upaniṣads (the Śākta and Śaiva) which constitute the goal of human life through their state of perfect equilibrium (*sāmarasya*); and he does so by pointing out, individually, their gross forms as deities composed of the qualities of *sattva* and *tamas*:
