"O Mother Light! That which is perceived in the heart by means of knowledge is the essence of meaning, light, swift and pervasive."
That which is the mark of smoke and that which is heavy—
those two, sattva and tamas, are your body.

By the words beginning with *jyotirambā* and so forth: the address *he amba* (O Mother) is as before. In the *arthamaṇḍapa*—which consists of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*) that are the objects of the activity of the five senses, and which comprises the functions of the elements and so on—there is a light that has spread forth subtly. [As it is said: "Like the awn of a wild grain (*nīvāra*), thin, yellow, radiant, and resembling an atom; at the tip of that flame, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established."

That light of the Self (ātma-jyotis), which is to be contemplated as having the form of the crest (śikhā) described in the Śruti—"He is Brahmā, He is Śiva, He is Hara, He is Indra; He is the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling Sovereign"—is the light of the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna-jyotis) consisting of all deities and possessing the previously mentioned dual-pure (dva-rajas) nature. Furthermore, the author will refer to this very light in the fourth Vimarśa with the words, "O Mother, by the crest of light, the haughty darkness residing in the mind within the person is destroyed," and so forth. That light [is to be contemplated] in the heart, that is, in the space of the heart (hṛdayākāśa).

By means of *vidyā*—that is, by means of the function of direct, immediate intuition (*aparokṣa-sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), which consists of the meaning of the verbal root, suffixes, and nominal stems of the various forms of the root *vid* as stated in the rule: "The root *vid* [is used] in the sense of existence (*sattā*), in knowledge (*jñāna*) as 'he knows' (*vetti*), in investigation (*vicāraṇa*) as 'he investigates' (*vindate*), and in attainment (*prāpti*) as 'he finds' (*vindati*)"; and by that which is "beheld" (*īkṣita*), meaning directly realized—as in the passage "He thought (beheld): 'Shall I now create the worlds?'"—which possesses the activity of vision already arisen; and that which consists of knowledge (*jñānamaya*) and that which consists of action (*karmamaya*), the light characterized by smoke.

That which has a mark like the mark of smoke—meaning, as stated in such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as "having become smoke, he becomes a cloud" and "the smoke-bannered, red-eyed one"—consists of Vedic rites whose transcendental nature is revealed by hidden intentions; and it also consists of the fruit of those rites, the agent, and the enjoyer. Therefore, having fallen away, it is heavy. After the realization of its worthlessness, it dissolves of its own accord. Or, for the sake of maintaining the world, it takes the form of the Teacher of the World and is thus supreme.

That which has smoke as its sole mark (dhūma-lakṣma) is so called through an etymological analysis (*vigraha*) of its action; or, in comparison with the previously mentioned form consisting of light (*jyotirmaya-jñāna*), it is the gross form. Regarding the word *guru*, Amara states: "The word *guru* [is used] for Jupiter, for the most excellent, for a teacher, for a father, and for that which is difficult to bear. And in the reading *tac ca tam*, the masculine gender is used because of the prominence of the subject (*uddeśa*). That male form is the pavilion of objects (*arthamaṇḍapa*). Those two previously mentioned—knowledge and action, or *sattva* and *tamas*—are your body (*vapuḥ*); they have issued forth (*prasṛta*) and are perceived in the heart by means of wisdom (*vidyā*). This is the connection with what precedes.

The essential meaning is this: by this, it is understood that the body consisting of Vedic knowledge and action has issued forth simultaneously for the sake of both you and your husband, the Puruṣa who is the essence of the sacrificial hall (*arthamaṇḍapa*). Thus, the very realization [of this] is the fruit of the *vidyā* of full being, consisting of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). This has also been stated in the Śruti: "Someone, having departed from this world, knows the Self, thinking 'I am this. Someone does not recognize his own world; he is indeed bewildered by Agni, exhausted by smoke."

"He does not recognize his own world. But he who knows this Agni Sāvitra—he, having departed from this world, knows the Self as 'This am I,' and he recognizes his own world. By this passage situated in the context of the Brahmavidyā concerning the Agni Sāvitra, it should be understood that—just as between speech and meaning—between knowledge and action as well, there exists a state of being composed of *sattva* and *tamas* respectively, by virtue of their individual status as primary and subordinate factors, through the power of the diversity of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is the overall purport of the collection [of texts]. (19)

In this way, by demonstrating the distinction between the triad of word, meaning, and form—corresponding to the distinct systems of Vedic knowledge and action, and the Vedic Sāṅkhya and Yoga—he also shows the unity of the fruit, which consists of the sixfold lineage of the Guru across the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvagurvaughaṣaṭkatā*). Thus he says:
"O Caṇḍikā, you indeed exist within the side-glance of Rudra, and having beheld [him] as he was being born..."
Just as the two teachers of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga were desired with full agreement and accompanied by proof. || 20 ||

By the words "tvaṃ hi" and so forth: O Caṇḍikā! [The name is derived] from the verbal root *caḍi* meaning "anger"; thus, this vocative is intentional, signifying the Goddess who consists of anger in a form other than her own essential nature. You are the counter-correlative to the cognition of the meaning of our speech; that is the meaning of "tvam". For (hi) because you are the two instructors of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga—either Sāṃkhya and Yoga themselves, or the two instructors of those two paths. The pair of these refers to the two paths of knowledge consisting of the scriptures of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), which are the means for the individual manifestation of the meanings of speech.

Regarding the statement by Śrī Harṣa: "By means of the four stages—study, comprehension, practice, and dissemination—induced through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he himself made the fourteenfold nature [of the sciences] manifest; I do not know why he himself [is not counted] among the fourteen sciences," this refers to the two [stages] among those [four] in the *Naiṣadhīya-vidyās*. It is like a pair of numbers or a pair of properties that appear as contradictory paths. The meaning is that it takes the form of the two teachers who instructed them. However, in the case of the object [the sciences], they consist of the Vedic word and its meaning.

The meaning is that there are two paths of the yoga of knowledge, distinguished by engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), as well as the two teachers who instruct them. "Beholding the one being born" means seeing one undergoing birth. "Residing within the side-glance of Rudra’s son"—Rudra’s son refers to those such as the six-faced Kārttikeya, who is born of Rudra; you cause him to turn toward, that is, you set him in motion toward, the two instructors of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. You are "residing within the side-glance of Rudra’s son" because you yourself proceed for the sake of the engagement and withdrawal of those two instructors.

With the intention of subsuming the two paths [Sāṃkhya and Yoga], the meaning is that you either exist as Prakṛti within the side-glance of Rudra, or you abide in the side-glance of Rudra. Therefore, those two are the teachers of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga. "Possessing the arising of consent and concentration" (*jātasammatisamādhikam*): *sammati* is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), and *samādhi* is practice according to reality. That in which these two have arisen is "possessing the arising of consent and concentration. [This occurs] simply upon perceiving [the Lord] being born.

Upon merely beholding [the world] as it is being born—characterized by activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*), which are synonymous with creation (*sṛṣṭi*) and dissolution (*saṃhāra*)—you become the object of Rudra’s sidelong glance due to the inherent nature of *prakṛti*, which consists of that very activity and cessation synonymous with creation and dissolution. Regarding the two readings, "you indeed become the object of Rudra’s sidelong glance" and "just as desired by the one who has attained consent," you are the one whose form is the aforementioned imperishable supreme sovereignty; you indeed become the object of Rudra’s sidelong glance.

How so? The meaning is as follows: the two teachers of the previously mentioned paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga have reached a consensus through their mutual harmony. Therefore, observing that [the desired goal] is arising exactly according to one's wish (icchānurūpyeṇa), you come to reside within the side-glance of Rudra’s laughter. The point is that, in both ways, the identity of the fruit of Vedic Sāṃkhya and Yoga is indicated either by your residing in the side-glance of Rudra’s laughter along with the resolution thereof, or by your own attainment of composure arising from that [resolution].

Therefore, in the Gītā as well, the Blessed One taught the identity of the fruit through such passages as: "The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṅkhya and Yoga as distinct; even by being properly established in one, one obtains the fruit of both. (Gītā 5.4) Thus, he taught that the fruit is one through right practice and right establishment. || 20 ||

Thus, having demonstrated the identity of fruit between knowledge and action— which correspond respectively to the meanings of the Vedic words *sāṅkhya* and *yoga*— by resolving their apparent contradiction, and having described how those two alone function as the full moon (*pūrṇimā*) and the new moon (*amā*) serving as the causes for the creation and dissolution of the world through the reverse and direct orders of the Vedic path, he also summarizes the subject matter of the treatise: "In Śiva, she who effects the immersion of the world into her own self-luminosity becomes the Full Moon."
Indeed, by making your form appear otherwise than it truly is— though it is already full— you are perceived as Kūhū.

By the words "self-luminous" (*svaprakāśam*) and so forth: O Bhavati! [The meaning of the vocative is: O you who consist of the worldly knowledge and action pertaining to the referent of the word *bhū* (earth), which is a body of *rajas* composed of the previously mentioned union of the portions of *sattva* and *tamas*; O Śivā, whose nature is auspiciousness; or O Kālaśivā, or Jīvaśivā! [The term] *saprakāśam* means accompanied by light (*prakāśa*), that is, together with luminosity, in whatever manner that may be. As for *kṛtamajjanam*, it means immersion performed by the luminous one.

"Having performed the immersion (*majjana*) and the ritual bath (*avabhṛtha*), and having performed the bathing of the limbs (*aṅgasnāna*). Regarding the reading *svaprakāśakṛtamajjanaṃ*: it means "having performed the immersion in the manifestation of one's own nature. The world is like the full moon; it exists within the expansion of knowledge consisting of both word and meaning, which comprises the two paths of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, or the fivefold set of duties (*kṛtyapañcaka*).

In this world, [She] is the Full Moon (*pūrṇimā*), meaning She manifests the nature of the fivefold functions—Speech, Meaning, and so forth—as well as their perfect form, through the sequence of the unfolding of the locations, efforts, and other factors for the production of vowels and consonants (such as "the throat is the place of origin for *a*, *ku*, and *visarjanīya*"), or through the unfolding of the fivefold functions consisting of the knowledge and action regarding those [phonemes], including the processes of adding and removing specific vowels and consonants as required by each respective case. Thus, even in the progression of time, Your form remains entirely full.

Acting otherwise, by milking desires that are rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), you cause [the world] to vanish through its incompleteness; thus, indeed, you are perceived as *Kuhū*. Here, by the word "you are perceived" (*pratīyase*), [it is meant that] within the garland of phonemes of the *Mātṛkā*—which will be described as divided into the various traditions such as the Māheśvara, Nārāyaṇīya, and Svāyambhuva—in the fourth *vimarśa* (contemplation) to be described, there occurs the unfolding of the universe through secret speech. This occurs within the nature of "I" created by both *vidyā* and *avidyā*, and the nature of "I" free from desire (*akāma*), through the division of the *hādi* and *kādi* *vidyās* and the various types of partial and total contractions (*pratyāhāra*) in direct and reverse order, such as *ajha* and *jalā*.

And by means of the concealment of the letters *ha* and *ka* within the two modes of *anuloma-pratyāhāra* (direct and reverse withdrawal), there occurs the manifestation of the power (*kalā*) named *Amā*; and by returning to that very sequence through reverse withdrawal (*viloma-pratyāhāra*), starting from the *sakāra* and *hakāra* and ending with the full nasal (*anusvāra*)—which represents the *visarga* of Śakti and Śambhu—one proceeds through the sequences consisting of *so'ham* or *haṃsaḥ-aham*. By concealing the letter *ha* alone, one realizes the form of the power named *Soma*; and by concealing both the letters *ha* and *sa* (or *ha* and *sa*), one realizes the form of the power named *Oṃ*.

The secret is this: when the full form itself is made otherwise by concealing its own fifteen-part limbs, who is the creator? It is Prajāpati who is invoked through the process of dissolution into the solar form of the conscious vital breath (*prāṇa*); or rather, she is summoned for the sake of creation into the lunar orb of the downward breath (*apāna*). By this etymology, the Great Power of Time (*Mahākāla-śakti*)—whose characteristics will be described and who extends from the processes of creation and dissolution up to Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī—is understood by the word *kuhū*. This is the secret.

Therefore, in the Vedic ritual worship (*vaitānika-vaidiki-upāsanā*)—from the dimensions of the sacrificial altars (*dārśika-vedi*) up to those of the Soma-altars (*saumika-vedi*)—and in the architectural layouts (*vāstu-kalpa*) consisting of the triad of direction, place, and time, as well as the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), there is also the ritual of the *kalā-mātṛkā-vedi* consisting of the triad of tone, sound, and phoneme, and the six paths. Regarding this, it is said: "The transverse [side] behind consists of thirty steps; the eastward [side] consists of thirty-six; the transverse [side] in front consists of twenty-four. Ten and ten make twenty; the *virāj* consists of ten syllables; food is the *virāj*; through the *virāj*, one obtains the enjoyment of food."

By means of such [passages] as these, just as the attainment of the *virāj* through each individual word (*pratipad*) is described in the third *anuvāka* of the second *prapāṭhaka* of the sixth *kāṇḍa* of the *Taittirīya-saṃhitā*, so too, for the sake of attaining the fruit of encompassing all food (*annāvaraṇa*), there is the horizontal current (*tiryaksrotas*) consisting of thirty western syllables and words, extending from the vowel 'u' (the unsurpassed form) and the visarga up to the semi-vowels; and the eastern and upward current (*prācīnordhvasrotas*) consisting of thirty-six syllables, extending up to the aspirated and nasalized (*soṣmakūṭa*) phonemes.

Furthermore, within the twenty-six phonemes beginning with the *anuttara-visarga* and ending with the *sparśa*, by means of the contraction (*pratyāhāra*) of the initial and final phonemes—namely *aham* and *ā*—which contains the essence of the twenty-four principles (*tattva*), and according to the sequence of the ancient horizontal stream (*tiryaksrotas*), there is taught an indivisible Great Saying (*mahāvākya*) in the form of "vaḥ, vaha, akṣaṃ, mā, ahamā, vahākṣamahamā. This is accomplished through symbolic Vedic and Sāṅkhya contractions of phonemes, which serves to awaken the realization of the identity with the nature of Sadāśiva within the blink of an eye.

Thus, through the scholarly skill of unveiling the wealth of one's own self—which is the unfolding of the universe as spoken in the *Gupta* [scriptures]—whether by Vaidikas, Tāntrikas, great worshippers (*mahopāsaka*), or preeminent investigators, the unveiling of the sovereign wealth of one's own self, such as the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and the meaning of the Nidāgha [teachings], should be inferred. And the poet will also state in the fourth investigation: "The interior of the moon, which is a digit within the ocean of true nectar, whose seat is the sixteen-fold digit of the womb..."

"In the case of Śivā, you have taken refuge in the lotus of the heart and head, which is born from the smiling [deity] and consists of the collection of sixteen vowels containing the emission (*visarga*) in the form of the Absolute (*anuttara*), and which comprises the thirty-six letters of the Mother-phonemes (*mātṛkā*). By such words, [the Goddess is described as] resting solely in her own essential nature within the two lotuses of the heart and head; having entered the yogic sleep of internal closing (*antarnimeṣa*); consisting of the fifth *preta*-bedstead of Sadāśiva; and being the perfection of the self whose form is the Absolute. This is indeed [the description] filled with hidden intentions regarding the path of smoke (*dhūmamārga*), which is dominated by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The particle *kila* signifies that which is beyond perception (*pārokṣya*). It is a particle whose meaning is unreal (*alīka*) with respect to the path of light (*arci-mārga*), where knowledge (*vidyā*) is predominant. In reality, however, because both—the internal and external—consist of the powers of time (*kāla-śakti*) and the person (*puruṣa-śakti*), appearing as such through the mere distinction of names despite being essentially the same, the particle *kila* indicates the unreality of time. This is because both the forward and reverse sequences, as well as the sequential and non-sequential orders of time-power, are characterized by the fivefold functions of knowledge and ignorance (*vidyā-avidyā-kṛtya-pañcaka*) regarding the objects of speech that are either proximate or remote, and they manifest as the form of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī. Thus, the particle *kila* serves to awaken one to the illusory nature of time.

This indeed is the nature of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī as "the Attractor of Time": that she displays differentiation within her own essential nature, as well as displays herself as the cause of the fivefold activities performed in both direct and reverse order.

All of this is found in the *Taittirīya-śākhā*, in the third book (*kāṇḍa*), fifth chapter (*praśna*), first section (*anuvāka*), in the introduction to the commencement of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice: "He who should know these two [sacrifices] in their direct order (*anuloma*) and their reverse order (*pratiloma*)—the period following the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is their direct order, and that which precedes the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is their reverse order. If one were to perform the full moon sacrifice first, he would perform them in reverse order; both [sacrifices] would then fail as they are being performed in reverse order. One should offer the two *sārasvata* oblations beforehand; for the new moon is indeed..."

This has been demonstrated by such passages as: "He seizes these two in accordance with Sarasvatī; as that [breath] swells, he too swells along with it. In brief, the essential nature of things is this: the pentad of functions consisting of knowledge, action, and will exists as if mutually opposed, yet it is bound to both the Vedic and Sāṅkhya-Yoga paths, comprising a pentad of functions characterized by both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) order. || 21 ||

This very sixfold path (*adhva-ṣaṭka*), which consists of time, the person (*puruṣa*), the triad (*tripuṭī*), and the two powers (*śakti-dvaya*), is multiplied by the three previously mentioned qualities (*guṇa*). Starting from the *kāṣṭhā* and *kalā* as described in the verse, "Eighteen *nimeṣas* are a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those are a *kalā*," and so on up to the *brāhma*, *divya*, *pitrya*, *prājāpatya*, and *gaura* [measures of time].

In the Śrīcakra, which is the Great Measure (Mahāmāna) of the Time-Person (Kālapuruṣa) consisting of the ninefold measures of time mentioned as "the solar, the civil, the lunar, and the sidereal—these indeed are the nine," there is also the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with the fourfold ultimate measures of time—namely the *pitṛmāna* and so forth, designated as *divya*, *prājāpatya*, and *brāhma*—which constitute the four corners of the Śaiva system. Furthermore, for the sake of application in ritual action (*karma*) and meditative worship (*upāsana*), there exists that which consists of the sequences of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as expressed in the passage beginning with "of the two bodies, of creation and dissolution."

Demonstrating the distinction in the sequence of meanings such as emission and withdrawal that will be explained hereafter, he concludes with a statement in the form of a *sūtra* for the sake of the primary reflective awareness (*saṃvimaśa*) of the beginning:
"That which is the interval between fullness and contraction, therein [the Goddess] Kālī resides in the sequence of differentiation."
Today’s time, which displays the agitation of the sequential divisions [of the day], remains to be consumed. || 22 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*, composed by the great poet Śrī Kālidāsa.

By the phrase "of fullness and thinness," etc.—the meaning is as follows: the interval between fullness and thinness refers to the intermediate state between the condition of fullness and the condition of thinness, and between the nature of fullness and the nature of thinness. It is like the junction of stages in a person's life, consisting of the manifestation of youth and old age, occurring between the states of knowledge and ignorance. Furthermore, it refers to the temporal junction within the sequence of time, specifically the transitional moment between the eighth day of the bright and dark fortnights at dusk.

In the phrase *vijahatkrame*: that in which the sequence of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and creation, as well as the sequence of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and withdrawal, are abandoned—either at the time of the emergence or destruction of the states of knowledge (*vidyā*), youth, or old age; or at the time of the emergence or destruction of the states of ignorance (*avidyā*), childhood, or decrepitude. Likewise, even within the sequence of time—that in which the sequence of the light of creation consisting of moonlight and the sequence of withdrawal consisting of darkness are abandoned—at the juncture of the appearance of the lunar days (*tithi*) named *rākā* (full moon) and *kuhū* (new moon).

You, who abide respectively as the object and the locus—according to your authority and suitability—in the junction of the eighth day of the bright fortnight, which is equal to either the manifestation of the youth of knowledge (*vidyā*) or the destruction of the youth of ignorance (*avidyā*), and in the junction of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, which is equal to the manifestation of the youth of ignorance or the destruction of the youth of knowledge, as well as in the lunar days named Pūrṇimā (Full Moon), Amāvāsyā (New Moon), and Kuhū, which are the fullness of both of those states. You.

"Displaying the agitation of the sequential division"—that is, that in which there is the agitation (*sambhrama*) regarding the sequential division (*kramavibhāga*) which has been shown (*darśita*), i.e., manifested (*prakāśita*), namely the sequential division of the emanation and withdrawal of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). This occurs at the time of the junction between the emanation and withdrawal of knowledge, as well as at the time of the withdrawal and emanation of ignorance. Such is the "present" (*adyatana*), according to the etymology: that by which the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of knowledge, ignorance, and so forth, is consumed (*adyate*) and expanded (*tanyate*).

The meaning is that conventional time consists of the incomplete creation and dissolution of knowledge and ignorance. You desire—that is, you wish—to devour or consume this. Regarding the term *kāla* (time), there is a confusion regarding the sequential divisions shown—meaning it has been revealed or manifested by the Kaṭha Śruti, such as: "The seer (*darśa*), the seen (*dṛṣṭā*), the visible (*darśatā*), the universal-formed (*viśvarūpā*), the beautiful to behold (*sudarśanā*)," or it refers to that which has produced vision. The sequential division consists of the ancestral and celestial [paths], and the junctures of night, day, and dawn.

He desires to eat—that is, to consume—the present time consisting of the bright and dark fortnights, which is characterized by the junctions of those respective fortnights; this time is manifested from the eighth day of the bright fortnight until the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and again from that start until the eighth day of the bright fortnight. It is a time of intense agitation (*sambhrama*) consisting of the sequential divisions of the junctions between the nights and days of the ancestors (*pitrya*) or the junctions between the days and nights of the gods (*divya*). He seeks to devour this time, which is established through the divine, Prajāpati’s, and Brahma’s mental faculties, and which is fit to be consumed as the ultimate reality.

In the reading *īhate*, the subject should be understood as the very interval between fullness and depletion. This is because the White Eighth (*śuklāṣṭamī*)—which is the form of Sṛṣṭikālī, described as "adorned with a forehead-region shining with the moon of the eighth day"—is of the nature of the intermediate period presided over by the moon that is a limb of the face of Śuddhavidyā Tripurasundarī. Likewise, on the Black Eighth (*kṛṣṇāṣṭamī*), since it marks the time of sunrise which initiates the worldly activity of the ancestors, just as the rise of the sun destroys the darkness of night, so too at the commencement of the Black Eighth [the darkness of ignorance is destroyed].

The sense is this: because the destruction of the paternal darkness belonging to the bright fortnight has been accomplished, and because the paternal ritual activities such as the *śrāddha*—which consist of the majesty (*vibhūti*) of the time of withdrawal (*saṃhārakāla*)—have proceeded without obstacle, agency belongs to the eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, which are the junctions of the day and night of the ancestors (*pitṛrātryahassandhi*), existing as a form intermediate between fullness and thinness. This is stated in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*, in the context of calculating the measures of time for humans, ancestors, and so forth: "The sun divides the human worldly [time] by means of days and nights."

Night is for the sleep of beings, and day is for the activity of their actions. A month constitutes the night and day of the ancestors (pitṛs); their division is as follows: the dark fortnight is their day, and the bright fortnight is their night for sleep. Thirty-two human months are said to be one month of the ancestors. Three hundred and sixty human months constitute a year of the ancestors as it is reckoned by human measure. Furthermore, that which is a hundred years by human calculation—

The calculation of time according to the Brahma-measure has been briefly shown there [in that same text] by such passages as: "Those years of the ancestors are indeed reckoned as three; ten months and more are proclaimed here as the measure of the ancestors. Therefore, all that is stated in the section on ritual action and worship—such as the counting of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī among the five parvans and the prescription of the Śrāddha on the new moon—is consistent with this very principle and is supported by valid reasoning.

In this very manner, by relying on the numerical measurement of time multiplied by the number of full and partial days, this same verse applies to the divine measure described in the *Aśvamedhika* Śruti as "The year is indeed one day of the gods," to the Prājāpatya measure—which is synonymous with the actual solar measure stated as "the Mahāyuga is the actual solar year"—and to the Brāhma-Kalpa measure stated as "four thousand Yugas are called a day of Brahmā."

By means of understanding the gradations of the revolution of the celestial sphere and time—extending up to the measurement of Para-Vāsudeva, which consists of the couple of Śiva and Śakti whose forms are the series of worlds arising and perishing through successive opening and closing [of the eyes]—one should integrate all things into the reality of the Supreme Self. However, for fear of excessive prolixity, I shall desist here. May there be auspiciousness!

In this first *vimarśa*, which consists primarily of aphorisms (*sūtra*), the commentary (*bhāṣya*) titled *Cidagnicandrikā* has been composed by Dhanadānandanātha; it is a divine female partridge (*divyacakorikā*) that grants the fulfillment of all aims. One should investigate therein the nature of the pair consisting of the Great Mother (*mātṛ*) and the Knower (*pramātṛ*). Those who have attained the state of the Puruṣa through the act of filling [the void], having approached and honored the venerable embodied form, [should proceed].

If they are truly desirous of beholding Me, let them unveil the vision of the divine state shining intensely within. (3) Even those who have attained the supreme purification from the impurity of *āṇava* and other stains, or who possess the sovereign power of mantric vitality (*māntravīrya*), or even the state of being a slave to the Kali age—if they behold this divine female Cakorī shining intensely within, they shall be truly desirous of beholding Me. (4) Let everyone enjoy this wealth belonging to My own Self—ninefold, not lacking anything else, and consisting solely of the treasure of one's own nature. (5)

The movement of the Westerners is considered to be from left to right, like that of our own [ancient] letters; whereas for us, the ancients, the movement was from right to left. Those who dwell in the eastern and western directions stand upon the paths of the right (*savya*) and the left (*apasavya*). *Sava* is said to mean sacrifice (*yāga*), for that is the livelihood of the ancients. That which is *apasavya* is indeed non-sacrificial; it is the livelihood of the Westerners. The Vedic path is the right-hand path, while the Yavana path is the left-hand path. The *Kaula* is the state of their essential identity (*sāmarasya*), for the *Kula-dharma* is indeed the right-hand path.

Therefore, for those established in their own duty (*svadharma*), both worldly enjoyment and liberation reside in the palm of their hand. (9) This is well-guarded as a secret situated upon the crests of the *Śrutis*; this very state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) among all philosophical systems is the thought of the Poet. (10) Indeed, under the guise of the *Kālikā-stotra*, the heart of the Poet is here being revealed by me; I touch the heated axe [of truth]. (11) Thus, at the beginning, even the promise is like a *sūtra*; in this matter, that *sūtra* is the authority for one who moves freely like a river’s current. (22)

Thus ends the first inquiry, which serves as a summary of the aphorisms, in the *Divyacakorikā* commentary on the *Cidgaganacandrikā*, composed by Agnihotra Śarman of the Śālikarā lineage, the delight of Dhanada and Ānandanātha. May there be an offering at the pair of lotus feet of the Supreme Śiva-Śakti, the bliss of the venerable Mother Kāmākṣī. Śrī Śrī Śrī.
Oṃ.
Salutations to the Supreme Deity.
The Moonlight of the Consciousness-Sky.
Adorned with the divine cakorī bird;
this is the second reflection.

Thus, by means of this textual composition consisting primarily of Sūtras and the first section of the Vimarsinī, having established the identity of the nature of speech and meaning—which consists of the aggregate of sound (nāda) and the non-sound (anāhata)—through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the two paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and by way of their non-difference from the power of Time (*kāla-śakti*), [the author] proceeds to discuss therein, starting with the verse "That which is the speech uttered as 'I' am" (*yāhamityuditavāk*), the triad of the Path of Speech (*śabdādhvan*)—comprising phonemes, words, and mantras—and the triad of the Path of Meaning (*arthādhvan*)—comprising limited powers (*kalā*), categories (*tattva*), and worlds (*bhuvana*)—both of which are employed in the sequence of the fivefold cosmic acts, such as the creation of the aforementioned struck (*āhata*) and unstruck (*anāhata*) speech and meaning.

In that which is the fundamental ground, the manifestation of the reality of the *nāda-brahman*—which is both supreme and non-supreme, gross and subtle, and consists of the sixfold reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) to be described as the *bindu* and the emission (*visarga*)—and which is the body of universal knowledge consisting of the equilibrium of the supreme and non-supreme *vidyā*, composed of the sixteen divisions of time and the sixteen vowels; therein [resides] the digit (*kalā*) known as the manifestation of the Śākta-unsurpassed emission (*anuttara-visarga*), and the digit in the form of the Śāmbhava-unsurpassed emission, which, by virtue of being the nature of the *kāmakalā* consisting of the three *bindus* non-different from the three mandalas, comprises the eight-fold totality of the remaining fourteen forms.

Having in mind the manifestation of the fourteen sounds of the *mānava* [alphabet]—which have evolved as the unfolding of the meaning of speech in the form of the fourteen worlds of knowledge (*vidyā-bhuvana*) and so forth, beginning with the fourteen threads (*sūtra*) of Māheśvara—and intending therein to first refute, by way of incidental discussion, the non-Vedic systems such as the exceedingly gross Cārvāka, Kṣapaṇaka, and Mādhyamika views among the six types of Buddhist doctrines within the expanse of the "lower knowledge" (*aparā-vidyā*) mentioned in the passage: "Two knowledges are to be known: the higher (*parā*) and the lower (*aparā*").

Even in the systems of Vaidika, Rāmānuja, Pūrṇaprajña, and others, which demonstrate the distinctions of the paths of meaning (*arthādhvan*), [the author] first declares the eternal liberation of the wise person— even one who, through the conceptualizing intellect consisting of the triad of subject, object, and means of knowledge, perceives the manifestation of objects or the self as being merely constructed by speech, yet directly realizes the expansion of his own objects through the stainless reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Goddess of Speech, whose nature consists of the resonance (*nāda*) of his own essential form— by means of the two verses beginning with "mātṛmeya... "The conceptualizing intellect produced by You, which arises in the form of the means consisting of 'subject' and 'object'..."
O Goddess, for what wise person would there not be liberation by means of that [knowledge] regarding Your stainless true nature? 23.

Regarding the phrase *mātṛmeyeti*: O Goddess! According to the list of verbal roots (*dhātupāṭha*), the root *div* signifies "play, desire for victory, gambling, worldly transaction, praise, joy, intoxication, sleep, and movement. Thus, this vocative is intended to mean that You are the one whose nature consists of speech and meaning, which are the causes of play and the other aforementioned activities. The term *mātṛmeyasādhanātmikā* means that You are the essence of the instruments of the knower (*mātṛ*) and the known (*meya*). The instrument of the knower is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The gross instruments of the known are the sense organs of action and knowledge, along with their physical seats (*golakāni*). She is so described because Her nature is the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpadhī*) whose form is the act of cognition (*miti*). Alternatively, She is the one whose very form is the Self (*ātman*) of all those [instruments].

That conceptualizing intellect—whether it be an intellect that conceives of distinctions, an intellect free from such conceptions, or, as it is said, "the body emaciated by diseases is called 'kalpa' (conceptualization)," meaning the cognition of the distinction between the body and the self—is created by You within You Yourself, who are the embodiment of word and meaning; it unfolds and shines forth externally. By means of that conceptualizing intellect, Your own nature—the nature of the pair consisting of sound and resonance, which is the great ocean of word and meaning—is perceived as being this very natural form of Yours. This is the sense.

"Stainless" (*akalaṅkita*) refers to the Knower (*viduḥ*), that is, the one who knows. The sense is: of which perfected being (*siddha*) or practitioner (*sādhaka*)? It is not [mere] liberation. For the dualistic cognition—which consists of the means of proof (*sādhana*) such as the triad of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and so forth—arises as something constructed solely by the powers of speech, objects, parts, and time. Precisely because it is constructed, it does not touch the underlying ground (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Therefore, the meaning is that the wise person, or the reflective investigator—indeed anyone at all—does not defile the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), which is by nature unattached consciousness, consisting of great supreme bliss and being without support; thus, everyone is eternally liberated. By this, it should be understood that the distinction between the empirical and the ultimate regarding the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge is intended, as well as the fact that the triad of the knower and so forth contains within it a portion of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). || 1-23 ||

Having thus asserted that even the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpa-buddhi*) of the ordinary triad possesses a nature free from the stains of the ordinary, [the author] now characterizes the mode of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that very intellect which examines its own nature— [an intellect] which, by abiding as the central pivot between those two, constitutes the primary seat (*pīṭha*) for the principles of both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*):
"That which consists of both sequence and non-sequence, characterized by the reflective awareness of both non-sequential and sequential [orders], [is] sequence-and-non-sequence itself."
Beholding you, Śiva, who are beyond succession yet abide in the center, this noble lineage is your very abode.

By the words beginning with *akrama* and so forth: that which consists of both *krama* and *akrama*. *Krama* is characterized as will be described hereafter; it is established in the *Kādimata* as the sequence of the phonemes of the *mātṛkā*. *Akrama* is established in the *Hādividyāmata* as the sequence of the *mātṛkā* consisting of vowels and *nāda*. That which consists of both is an epithet of the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpa-buddhi*) regarding the verbal *mātṛkā*. However, in the case of the conceptualizing intellect regarding the objective *mātṛkā*, [it is said]: "Knowledge of the *krama* depends upon the Guru and brings about the supreme perfection of the Command (*ājñā*). O Great Goddess, through knowledge of the *krama*, the three worlds are swallowed up."

"The letter *ka* is of the nature of wrath (*krodha*), while the letter *ma* bestows auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). One should produce auspiciousness within wrath; such is the sequence, which is the sequence of time. This means that the conceptualizing intellect consists of both sequence and non-sequence, as characterized in other Tantras and to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru. The characteristic of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of both non-sequence and sequence is as follows: the reflective awareness of non-sequence is the creative emission (*sṛṣṭi*) of the *mātṛkā* consisting of vowels and *nāda*, whose characteristics will be described hereafter. The reflective awareness of sequence is the withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of *nāda* through the *mātṛkā* of phonemes (*varṇa*). The [characteristic] of both is the combination of these two.

In the same way, it possesses the characteristic of both sequence and non-sequence (*kramākrama*), consisting of the previously mentioned *varṇa*, *svara*, *nāda*, and *mātṛkā*, as well as the sequence and non-sequence of word and meaning. For this very reason, it is "non-sequential" (*akrama*); it is called non-sequential because it does not proceed—that is, it does not reach [any object]—due to its unimpeded movement. For this very reason, it is "situated in the middle" (*madhyaga*), being situated in the midst of Śiva, the individual soul (*jīva*), and transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). It is Śiva, the Śiva who is the practitioner (*sādhaka*). And you, who are indeed of three kinds, and You yourself. "Sat-kula" means the lineage (*kula*) of the true ones—of those whose nature is the truth of worldly transaction—who are the rays of the lunar asterisms, namely the triad of subject, means of knowledge, and object.

Alternatively, [it refers to] either the threefold nature of the world-creation and other causes as described in the *Nāciketa-agnicayana* section of the *Brahmavidyā*, namely: "The triad is indeed preeminence (*jyaiṣṭhya*): mother, father, and son; the triad is procreation: the lap, the womb, and the middle [the child]"; or the three classes of beings designated as Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya, whose bodies are composed of the three qualities (*bhāva*); or the threefold nature consisting of substance, quality, and action; or the three forms of genus, action, and substance.

The *satkula* (the true lineage) is the collection (*kula*) of the condensed portions of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*), or of the threefold emanations beginning with Śākta; the meaning is that it consists of a homogeneous group. As it is stated in the Tantra: "The *kula* is remembered as being of the same class. This [lineage] is of the nature of the manifestation of the aspect of "this" (*idamaṃśa*). It belongs to You—whose nature consists of both Consciousness and Unconsciousness, being non-different from knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—and it is Your mouth, consisting of the five senses and the seven vital breaths in the head, insofar as it is the manifestation of the five channels and seven streams to be described hereafter.

Alternatively, your face is the manifestation of the lineage of Gurus—also known as the Mānava, Prajāpati, and Apara lineages—or it is the triad consisting of the Divine (divya), the Siddha, and the others. Or, if the reading is "your seat" (tavāsanam), the meaning is that it is the form of your sacred seat (pīṭha). Having perceived this, the conceptualizing intellect formed by you does not defile your true nature. This applies either to one who knows that [nature] or to the discerning observer. The connection with the previous verse is: "For whom is there not liberation? (2-24).

Although I am indeed eternally liberated in the manner described, nevertheless, because the *āṇava-mala*—induced by the *māyīya-mala*—acts as an obstacle to the experience of the bliss mentioned, its mere removal depends upon you; thus, he says, "I entreat you":
"By Māyā, which is capable of creating the distinction between the object and the subject, [the soul] moves through the successive stages of the limbs..."

"O Mother, destroy that state of minuteness which resides within me and which remains outside, longing for a protector"—this is the meaning of the verse beginning with *vedya-vedaka*. The term "O Mother" (*amba*) is a vocative, as explained previously. By the phrase "skilled in the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower" (*vedya-vedaka-vibheda-dakṣayā*): the "distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower" (*vedya-vedaka-vibheda*) refers to the separation between consciousness (*cit*) and its content (*caitya*), or between the content (*caitya*) and consciousness (*cit*). This distinction—whether the object is formless or possesses form—is of a nature distinct from the conceptualization of different forms, such as the appearance of a city of Gandharvas or the perception of one's own head being cut off. It is "skilled" (*dakṣayā*) in that it is capable of sustaining such a distinction.

"By *māyā*": *māyā* is that by which one's own nature is measured—that is, delimited—by itself; thus, it is the manifestation of duality established through etymology, consisting of the form of word and meaning. "Attaining the sequential limbs" means attaining those limbs—the body of word and meaning—which possess the sequence of either the previously mentioned emission (*sṛṣṭi*) or withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). For this very reason, she is "desiring the external sense-organ" (*bahirakṣakāṃkṣiṇī*): the external sense-organ is the organ of speech directed outward, as well as the external sense-organ consisting of the union of the perfected meanings of the letters of the *Mātṛkā* and their respective contractions (*pratyāhāra*). She desires these, and is therefore called "desiring the external sense-organ."

That which is "minuteness" (*aṇutā*)—consisting of the two kinds of innate impurity (*āṇavamala*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter, serving as the cause of limited knowledge (*kiṃcidjñatā*), and constituting the state of being a *jīva*—resides in me, that is, in the Self (*ātman*) whose nature is the cognition of "I. Abandon that! The intended meaning is: "By severing my head, which consists of the innate impurity, make me, who am Sadāśiva, the fifth corpse upon the couch. Furthermore, he will later state the immovable nature of the fifth corpse on the couch, who is Sadāśiva, with the words: "The corpse abandoned of coming and going in Śiva," and so forth.

The nature of the two-fold *āṇavamala* is stated in the *Tantrasāra*, at the point of establishing the supremacy of the Trika scripture: "The loss of freedom for consciousness, and the lack of consciousness regarding freedom—this is declared to be the two-fold *āṇava* impurity, due to the forfeiture of one's own true nature. (2-3-25)

Thus, after the removal of the root impurity of *āṇava* consisting of the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*), the fulfillment of purpose—consisting of the dissolution of the three kinds of agency such as that which has already begun (*ārabdha*)—is accomplished by your very activities alone. Therefore, the state of abiding without means is spontaneously established; thus he contemplates the innate state (*sahajāvasthā*) with the words beginning "karma" and so forth.
For indeed, that karma which consists of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is accompanied by the power of the individual soul through *māyā*,
is dissolved by you through your functional activities (*vṛtti*).
O Goddess, [he destroys] darkness as the sun does with its rays, or as [it melts] frost. || 26 ||

O Goddess! By Māyā—which functions in conjunction with the aforementioned state of being the individual soul (jīva) and which consists of the manifestation of the differentiation of objects—action (*karman*), that is to say, action consisting of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as auspicious and inauspicious ones, is produced; this is the remainder of the sense. That action is indeed dissolved, just as darkness is by the rays of the sun; it is certainly destroyed by Your powers (*vṛtti*).

In this context, since Māyā—which consists of the manifestation of the differentiation of objects—is rendered ineffective without the specific qualification of being accompanied by the state of atomicity (āṇubhāva), and since it is precisely the atomicity consisting of the power of obscuration (āvaraṇa-śakti) that, in relation to that [Māyā], serves as the cause of transmigratory existence, the dissolution of the Kārmaṇa-mala is established by nature through the continuous flow of Your activity, which removes both of those Āṇava-malas—just as the rays of the sun dispel deep darkness. This is the meaning of the particle *hi*, which indicates what is well-known.

Alternatively, the word *hi* may signify a reason (*hetuvācaka*). For (*hi*), because—just as one observes the maintenance of the conduct of all women with whom one has had relations through one's own mental states (*vṛtti*) by means of dispelling the turbidity of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) inherent in those respective actions—so too, by the rays of the sun, the impurity consisting of latent impressions and karma (*kārmaṇa-mala*) is itself destroyed in accordance with the functioning of each respective time, as if it were darkness; thus, it becomes as if dissolved by your own mental states. Therefore, the connection with the preceding verse is: "Abandon the state of being an atom (atomicity) while abiding in me."

And thus it has been stated in the *Mālinīvijaya* as well: "Therefore, time is not capable of creating a distinction within consciousness; nor is this time able to become a differentiator of the object of knowledge (*vedya*)," and so forth. Having thereby refuted time’s capacity to differentiate between the object and the subject, [it continues]: "Therefore, once the existence of the Sun [of Consciousness] is established, what fool indeed would say: 'How is it that He is filled with His own rays throughout the entire universe? Thus, since this Light is established, whatever conceptualizations of light there may be..."

Therefore, all those women who have enjoyed [him] protect their conduct; and since manifestation is unestablished, what am I, what are you, and what is even darkness? What could possibly exist, or how could there even be silence? Therefore, for entities that have attained the state of Bhairava through identity with manifestation, even time is unable to do anything at all.

By these and other such statements, it is explicitly proclaimed that even for those who have attained the state of Bhairava through identity with the light of their own self-functioning (*ātmavṛtti-prakāśa*), and who thus possess innate diversity, the Lord Kālaśiva—though entirely independent—is rendered powerless by that very differentiation. What need is there to mention the wretched Māyā, which possesses the nature of a limited soul (*aṇu*) as its collaborator? The sense is that the majesty of your functions, like the rays of the sun, resides in a realm inaccessible to mind, speech, and the rest, acting to destroy darkness. In the reading *himam* (snow), the syntactical connection is: "Just as snow is dissolved by the rays of the sun, so is karma dissolved by [your] functions. (4-26)

He says that when the three lotuses— named after the three actions beginning with *ārambha* (commencement)— are dissolved, there is also the attainment of the direct realization of Your essential nature:
"O Mother, by means of this secret and reverse practice (*viparīta-caryā*), which makes the mind consisting of consciousness identical with the object of the senses, [the realization is attained]."
Your all-consuming form is attained, in which all dualistic functions have been made equalized. || 27 ||

By the words beginning with *cinmayī* [the author says]: O Mother! Therefore, from this dissolution of *kārma-mala* or the removal of *āṇava-mala*, [She is] through the secret one—whose body is merely the vibration within the cave of the heart. For this very reason, because of the root *guhū* meaning "to conceal," She is either that which conceals the true nature of things or that which has become a secret. Nevertheless, She is visible to the senses; Her visible body consists of the phonetic form from *A* to *Kṣa*, and the form of the *Artha-kṣa* (the letter *Kṣa* as the essence of meaning) which has the appearance of a burnt cloth.

That is to say, it is devoid of the clinging to "I-ness" (ahantābhiniveśa), consisting merely in the functioning of the body, senses, and so forth at that moment. For this very reason, it is through "contrary conduct" (viparītacaryā)—which is distinct from worldly norms and takes the form of unconventional actions—that all dualistic functions have been rendered equal in flavor (samarasīkṛta). In that state, all dualistic functions—the entire range of opposing experiences such as pleasure and pain, gain and loss, and so on—have been brought to a state of aesthetic unity (sāmarasya). [This is] yours, who are of the nature of both word and meaning.

"Ghasmara" means that which devours all by virtue of having the nature of pure luminosity (*prakāśa*). "Vapuḥ" (body) is so called because of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "that in which the seed-syllables of speech and meaning—such as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and so forth—are deposited. Thus, it refers to a body consisting of the triad of *nāda*, speech, and meaning, comprising the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and the rest, which is burning and composed of space (*vyomamaya*). It has been "rendered conscious" (*cinmayīkṛtam*). That which was previously non-conscious (*acinmaya*) is now made to become conscious; thus, being "rendered conscious," the suffix *cci* is used in the sense of a transformation into something that was not previously so.

This is obtained from the indicative mark (liṅga) mentioned in the preceding verse: "Kill that subtle state residing within me. The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "by me as the practitioner (sādhaka), or by the practitioner who is non-different from me. Therefore, because the practitioner and the "I"—which consist of the nature of association and superimposition respectively—are of a single form in their literal and figurative meanings, the attainment of the realization of their identity is indeed implied by the sense of the passage. This is the intended meaning.

Here, by the two qualifying adjectives ending in the *cvipratyaya* suffix—namely, "made of consciousness" (*cinmayīkṛtam*) and "having made all dualistic functions into a state of equal flavor" (*samarasīkṛtākhiladvaitavṛtti*)—it should be understood that even the aggregate of the ordinary body, senses, and so forth becomes composed of consciousness over time through the power of the practice of *sāmarasya*. Thus, following the sequence of the great subject matter (*mahārthaprameya*), this reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is intent upon the "I" as the cognizer; therefore, it should be known that the object of reflective awareness (*vimarśaprameya*) has also been indicated. (5-27)
Therefore, he says that non-attachment is indeed attained:
"O Śivā! Those powers characterized as the instruments which move within your sky-like consciousness-self,"
For you abide on that upward path, having abandoned all effort toward the expansion of external states. || 28 ||

"Those which move," and so forth. In Śiva, whose nature is that of the practitioner (sādhaka) and Śiva himself; or "O you who are the embodiment of all auspicious desires" may be taken as an address. In your conscious self—the void consisting of consciousness, the internal space (daharākāśa)—those powers which move and circulate are characterized as instruments (*karaṇa*). An instrument is defined as an uncommon cause possessing activity; thus, they are characterized as the external and internal organs. The meaning is that they take the form of the external and internal organs, such as breath, speech, hearing, and so on. Those powers which move and circulate...

The root *carabhakṣaṇa* means that they enjoy the mere experiences of food, drink, and so forth; thus, the meaning is "you," who are the form of the Mistress of Space (*Vyomeśvarī*), the collective totality of all powers (*sarvaśaktisamaṣṭi*). "On the path leading upward from that" means on the path of the sixfold way (*ṣaḍadhvan*) consisting of sound (*nāda*), speech (*vāk*), and meaning (*artha*), which lies above those powers characterized as the internal and external organs. "With the effort to expand beyond the state of the external" [means: [The rest of the passage continues: ...the expansion of the state of the external has been abandoned. "O you who are the supreme power of consciousness" means the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) which is the supreme reality. "O you who are the supreme power of bliss" means the power of bliss (*ānanda-śakti*) which is the supreme reality. "O you who are the supreme power of will" means the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) which is the supreme reality. "O you who are the supreme power of knowledge" means the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) which is the supreme reality. You remain as one who is thus described: she by whom there is the exertion of "yawning"—that is, the manifestation—of the external states beginning with waking and ending with deep sleep, even though they have been liberated. The particle *hi* is a nipāta used to indicate a well-known fact. It is the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) to manifest these external states, and that [nature] consists of attachment to the worldly cycle of material existence (*prākṛta-saṃsāra*). The sense is that, since even that has been liberated by your consent, the state of non-attachment is attained.

Alternatively, the meaning is: you are that very Prakṛti, consisting of the power of cessation (nivṛttikalā), in whom there is the mere effort of the unfolding of the external state—which is the nature of the fourth state (turīyāvasthā)—of the liberated ones who have attained bodiless liberation (videhakaivalya). In either case, the sense is that you are unattached. And so, in the *Saundaryalaharī*, the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpūjyapāda says: "Fifty-six on earth, fifty-two in water, sixty-two in fire, and fifty-four in air..."
"Those rays which number thirty-six in heaven and sixty-four in the mind—even above them is the pair of your lotus feet. (6.28)

Henceforth, [the text] indicates that the perceived dualistic functions serve as aids for attaining the bliss of the unattached Self; thus, even within the three sequences beginning with the "Abode" (dhāman) to be described in the third *vimarśa*, it points toward the natural vomiting of the seven-times-sevenfold [elements] through the manifestation of the world spoken of in secret:
"O Sovereign Goddess, you who are the abode of the qualities of consciousness beginning with the peaceful void, you vomit forth in seven ways!"
You lead those who have taken refuge to no other auspicious state than that which transcends the plane of duality and non-duality. || 29 ||

Regarding the word *saptathā*: "O Īśvarī" is an intentional vocative. The meaning is: you who consist of the sixfold reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) whose characteristics are about to be described; you are the locus of the qualities of tranquil consciousness (*śāntamukhacidguṇāspadam*). As for "tranquil-faced consciousness," it is that consciousness which is tranquil, as well as its qualities such as omniscience and so forth. [As stated: "The aggregate of the six—complete sovereignty, valor, fame, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion—is declared to be *bhaga*. Likewise: [the power to know] the origin and destruction of beings, their coming and going..."

"He who knows both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) is to be called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). Thus, according to this definition, [the following] exist upon the path of the six *adhvans* consisting of the supreme vitality (*prāṇana*), sound (*nāda*), and the digit of the point (*bindu-kalā*): omniscience and the rest, tranquility and the rest, and desire, anger, and the rest. Furthermore, on the path of the six *adhvans* of his own consciousness—which consists of the sixfold contemplation (*parāmarśa*) of the phonemes whose characteristics will be described later—and on the path of the six *adhvans* of the letters of the *mātṛkā*, there exist those things which, in the *Saṃhitās* and other texts, are known by the names "alliance," "war," "march," "halt," "double-dealing," and "seeking shelter," and which consist of verbal expression, meaning, and action.

The abode of all these is the void (*vyoma*). You reside there in seven ways, through the various distinctions of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and the threefold set (*tripuṭī*). This occurs within the locus of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyomadhāman*) by way of the seven streams consisting of the functions of the mind, the intellect, and the five sense organs.

In his consciousness and in the *nāda*, there occurs a sequence consisting of a sevenfold manifestation known as the stages of commencement (*ārambha*), infancy (*taruṇa*), youth (*yauvana*), maturity (*prauḍha*), its end (*tadanta*), the *unmanā* state, and the state beyond stability (*anavasthā*); and likewise, a sevenfold manifestation corresponding to the seven musical notes—from *ṣaḍja* to *niṣāda*—as taught in the science of music (*gāndharvaveda*). Furthermore, there is also a ninefold sequence of the *unmanī-nāda*, whose characteristics will be described later, beginning with the *candrarodhinī* and culminating in the *bindu* of his unsurpassed form. This is also indicated in the aphorism.

This is according to the sequence of the creation of the phonemes of the Māheśvara Mātṛkā, characterized by the sounds described as "He sounded the drum five times" (*nanāda ḍhakkāṃ pañcavāram*), beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the *praṇava* (Oṃ) on the mountain of the Unsurpassed (*unmanā*). Furthermore, even within the sequence of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of their respective denotative meanings, [it is said]: "From Him arise the seven vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the seven flames, the seven fuels, and the seven tongues; these seven worlds exist within which move the seven vital breaths, hidden and deposited in the cave of the heart."

"From Him all oceans and mountains arise; from Him flow rivers of every form; and from Him come all herbs and juices, by which this inner self (antarātman) exists as a being. And: "Seven are your fuel-sticks, O Agni, seven your tongues, seven your seers, and seven your beloved abodes," and so forth—by virtue of being the cause of the entire creation, beginning with the seven vyāhṛtis, the groups of letters as primary and secondary forms, and extending to the end of the world-system from Loka to Aloka, as revealed by all the Vedas such as the Taittirīya Yājñikī and Mahānārāyaṇī Upaniṣads.

And by way of the manifestation of the self’s power consisting of the sevenfold stream elaborated in the Sāṃkhya treatise, the meaning is that you, being possessed of vital breath (*prāṇavat*), vomit forth the very sky as a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of unsurpassed form in various shapes. Thus, the Sāṃkhya Sūtra states: "The root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are both natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only a modification; the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither nature nor modification. In this context, the root-nature is the form of the Sāṃkhya-praṇava.

The seventh and eighth [kalās] also exist in the form of transformations (*vikṛti*) characterized by the non-supreme form (*anuttarākāra*), due to the intention to express the distinction between the Vedic word and its meaning; thus, they are "untransformed" (*avikṛti*). However, the secret truth is that the ninth is "untransformed" (*avikṛti*) because it is devoid of transformation, owing to the single nature of the Vedic word and its meaning. For this very reason, the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, and so on, arise from the various enumerations of the phonemes of their respective *mātṛkā*s; this is another Vedic secret: "O You who abide as the void (*vyoman*) in this manner, You are She."

By means of dualistic activity—that is, by means of the functioning of duality. She is *nārī*, one whose form is that of a woman. The meaning is that she has conducted herself through the worldly dealings of humans—the manifestation of the universe expressed in secret—by means of human conduct. For this very reason, she is "one who transcends the state of non-duality. Having even surpassed the state of non-duality, which is the fourth state (*turīya*), she transcends it; she turns away from enjoyment toward the distinction of objects of knowledge by way of the path beyond the fourth (*turīyātīta*). Thus, she is "one who transcends the state of non-duality."

Alternatively, [the term *nivṛtti*] may be derived from the verbal root *laghi*, meaning "to cease from eating," in accordance with the Vedic scripture: "The other, not eating, gazes on. Or, the construction may be understood as follows: even though she has entered the state of duality, she is intent upon ceasing from enjoyment by virtue of her non-difference from the power (*śakti*) of the Lord. Furthermore, within the sequence of the letters of the Mātṛkā arising from the Unsurpassed Sound (*anuttaranāda*), at the beginning of creation, there are two instances of the letter *a*, consisting of one and two morae respectively, which constitute non-duality (*advaya*). Her state (*pada*) consists of the three points (*bindu*).

Having transcended the sequence of sounds such as *pluta*, *raṅga*, and so forth, she leaps beyond them; thus she is "the one who has leaped over the non-dual state" (*advayapadātilaṅghinī*). Being such, she leads—meaning she causes to attain—the "dependents," those for whom a refuge has arisen, and the practitioners who rely upon the form of the Unsurpassed (*anuttarākāra*). She leads them to "Supreme Śiva," who exists as if distinct from the self through indirect perception, appearing in the form of either the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Lord (*īśvara*). The verb *nayati* (to lead) takes two objects. Alternatively, she leads the dependents, the practitioners, to Supreme Śiva by means of an exchange between the primary and secondary objects.

"Or" (*param*) means the individual soul (*jīva*). "And" (*ca*) means the individual soul or the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), according to one's wish. "You lead" (*nayasi*) means you cause [them] to reach. Likewise, "those who have taken refuge" (*āśritān*) means those who have taken refuge in You. "The perfected ones" (*siddhān*)—You do not lead them to another Śiva, but rather cause them to attain Śiva whose very nature is the Self (*ātmarūpa*). Thus, there is a difference in syntactic connection (*samanvaya*) either through repetition (*āvṛtti*) or by dividing the words (*padabheda*). At that time, by means of a dual function (*dvandvavṛtti*) consisting of the attainment of the Self, [She is] "one who transcends the two states" (*dvayapadātilaṅghinī*). The "two states" (*dvayapadāni*) are the previously mentioned states such as waking (*jāgrat*) and so forth, or the cosmic processes such as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth.

The compound *dvayapadātilaṅghinī* should be explained through an analysis involving the causative suffix (*ṇic*) as "she who causes those who have taken refuge to transcend those dualistic states," which exist in the form of pairs such as waking and sleep or creation and dissolution that are mutually opposed. Furthermore, it should be understood that this Goddess—being the *devataraṇī* (the one who enables crossing) mentioned in the mantra, "O Mother Earth, we invoke you, the wife of the upholders of truth, for protection... the wide-reaching, the giver of good shelter, the excellent guide"—is she who, in her form as the Mother of the Gods, leads the perfected ones (*siddhas*) precisely to the Śiva of the Self. (7–29)

With the intention that you, who possess the characteristics thus described, cannot be determined even by the primary function of speech— which is the collective totality of the four levels of speech (para and so forth) mentioned in the Vedic scripture, "Speech has four measured quarters"— let alone by *vaikharī*, he says: "She who, as *parā*, resides in the subject (*pramātṛ*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*), and whose form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)."
O Mother, that speech which is manifested through the three states does not even speak of You; how much less so, then, can it be Vaikharī?

By the words "She who does not cross over" (*yā māpratarī*) and so forth: she is the supreme Speech (*vāk*) whose name is Parā. She resides in the subject (*pramātṛ*), in the Self (*ātman*), and in the eldest Mother (*jyeṣṭhā ambā*). According to the etymology "she who pervades (*vyāpnoti*) cognition (*pramā*)—that is, that which possesses the function of conforming to reality"—she exists in the pervasive Self. This means she is the substratum for the conceptualization of the three folds (*triṣuṭī*). Being of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), she consists of specific knowledge (*viśeṣajñāna*). She is "seated" (*niṣeduṣī*); she is the "inner" (*pratyak*), meaning the inner Self (*pratyagātman*).

This Speech, illumined by the threefold states—namely the three modes known as *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*, or alternatively by the forms of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*)—declares to you: "He is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). O Mother! What need is there to mention *vaikharī*, which is illumined by a single state? It goes without saying that *vaikharī* declares you to be the inner self.

Even Parāvāk, though existing as the innermost subject within the Great Measurer (Mahāpramātṛ) and though manifested through the threefold states beginning with Paśyantī, is unable to express herself in her own essential nature as Mahākālī due to the contradiction between agent and object; thus she says, "I am the inward Self. What need is there to mention that this applies to the state of Vaikharī? This is the intended meaning. Regarding the reading "na vakti" (she does not speak): the sense is that even Parā herself, though manifested through the threefold states, does not speak of you, let alone Vaikharī.

The sense is that, in both ways, speech is simply incapable of expressing You, whose nature is its own self. Therefore, even such scriptural passages as, "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it," refer to You—who are of the nature of the Great Contemplation (*mahāvimarśa*) transcending both [the states] beginning with *parā* and ending with *vaikharī*, and those beginning with *parā* and ending with *parā*—whether they be enumerated in direct or reverse order; for both *parā* and *vaikharī* are of the nature of the Fourth (*turīya*). Thus, You are expressed neither by way of creation, maintenance, or withdrawal, nor by way of the Fourth state which is the equilibrium of those three.

Being unable to speak, yet manifesting existence solely as the true nature of the Great Contemplation (*mahāvimarśa*) which transcends those four [states], the word *vācaḥ* (words) is used in the plural to express this intention; nevertheless, because its own essential nature is inexpressible, it declares through its own voice the withdrawal from that nature along with the mind, saying: "from which words turn back. For this very reason, in the *Śrīsaṃvitstotra*, the nature of speech consisting of the Great Contemplation of five steps is described thus: "O Best of Kine, neither a word nor a cognition can be conceived otherwise."

"They cannot be conceived [as identical] because they have that as their nature, and likewise for the 'I-maker' (ahaṃkartṛ)"—the term *ahaṃkartṛ* is a single word; its meaning is "the user of the word 'I'. (8.30)

Now, [the author] explains how Kālikā— who consists of the Great Reflection (*mahāvimarśa*) and whose form is Speech— also assumes the nature of the seven *vyāhṛtis* by vomiting forth the seven streams previously mentioned, such as the Fourth (*turīya*) and that which transcends it, through her abiding in the central center of both the triad of powers of action (*kriyāśakti*) consisting of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal situated below her own essential nature, and the triad of powers of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) consisting of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*. "The three powers of Speech, whose bodies are *nāda*, *bindu*, and the letters, are upward-moving reflections."
O beloved of the Lord, those [mantras] are uttered below you in the abodes of withdrawal, maintenance, and emission.

By the words "nādabindu" and so forth: O Beloved of the Lord! This is an intentional address meaning "O You who are the form of the speech of the Lord, whose nature is the meaning of the Gāyatrī-mantra of the Great Virāj mentioned previously. "Of the *giraḥ*" means of the Goddess of Speech, whose body is the meaning of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*) consisting of great reflective awareness (*mahāvimarśa*). "Sprays of upward-moving reflective awareness" refers to the sprays of that reflective awareness which has ascended to the higher plane; they are its triple-atomized particles (*trayasareṇu*). In the reading "vimarśaśaktikāḥ," the meaning is "the minor powers of the very nature of reflective awareness."

"Three" means numbering three. They consist of the forms of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi*. *Nāda* is that which is called the "unstruck" (*anāhata*), a specific type of unmanifest sound synonymous with the desire to speak; it corresponds to the world of *janaloka*. *Bindu* is a specific modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) consisting of the determination of the form of what is to be spoken; by the etymology "it binds" (*bindati*) or "it vibrates" (*spandate*), it corresponds to the world of *tapoloka*. This is because of the verbal root *tap* in the sense of "perception" (*ālocane*), meaning it consists of the modification of the intellect known as the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

*Lipi* is a synonym for the aggregate of superimpositions consisting of the nature of "I-ness," "mine-ness," and so forth; it occupies the place of the *vyāhṛti* (the intermediate utterance) of *Satyaloka*. It is a specific resonance (*dhvani*) whose manifest form is the equilibrium of empirical and ultimate existence. Thus, they possess a threefold form. *Tvadadhaḥ*: below that which consists of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccitsukha*). They are the *vyāhṛtas* situated within the abodes of integration, maintenance, and emission.

The meaning is that by way of reversal, the *vyāhṛtis* of *jana*, *tapaḥ*, and *satya* are also recited in the very positions of the reversed *vyāhṛtis* mentioned as *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. The sense is that the words conventionally designated by the names of the letters beginning with *nāda* and *bindu* are themselves employed in the process of manifestation (*arthaprakriyā*) in the forms of dissolution, maintenance, and creation. Thus, she is described through the method of *prauḍhavākya* (bold assertion) as being the embodiment of such word and meaning, abiding as the form of *parāvāk* at the central pivot between the two.

By this, the supreme [speech] (parā) possesses a threefold nature in its external state as Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī, and in its internal state as the aspect of reflective awareness (vimarśa) consisting of Nāda, Bindu, and Kalā; thus, together with its own essential form, it consists of seven streams in its sixfold nature.

Regarding the state of being composed of the triad consisting of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*, the term "Great" (*mahaḥ*) refers to the fourth *vyāhṛti*. When the distinction of the threefold nature of its own essence—consisting of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *kalā*—along with creation, maintenance, and dissolution, is intended, its state as "beyond the fourth" (*turīyātīta*) is to be understood in relation to that threefold nature of its own essence; this and other points are to be inferred accordingly. For this very reason, even the Śruti, on the occasion of describing the nature of the fourth *vyāhṛti*, states: "These three *vyāhṛtis* are indeed 'Bhūḥ', 'Bhuvaḥ', and 'Svaḥ'. Of these, there is this fourth... and so forth.

Mahācamasya declares: "Maha! This is Brahman; that is the Self (Ātman); the other deities are its limbs," and so forth, thereby establishing that the Great Vyāhṛti consisting of the *turīya-nāda* (the fourth sound) is itself the nature of Speech, Meaning, and Brahman. And at the end [it says]: "These indeed are the four [sets of] four; there are four [sets of] four Vyāhṛtis. He who knows them knows Brahman."

By stating, "All the gods bring an offering to him," and so forth, [the text] proclaims aloud—by way of the sequence of the four great purposes—the nature of Brahmanhood for one who knows its true essence, on the basis of the quality of being worshipful to all the deities; such is the direction [of the argument]. (9-31)

Having thus described how [the universe] consists of the seven *vyāhṛtis* and the seven streams through the two sets of the triad of speech and meaning, he praises [the Lord], praying for the vision of the Fire-Śiva (Agni-Śiva), who is the fourth abode of fire transcending the three mandalas consisting of moon, sun, and fire, and who is the form named Time situated in space, composed of the wheel of the *saṅkarṣaṇa* fire:

"May that abode which moves like the wind in the sky, situated between the moon and the sun— the nature of which is vision and action, and which is composed of nectar— move within the station of the fire-stick."
O Mother, show me Śiva there in that supreme sky which has its peak above.

By the words beginning with *dṛkkriyā* [the author says]: O Ambikā! [He is] situated between the moon and the sun, which consist of vision (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*). Vision and action consist of knowledge and activity. He is situated between those two, the moon and the sun. Like the wind, that is, like the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), he moves in that sky which is the abode of nectar (*sudhāma*). In the reading *sudhāmaya*, it means consisting of the immortal power of life (*jīvaśakti*). He moves; that is, he circulates by means of the vital breath. Alternatively, according to the root *car* meaning "to eat," the sense is that he consumes the fourfold food.

Regarding this, scripture also states: "The wise one, ageless, stands partaking of the first portion of food," thereby describing his status as the first consumer of the fourfold food; and likewise: "Within the slender, yellow, radiant, and subtle crest-like flame, which resembles the awn of a wild grain, the Supreme Self is established. He is Brahman, he is Śiva, he is Hari, he is Indra, the Imperishable, the Supreme, the Self-ruling Lord. Thus it describes that very [Self] as being composed of all the deities.
