And in the *Śārṅgadharasaṃhitā*: "The vital breath (*prāṇapavana*), residing in the navel, having touched the interior of the heart-lotus, emerges from the throat to drink the nectar of Viṣṇu’s feet. Having drunk the ambrosia of the sky, it returns with speed, gladdening the entire body and enlivening the digestive fire. Smṛti as well clarifies this very point.

In the reading *khecaratvānalayaṣṭidhāmayat*—it means that which has as its abode (*dhāma*) the abode of the fire residing in the staff (*analayaṣṭi*), namely the space of the small ether (*daharākāśa*) consisting of the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*). Let it move about (*caratu*) or let it consume (*bhakṣayatu*). The verb in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) here expresses a possibility. The sense is that its movement or consumption is established by inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of the effect, which is the digestion of the four kinds of food.

That which is the peak above that—the supreme sky which takes the form of the peak above such a *daharākāśa* (the inner space consisting of consciousness)—exists; this is the ellipsis. According to scriptural and sūtra authorities such as "Brahman has the ether for its body" and "The ether [is Brahman] because of its characteristic marks," there exists a consciousness-made void (*cinmaya-vyoman*) in the form of the *brahmabila*, the *dvādaśānta*, and so forth; in that sky (*khe*), show me Śiva. You are *Sarvamaṅgalā*, whose very form is the *daharākāśa*.

The summarized meaning is: "Make manifest Śiva, who is your own essential nature, the embodiment of all auspiciousness, and whose essence is the abode of Brahman at the *dvādaśānta*. This is because, in the *Śikṣāvalli* of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, beginning with the passage, "That which is this space within the heart; in that [space] is this person consisting of mind, immortal and golden," the fruit of liberation is presented through the words, "He attains self-sovereignty (*svārājya*)," and so forth. (10.32)

Thus, having described the nature of the seven *vyāhṛtis* and the seven streams as being composed of the sequence of three and four objects through the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the three mandalas, he now clearly describes the nature of the nine Brahmans as being useful for the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*) of the five objects to be taught hereafter—[nine Brahmans] formed by the triad of the previously mentioned equilibrium of word and meaning: "The triad of speech beginning with *vaikharī* is the object (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and [the agent] (*iti kartṛ*) in the subsequent [state]; this is the definition."
They remember Your other, manifold form, which consists of arising, persistence, and dissolution. || 33 ||

By the words "vaikharī" and so forth: "in the Supreme" (pare) means in that which has the nature of *parā-vāc* (the supreme speech), that is, in the Great Knower (*mahā-pramātṛ*) whose essence consists of the non-differentiation of word and meaning. Or, "O Supreme One" (*he pare*) may be taken as an address to Her who is the very form of *parā-vāc*, namely Kālī. The sense is that *parā* consists of the aggregate of the nine Brahmans, being the triad of the threefold functions of word, meaning, and action—which are synonymous with knowledge, action, and their state of equilibrium. This triad comprises the three forms of speech known as *vaikhārī*, *madhyamā*, and *paśyantī*. These constitute the triad of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the means of knowledge (*mānam*), and the agent characterized as the knower (*kartṛ*).

"In due order, the object of cognition and the means of cognition" refers to the definition—that is, the essential nature—of the agents, namely the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the knowers (*pramātṛ*). The sense is that this occurs "in the context of the objective sphere. Regarding the reading "the object of cognition and the means of cognition are the definition elsewhere," "elsewhere" means in the context of the objective sphere; that is, within the nature of the knower characterized by duality. "The object of cognition and the means of cognition" means that the means of knowledge is the instrument for measuring the duality that constitutes the object of knowledge; it is the definition, the essential nature [of the knower].

Having thus described the body consisting of difference and non-difference, he now describes the body of their essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with the verse beginning "udbhava" and so forth. It consists of emergence, maintenance, and dissolution—that is, it takes the form of creation, preservation, and withdrawal. It possesses manifold differentiation (*bhūribheda*), being endowed with even greater diversity due to its inherent nature of both difference and non-difference as previously mentioned. Therefore, they remember Your other body—the form consisting of the essential identity of the insentient and the sentient—as the word "rememberers" is to be supplied as the subject.

Regarding the reading *smaranti yat*: the meaning is that they remember that other body which possesses many divisions, consisting of the essential harmony (*sāmarasya*) of the nine vowels beginning with *a, i, u, ṇ*. || 11-33 ||

Having thus analyzed the triad of triads consisting of the equilibrium of difference and non-difference, he explains therein— within the form of the nine *yoni*s— the fivefold flow (*pañcavāhatā*) of Śiva and Śakti through their relationship as support and supported: "That whose form is unseen, yet which is the universal form— that is the Lord’s body, the state of supreme peace."
Therein, O Mistress of the Family (Suveśī), that which is your arising, the emanation consisting of five currents, takes its support. 34.

By the words beginning with *viśvamūrti* and so forth: O Kuleśī! *Kula* is a collection of similar things; *Īśinī* means its controller—this is the vocative address. That whose form (*mūrti*) consists of the universe, which comprises the eighty-one parts beginning with *Vyomavyāpin*, or else, according to the method of the *Liṅgānuśāsana* which states, "The term *viśva* may refer to one who identifies with the gross [body], or *viśva* may mean 'the name for everything'," it possesses a form in the shape of the universe as the name for all things, or a form consisting of one who identifies with the gross.

Nevertheless, "whose form is unseen" (*adṛṣṭavigraham*): "unseen" means beyond the range of the physical eye; "form" (*vigraha*) refers to a manifold grasping, that is to say, the nature of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of dualistic cognition—this is the meaning according to the sequence of sense. Furthermore, according to the sequence of words, it is "whose form is seen by the letter *A*"—the letter *A* being the root of the phonemes of the Mother-Syllable (*mātṛkā*) and the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*)—and thus it is such [a form]. "Your state of peace" (*tvatpraśāntipadam*) is the locus of Your tranquility.

Regarding the reading *tatpraśāntipadam*: it is the place of rest for this Lord who consists of both word and meaning; or, it may be designated as the "place of rest" (*praśāntipada*) because it is beyond direct perception (*parokṣatvena*). As for His body of sovereignty (*aiśvaryavapuḥ*), which—as previously stated in the *Vimarśa*—consists of the mountain of *ka-ī-a-sa*, or which is related to the Lord or non-different from the Lord, and which consists of both word and meaning: within that very body is Your arising, which takes the form of the unfolding of the five functions of the cognitive senses consisting of the five-syllable rosary.

Or rather, it exists in the form of the fivefold functions beginning with *khecarī* that will be described hereafter. That is your arising (*udaya*). Emission (*sṛṣṭi*) consists of the flow of the functions of the five organs of action, which takes the form of the expansion of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) pregnant with knowledge (*jñāna*). It also consists of the flow of the functions of the five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), which takes the form of the expansion of the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) pregnant with action. And it consists of the flow of the five powers beginning with *khecarī*, which takes the form of the expansion of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of both; this emission, being of such a nature, she takes as her support.

The meaning is that your arising—which, as stated in the Śruti, is "suveśatam" (well-pervaded), consisting of the form of having entered into the created world—is the locus for the creation of the five breaths (*pañcavāha*). The sense is that your very entry [into the world] is designated as the creation of speech and meaning.

Here, by the power of the epithet *kuleśī* (the Mistress of the Kula) as a qualification of Kālī, and by the power of the epithet "whose form is the universe yet whose body is unseen" (*viśvamūrty-adṛṣṭavigraha*) as a qualification of the Lord whose body consists of both word and meaning, [she resides] within the Śrīcakra—which is composed of the universe and consists of the state of non-dual identity (*sāmarasya*) between the nine *yonis* and the *nāda*—within the Bindu and Triangle wheels which consist of the Tripurā-unity and its non-dual identity, and within the eight-spoked wheel and the eight-petaled lotus which correspond to the state of non-dual identity of the threefold set of internal and external sense organs (*buddhīndriya-tripuṭī*).

It should be understood that, through subtle observation, the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)—consisting of the union of the two pairs of wheels (the four-cornered Śiva-wheel and the five-cornered Śakti-wheel)—is also indicated by the thread [of the teaching]. This equilibrium is characterized by the embrace of the two lotuses of ten and sixteen petals, which consist respectively of the sun and mind on one side and the inner and outer circles of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), senses, and the activity of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) on the other; and of the two fortresses (*bhūpura*), which consist of the inner and outer ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

This has been stated in the *Lalitātriśatīnāmottarapīṭhikā* of the *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa*: "In the triangle is the Bindu; joined to it are the eight-spoked [wheel], the eight-petalled lotus, the ten-spoked, the sixteen-spoked, and the Earth-fortress (Bhūpura) with its nine gates. He who knows the inseparable relationship between these wheels—belonging to the Śaivas, the Śāktas, and the Cakras themselves—is a knower of the Cakra. (12.34)

Thus, having established the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti through their relationship as support and supported within the ninefold wheel of origins (*navayonicakra*), he now elucidates the creation of word and meaning—which serves as the means for the sequence of the five vehicles (*pañcavāha*) to be described later—by way of being like waves upon the ocean of the supreme speech (*parāvāṅmaya*), which consists of the four oceans of the Vedas as established by the previously cited scripture: "Speech has four measured quarters.
O Ambikā! That supreme power which vibrates within you is indeed like the waves of the ocean.
The fivefold purpose of the components of the *śiñjikā* exists as various subtle forms. (35)

By the words "yā pare" and so forth: O Ambikā! that Śakti who flashes forth as the nature of the supreme word (parāvāk)—in her, in you; that is to say, in you who possess that very form. Like the waves of the ocean, like the surges of the sea—those objects consisting of sound, touch, and so forth, whose limbs are specific sounds of ornaments for the feet consisting of the operations of knowledge and action (jñāna-kriyā), namely those forms of universals, individuals, substances, qualities, and actions, or those forms of the four aims of human life and their state of equilibrium (sāmarasya)—of these objects, which are the very bodies of the [four] aims... [the text continues].

The meaning is as follows: according to both definitions in the *Amarakośa*—"*artha* is used in the masculine sense of 'wealth' (*samaṃśaka*)" and "*artha* means 'denotation,' 'wealth,' or 'object'"—there is a pentad of denotable meanings, as well as a pentad of meanings belonging to the components of the *śiṃjikā*. It exists in that form, possessing various subtle structures—that is, endowed with knowledge distinguished by manifold subtle forms. Like an internal ocean consisting of a succession of waves accompanied by sound, the heart within is resonant; it exists through the very body of subtle conventional sounds as either the pentad of objects (*viṣaya*), the pentad of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), or even the pentad of denotable meanings (*abhidheyārtha*). This is the intended sense.

Now, by the force of the simile that the fivefold objects of meaning are like waves in the ocean, and by the force of the qualification "having *śiṃjikā* as their constituent part," it is also illuminated that within the Creative Power (*sṛṣṭikālī*), who—like the ocean—is the foundational substratum consisting of the supreme power of the Word (*parā-śabda-śakti*) in the form of a fourfold expressive capacity, the fivefold nature of the fivefold objects of meaning also exists solely through the body of the Word.

All of this will be examined in the fourth chapter, during the commentary on the verse beginning: "In that ocean of the nectar of existence, which is a raft of bliss filled with the ambrosia of the five objects. Therefore, we shall desist here. (13–35)

Having thus described the nature of the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevatā*) as common to both the internal and external, consisting of three, four, and five meanings in the form of the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*), [the author] now begins the description of the sequence of the four meanings, which consists of the four faces of Sṛṣṭikālī. This is done by expanding upon the pervasive power of time externally, together with the manifestation of the inner Self in the manner previously stated—namely, "by means of the internal and external forms of the Person and Time"—and by employing the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with the Bindu at the *dvādaśānta*, as referred to in the statement: "They say there is a thirteenth month even within the cosmic cycle (*kalpa*) of the year consisting of twelve months."

O Mother of the triple-pathed river! Your face is the host of powers (śakti) consisting of the three [states], which here constitutes the arrival of the fourth state through the stages beginning with the first,
following the sequence of the twelve.
It was manifested and proclaimed in the world by those [who possess] the fourfold marks. || 36 ||

By the words "Your face," and so forth: O Goddess with three paths for your eyes! The "three" refers to the triad of reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the letters *a*, *i*, and *u* which will be described in the process of the arising of the letters of the Seed (*bīja*) and the Source (*yoni*). They consist of the play of the triad of emissions (*visarga*)—the Śāmbhava, Śākta, and Āṇava—and take the form of the knower (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), as well as the forms of knowledge, contemplation, and action. They take the form of the gross, subtle, and causal bodies useful for those [states], and the forms of their respective states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as the divisions of time—past, future, and present—which are the cause of all that.

"Paths" (panthānaḥ) refers to the specific paths for the realization of reality. Their collection is the "threefold path" (tripatha). [The vocative] "O Leader of that" (tasya netri) means "O Guide," or alternatively, "O she whose eyes are the three paths itself" (trayaḥ panthāna eva netrāṇi yasyāḥ sā tripathanetrī)—this is the meaning of the vocative. Here, it refers either to the fivefold subtle body (sūkṣmavigraha) and its objects mentioned in the preceding verse, or to the fourfold ocean of speech beginning with the Parā, which expresses those [five].

In accordance with the Turyathāgama, [it exists] in the fourfold form of the Mātṛkā-vowel-section as the four sūtras beginning with *a i uṇ* which signify the nine vowels divided by the nine nādas; in the fourfold form of the four vowel-groups consisting of *ṛ ṛ lṛ lṝ*; in the fourfold form of the four diphthong vowels consisting of *e ai o au*; in the fourfold form of the four levels of speech (*vāk*) beginning with Parā and Paśyantī; and in the fourfold form of the four accents beginning with Udātta—thus within the four Vedas composed of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), and likewise within the sequence of word and meaning.

It is called *turyadhāgama* because it leads one to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) through its fourfold form—consisting of the fourfold adjuncts of the gross, subtle, causal, and great-cause; the fourfold states beginning with waking and ending with the fourth (*turya*); and the fourfold functions beginning with creation and ending with concealment regarding space, location, time, and emanation—and because it exists within the sequence of word and meaning that constitutes the universe. Alternatively, it is *turyadhāgama* because it itself becomes like the fourfold scripture (*caturvidhāgama*).

The meaning is that it reveals its own nature in four ways: by way of the four vowels (*cātusvarya*) and so forth, and by way of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) and so forth. For this very reason, it consists of five aspects: it is the nature of the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*) by way of the twelve vowels to be described hereafter, and by way of the supreme great resonance (*mahānāda*) and the point (*bindu*) of the twelfth state; it is the nature of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) by way of being the wheel of the twelve zodiac signs; and for this very reason, it is the "multitude of powers" (*śaktibṛnda*), because within it the various limiting powers (*upādhi-śakti*) are gathered together.

The term *śaktibṛnda* refers to that in which the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are gathered together; the meaning is that it possesses the characteristics of the wheels (*cakra*) to be described in the third *vimarśa*, and consists of the entire multitude of powers. "Your face"—that which exists as your face, that is "your face. Regarding the phrase "by the triads beginning with the state": the word *pada* (state) refers to waking (*jāgrat*), which is the first among the four triads. By means of these [triads], there are: waking-waking, waking-dreaming, waking-deep sleep; dreaming-waking, dreaming-dreaming, dreaming-deep sleep; [and so forth].

Through the four triads consisting of waking-in-sleep, dreaming-in-sleep, and deep sleep-in-sleep; and through the forms of the fourth-waking, the fourth-dreaming, and the fourth-deep sleep—there are twelve sequential stages (*dvādaśakramapada*). This very point has been stated by citing the words of Jayaratha and the *Nāgama*: "The one [reality] is the form of its own nature (*svarūparūpa*); it is threefold through the distinctions of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution. Each of those is also fourfold through arising, persistence, dissolution, and rest."

The "twelve-fold sequential word" (*dvādaśakramapada*) is so called because, through twelve sequential words consisting of groups of four and three—namely, the forms of the vowels *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*, *am*, and *aḥ* (comprising short, long, and protracted forms)—the reality of emanation and the other cosmic processes is traversed and attained, and the reality of one's own essential nature (*svarūpatattva*) is reached therein.

In the reading *jṛmbhitaṃ bṛṃhitam*, [it is understood] by way of the sequence of speech (*vāk-krama*) at the end of the syllable-sections (*svarakhaṇḍa*) consisting of sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, and twenty-one letters; by way of the sequence of the inner and outer Puruṣa and Time (*kāla*) as taught in such Śruti passages as, "The ten fingers of the hand, the ten toes of the feet, and the self is the twenty-first," and "The twelve months, the five seasons, these three worlds, and yonder sun make the twenty-first"; and also by way of the sequence of word and meaning (*vāgartha-krama*) in the form of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) and the seven subsequent meters (*chandas*) beginning with Gāyatrī and ending with Bṛhatī.

The meaning is that it has increased. Regarding the phrase "consisting of *bhā*s" (*bhātmaka*): even in the system of measuring time by means of the lunar mansions (*nākṣatra-kāla-māna*), which is indicated by the epithet "Kālīmukha," since each individual mansion consists of four quarters (*pāda*), and since each individual zodiac sign (*rāśi*)—which constitutes the twelve-sign wheel—is itself composed of a nine-part wheel of nine-divisional portions (*navāṃśa-cakra*), the full moon day conjoined with the Citrā mansion (the Caitrī) is likewise "Kālīmukha" consisting of *bhā*s even according to the conventional lunar measurement (*vyāvahārika-cāndra-māna*).

Likewise, even in the conventional solar measurement—designated by the names of the months corresponding to the zodiac signs beginning with Aries and Taurus—the essence is indeed that of *bhā* (light). The "mouth of Time" (*kālamukha*), consisting of years, yugas, and so forth, is a multitude of the powers of time, which are of the nature of the rays of the sun's light. It is fourfold by way of the two solstices (*ayana*), the equinox (*viṣuva*), and the two transits (*saṃkrānti*). It is fourfold [also] by means of the four triplets (*trika*), which consist of the collective totality of three months; by those four triplets, [it is established] through the steps (*pada*) and so forth.

Because each triad of months is constituted by being "sandeshita" (enclosed) by two solstices (*ayana*)—namely the two transits (*saṃkrānti*) called *Haripada* and *Ṣaḍaśītimukha*—or by an equinox (*viṣuva*), the twelve-fold sequence, consisting of twelve months, becomes fourfold as the form of Time (*kāla-rūpa*). Being fourfold, it becomes "jṛmbhita" (expanded) or "bṛhita" (augmented). This very twelve-fold sequence will be explained further ahead in the third *vimarśa*; therefore, we shall desist here.

In this very sequence, the correlation of the duration of time up to the end of a thousand cycles of four yugas—the day of Brahmā—and the correlation of the fourfold classes of speech pertaining to the elements and their derivatives, are to be inferred as far as possible; such is the summary. (14–36)

Having thus explained the manifestation of the Person (Puruṣa) as the meaning of the Unstruck Speech (Anāhatavāg) through the state of equilibrium (sāmarasya) of direction, place, and time, [the author] now desires to explain the emergence of the phonemes of the Struck Mātṛkā (Āhatamātṛkā) from the manifestation of the meaning of the Struck Speech (Āhatavāg). This is preceded by the sequence of the phonemes and the consciousness of the abodes (dhāma) required for the worship of the Wheel of the Vṛnda to be described hereafter, and it occurs through the state of equilibrium of the three wheels named Prakāśa, Ānanda, and Mūrti. In this regard, he characterizes Agni, Sūrya, and Soma—the impellers of the conceptualizing intellect—as being of the nature of the Bindu of Unstruck Speech and Meaning, acting respectively as the means of knowledge (māna), the object of knowledge (meya), and the knower (mitṛ): "characterized by the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower."
O Mother, the three abodes of the Moon, the Sun,
and Fire are indeed marked by you with the vowels, which are divided according to the lords of the zodiac signs, O Dispeller of Sins.

By the words "māna-meya" and so forth: O Ambikā! [You are] characterized as the means of knowledge (*māna*), the object of knowledge (*meya*), and the knower (*miti-netṛ*). According to the grammatical rule that a word at the end of a *dvandva* compound is connected with each preceding member, the leader of the means of knowledge (*māna-netā*) is Soma; the leader of the objects of knowledge (*meya-netā*) is Sūrya; and the leader of the act of knowing (*miti-netā*) is Dahana (Fire). Their nature as the means, object, and knower of knowledge consists respectively, in the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking, in their capacity as the individual egos named Prājña, Taijasa, and Viśva, and in their capacity as the cosmic egos consisting of Īśvara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Virāṭ.

And those three—the Moon, Sun, and Fire—residing in the three abodes, having reached the threefold abode of the *tripuṭī* (the triad) consisting of sound (*nāda*), non-sound (*anāha*), and the form of the tranquil light that is the object of the three Vedas to be described hereafter—both collectively and individually, according to their will—and having reached the threefold abode of the states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking; finally, in the manner of the threefold division of the *tripuṭī*, they have gone to the *amā* (the New Moon), which is the digit of the *māyā*-related lunar phase, meaning the full *anusvāra* nature belonging to Śambhu and the process of emission (*visarga*).

They "go" (gacchanti) means they "attain" (prāpnuvanti); thus, they are "Amagas" because they sequentially attain the state consisting of the supreme perfection of form (*anuttarākāra-sampad-rūpa*)—which is both of the nature of knowledge (*vidyāmayī*) and of the power of emission (*śāktavaisargikī*). The meaning is that, having attained in the third *vimarśa* the "Amākalā" which consists of the great measure (*mahāpramāṇa*) and great capacity (*mahākṣama*) as will be described, they then attain in the fourth *vimarśa* the "Amākalā" which consists of the capacity of the "I" of the power of emission (*śāktavisargāhamakṣamayī*) and the perfection of the equilibrium between knowledge and ignorance (*vidyāvidyā-sāmarasya-sampad-rūpa*), by way of returning to oneness with the Great Subject (*mahāpramātṛ-aikya-pratinivartana-krama*).

In the sequence thus described, the present individual presiding deities—the Moon, the Sun, and the Fire—are distinguished by the divisions of the triad of *apāna*, *prāṇa*, and *vyāna*. They are characterized by the vowels—*a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth—which are derived from the "heap" (*rāśi*), meaning the collection of sounds, by being divided according to the "kingly rule" (*rājividhi*), that is, by the arrangement of rows, having been separated from that heap. These [deities] are indeed the very droplets of the *vippṛṣ* (the Great Goddess). Thus, in order, they are the forms of Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī. Indeed, they are simply the spray of the *vippṛṣ*.

Herein is the process of the origin of vowels according to Atri: In a previous kalpa, the Moon—which possesses the power of internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) latent within it, which identifies with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and whose nature is the beginningless *anuttara-nāda*—having emerged from the collective deep sleep that constitutes its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the beginningless *anuttara-nāda*, desired: "May I become through the nature of the reflective awareness of the vowel *a*. At that moment, the vowel *a* originated.

When that very letter *A*, which externally manifests the unsurpassed bliss of the internal resonance (*nāda*) it has experienced, transforms into the long *Ā*, at that very same moment, the letter *I*—which signifies its will (*icchā*)—and the letter *U*—which signifies its unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—come into being. Since at that time there can be no resting place for the form of the Unsurpassed (*Anuttara*) without the impulse of will toward governance (*vineśana*) through the internal power of action (*kriyāśakti*), nor without the bliss of unfolding, the powers of governance and unfolding themselves transform into the long vowels *Ī* and *Ū*.

Thus, within the pair of triads consisting of the internal and external divisions—namely, the short and long vowels which signify the two [internal and external] cognitions—the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) exists in each instance as the essence of the equilibrium of the internal *rakta* (the red/active). Furthermore, through the pair of short and long phonemes externally, there is the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*); and in this very same way, the nature of each individual string (*dāma*) is also to be known solely through experience. In this manner, the same should be inferred for the others as well.

The process of creation from the remaining ten vowels, along with the process of the origin of all the phonemes of the Mātṛkā in that context, was likewise declared in the *Tantrasāra* during the section on the determination of the Śāmbhava means (*upāya*): "In that regard, there are first of all three primary powers of the Supreme Lord: Anuttara (the Absolute), Icchā (Will), and Unmeṣa (Expansion). These are themselves the triad of reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), namely: *a*, *i*, and *u*. For this very reason, it is so even in the *Māheśvara-sūtras*."

It should be understood that even in the *Śrīnandikeśvarakārikās*, a reasoned determination has been made that the sūtra was indeed begun as ‘a i u ṇ’. From these very three acts of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), the entire expansion of all powers (*sarvaśaktiprapañca*) is discussed. For rest in the Absolute (*anuttara*) alone is Bliss (*ānanda*); rest in Will (*icchā*) alone is Lordship (*īśana*); and rest in Expansion (*unmeṣa*) alone is Height (*ūrbhiḥ*). That which is called the commencement of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*) is precisely this triad of reflective awarenesses: ‘ā ī ū’.

And here, the first three reflections, because their essence consists solely of manifestation (*prakāśa*), are solar in nature; the final one, because its primary quality is the bliss of the nature of repose (*viśrānti*), is lunar in nature. As long as there is no entry of the element of action (*karman*), it remains thus. But when action enters into Will (*icchā*) and Sovereignty (*īśana*), that which is then called "the desired" and "the governed" possesses two divisions: the sound *ra* through mere manifestation, and the sound *la* through repose, because *ra* and *la* possess the inherent natures of manifestation and stasis, respectively.

And that which is being willed (*iṣyamāṇa*) is not manifest like an external object; for if it were of a manifest form, it would simply be a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*), and not a will (*icchā*) or a lordship (*īśana*). Therefore, precisely because of its non-manifest nature, there is only the sound (*śruti*) of *ra* and *la*, but no stable existence as a consonant (*vyañjana*). These four phonemes (*varṇa*)—*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, and *lṝ*—are neuter because they bear the shadow of both [the Absolute and Bliss]. When the expansion of the Absolute (*anuttara*) and Bliss (*ānanda*) occurs within the [powers of] Will and the rest, then there are two phonemes: *e* and *o*. Here too, due to the union of the Absolute and Bliss, there are again two phonemes.

"ai au"—this is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). These are the four phonemes: "e ai o au. Then again, at the end of the power of action, everything that has become an effect enters into the Absolute (*anuttara*); until that point, it remains as the *bindu*, which is pure light by virtue of having consciousness alone as its essence—namely, "aṃ. Then, right there, the emission of the Absolute (*anuttara-visarga*) arises—namely, "aḥ. Thus, this group of sixteen is said to be the nature of the seed-syllables of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*).

That which arises from it consists of phonemes (*vyañjana*) and takes the form of the *yoni*. Therein, from the Absolute (*anuttara*), the *ka*-group [arises]. From Faith (*śraddhā*) and Will (*icchā*), the *ca*-group; from Will accompanied by action (*sakarmikā icchā*), the two groups, the *ṭa*-group and the *ta*-group. From Expansion (*unmeṣa*), the *pa*-group. Through the conjunction with the fivefold Power (*śakti*), there is the state of five groups of five. From the threefold Will itself come *ya*, *ra*, and *la*. From Expansion comes the letter *va*. From the threefold Will itself come *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*. From the Emission (*visarga*) comes the letter *ha*. The letter *kṣa* is born from the union of the *yoni*.

Thus, this Blessed One is indeed the unsurpassed Lord of the Kula (*kuleśvara*). And his is the one and only Kaulika power of emission (*visarga-śakti*). By means of this, from the form of bliss (*ānanda*) onwards, up to the limit of external creation, the very cognitions of the categories (*varga-parāmarśa*)—as they vibrate—attain the state of being external objective principles (*tattva*). And this emission is threefold: the *āṇava*, which consists in the repose of the mind; the *śākta*, characterized by the awakening of the mind; and the *śāmbhava*, which consists in the dissolution of the mind.

Thus, when there is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of this much—that emission (*visarga*) alone is the power (*śakti*) of the Lord in the generation of the universe—by virtue of its very indivisibility, then the one Lord alone becomes both the possessor of power (*śaktimān*) and the power (*śakti*) itself through the division into seed (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*). When there is a reflective awareness of the eight [groups] separately, along with the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), there is a group of nine. When each individual reflective awareness is predominant, there is a nature consisting of fifty. Even here, by reflecting upon the possible divisions of parts, there is a form consisting of eighty-one.

In reality, however, the six cognitive reflections (*parāmarśa*), becoming twelve through the process of expansion and reabsorption, nourish the Supreme Lord’s state of being filled with the power of the universe. These very reflections, as powers (*śakti*), are described as the divine Śrī Kālikā Bhagavatī. These same reflections, in their form as power, assume the nature of Śuddhavidyā and Vidyeśvarī. Furthermore, within the realm of Māyā, they manifest as distinct divisions and assume the state of the phonemes of Māyā.

When those [entities] are perceived within the Paśyantī, Madhyamā, and Vaikharī levels, having attained a state of worldly transactionality through their inherent nature as external forms; and when they are revived by these aforementioned pure reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*), which serve as their very life-force—then they become endowed with vitality (*savīrya*). And such entities are the bestowers of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*).

Thus, for one who perceives the Self as consisting solely of the repose of all reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), wherein the distinctions of all the *tattvas*, elements, and worlds are reflected, there is liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) through the Śāmbhava immersion (*samāveśa*) characterized by freedom from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpatā*). On this point, there are these verses: "Just as the entire world with its manifold arrangements shines within a mirror, so does everything shine here within the Self."

In the *Tantrasāra*, the Śāmbhavopāya is elaborated upon with a focus solely on the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the process of the creation of phonemes (*varṇasṛṣṭi*), stating: "Consciousness (*bodhaḥ*), by following the savor of its own self-reflection (*nijavimarśarasānuvṛttyā*), reflects upon the universe; but the intellect (*tukuḥ*) does not do so in that way," and so forth. Therefore, one should understand that even for all phonemes, there exists individually the nature of the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*). Furthermore, hereafter, the sequences of abodes, consciousness, and phonemes will be briefly analyzed for the sake of their utility in spiritual practice (*upāsanā*).

In this same way, regarding the process of the production of sound, just as the sixteen lunar vowels—from *a* to the visarga—residing in the gentle-sounding (*saumya*) section which is the root of the rosary (*akṣamālā*), are pervaded by the sixteen digits (*kalā*), so too is the mind (*manas*), which is their root. Since the mind is pervaded by the number sixteen through its manifestation as the sixteen digits in the form of vital breath (*prāṇa*), faith (*śraddhā*), ether (*ākāśa*), air (*vāyu*), fire (*tejas*), water (*jala*), earth (*pṛthivī*), the senses (*indriya*), mind (*manas*), food (*anna*), vigor (*vīrya*), austerity (*tapas*), mantra (*mantra*), action (*karman*), world (*loka*), and name (*nāma*), the mind remains as a mere name during deep sleep and at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), along with all [the other elements].

Along with its digits, it dissolves into the self of the vital breath (prāṇa) which is characterized by ignorance; likewise, the moon, remaining as a mere name, dissolves into the solar self during the new moon, which is like the night of ignorance. Then, on the day consisting of knowledge, like the mind endowed with sixteen digits, the moon—also endowed with sixteen digits—rises and shines during the full moon of knowledge.

Just as the dissolution of the moon through its conjunction with the visible sun brings about its disappearance, so too the dissolution of the mind—occurring during the state of inert deep sleep—through its conjunction with the Prāṇa-sun, the churner of the universe, leads to rebirth. Likewise, just as the moon’s union with the form of the Saṅkarṣaṇa fire results in its non-return, so too the mind’s union with the form of the fire of consciousness within the primary Prāṇa-sun bestows liberation known as *anāvṛtti* (non-return).

Therefore, the parts of the wheel of time (kālacakra) consisting of the year of sixteen months belonging to the Goddess are [manifested] within oneself as sixteenfold in the form of the subtle mind (manas) consisting of sixteen digits (kalās), and as twelvefold in the form of the ten gross senses joined with the mind (manas) and intellect (buddhi).

Furthermore, even regarding the personification of time (*kālapuruṣa*) in terms of external conventional solar and lunar measures, there is [a distinction] starting from the *nimeṣa*, *kalā*, lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays, lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), yogas, and karaṇas, up to the twelve transits (*saṃkrānti*) consisting of the two solstices and two equinoxes, as well as the conventional usage of Aries (*meṣa*), the month of Caitra, and so forth. Likewise, there is a distinction based on the differing views regarding the five seasons or six seasons as explained in the *Nirukta* of the Śruti, such as: "In this [year], there are six seasons, or nine... and so on.

Likewise, when it is intended to express the consonance between the calculations of the lunar days (*tithi*), fortnights (*pakṣa*), months, and so forth as stated in the *Devīmāna*, and the ultimate reckoning of time—ranging from the month measured by six-day periods (*ṣaḍaha*) according to the Vedic injunction, "Having completed these months with six-day periods, they omit a day," and including the years ending in *saṃvatsara* and *parivatsara*, down to the days, months, and years of the conventional *bārhaspatya* and other *sāvana* measures, and the ultimate measures such as *pitrya*, *divya*, *prājāpatya*, *vairāja*, *brāhma*, and the state of *mānasāmarasya*. (Note: This passage discusses the reconciliation of various systems of temporal measurement—from the ritualistic *ṣaḍaha* cycles of the Vedas to the astronomical *bārhaspatya* year, and further to the transcendent measures of the cosmic cycles and the ultimate equilibrium of the mind.)

In that context, within the body of a month consisting of thirty days—which is composed of two fortnights (pakṣa) each made up of fifteen lunar days (tithi), totaling three sets of five times five lunar days—there is the attainment of a single fortnight comprising sixteen lunar days. This occurs because the full moon (pūrṇimā) is divided into two forms by the distinction between Anumati and Bheda, and the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is likewise divided into two forms by the distinction between Sinīvālī and Kuhū. Just as this is the case in the conventional [calendar] consisting of lunar, solar, and civil months, so too in the system of the Goddess (Devīmāna), there is the attainment of a fortnight containing eighteen lunar days for the purpose of a month consisting of thirty-six lunar days.

And because it is accomplished by being counted together with the daily and the occasional [observances]; likewise, even regarding the two principles of the year—the *kalpa* as the self and the person—there is a distinction in the natural measures such as the lunar, solar, and civil days.

Just as in the case of the common (prākṛta) month, half-month, and lunar day, where numbers such as twelve, twenty-four, sixteen, eighteen, and so forth are obtained for the days according to their respective origins and desires; likewise, even in the divine measures—known by the synonyms *divyamāna*, *mānavamāna*, *prājāpatyamāna*, *brāhmamāna*, and *aparamāna*—the numbers thirty-six, eighteen, and so forth, corresponding to the lunar days and days of the month, are obtained respectively in the divine, human, progenitor (prājāpatya), and Brahma measures. This is because, according to the technical definition of the Goddess's measure (*devīmāna*)—which concludes with the completion of the cycles of years, the ages (*yuga*), and the full mandala—the results are obtained through calculations based on eight, twelve, and sixteen parts.

They proceed by means of a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*). There are indeed six seasons; verily, they find firm support in the seasons. There are two six-day periods; these amount to twelve days. Man consists of twelve parts: two thighs, two arms, the trunk, and the head—these are four limbs—and the two breasts make twelve. "Man indeed consists of sixteen parts. Thus they revolve around the man. There are three six-day periods; these amount to eighteen days. Nine and nine more; for there are nine vital breaths in man.

"The vital breaths turn back toward those [other] vital breaths. There are four six-day periods; these amount to twenty-four days. There are twenty-four half-months in a year; thus they turn back toward the year. 'The year is indeed unstable,' they say, 'for it is greater than a firm foundation. This much, indeed, is the Vedic exposition of the year: by means of the month, they proceed, finding a firm foundation month after month. Thus, in the section concerning the Aśvamedha and other subsequent sacrifices.

In the eleventh anuvāka of the fourth praśna of the seventh kāṇḍa of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, it is stated that they are "characterized" (lakṣitāḥ) in order to express that speech and meaning are the foundation of linguistic usage through the equality of the *puruṣakalpa* and *kālakalpa*; such is the secret of the arrangement of speech and meaning (*vāgarthakalparahasyam*).

Therefore, in the *Sāmidhenī-brāhmaṇa*, regarding the fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses consisting of three-footed *gāyatrī* meters, the fruit of attaining the deity of the year (*saṃvatsara*) is explicitly stated through the calculation of their syllables being equal in number to the days and nights of a year: "Their syllables are three hundred and sixty; so many are the nights of the year; by [the number of] syllables, one indeed attains the year. And in the *Saundaryalaharī*, the venerable Guru Śaṅkarapāda [states]: "On earth..."

"Your pair of lotus feet is even above those rays which number fifty-six in water, fifty-two in fire, sixty-two in air, fifty-four in ether, thirty-two in each of the two [subtle elements], thirty-six in the mind, and sixty-four in the intellect"—such are the words praising the lotus feet of the Goddess. And in the *Mānasollāsa*: "By means of the fivefold division of the ten [stages], the playful manifestation of the universe..."

Since she is the witness and consists of syllables, she is therefore the fifteen-syllabled one (*pañcadaśākṣarī*). Likewise, the words of great poets such as Kālidāsa—"O Mother! Your divine form, with the netherworld for feet, the earth for hips, the sun and moon for breasts, the directions for face, and the clouds for hair—before this form, the millions of gods beginning with Hari, Brahmā, and Indra act like mere insects"—are a hymn to your form whose sole purport is the state of mutual containment between word and meaning; enough, then, of wandering among the branches [of secondary arguments]. (15–37)

Thus, having characterized the state of being the womb within the womb of both the *vāk* (speech) and *artha* (meaning)— namely, *Ahaṭā* and *Anāhaṭā*, *Kālī* and *Kālakalpa*, which consist of the three *bindus*— he also establishes their state of non-duality as the *anuttara-praṇava* through the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka*) pertaining to the times of emanation,

maintenance, and withdrawal: "O You who are the refuge for those unable to cross over [the ocean of existence], other than [the ordinary], You arise from Your own state, which is of the nature of Śiva."
From non-duality, the manifestation of consciousness as object is the vision; here, its reflective awareness is the expressive vowel. || 38 ||

By the words "āhata" and so forth: "The source that is struck, other, and difficult to cross. "Struck" (āhata) refers to the time of emanation (sṛṣṭi). "Other" (itara) refers to the time of maintenance (sthiti), being of the nature of mental reflection (manovimarśa) and thus having the form of the "unstruck" (anāhata). Or, it is "difficult to cross" (duruttara) because it causes one to cross over suffering known as the cycle of birth and death (saṃsāra). Alternatively, it is "difficult to cross" because it delivers one from the suffering of the cycle of birth and death known as saṃsāra. It is characterized by the adjunct of the third level of consciousness (tārtīyājñāna) at the time of withdrawal (saṃhāra) known as death; or, it is characterized by the adjunct of the fourth bliss (turīyānanda) at the time of the cycle of saṃsāra through the knowledge of Śiva known as the Immortal (amṛta).

The meaning is that [the Heart] consists of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) which exists during the four states—creation, maintenance, dissolution, and the fourth (*turya*)—of those [beings] whose difficult-to-cross [cycles of rebirth] have been brought to an end. Therefore, it is said: "The syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*: these two emerged from Brahmā in ancient times after piercing his throat; therefore, both are auspicious. Thus, it refers to the space within the heart (*daharākāśa*), which is the substratum and the very form of the meaning expressed by the auspicious *praṇava*.

In the reading *śivātmikām*, the meaning is that it is an address to Kālī, *he śive maṅgale*, [meaning] "O auspicious Śivā," who is the form of the syllable *praṇava* which denotes auspiciousness. She is "the body of the expansion of the consciousness of objects" (*viṣayacitprathātanuḥ*). She is called *viṣayacitprathātanuḥ* because she first expands—that is, spreads—the expansion of the knowledge of objects (*viṣayajñānavistṛtim*), and subsequently destroys it.

The essential meaning is this: first, by means of its own differentiation, it bestows the cognition of objects; subsequently, through the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it bestows the cognition of non-difference even for an object that was previously perceived as distinct. In the phrase "just like the reflection of vision" (*dṛgvimarśa iva*), the word *iva* carries the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*. Alternatively, because it is an indistinct reflective awareness, it is "equal to the reflective awareness of knowledge" (*jñānavimarśatulya*); thus, by virtue of expressing an indistinct meaning, it denotes a slight similarity. By this, it is indicated that reflective awareness is an attribute of the knower.

Regarding the reading "iha" (here): the meaning is "in this context," namely, within the three mandalas composed of your own *vippṛ* [vibration] as characterized in the preceding verse. The "designator" (*vācaka*) is that whose form is non-different from the activity of the speaker, which consists of the pulsation of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*). The "vowel" (*svara*) is a particular sound (*dhvani*) known as the *praṇava* or *oṃkāra*, which shines by itself or is pleasing to the senses. From your non-dual state (*advayāt tvatpadāt*), that is, from the locus of the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) consisting of the non-dual day (*ahar*), it "arises"—it manifests in the form of the four measures (*mātra*) consisting of the short, long, protracted, and the final *pluta* [measure].

The vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), consisting of inhalation and exhalation, takes the form of the utterance of the *samarasya* (state of equilibrium) of the letters *sa* and *ha*, which correspond respectively to the awakening of the mind and the power of emission (*visarga*). When this very utterance, together with the nasal bindu (*sabinduka*), takes the form "so'ham," and the portions of the consonants—the letters *sa* and *ha* alone—are discarded, the *praṇava* remains. Since that *praṇava* is of a single nature throughout the processes of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, as both word and meaning, and because there is an absence of articulatory points (*sthāna*) and efforts (*prayatna*) in the unstruck (*anāhata*) vibration of the breath, it possesses the quality of being a sound that arises without being struck.

By the use of the *ātmanepada* ending in the verb "udayate" (it arises), it is understood that the fruit of the action consisting of arising accrues to the Self (*ātman*); thus, it is also indicated that its status as a witness is eternal. For this very reason, the manner of the origin of the *praṇava* is likewise recorded in scripture: "From the *mūlādhāra*, the letter 'A' flashes forth; from the cavity of the navel, the letter 'U'; in the middle place, the letter 'M'; and from the throat, the *bindu*, by the power of the moon's rays. From the center, the *nāda*; and at the head, the *śakti* is said to be; and at the limit of the twelve [finger-breadths], the *oṃkāra*. Meditative in form, like the sun, it is the leader of the worlds, the universal embodiment. (16–38)

Thus, describing the state of the unstruck resonance (*anāhata-praṇava-nāda*)—which has entered into the relationship of signifier and signified through the three functions—as having both the fivefold functions (*pañcakṛtya*) and the state of being struck and unstruck, [the author] shows, by means of a variant reading in the sequence of its fivefold resonance, that the Supreme Lord Śiva—the foremost of practitioners whose body is composed of sound, who is both immanent in and transcendent of the universe, and who is the enjoyer of the primordial ground—is of the nature of *Kāmakalā* and is knowable solely by Mahākālī:
"O Mother! The Vaikharī sound, born from the effort of the organs of speech and the locus [of articulation], resounds as the 'struck' (*āhata*)."
Furthermore, this mental [suffering] is unsurpassed, being unstruck, perfumed, and characterized by your own perception; it is the highest of the high. || 39 ||

By the words beginning with *amba*, etc.: "O Mother" (*amba*) is a vocative as before. "In the abodes" (*dhāmasu*) refers to the locations such as the throat, palate, and lips; elsewhere, it refers to the lute, flute, drum, and so forth. "By means of the instruments" (*karaṇaiḥ*) refers to internal operations such as the closing and opening of the vocal organs; elsewhere, it refers to the operation of external means such as the strings, fingernails, fingers, and plectrum. "By effort" (*prayatnena*) refers to the form of internal and external articulation; elsewhere, it refers to efforts such as the teacher's instruction and the student's study. Thus, [the sound] is produced.

It is produced by the effort of articulation (*dhāmakaraṇaprayatna*). It is *āhata*—thoroughly cultivated (*ā-samantāt kṣuṇṇa*) in the form of either the path to ultimate liberation (*naiśreyasa*) or the path to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), through the self (*ātman*), knowledge (*vidyā*), the arts (*kalā*), and so forth. In other cases, it is *āhata* in the sense of being utterly destroyed (*ā-samantāt hata*) due to straying from both paths, and is thus nearly burnt. For this very reason, it is said in the *Śikṣā*, an auxiliary of the Vedas (*vedāṅga*): beginning with "The mind strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air (*māruta*)," and continuing until, "That which has come from a false teacher (*kutīrtha*) is burnt, discolored, and consumed."

"Thus, such an utterance is sinful; thus, such an utterance is auspicious. Likewise: "The Brahman [Veda] becomes manifest when it has come from a true teacher (*sutīrtha*), is clearly articulated, well-established in its own tradition (*svāmnāya*), and is employed with a beautiful tone and by a skillful speaker. For this very reason, it is called *vaikhara*: it is *vaikhara* because it certainly (*vai*) takes (*rāti*) or grasps (*gṛhṇāti*) the cavity of the ear (*kham*). Because its sound is struck forth through the repeated recitation of one's own guru, it takes the form of knowledge consisting of the Vedas, Upavedas, and so forth.

Otherwise, it is censurable in form due to its harshness to the ear, resembling the distorted and awkward braying of a donkey; such is the sound that vibrates and manifests. This, moreover, is the *anāhata* (unstruck) sound, which is devoid of the previously mentioned second characteristic of being "as if burnt. Regarding the sequence of meaning and the sequence of words: "The Self, having come together by itself, joins with the objects through the mind, by means of the desire to speak."

"The mind strikes the fire of the body; it impels the vital air. Thus, having assumed the form of non-extension through the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) mentioned [in that verse], the mental [sound] comes to rest within the mind itself by virtue of its identity with the emission of power (*śāktavisarga*). Alternatively, "it" refers to the sound whose body has been struck—that is, worn down—by the repetition of the initial striking characteristic on either of the two paths: the path to supreme bliss (*naiśreyasa*) or the path to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), consisting of the categories of Self, Knowledge, and so forth. Or rather, the mental [sound] comes to rest within the mind itself in the form of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the emission of power.

Alternatively, the meaning is that being the very nature of direct experience (*sākṣādanubhūtatva*), the Unstruck (*anāhata*) becomes the form of the son through the continuum of the consciousness of the emission (*visarga*) characterized by the repose of the mind (*cittaviśrānti*)—in the form of a continuum of knowledge consisting of the heart's agitation—as stated in the seventh section of the *Praśna* book of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*: "Therefore, the son is the heart; therefore, from this world they do not desire that world, for the son is indeed the heart. For this very reason, because the power of sound whose essence is the living self (*jīvātman*) in the form of the heart’s exertion is not for the purpose of sacrifice, it abandons the gods and enters into the plants (*vanaspati*).

It is said that even for her, who is of the nature of form (*rūpa*), there is the capacity to protect from the hell named *puṃs* by means of the quality of being a son—which consists in the exertion of the heart and the knowledge of the Dharma; furthermore, she acts as an assistant in attaining the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) of obtaining the bliss of one's own true nature. This is consistent with what is recited by the Brāhmaṇas here in the context of the Soma sacrifice, during the occasion of the handing over of the staff to the initiated.

For in that regard, in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, in the sixth book, first section, fourth anuvāka, it is said: "Speech indeed departed from the gods, not remaining [with them]. It entered the trees; that speech speaks in the trees—whether in the drum, in the flute, or in the lute. When one gives the staff to the consecrated [sacrificer], he wins speech itself. This sound, though unstruck (*anāhata*), is perfumed by you; it is cognizable by you, it is the knower of what is cognizable by you, and it is the supreme knower of what is cognizable by you. Thus.

"Perceived by you" (*tvadupalakṣya*) refers to *uttara* (the subsequent). Even according to the alternative reading "perceived by you" (*tvadupalakṣya*) as "supreme" (*uttama*), it manifests in four or five ways like a struck sound. In the case of its fourfold manifestation: 1. It is "perfumed" (*vāsita*), meaning it exists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). It is the sound whose nature is the Supreme Word (*parāvāk*). 2. "Perceived by you": it is to be known by you alone through the nature of the Visionary Word (*paśyantī*). 3. Then, manifesting outwardly in the form of the Intermediate Word (*madhyamā-vāk*), it is indeed perceived by you; thus, it is "one who knows what is perceived by you. (Note: In the fivefold division, this would be further distinguished by the addition of the Word of Experience, *vaikhari*.)

"Vit" means one who knows (*vetti*). A "knower" (*vidvān*) is one whose nature consists of knowledge (*vidyātman*), meaning one who investigates the reality of his own essential form (*svarūpatattva*) and whose very being is sound (*śabdarūpa*). Such a person is a "knower of that which is characterized by You" (*tvadupalakṣyavit*). By virtue of this, he becomes a knower of the reality of Your essential form through an incomplete realization. Furthermore, by manifesting externally in the form of articulate speech (*vaikharī-vāk*), he becomes not only a knower of that which is characterized by You, but even more so a "knower of the knower of that which is characterized by You" (*tvadupalakṣyavittara*). Thus is this fourfold perspective of manifestation.

Even regarding the fivefold expansion (*pañcavidhasphuraṇa*), in the final portion of the commentary on the forty verses in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*, the sequence of the five-fold meaning—also known as the sequence of the five stages beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with manifestation (*bhāsa*)—is described as follows: "the appearance of the four lost objects; the persistence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three dissolved objects of knowledge; the state of being a knower who devours both the object and the means of knowledge; the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the object accompanied by conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*); and the appearance of the object devoid of conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). This is the sequence of the five-fold meaning that has been defined.

In this context, what is intended by the term "the sound struck by the first measure" (*prathamāhata-śabda*) is precisely the self-nature of consciousness (*svātmatattva-vimarśa*), which is synonymous with the manifestation of the fourfold objects that have been dissolved through non-difference from that [consciousness]. Through the maturation of that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it transforms into the form of the three *bindus*, being perfumed by the persistence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the three dissolved objects of knowledge. Furthermore, manifesting externally as *nāda*—which is synonymous with the reflective awareness of objects accompanied by conceptualization (*savikalpaka-meya-vimarśa*) and refined by its own latent impressions—it attains the state of *sphoṭa* in the form of the intermediate speech-sound (*madhyamā-vāk*).

Furthermore, by attaining the very nature of self-reflection (*svātmavimarśa*) in the form of the manifestation of the object of non-conceptual cognition—which is another synonym for *vaikharī*—even though it is similar to the external *vaikharī* form, it rests in its own bliss through the state of non-duality (*sāmarasya*) between sound and the source of sound, and thus becomes nothing other than its own essential nature; this is the transcendence of the fivefold manifestation of sound. Both of these points are clearly demonstrated by both scripture (*śruti*) and tradition (*āgama*): "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them."

The manifestation of the fourfold nature of sound is indicated by the Vedic revelation: "Three [quarters] are hidden in the cave and do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech humans speak. Furthermore, the manifestation of its fivefold nature is indicated by the Āgama: "Reflection (vimarśa), the Bindu, the Nāda, the Sphoṭa, and the Word (śabda)—this is the sequence of speech. Regarding the reading "uttara" (the transcendent): the practitioner, who consists of the universe, is called "uttara" because he transcends this [world] by virtue of his essential nature as that which transcends the universe.

Likewise, even in the reading *uttama*, the meaning is that [the state] is called *uttama* because from it one becomes free from darkness (*udgata-tamaska*) through the manifestation of the nature of the *mātṛkā-kuṇḍalinī*. Thus, in the thirteenth chapter of the *Agnipurāṇa*, beginning with the words "I shall describe the wheel of channels" (*nāḍīcakraṃ pravakṣyāmi*), the sequence of the fivefold worship of sound suitable for the meditation on the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*)—preceded by the etymological definitions of terms such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*—as well as the description of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) itself, preceded by its non-difference and coordination with sound, is to be seen in that very same place.

Furthermore, in this context, as stated in the *Dhātupāṭha*: "The root *vid* exists in the sense of being (*sattā*); in the sense of knowing, it is *vetti*; in the sense of deliberation, it is *vinte*; and in the sense of attainment, it is *vindate* and *vindati*," these are indeed distinctions in the meanings of the verbal roots. "I take refuge in that God who illumines the self through the intellect, whom [the Lord] creates as Brahmā in the beginning, and who indeed imparts the Vedas and the Vedāngas to him—[I], desiring liberation."

Thus, for the sake of understanding the nature of the sacred seat (*pīṭha*) of the deity—which is the incarnation of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) whose consciousness is awakened by the sentences of the Upaniṣads—it should also be considered through subtle vision that these [deities] are described as being of the nature of the four Vedas taught therein, or as being of the nature of the five Vedas; this too is a secret.

Furthermore, the poet will state this very same intention in the third *vimarśa* through the instruction on the worship of the *pīṭhas*, cremation grounds, and so forth; and in this *vimarśa* as well, by means of the difference and non-difference between word and meaning, starting with the verse: "That which You illuminate, the object whose body consists of both the substrate and its attributes, is manifested in the Lord," and so on. Enough of this elaboration. Even regarding the sequence of meaning, the fivefold manifestation of sound and the rest will be clearly established during the commentary on the verse "filled with the nectar of the fivefold meaning" in the fourth *vimarśa*; therefore, it is not analyzed here. (17–39)

Thus, having discerned the state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) between the unstruck (*anāhata*) and struck (*āhata*) speech, meaning, and sound, he demonstrates the nature of the vowels as being composed of the three abodes (*dhāmatraya*), the digits (*kalā*), and the two-fold characteristics of mutual womb and seed (*yonibīja*); this is described in the very first verse regarding the measure, the object of measurement, the means of measurement, and the knower. Furthermore, through the union of the two inherent qualities that delight the King [of Speech], he reveals their vowel-form:
"The digits of the one whose majesty is devoid of the six vowels, which are also bereft of the *sarga* [visarga] and the *bindu*, belong to the auspicious *Śuci*."
All the digits of the moon are, O Śivā,
the vowels which are the supreme wombs that have held the seed-syllables.

By the phrase "excluding the neuter" (*ṣaṇḍavarjam*) and so forth: O Śivā! [This is] either a vocative meaning "O you whose nature is the desire for auspiciousness," or a locative used with the intention of expressing the locus, meaning "in the auspicious practitioner whose form is the desire for auspiciousness. "Excluding the neuter" means excluding the four neuter vowels consisting of the previously mentioned group of sounds—*ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, and *lṝ*—which bear the shadow of both illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflection (*vimarśa*). The remaining digits (*kalā*) belong to the one possessing the brilliance of fire, namely the Sun; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. This applies even within that collection of twelve vowels.

Those which are devoid of the *sarga* (visarga) and the *bindu*, namely the remaining eleven vowels together with the *bindu* of meaning (*arthabindu*), or the ten vowels devoid of the triad of *bindus* consisting of the *visarga*, the *pūrṇa-anusvāra*, and the [ordinary] *anusvāra*—these are the *kalās* that come before the *śucaḥ*. In the reading "in the auspicious" (*śubhe*), the meaning is that they become *kalās* in the fire of Śiva, which is of the nature of the practitioner and has the form of auspiciousness. All of them indeed mean the sixteen vowels; they are the *kalās* of the Moon (*śaśin*).

Intent upon the held seed (*dhṛtabīja*): that is, in such a way that it becomes "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*), [occurring] within those seeds already held—which consist of the previously mentioned threefold, sixfold, twelvefold, and so forth types of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—or else within those forms of the womb (*yoni*) to be described hereafter, namely the *nahnāyoni*, *śaṅkhayoni*, *padmayoni*, and *divyayoni*; or else, in such a way that it becomes "various" (*vividha*).

When the seed-syllables (*bīja*) have been established, all vowels—whether numbering thirty-eight together with the three *mūrtikalās* consisting of the aforementioned reflections on *a*, *i*, and *u*, or numbering thirty-five when excluding those [three] and including the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*—are indeed the digits (*kalā*) of the Moon, being intent upon them and possessing their significance. In the reading *vidhṛtabījatatsvarāḥ*, "the seeds" refers to the thirty-five syllables consisting of the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*.

The vowels are for the purpose of pronouncing those seed-syllables (*bīja*) with ease. It should be understood that all these vowels are the *kalās* (energetic aspects) of the Moon—of the Sādāśiva-moon, who consists of two forms, the conventional and the ultimate, and who is composed of the two vowels, short and long, representing the unsurpassed form. Excluding its two conventional formal *kalās*, they number thirty-three.

And among those, within the seven *mūrtikalās*—which consist of the seven groups of the Seven Mothers (*saptamātṛkā*) and the seven *Kṛttikās*—one is the female form (*strīmūrtikalā*) named Ambānnā, consisting of either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*) among the kārakas. The other, however, is the male form (*puruṣamūrtikalā*), which is another synonym for the *nakṣatra* Abhijit, and consists of either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) among the kārakas.

For this very reason, the description of these seven forms of Kṛttikā by the name of the constellations (*nakṣatra*) is stated even in the Śruti: in the *Mahāgnicayana-kāṇḍa* of the *Taittirīya-saṃhitā*, in the fourth section of the fourth chapter, fifth lesson; and in the Brāhmaṇa, in the first book, and again in the second book of the Saṃhitā, it says: "Ambā, Dulā, Nitatni, Abhriyantī, Meghayantī, Varṣayantī, and Cupuṇīkā—by these names you are known."

The secret [of this teaching] is that in such passages as "the seven Kṛttikās," "the Brāhmaṇa is indeed the twenty-eighth among the lunar mansions," "there is a lunar mansion named Abhijit, above the Āṣāḍhās and below Śroṇā," and "Prajāpati had thirty-three daughters; he gave them to King Soma, but he went to Rohiṇī," there is the intentional attribution of the status of being the daughters of Dakṣa to the syllables themselves. || 18–40 ||

Thus, he says that the entire *mātṛkā*, differentiated by the distinctions of vowels, consonants, alternative synonyms, seeds (*bīja*), matrices (*yoni*), and designations (*saṃjñā*), is indeed the body of the Supreme Lord himself—consisting of action (*kriyāmaya*)—which has been accomplished through the "falling upon the cattle" (*paśupāta*) of the *mātṛkā* (to be described below) and the grace bestowed upon one hundred thousand cattle; which possesses the previously mentioned supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*) of one hundred thousand [verses]; and which unfolds through the manifestation of the universe as spoken in secret.
He states: "The *mātṛkā*, divided by the rules for seeds and matrices, is the mother characterized by the merit of [human] beings."
O Mother Śakti! Your body, consisting of action, triumphs as the supreme form of the Great Goddess. || 41 ||

By the words "born from seed" (*bījayoni*) and so forth, O Child, the distinction between the method of seed (*bījavidhi*) and the method of womb (*yoni*) is meditated upon. The method of seed is that which, even without union with a womb, is by nature the form of the vowels—another synonym for which is "consisting of self-shining bliss."

The "Method of the Womb" (*yonividhi*)—which is a synonym for the Supreme Emission (*anuttaravisarga*) of Śakti, also known as the Great Womb (*mahāyoni*)—is as follows: since it lacks the bliss of emission inherent to itself according to the conventions of the Kama-shastra, its state of being self-radiant bliss (*svaratva*), which is a synonym for the nature of the bliss of dependence on the other, depends solely upon union with the seed-syllable of the Supreme Emission of Śambhu consisting of *bindu*. By the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*), the letters of the womb, from *ka* to *kṣa*, which are the effects thereof, possess a bliss that is dependent on another, characterized by their own luminosity. Such is the Method of the Womb, which consists in this dependence on the bliss of the other.

Intending this very point, it is said in the *Gītā*: "O son of Kuntī, whatever forms arise in all wombs, of those the womb is Brahman, and I am the father who provides the seed. Thus, differentiated by the distinction between the method of the seed and the method of the womb, she has become divided. Mātṛkā is the garland of letters consisting of manifest sound.

Elsewhere, there is the rule regarding seed (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*), which consists of the eightfold distinction of marriage rules—such as the scriptural injunctions for performing rites like "one should marry a woman of the same caste who is younger and possesses auspicious marks"—as well as the rule regarding male seeds of various species mentioned in the *Kāmaśāstra*, such as the hare, the bull, and the horse, and the rule regarding wombs such as the *padminī*, *śaṅkhinī*, *citriṇī*, and *hastinī*.

She is distinguished by the classification of the four types of lovers in erotic sentiment—namely the *anukūla* (favorable), *dakṣiṇa* (tactful), *dhṛṣṭa* (bold), and *śaṭha* (deceitful)—as well as by the classification of the eight types of heroines in erotic sentiment according to their origins and characteristics, such as the *svīyā* (one’s own wife), *parakīyā* (another’s wife), *sāmānyā* (common woman), and *punarbhū* (widow remarried). She is the source of the distinctions of caste and so forth, the matrix of speech, and the woman who embodies the brother. She is characterized as the mother of humanity; for according to the root *man* meaning "to know," *manavaḥ* are the mantras that serve as the causes of knowledge.

Regarding those [sounds] and their birth—the act of being born and the one who is born—there is the "Mātṛ-lakṣaṇā" (the characteristic of the Mother). She is called *mā* because she measures (*māti*) herself or her own manifestation without limit, or because she delimits them through forms such as names and mantras; thus, she is the Fortune (*lakṣmī*) of speech and its meaning. She is called *tṛ* because she crosses over (*tarati*), leaving behind her prior nature consisting of unstruck sound (*nāda*) and descending to the level of articulated phonemes (*varṇa*). Both of these, *mā* and *tṛ*, are the two Mothers (*mātarau*), namely Prakṛti and Puruṣa. She is the "Mātṛ-lakṣaṇā" because she characterizes (*lakṣayati*) those two, or because those two themselves are her characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, she is the Mother of Manu (*manuja-mātṛ-lakṣaṇā*).

Elsewhere as well, she alone is the motherly form and the very nature of the progenitor for human beings—those *manus* who constitute the lineage of Manu—and is thus *pārameśvarī*. She is the *pārameśvarī*, the power (*śakti*) consisting of action (*kriyāmayī*), whose nature is the operation of the Word and its Meaning belonging to the union of the Supreme Goddess (*Parameśvarī*) and the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*). Elsewhere, in the form of the succession of the lineage of Gurus, she is the one who leads one to the union of the Supreme Goddess and the Supreme Lord, or who bestows supreme sovereignty; thus she is both *pārameśvarī* and the power consisting of action.

She whose body is yours—either because she performs the fivefold cosmic functions such as creation through this [body], or because she is stretched out (tanyase) and expanded as the essence of those five functions, or because she is diminished or cast away through various etymological derivations—is the embodiment of sound and meaning; inseparable from you, that body is victorious, existing in supreme excellence. Regarding the reading *sukṛtamātṛlakṣaṇā*: "He made himself by himself; therefore it is called 'well-made' (*sukṛta*). That which is indeed well-made is indeed the essence (*rasa*)."

"For having tasted this essence, one becomes blissful. For who indeed could inhale, who could exhale, if this bliss were not in the ether? He alone causes bliss. Thus, it should be understood that the Self itself—whose nature is the light of the Word (śabda-jyotis) consisting of the activity described in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad*—is the meaning of the term "well-done" (*sukṛta*). (19–41)

Having thus established that the Great Cause-Nāda (mahākāraṇanāda)—which consists of the aggregate of the nine Nādas and is composed of the ten previously mentioned fire-energies (vahnikalās)—is the cause of the body of the Mātṛkā consisting of action, through the division of seeds (bīja) and matrices (yoni), just as the digestive Vaiśvānara fire is the cause of the aggregate of the ten vital breaths; [the author] now further establishes its status as the Abhijit asterism by virtue of being the cause of the triad of aggregates formed by the nine Nādas of action, which consist of the causal, the effected, and the active.
"He who, characterized by intellect (buddhi), restrains the time of the syllable 'A', which consists of action and is the Bindu."
O Supreme One, whose nature consists of the three qualities, you are the resonance that is the desired form for one [seeking liberation], yet you are the cause of the other. 42.

By the words "the point" (*bindu*) and so forth: *he pari* may be taken as a vocative, meaning "O You who are of the nature of supreme speech" (*parāvāgrūpiṇī*). Alternatively, it may be taken as a locative of location, meaning "in the Supreme Self whose essence is resonance" (*nādātmake paramātmani*). It is thus construed according to different readings. That resonance (*nāda*), which is one's own essential nature (*svarūpātmaka*), has assumed a body that is desired; its form consists of five aspects: vowels, phonemes, the point (*bindu*), resonance (*nāda*), and the digit (*kalā*). For this very reason, it is characterized by intellect (*buddhilakṣaṇa*). According to the etymology "that which characterizes intellect," it possesses a body consisting of knowledge (*jñānamayaśarīra*); and according to the etymology "that which is characterized by intellect," it possesses a body consisting of action (*kriyāmayaśarīra*).

By the etymological derivation "that which binds (bindu) and vibrates (spandate)," it exists as the *bindu* whose body is the vibration of knowledge and action at the central point within the midst of the five forms (*rūpa*). It governs that which consists of the imperishable (*akṣaramaya*)—the nature of the indestructible self of knowledge—and that which consists of action (*kriyāmaya*)—the nature of the self of action composed of the syllables of Śiva. It regulates that which consists of the imperishable as the causal form rooted in indestructible knowledge, and that which consists of action as the effect-form; and it regulates that which consists of the indestructible syllables and knowledge. Thus, the syntactical connection of the single word is "it governs the womb" (*yoniṃ yantrayati*).

The connection should be understood through the form of the verbal root ending in the suffix *kyap* in the sense of "acting," as in: "Nāda itself acts like a controller. You are the embodiment of the threefold nature; that is, you are the very essence of the threefold nature consisting of cause, activity, and effect. You become the cause—the source—of another's transformation into the form of an effect, which is composed of activity. The meaning is that, abiding in the middle, you transform your own self into the dual form of both cause and effect, being yourself the embodiment of activity.

Regarding the reading *asya kāraṇam*: the meaning is that it is the cause of this very *anuttara-nāda* (the unexcelled sound), which, having taken the form of an action, has evolved into the effect known as the *akāra-nāda*. As for the phrase *tritayadharmarūpiṇi*, in the short-vowel reading, it should be understood as an adjective qualifying either the Supreme Self in the form of *parāvāk*—addressed in either the vocative or the locative case—or the one whose nature is *nāda*.

Thus, it is established that even the difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) between Kālī and Kāla—who are, respectively, the *parāvāk* and the *nāda*, and who consist of the aggregate of the triad of effect, cause, and action, as well as the aggregate of the two groups of six consisting of *nāda* and *anāda*—is merely produced by the exchange of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*) based on [the Lord's] will; it is not real, just like the illusory appearance of an elephant or a bull in a painting. Therefore, everything is beyond reproach. (20–42)
