Having been addressed thus, he says that the manifestation of vibration occurs solely through the connection with the power of your vital breath (*prāṇakriyāśakti*), which resides in the center like a waveless ocean due to its relation to the wind of Mahākāla, the Lord of the Universe, whose nature is the Great Cause-sound (*mahānāda*):
"The first wave is exertion (*udyama*), and the subsequent one belongs to the waveless ocean of consciousness of Śiva."
O Sovereign Lady, prior to the assumption of a previously unaccumulated state, Your body was as vast as the great ocean within the sky.

By the words beginning with "udyama" (exertion), etc.: O Īśvarī! [The meaning of the vocative is as follows: prior to Your assumption of the state of insentient matter (*acitpadaparigrahātprāk*), You are the regulator by means of Your abiding in the middle between the inner triad of the vital breath's vibration (*prāṇaspanda*)—which consists of the previously mentioned upward desire and unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—and the outer triad of the vital breath's vibration—which consists of the waves of the command of bliss (*ānandeśanormyātmaka*). This refers to You, who are composed of consciousness (*cinmayā*) and consist of the subsequent vitalization (*uttaraprāṇanādātmikā*), prior to Your assumption of the state of insentient matter.

In the sequence of words (*śābdakrama*), this means prior to the assumption of a limited form consisting of the vibration of the breath—which is insentient and arises from the external Anuttara characterized by the triad of bliss (*ānanda-tripuṭī*). And in the sequence of objects (*arthakrama*), it means prior to the assumption of the vibration of the power of insentient action (*jaḍa-kriyā-śakti*). It is "waveless" (*nistaraṅga*) because there is an absence of transformation into activity conducive to the nature of waves, since it consists solely of the opposite will (*viparītecchā-mātra*) derived from the verbal root *vaś* (to desire) through the transposition of its syllables, [thereby signifying] the ocean of the consciousness of Śiva.

The ocean of the consciousness of Śiva is free from the waves of the activity of effects consisting of waves [of desire], being the ocean of the consciousness of Śiva whose body consists merely of the unfolding of will (*icchā-unmeṣa*). Likewise, by virtue of its nature as the will for the opposite, it consists of the continuous waves of the activity of effects; and in the sequence of objects, it is the ocean of the external-facing consciousness of Śiva. Its first vibration is the exertion (*udyama*), occurring through the body of the supreme will (*anuttara-icchā*) and the supreme unfolding (*anuttara-unmeṣa*).

The meaning is that *unmeṣa* (the opening) is indeed synonymous with *udyama* (exertion), based on the etymological derivation that it "controls the opening" (*unmeṣaṃ yamayati*) through mere internal effort, whether it be the manifestation of a contrary joy consisting of external instruction or [the joy] within and without which consists of the cause. The underlying intention is that the subsequent *spanda* (vibration) is understood to be an effect, by virtue of its being a great arising in the form of a wave.

*Uttara* is so called because the practitioner is raised up from this state, whether by means of inward-turned or outward-turned orientation; it is the vibration (*spanda*) occurring subsequent to the aforementioned apprehension of the state of consciousness (*cit*), consisting of the triad of verbal bliss or the triad of objective bliss. Being a wave in the form of the activity of an effect, it exists in the *vyoman*, that is, in the internal space (*daharākāśa*). It is the "great rising" (*mahodaya*), meaning the emergence of splendors (*mahaḥ*), which are either lights or festivals.

Your body becomes the form of rising splendor, or the form of a rising festival—Amara states that *maha*, *udbhava*, and *utsava* are synonyms. It is either the causal vibration (*kāraṇaspanda*) consisting of the rising nature of the triad of verbal bliss (*śābdānandatripuṭī*), or the triad of objective bliss (*ārthikānandatripuṭī*) consisting of the rising nature. If [the Self] is transcendent to the universe, it exists as the Lord of Yogins (*yogīśvara*) or the ascetic (*yati*) in the form of a mass of rising splendor through the manifestation of action both internally and externally in the form of waves; or it becomes the Lord of Enjoyment (*bhogīśvara*) or the sovereign (*bhūpati*) in the form of a mass of rising festivals—this is the intended meaning.

If the intention is to take *vyomanīśvarī* as a single compound word, then by its connection with the *lṛk*-compound, the meaning of the vocative case is "O you who are the regulator of the function within the subtle ether (*daharākāśa*)! In the reading *tataḥ* (instead of *tathā*), following the prior inclusion of the word *acinmaya* ("consisting of the insentient"): just as, according to grammarians, the first vibration (*spanda*) occurs prior to the inclusion of the word *cinmaya* ("consisting of consciousness"), being insentient due to verbal cognition and having mere exertion as its body; so too, prior to the inclusion of the word for insentient action (*jaḍakriyā*) which pertains to the object, the first vibration, though consisting of consciousness, is insentient with respect to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

The meaning is as follows: first, there is the mere effort within the body itself; thereafter, the vibration of verbal knowledge or the vibration of objective action, being transcendent to the universe, becomes the "greatly arising wave" (*mahodaya-ūrmi*) in the form of a wave of activity and its effects. In the reading *mahodayāḥ* (feminine gender), it should be understood that "woman" (*strī*) is a specific designation for the body. (21–43)

Thus, having described how this very triad consisting of agent, object, and action takes on the form of the Great Arising (*mahodaya*) through the nature of knowledge and action, he now demonstrates its great significance as the triple and quadruple flow—consisting of five attributes whose characteristics will be explained below—by means of its various locations, namely the states of the Sky-farer (*khecarī*), the Gaze-possessor (*dṛkvarī*), the Quarter-farer (*dikcarī*), and the Object-farer (*gocarī*): "O Mother! This expansion, which has resorted to the Sky-farer state within the direction of the breath..."
The cow, having followed the circle of fodder and reached the place where she grazes, became [your] very own. 44.

By the words beginning with *sphāritā* (*svāditā*), etc.: "O Mother" is an address containing a reason (*hetugarbhitasaṃbuddhi*). This is the very seeking (*eṣaṇā*). It consists of the first vibration and exertion (*udyama*) of the triad of agent, object, and action mentioned previously; it is the Will (*icchā*). "Made to expand" (*sphāritā*) means it has been brought to a state of throbbing manifestation, revealed in the form of a wave consisting of the second vibration. In the reading *svāditā janani neyameṣaṇā*, the meaning is: "O Mother, this seeking has not been tasted."

The meaning is that the resolve for creation—being of the nature of play, as stated in the passage, "The Lord’s creation is mere will; others say it is for the sake of sport"—is devoid of egoism and thus has not been experienced through craving for sense objects. This is stated by the Śruti: "One [the Self] eats, while the other looks on. Alternatively, the meaning is that the power of man (mānuṣī śaktiḥ) has not been tasted, whereby one becomes a human being. In the sky (khe), both in the internal space (daharākāśa) and the elemental space (bhūtākāśa), she remains unresorted to (asamupāśritā).

Taking recourse in *aṃ*—which is the mere vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of the Śākta supreme emission (*anuttara-visarga*)—and in *aḥ*—which is the mere vibration of the resonance (*nāda*) of the Śāmbhava supreme emission—and yet not taking recourse [in them], let her move in the void (*kha*), whether in the internal space (*daharākāśa*) or the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). By this, let her become the power named Khecarī; thus, the verb is used in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) to express a prayer. In the reading *khecaraty asum upāśritā*, it means that having taken recourse in the vital breath (*asu*), she moves in the void; she is one who moves solely within the internal space.

The one named *khecarī* within moves only in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), while the one named *khecarī* outside is the power of the *mudrā*. This is the meaning. As it is stated in another tantra regarding the definition of the *khecarīmudrā* through the distinction of their respective characteristics: "With the internal as the object and the gaze directed outward, free from blinking and opening—the eyes—this is that *khecarīmudrā*, hidden in all tantras. In this same way, the definitions and other characteristics of the powers of the *mudrās* should be understood in what follows as well. [In] the direction.

By connecting with the first reading, *caratvasamupāśritā*, or by connecting with the second reading, *caratyasumupāśritā*, the construction is as before: she is either the power (*śakti*) or the mudrā named *Dikcarī*. *Akṣacakra* refers to the wheel of the letters of the Mother (*mātṛkā*), which is the wheel of phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* through the process of pratyāhāra, as well as the wheel of the sense organs (*indriyacakra*). *Anujagmuṣī* means having followed after. *Gavī* is the power named *Gocarī*.

The meaning is that because the word *go* denotes the sense organs—such as the eye and speech—and their functions, the power (*śakti*) named *Dṛkcarī* is also the *mudrā* whose form consists of the sense organs such as speech. Therefore, she has attained the state of being an object of perception (*gocarapadā*). The term *gocarapada* refers to the locus of the contact between the sense objects and the sense organs. This is because the word *go* [is used in the following senses], according to the *Amarakośa*: "In the feminine, *go* [denotes] heaven, the arrow, cattle, speech, the thunderbolt, direction, the eye, the sun, the earth, and water; in the masculine, it denotes the target and the gaze. [And also: "*gauḥ*, *gmā*..."

In the *Sāṃkhyasūtras*, the term *kṣmā* is listed as a synonym for the earth (*bhū*); thus, its denotation of "earth" is also understood. [The phrase] "the place of movement on the earth" refers to one who has attained the state of the range of what is reached and what is not reached. *Svayaṃbhava*—the power (*śakti*) and mudrā named *Bhūcarī*—is used in the sense of a prayer or an address, functioning as a vocative.

Regarding the reading *bhavaḥ svayam*: from the root *bhū* in the sense of "existence," *bhava* means "that which exists. Thus, it refers either to Śaṅkara, whose body is pure existence; or to the Self-born Brahmā (*svayaṃbhu*), who is of the nature of primordial matter (*prakṛti*); or, since the word *bhava* denotes both transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) and Śiva, according to the respective context, it may refer to the form of either the individual soul (*jīva*), Śiva, or transmigratory existence. The meaning is that he exists as the very essence of Śiva.

Thus, here, by the power of the pun on the word *bhava*, there is the secret of the four aims of human life embraced within the ninefold resonance (*nāda*) of the Śrīcakra—whether conceived as non-dual through the desired state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) with either the four or five Mudrās and Śaktis, or as distinct—and which, through the fivefold meanings of the words *maṅgala*, *janman*, *jīva*, *śiva*, and *saṃsāra* (referring to the pentad of Svayaṃbhu, Brahmā, Khecaryā and the other five Śaktis), culminates in liberation (*mokṣa*), known as the bliss of one's own essential nature.
Furthermore, it should be understood by the wise that the secret of the fifth human goal (*pañcamapuruṣārtha*) has also been slightly unveiled through subtle scrutiny. || 22-44 ||

He explains the fifth [state], which is the nature of the *prakṛti* with parts externally and the nature of the supreme, partless *parā-nāda-prakṛti* internally, within the fivefold powers of the *mudrās*—the *khecarī* and others, along with *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi* mentioned in the previous verse—by their inclusion within one of the aforementioned categories; namely, how the four [powers] exist externally in the form of speech and meaning as the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*), and the four aims of life (*caturvarga*), etc.:
"O Mother, that quartet beginning with *khecarī*, together with its essence (*sāra*) and parts (*sāṃśa*), is Your external body."
That which devours the distinction between duality and non-duality is partless, not external, and indeed beyond the reach of words.

By the words "beginning with Khecarī" and so forth: O Mother! that quartet beginning with Khecarī—which, according to the previously mentioned method, is a quartet formed by the intended unity of either Gobhūcarī and Dṛkcaryā or Dṛgdicaryā—is the *sāra* (essence), meaning its stable constituent part, like thickened milk, butter, or ice. That is Your external body (*bahirvapuḥ*), which consists of speech and meaning; the sense is that it is Your external body of sound (*nāda*) as it functions through the aggregate of the physical body and the senses.

In the case of the two alternative readings, *haṃsam amba* or *sāśam amba*, the meaning is that [the body] is endowed with parts by way of the names and forms of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), either as the play of the Śāmbhava emission (*visarga*) or as the play of the Śākta emission. That "body" (*vapuḥ*) is the devourer (*ghasmara*) of the dual division—that is, the consumer of both the dual division consisting of name and form and the non-dual division consisting of the vibration of the vital breath; or rather, it is the illuminator of both.

That body which consists of the supreme *nāda* (sound) made of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is partless; for there is no distinction between name and form, or because it is one with the Light (*prakāśa*). This is the intended meaning. Therefore, it is "not external" (*abāhiḥ*), as it does not exist outside. For this very reason, it is "not a word-object" (*na vākpadam*); a "word-object" (*vākpadam*) is that which is reached or can be expressed by speech (*vācā padyate*). Since it is not such [an object], it is "not a word-object. The meaning is that, because its sole body is *nāda*, it is beyond the range of speech.

Alternatively, the phrase "that partless body of sound (nādaśarīra) is neither external nor internal" contains an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) for the purpose of questioning: "Is it not internal?"—meaning, it is indeed internal. If one asks why, it is because it is being traversed by the very nature of speech itself, through the form of the nine sounds (*navanāda*) described as follows: "Bindu, artha, candra, rodhinī, nāda, nādānta, śakti, vyāpikā, samana, and unmanā are proclaimed as the nine sounds," which constitute the function of the fourfold speech beginning with Parā and Paśyantī; thus, it is of the nature of being traversed by speech itself.

Therefore, it is "not external" (abahiḥ), meaning it is internal both in its objective body and its verbal body; or the meaning is that it does not exist outside of the letter 'A'. Or, the relationship of cause and effect may be applied as one pleases. Because it is not external, it is therefore partless (niraṃśa). Because it is partless, it is therefore the devourer of the distinction between duality and non-duality. For this very reason, it is the "word of speech" (vākpada); the sense is that it is eternally present in the form of speech. In the reading "abahir nu vākpadam," the particle *nu* indicates deliberation (*vitarka*).

The meaning is: why is it internal (*ābhyantara*) because it is accessible to the mind (*manogamya*)? If one asks why, the intention is that the word *vāk* (speech) is indeed accessible to the mind, since it is traversed by speech as well. This has also been stated in the Śruti: "What one contemplates with the mind, that one speaks with speech; that one performs through action. Alternatively, *nu* signifies certainty: the word *vāk* is indeed within the range of speech alone. If one asks why, it is because it is not external (*abahiḥ*). It should be understood as being focused on the coiled serpent (*sarpakuṇḍalī*) of the waters (*āpya*).

Therefore, the sense is that it is merely a matter of words. Alternatively, *nu* may signify doubt; thus the meaning is that, according to the scriptural statement, "It is to be perceived by the mind alone," it is to be attained solely through inquiry. || 23-45 ||

Now, demonstrating through the outward and inward movement of the goddess Parāvāk—who consists of the fivefold vital functions—along with the body of sound (*nāda*) composed of the inner reflection of all things, [the author] shows the state of *kula* and *akula*, as well as the state of *akula* and *kula* regarding Śiva and Śakti, and demonstrates that Śiva is the locus of rest for Śakti:
"O Mother! Your body of fivefold functions has emerged; Śakti, having bestowed the splendor of *Kula*, is seated upon her throne."
Since you have come from the lineage of Śiva, you shall find rest there once again. 46.

By the words beginning with *paṃcavṛtti* and so forth: O Mother! You, along with Śiva, have offered—that which has been mutually bestowed—the *kulaprathāsanā*. The *kula* is the collection of like categories, such as the triad of sound (*nāda*), speech (*vāk*), and meaning (*artha*), as well as the five currents (*pañcavāha*) and so on, and the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) and so forth; for it is said, "The *kula* is remembered as that which is of the same class. Its *prathā* is its expansion; that is to say, its manifestation.

In the reading *prabhāsanā*, the meaning is: the illumination (*prakāśa*) of the *kula*—that is, the collection of similar elements such as the *tripuṭī*, or the family-dharma of the four castes and so forth. She whose seat (*āsana*) is such an expansion (*prathā*) or power (*prabhāva*) is [the Goddess]. For this very reason, she has a body consisting of five functions (*pañcavṛttitanu*).

In the state where your family-lineage (*kulaprathā*) has been offered to Śiva, you expand—that is, you extend—the functioning of the five senses and so forth; and in that state where your family-lineage has been offered to Śiva, you likewise dissolve the functioning of the five senses, the five elements, the vital breaths, and so forth. Thus, you are "the body of the five functions" (*pañcavṛttitanuḥ*). You [proceed] from *Akula*—from the *Nāda* in the form of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) situated at the Mūlādhāra, or from that which is devoid of the qualities of the family-lineage of phonemes and forms—from Śiva, that is, from the *Jīva-Śiva*.

Likewise, although the *kula-dharma* exists through the predominance of *nāda*, it is understood that [the state] is devoid of connection to the *kula-dharma* due to the predominance of *varṇa*, arising from the *akāra-nāda* located in the *brahmarandhra* at the thousand-spoked [lotus], from Śiva, from Paraśiva, and from that which is devoid of *kula*.

From the verbal root *vaś* meaning "desire," through a permutation of letters (*varṇavyatyaya*), there arises the word *vaśā*, signifying the Power (*śakti*) that has emerged from the Jīva-Śiva—whose synonym is desire (*icchā*) and who is listed in the *siṃhādi* group of roots—or from the Supreme Śiva (*paraśiva*). Having again united with that Jīva-Śiva or the Supreme Śiva according to the distinction between the *kula* and *akula* natures, you attain rest (*viśrama*) therein, whether in the Jīva at the thousand-petaled lotus of the *kula*, or in the Supreme Śiva at the thousand-petaled lotus of the *akula*. You reach [that state].

Furthermore, regarding the reading *eṣa viśramaḥ* (this is rest): the meaning is that this very process of the departure and arrival of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Supreme Śiva constitutes your "rest," which takes the form of the *āṇava-visarga* characterized by repose. Therefore, both the *kula* and *akula* possess the nature of Śakti and Śiva, being essentially the individual soul and Śiva. As it is said in another Tantra: "The six wheels within the Mūlādhāra constitute the state known as *kula*. Therein, O Goddess, are the three knots, which are encompassed by two of those wheels. (1)

"The two wheels of Earth and Water, arising from the location of the *brahmagranthi*, are composed of Fire and Sun, great and full of splendor. The two wheels composed of Wind and Space, described by the term *viṣṇugranthi*, are made of fire (*taijasa*) and bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*). The two excellent wheels, described by the term *rudragranthi*, are the great abode of auspiciousness," and so forth. And in the *Kaulopaniṣad*: "They say that *Akula* is Śiva, and *Kula* is declared to be Śakti."

"The continuous connection between the Kula and Akula is designated as Kaula. Furthermore, there is the statement in the *Lalitāsahasranāma*: "Kaulinī is the Yoginī of Kula. By this, it is established that Mahākālī’s being the body of the meaning of Śiva and Kālā through her non-difference from the soul of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is explicitly stated; and likewise, that Kālaśiva—who has action and speech as his body—is the locus of repose for Kālī. (24–46)

Having stated this according to the established rule, he says that the aforementioned pentad of powers— Khecarī and the others— is itself designated by the five names Śiva, Śakti, and so forth, through the distinction of intending either the substrata or their attributes, by way of a logical pentad of functions consisting of the five elements: "Indeed, your pentad of functions,
which consists of the functions of the qualities of the five elements, is perceived as such."
That which is named Dharmavṛttikṛtasiddha and that which is named Dharmavṛttikṛtaśakti belong to you. || 47 ||

By the words "by means of yoga" (*yuktitaḥ*) and so forth: O Mother! Your fivefold activity (*vṛttipañcaka*), which consists of the previously mentioned forms such as Khecarī and the rest, [arises] by means of yoga—namely, from that which is called *melāpa* (union) and from the attainment of knowledge (*jñānasaṅgati*). According to Amara, "yoga" is used in the senses of preparation, means, attainment of knowledge, and application. It is the activity within which the five elements and their qualities, such as sound and the rest, reside. That is the fivefold activity.

Likewise, the fivefold function (*vṛttipañcaka*) exists within the five elements and the [five] qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, by means of different grammatical analyses (*vigraha*), it is characterized as "the function of the qualities of the five elements. For this very reason, it is called "that whose names are established by the functions of the substrata" (*dharmivṛttikṛtasiddhanāmaka*): that is, the fivefold function whose names—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—are established by the functions of the substrata, such as Vāmadeva and others, and by the activities of creation and so forth, such as "earthly odor" and the like.

Likewise, by those whose conduct is in accordance with *dharma*—such as Vyomeśvarī, Khecarī, and others—and by those such as Gandhavatī and Pṛthivī, the name "Kṛtaśakti" (Power of the Kṛta Age) is established, as is the name "Kriyāśakti" (Power of Action) pertaining to the Kṛta and other ages. These indeed belong to you alone. Regarding the reading "the name Kṛtaśakti": the meaning is that the very name "Kṛtaśakti," which pertains to the functions of *dharma*, becomes the "Siddha-named" (named after the accomplished ones) through the intended reference to the functions of the substratum (*dharmivṛtti*); it is also the "Śikṣita-siddha-named" (named after those perfected through training) because of its state of being most venerable.

Just as there is a distinction of powers (*śakti*)—such as Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, and Gāyambikā—due to the desire to express a difference in attributes (*dharma*), and likewise the identity of Kāla and Śiva due to the desire to express the unity of their substrates (*dharmin*); so too, there is a distinction among the perfected beings (*siddha*) such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva due to the desire to express a difference in substrates, while the identity of the power as Bhūtaprakṛti, Kālī, and so forth, due to the desire to express the unity of the substrate, is exactly the same. Thus, in either of these two pairs, because of the identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), the meaning is that Prakṛti or Puruṣa is indeed ninefold.
By this, it is established that the relationship between knowledge and action as attribute and substratum is also a matter of will. || 25-47 ||

Having spoken thus, he says that one who knows the pentad of elements together with their powers— which consists of the bliss of the five Brahmans differentiated merely by the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and so forth— as being the form of your own Unmanī-nāda, is indeed one who has accomplished his purpose: "The pentad of Siddhas beginning with Brahmā,
and the pentad of Śaktis beginning with Bhāratī."
That person who remembers your form on the path of the Siddhas during the full-moon festival is victorious. || 48 ||

"Beginning with Brahmā": this means beginning from Brahmā, consisting of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. "The pentad of the Siddhas," and likewise "the pentad of Śaktis beginning with Bhāratī," meaning consisting of Bhāratī, Lakṣmī, Gaurī, Vāmā, and Ambikā. That person, even though born as a practitioner (*sādhaka*), remembers Your form as *unmanī*; he brings the form condensed by the nature of the *unmanī-nāda* within the range of his memory.

This practitioner, having ascended through mindfulness to the form of your *unmanī* state, possesses the mental activity (*vṛtti*) of *nāda-unmanī*. He triumphs—that is, he exists with supreme excellence—on the path of the perfected ones (*siddhavartmani*). Regarding the reading *siddhaparvaṇi*: a "parvan" is that which fills a count; it is a reckoning. Furthermore, even within the multitude of rays, he is one whose mental activity is *unmanī-nāda* at the *bindu* of the *dvādaśānta*; he consists of the *mātṛkā-vidyā-pīṭha*, which comprises the fourfold reflective awareness (*turīya-vimarśa*) and the sequence beginning from the earthly element up to ether, as will be described hereafter.

The suffix *kip* is used in the sense of "practicing" (*ācāra*), meaning that she herself acts by means of the power of Jayākālī. The meaning is that she becomes one who completes the number of the assembly of Siddhas. By the word "remembers," the intention is: if such is the fruit for the rememberer alone, how much more so for the knower? || 23-48 ||

Now, in order to dispel the practitioner's notion of the differentiation of objects, he states that the cause of creation is latent impression (*vāsanā*): "O Lord, whatever object You manifest, that is created as having the body of both subject and predicate."
That light which exists here, when fashioned by you, assumes various forms and attains the state of creation.

By the words "thou," and so forth: here, within the form of the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti, which consists of the *unmanī* and *nāda*, the meaning is "thou art such a one, whose nature is the bindu and nāda of reflective awareness. The sense is that thou manifestest toward whichever practitioner (*sādhaka*), acting as light itself in the form of that which is to be manifested.

The term *dharmidharmatanuḥ* means that which extends (*tanoti*) or expands (*vistārayati*) either the substrate (*dharmin*) as its own nature through the property (*dharma*), or conversely, the property consisting of the body of speech and meaning—composed of the aggregate of body and senses—as the nature of the substrate; or it causes one of the two to diminish. Thus, it is called *dharmidharmatanuḥ*. Alternatively, by the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*), the meaning is that it possesses a body consisting of both the substrate and the property. For this very reason, it has "meaning" (*artha*) in the Lord (*īśvara*). It has the form of the object of meaning (*arthaśarūpa*) in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) of either a man or a woman.

Or rather, [the person] is created with the body of the subject (dharmin), the predicate (dharma), or both. For this very reason, the beloved woman desires either the illusory human goal consisting of gold and the like, or the goal of the experience of her own true nature, which consists of the fivefold activity and the proficiency of knowledge (*vidyā*); such is the meaning of "object" (*artha*). Regarding the term "in the Lord" (*īśvare*), the locative case is to be applied respectively according to the intention to express either the status of being the instigator (*prayojakatva*) or the status of being the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*). The meaning is that, impelled by the Lord or having the Lord as his locus, he comes to desire whatever desire is either illusory or composed of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*).

This has also been stated by the Blessed One in the *Gītā*: "Whatever form a devotee desires to worship with faith, I make that very faith of his firm. Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity]; the fruit of those of small intellect becomes finite. By such passages, it is shown that even the fruit of both types of human goals (puruṣārtha) is finite due to the smallness of their intellect.

It should also be understood that after the realization of one's own true nature (*svasvarūpatattva*), even the goal of human life consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya-puruṣārtha*) possesses finitude only from the perspective of being a "human goal," but not from the perspective of one's essential nature (*svarūpa*). From the perspective of one's essential nature, however, both knowledge and ignorance are infinite precisely because they are forms of the Self's manifestation (*ātmavibhūti*). Furthermore, in this context, the meaning implied is that since the Lord (*īśvara*) is defined as "the object" (*artha*), by being fixed solely upon Brahman—whether as the literal meaning or the implied sense—and lacking the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between those two which consists of the *nāda* (the primordial sound), the Lord too is essentially incomplete in his nature.

Therefore, [scriptures state]: "He who controls the mind from within, whom the mind does not know, whose body is the mind; He who controls the Self from within," and so forth. Furthermore, the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, beginning with "This is the Self, the inner controller, the immortal," also demonstrates that the status of being the inner controller belongs to the Lord alone—as the immutable identity of the incomplete reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa)—and not to the immutable Self (kūṭasthātman), because that would lead to an infinite regress. For this very reason, it is said: "The Lord is the outward unfolding (unmeṣa); Sadāśiva is the inward closing (nimeṣa)."

Another Tantra also confirms the Lord’s role as the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmitā*) by emphasizing His intent toward external manifestation: "That practitioner, though threefold, is created; [he is created] by You alone, consisting of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The implied meaning is that having become such a practitioner, he enters into creation as a constituent part of it. Furthermore, "the perfected one" (*siddha*) here means one who has been fashioned by Your *unmanī* state as previously described; "light" (*prakāśa*) is indeed of a nature non-different from Light itself.

The statement that this was performed by you, whose nature is the *unmanī* and *nāda*, even regarding Kālaśiva, is not intended to express his lack of autonomy; rather, following the maxim of "not disparaging," it is aimed at highlighting the predominance of the power of *nāda*. As it is said in the *Saundaryalaharī*: "If Śiva is joined with Śakti, he is able to manifest [the universe]," and so forth. He, having established such a nature, is the practitioner of the highest qualification (*uttamādhikārī*). He possesses those various forms; by his very freedom, he appears in the form of various places, times, objects, and so on.

"Sṛṣṭitām" means the state of being created, the nature of being created, or, in other words, conformity with creation. "Upaiti" means he partakes of; the sense is that he attains sovereignty over creation. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "It expands, as it were; it wavers, as it were. The intention is that from the perspective of others, he appears to partake in conformity with creation. For this very reason, it was stated by this same poet in the *Dvādaśamañjarikāstava*: "Human beings, animals, and gods—this triple world, submerged in the ocean of existence, consisting of the three qualities, is a manifestation of Māyā."
"And if, O Mother, even a sidelong glance were cast here somewhere out of compassion, this embodied being would immediately attain the state of a body composed of supreme bliss. (27-49)

Now, having spoken by means of the sound of the *unmanī* [state], which is of the nature of consciousness, he—while illuminating the impermanence of even the bodyless sound-body of the Supreme Deity (who consists of consciousness and whose other synonym is *citta*, being composed of latent impressions)—and while demonstrating that even in the sequence of the contraction of the Guru’s flowers about to be described, the lineage of Gurus and disciples rooted in the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) is the fundamental form of the word and its meaning, says:
"For you are devoted to the *citta*; without the variegatedness of objects, there is no state of non-*citta* for you."
If you are taught without the mandala of the object, how can there be the state of mind at the point of creation? || 50 ||

By the words beginning with "tvaṃ hi" (you indeed), the meaning is: you are of the nature of *unmanī* and *nāda*. For (*hi*) because of this, you expand (*tanuṣe*), extend, and [ultimately] dissolve the mind (*citta*)—according to the various etymological derivations [of the word *tanu*]. You are the embodiment of the power (*śakti*) which consists of both knowledge and action; for that very reason, you possess a body of consciousness (*ciccharīrā*). Therefore, for you (*te*), there is no state of being a mind directed toward objects (*viṣayacittatām*), even when in the form of an object, without the functioning of consciousness (*cidvṛttitām*).

In the reading *vinā citratām*—the meaning is: "without the state of being a function of the wonder of consciousness (*cit*) within the manifold variety of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For this very reason, it is said in another Tantra: "Consciousness itself first becomes the mind (*citta*); then, through attachment to objects, it assumes the form of the phenomenal world and is designated as 'the variegated' (*citra*). The sense is that [consciousness] is identified with the full moon because it is the face of the year (*vatsara*). "In the sky" (*khe*) means either in the internal space (*daharākāśa*) or in the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*). "There is no state of mind for us" (*naḥ cittatā*) means there is no mental activity (*cittavyavahāra*). In the reading *svena*, the meaning is: "by its own nature as pure consciousness" (*svacitsvarūpeṇa*).

Thus, having refuted the notion that the Supreme Deity possesses a nature consisting of an imagined mental state colored by objects—just as a crystal appears red through external influence—he demonstrates, by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the logic of "how much more so"), that even the negation of that [imagined state] follows as a consequence. He shows that within the sequence of the sixfold lineage of gurus—consisting of the *paraugha*, *mahaugha*, *divya*, *siddha*, *mānava*, and *śiṣya*—which is indicated by the *Mahārthakrama* and belongs to the insentient primordial nature (*prakṛti*) composed of the functions of cognition and action, even the lineage of gurus known as the *śiṣyaugha* possesses the nature of the Root Transmission (*kramamūla*), provided there exists the sovereignty of Word and Meaning.

He shows this with the words "of the disciple. Without the *arthamaṇḍala*—that is, without the category of objects of knowledge consisting of speech and its referents—at the boundary of emanation (*sargasīman*), on the path of the ultimate creation of speech and meaning which consists of the performance of desireless action (*niṣkāmakarmānuṣṭhāna*) that is the Śākta emission (*śāktavisarga*); if you [the disciple] remain as the one who possesses the fruit, in the form of the "residual" (*śeṣin*) subject who attains the results of knowledge and action—which are synonyms for "being a knower" and "being an agent"—then how could there be the expansion of manifold worldly activity (*vittatā citravyavahāra*)? This is the sense of the question expressed through the elision of the conditional particle (*yadi*) in a context of possibility.

The meaning is this: although there exists a relationship consisting in the superimposition of identity with agency and so forth in one who perceives the mere fruit of the act of observation while remaining of a different class (*asavarṇa*), he is nonetheless of the very nature of the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*) composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*). This is because he is capable of the conventional usage of "mind" (*citta-tattva*) and because he is fit for entry into the lineage of disciples and the succession of gurus. He is not like a pillar or a wall, nor is he like animals, birds, and other lower species, such that his conventional usage as "mind" would be unfit for address through speech.

Regarding the reading *kuto 'sti*: the clear meaning is that there is no state of being consciousness (*cittatā*) from any source whatsoever. The sense is this: while the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) remains in its status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatva*) toward the expression of people, there is an absence of coloring by objects; however, in its status as the predominant element (*śeṣitā*), how could there be any coloring by objects?

The literal meaning is as follows: since the status of being a knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth is impossible for the factors of the knower and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in the absence of an object of knowledge (*prameya*), the conventional usage of the term "consciousness" (*cittattva*)—which results in the establishment of conventional usage regarding the body, senses, and so forth, even though they are objects of knowledge consisting of consciousness—is merely established through superimposition (*adhyāropa*), and is not real, just like the conventional usage of "consciousness" applied to inert objects of knowledge such as pillars and jars.

Now, one might object: "If the mental activity (*cittavyavahāra*) directed toward the sphere of insentient objects of knowledge is indeed prohibited for the Supreme Deity, then alas, since that very mind—which is the aggregate of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), constitutes a part of the body of the 'Triad' (*tripuṭī*) consisting of either the Great Subject (*mahāpramātṛ*) or the object of knowledge, it would necessarily destroy the essential nature of Sṛṣṭikālī, who is the Consciousness-Power (*cicchakti*) of that Triad. Anticipating this doubt, [the text proceeds] with the meditation on her, whose belly contains the universe characterized by power (*śakti*), and whose body is the *unmanī*, the *nāda*, and *sṛṣṭikālī*.

Reaffirming the state of having a sunken belly mentioned in the verse, he refutes the variegated nature of the inert world— otherwise known as the diversity of creation— which is the object of her own consciousness-based latent impressions (*vāsanā*):
"If you alone are the progenitor here of that supreme state which transcends the variegation of the multitude of latent impressions..."
[O Goddess] whose belly bears the world characterized by power,
[you reside] upon the chest of the Son of Mānasa and Indriyaka.

By the words "vāsanā" and so forth: here, at the boundary of the emission of the triad consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—the ninefold resonance (*nāda-navaka*)—there is the one whose belly bears the world characterized by power (*śakti*). The powers are the previously mentioned Khecarī and others, which constitute the characteristic of the world. By the etymological derivation that "the world (*jagat*) goes (*gacchati*"), it refers either to the totality of the ninefold resonance which possesses movement, or to the world that is identical with that [resonance].

Alternatively, "characterized by power" (*śaktilakṣaṇa*) refers to the powers—namely the powers of will, knowledge, and action—which are synonymous with the "pervading power" (*śaktivyāpikā*). Or, it refers to the world common to both word and meaning, which is characterized by power and known as *unmanī* and *nāda*. She bears that [world], or she is borne by it; thus, she is "she whose womb bears the world characterized by power" (*śaktilakṣaṇajagadbhṛtodarī*). She is the progenitor of objects pertaining to the mind and the senses.

The objects of the mind, the senses, and the body are merely phenomenal entities, like those appearing in a dream. They give rise to objects pertaining to them—whether conventional or material—and thus [the Lord] is "the progenitor of mental, sensory, and bodily objects. Alternatively, in the reading *mānasaindriyakavastuno rasī*, it means: [He who possesses] the essence of both that which consists of the body of the mind alone and its object, as well as that which consists of the activity of the senses alone and its object.

The hidden intention behind the use of the dual number in "of those two" refers to the two things: the witness-consciousness (*sākṣibhāsya*) and the object perceivable by the senses (*indriyavedyavastu*). Alternatively, the construction may be understood as follows: [the Self] is with the imperishable reality whose body consists of the mind and the mere senses; in the chest, within the *dahara-ākāśa*; or with the rosary of letters (*akṣamālā*) which is speech and its meaning, characterized by power (*śakti*) and possessing a belly that bears the world—this being due to the desire to express non-difference from the reality of the Self, or through the intended use of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) to denote a characteristic state (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*). Such as you, described by these characteristics, are indeed absolute (*kevalaiva*).

If you are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpiṇī*), having the form of the previously mentioned *unmanī* and *nāda* alone, and are indeed devoid of the threefold distinctions such as "homogeneous" (*sajātīya*) and so forth; and if you are the progenitor of that—meaning the mother of the previously mentioned ninefold *nāda*-triad, or the producer of its mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and by the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is that there is also the latent impression of objects (*viṣayavāsanā*). Then you do not become a locus of manifoldness (*vicitratā*). Regarding the reading "not the supreme manifoldness" (*na vicitratāparam*): the supreme is only the latent impression, not manifoldness; for manifoldness itself is merely temporary. It is not a permanent latent impression belonging to that [consciousness].

Thus, the word *para* (the supreme) indicates the state of liberation (*kaivalya*) during the time of the creation of consciousness (*cinmaya-sṛṣṭi-kālī*), by virtue of being either identical with one of the two—the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or their diversity—or by virtue of its essential nature as the non-difference between the triad of sound (*nāda*), the void (*anavakāśa*), and the triad (*tripuṭī*). Since both are composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), there is no coloring by objects (*viṣayoparakti*). The intended meaning is that if even the latent impression produced by consciousness lacks coloring by objects, then the coloring of the consciousness that produces it is all the more remote from possibility.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since there would be no coloring by objects even for the consciousness-based latent impression (*cinmayavāsanā*), the very creation of the world would be impossible, and thus her status as the Mother of the World (*jaganmātṛtva*) would be lost. This doubt is dispelled by the specific qualification "she whose womb is the world" (*jagadbhūtodarī*), which signifies that her interior is never filled—even by the creation of millions of Brahmāṇḍas characterized by mental and sensory functions—just as it is in the state of dream. Thus, everything is perfectly consistent; this is the summary. (29–51)
By means of illuminating the world of words and their meanings— which consist of the ninefold sounds previously mentioned— he further confirms her status as the Mother of the World:
"This entire world is illuminated at all times by You, who sustain it in the form of sound."
O Mother! You have established the internal [reality] within the mirror of the intellect, and the external [reality] today through the path of the senses.

By the words "occurring at all times" (*sārvakālikam*) and so forth: "O Mother" (*he jananī*) is an intentional address. "At all times" (*sārvakālikam*) means pervading the three periods of past, future, and present, as well as the states of waking and the rest. "Internal" (*āntaram*) means that which exists within the inner self; it exists in the interior of the three worlds, and being "this" (*idam*), it is manifested by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). And the world (*jagat*)—which goes (*gacchati*)—is that which is perceivable by the senses; by the etymological derivation involving the addition of a letter (*varṇāgama*), it refers to the form of the subtle, transmigrating individual soul (*ātivāhika-jīva*).

In the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi-darpaṇa*), which is imagined as the immutable substrate (*kūṭastha-adhiṣṭhāna*) and stands in the place of a mirror—that is, in the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*)—there exists that which is held in a distinct manner. This consists of sound (*śabda*) maintained through the various functions of the vital breaths such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, and through the various functions of the senses and their movements; it takes the form of the tenfold vital resonance (*prāṇanāda*), the ten *vahni-kalas* that signify it, and the vowels (*svarādi*). By that which has this very held sound as its form—that is, by the supreme speech (*parā-vāk*) whose nature is sound, which constitutes the individual self (*jīvātman*)—it [the object] is perceived.

Thus, by you—who, like a parrot or a thrush, sustain the form of *vaikharī* speech through a nature that is inert, consisting of body and senses; and who, by sustaining that very form of speech, possess a nature that is the union of the inert and the non-inert—you are manifested (*bhāsyate*), meaning you exist as the *Bhāsā-Kālī* whose characteristics will be described hereafter, and you are also illumined (*prakāśyate*). Likewise, the external (*bāhya*)—that which exists outside, or, due to the non-difference between *ba* and *va*, that which is to be carried (*vahanīya*)—is [sustained].

This is because of the evidence from the variant reading *akṣarūḍhayā*, and because there is an intended non-distinction between the letters *va* and *ba*. "Present" (*adyatana*) refers to that which lasts only as long as the time of enjoyment, consisting of the locus of enjoyment, derived from the verbal root *ad* (to eat/consume). It is also that which is experienced only during the present states such as waking and creation. [The term] *akṣarūpayā* means by way of the aggregate of the organs of knowledge and action; and also by way of the form of the rosary of phonemes (*varṇākṣamālā*), which consists of speech and so forth directed toward the *vaikharī* sound—the specific function of each respective sense organ.

In the reading *akṣarūḍhayā*—the meaning is "by that which has become established through the functioning of the sense organs toward their objects. This connects with the preceding phrase, "is manifested by you" (tvayā bhāsyate). || 30-52 ||
Thus, he shows the ultimate limit of the worship of the ninefold sound (*nāda*) consisting of the three layers (*tripuṭī*), as described above:
"O gentle one! [It continues] until the seventh state of tranquility for the person abiding within all states of being."
To that extent, there is the state of being differentiated by the reflective awareness of duality; [but] at all times, it is permeated by the reflective awareness of existence. || 53 ||

By the words "as far as" (*yāvat*) and so forth: "O Mother! [those] existing within all entities. The meaning is as follows: according to the Jaiminiya Sūtra—"Words denoting action (*karma-śabda*) have 'being' (*bhāva*) as their primary meaning; from them, action (*kriyā*) is understood; for this is the meaning that is conveyed"—the word *bhāva* signifies the existence of phenomenal activity (*pratibhāsika-vyavahāra-sattā*). Since it denotes both internal and external activity, and because there is a rule that such activity possesses an equal ontological status (*samasattākatva*) with the two types of triads (internal and external) understood through the suffixes *kṛt* and *tiṅ*, [it is established] within the external triad that constitutes the meaning of the *kṛt* suffix.

Within the threefold structure (*tripuṭī*) whose meaning is "going" (*gati*), there is [the deity] in the form of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of the vocalized meaning of nouns—whether nasalized or non-nasalized, and whether ending in a suffix (*kṛdanta*) or not—and likewise in the form of the essential identity of the vocalized meaning of verbal roots, whether ending in a personal suffix (*tiṅanta*) or not; or else, in the form of the word and meaning of Kārtikeya the Seer (*kārtāntika-kārtikeya*). Here, the two persons—the previously mentioned teachers of Yoga and Sāṃkhya, Śiva and Kumāra—are intended either as the personification of all states of being, words, and meanings, or as the words and meanings residing therein.

In this regard, concerning all entities—which take the form of Bhavaputra as the initiators of the paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; which consist of agent, action, and so forth; or which exist as internal and external activities—the practitioner (*vārteṇaḥ*), the performer devoted to ritual action, who has been previously instructed in the path of Yoga, [attains] a state of aesthetic fusion (*sāmarasya*) with the six-faced Śiva-Kumāra-Kāla-Puruṣa, who possesses the six faces of the six sense organs with intellect as the sixth, and who dwells within all entities along with the six seasons.

Thus, for the reflective subject who abides within all entities—whether internal or external—which are characterized by the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) in their activity and take the form of the sons of Bhava; for one devoted to knowledge, such as the aforementioned Sāṃkhya teacher, who possesses the six faces in the form of the mind and the five sense organs; or for the Puruṣa who exists within all entities through equilibrium with the Time-Puruṣa who has six faces in the form of the six seasons—there is tranquility.

The seventh [state], called *śāntatātā*, consists of the delusion that there exists something distinct from the previously mentioned six types of intellect (*buddhi*), the six organs of action (*karmendriya*), or the six seasons (*ṛtu*). This occurs through the forgetting of the true nature of the Puruṣa and Kāla as described in the phrase "manifested internally and externally as Puruṣa and Kāla. It takes the form of the agent, the reflector, and so forth—the form of Puruṣa—or the form of Kāla, differentiated by the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*). Alternatively, it pertains to the Puruṣa who resides within all states of being.

Even for a perfected one (siddha) who is a supreme candidate, as long as he remains within the six transformations of existence accompanied by their constituent parts (kalās), even until such time as "sorrows appear as joys and poison appears as nectar."

And where the path of Śiva—as stated in the verse, "In which even saṃsāra acts as liberation"—is not mastered through proficiency, then within one's own self, as long as there appears some form of tranquility distinct from the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), whether consisting of the seventh state of *ātmakalā*, or in the form of the worship of the *praṇava* as either the word or its meaning; for that long, there exists the state of being permeated by perpetual *vimarśa*—that is, the state of being permeated by the *vimarśa* of all times and all conditions, or the *vimarśa* regarding all objective existents (*bhāva*). This is what is called "destiny" (*bhavitavyatā*).

The meaning is as follows: either there is a differentiation of the non-dual awareness (*advayavimarśa*), or the non-dual awareness itself [is differentiated] by means of duality; or else, there is a differentiation in the modes of non-dual awareness through its identity with the Self (*ātman*). This refers to the differentiation of the non-dual awareness—which consists of the two supreme forms (*anuttarākāra*) of *nāda* and phoneme (*varṇa*)—within the sequence of phonemes of the consciousness of the abodes (*dhāma*) that will be described hereafter. The implication is that when one resorts to resting in the Self, which is the six-limbed reality undifferentiated from the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) and is characterized by a natural tranquility and equanimity that is not artificial or caused by external objects, then the "external awareness" (*bāhyavimarśa*) comes to an end. || 31–53 ||

Now, when external reflection has reached its conclusion in the manner described, he says: "O Mother! That very world, which is composed of consciousness and is internalized within this very universe as latent impressions (*vāsanā*), shines forth through the power of Your own Maya—which shines all at once—as the Self that has become the Self of all beings; that indeed is You.

"O Mother! That which shines forth through Your qualities is called 'insentient' (*jaḍa*) by those who possess the notion of difference (*bhedadhi*) and the like, and it is gradually cast aside [by them]."
That which measures the form of the mind as its own form all at once—that indeed is You. 54.

With the words beginning with "O Amba," [the text says]: O Amba! By means of the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely, those such as the "all" (*sarva*), etc., those such as tranquility (*śama*), etc., and those such as desire (*kāma*) and anger (*krodha*), etc.—that which is the world, which is "throbbing" (*sphurat*), meaning manifesting according to its respective capacity through the Veda, is "removed" (*apohyate*) in due order—that is, by the sequence of the practice of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). That which is throbbing is shown to be of the very nature of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), and thus the sense of "I" (*ahaṃ*) is eliminated.

That which manifests in the form of restraint (*yama*) and so forth is indeed of the nature of the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*); thus, one is made free from erroneous notions (*viparyaya*). Likewise, that which manifests in the form of desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), and so forth is indeed of the nature of the sixfold path; thus, one is made free from erroneous notions. Furthermore, that which manifests in the form of desire, anger, and so forth is entirely demonic (*āsura*); by means of the removal of doubt through the destruction of the demonic world, and according to the sequence of one's own respective offices, the nature of the external waking state (*bāhyajāgrat*) is negated.

Although that threefold world is [in fact] only the cognition of difference (*bhedadhī*) that is being negated, for this very reason, the Śrutis declare with certainty that what is being negated—which consists of the cognition of difference—is indeed inert (*jaḍa*); and the Smṛti-authors likewise remember this; and the investigators (*vimarśakāḥ*) speak thus. (The meaning is: "By those who possess difference" (*bhedibhiḥ*)—if this is the reading—it is an adjective qualifying the *guṇas*, meaning "by the qualities that possess difference."

Having thus negated the threefold world—consisting of the empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-sad-rūpa*), the illusory appearance (*prātibhāsika*), and that which consists of the latent impressions of qualities (*guṇa-vāsanātmaka*)—the text reveals the world as the ultimate form of the Virāj, which is composed of the latent impressions of consciousness (*cid-vāsanā-maya*) and is one's own essential nature, by means of the passage beginning with "consciousness" (*cit*). "Tadākṛtiḥ" means that whose form (*ākṛti*) is like the form of that threefold world being negated; yet, by its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), it is "anākṛtiḥ," devoid of form. The sense is that this is because its essence consists of the latent impressions of consciousness.

In the reading where "anākṛtiḥ svataḥ" is treated as a single compound, it is stated that [the Self] exists by its own nature as the form of the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*), derived from the verbal root *ana* (to breathe). This [Self] exists as if possessing a non-manifest form; for this very reason, it is also [described] in the context of the non-recognition (*avakhyāti*) of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

The use of the word "asau" (that one) is intended to illuminate that she is composed of the seven planes (*saptabhūmikā*) and the aggregate (*piṇḍa*), even while possessing the qualities of knowledge, power, and virtue, by virtue of being the essential identity of the union of the meaning of the supreme seed-mantra which is the form of emanation. Furthermore, through a hidden intention, it indicates that she possesses a body consisting of mantras fashioned from the Śākta emission (*visarga*). That consciousness (*cit*) which shines forth once—since the nature of consciousness, which is one's own self, is a nature that shines forth all at once, its "shining forth once" must be understood as such—you are that very consciousness.

Regarding the reading *tvayāsi sā*, it means "by you," who are of the nature of both the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). Since consciousness shines by itself, the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) should be understood here in the sense of non-difference (*abheda*), intended to express the state of being (*bhāvārtha*), just as in the expressions "grain" (*dhānya*) or "wealthy" (*dhanavān*). As it is said in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "Śiva pervades the vast body of the universe itself, just as an elephant occupies its own large stable or a mirror. Within this very world, for those possessed of devotion to You, this [is the case].

By such statements as, "The world became something else entirely, abounding in joy and manifestation," even the various modes of the entire universe—such as the *pañcajana* (the five classes of beings) and *mānava* (humanity)—are described in other tantras as being composed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of consciousness; however, these have been omitted here for fear of excessive prolixity. (32–54)

Now, one might object that if the nature of the world as it exists in the waking state were thus negated in its entirety, the cessation of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would result in the blindness of the world; anticipating this, he refutes it by stating that only the portion consisting of the differentiation of its own insentience—which is a fault of the individual soul—is negated, and therefore there is neither the cessation of worldly transaction nor the blindness of the world:
"O Mother, that insentience of the world which, by its very nature, appears as differentiation starting from the level of *parā* onwards..."
But you, who shine forth within the mandala of the single goal, are remembered as the one who obstructs the path to old age.

Regarding the passage beginning with "O Mother, dullness... (*jāḍyamamba*): O Mother! In the "pavilion of objects" (*arthamaṇḍapa*)—which, by the word "with sound," consists of the fivefold denotable objects comprising substance, genus, quality, and action; or, in the alternative reading "in the pavilion of the four aims of human life" (*puruṣārthacatuṣṭayagṛha*), which is the very form of the pavilion of the four aims—or, according to the reading *arthamaṇḍale*, in the circle of the five aims of human life that are non-different from one's own essential nature, or in the form of those four aims—the meaning is clear.

The statement that *parā* is the "starting point" (*prabhṛti*) and the "limit" (*pāra*) intends to express its status as the boundary (*maryādā*), not that it is included within the three activities such as creation (emanation), as is the case with *paśyantī* and the others; for *parā* consists of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of consciousness. For this very reason, there is the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "That non-dual supreme speech (*parā vāc*)," and so forth; and the Vedic scripture (*śruti*): "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, they do not disclose."

And there is the passage beginning with, "Humans speak of the fourth state of speech. These [scriptural statements] indicate that the Supreme (parā) is non-different from the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā). "From difference" means from the nature of difference. The meaning is that the insentience (jāḍya) which appears in the world shines forth as having emerged from that [Supreme]; that is to say, the measure of insentience caused by difference is simply natural (naisargika). In the reading *nisargaja* ("born of nature"), the meaning is: the insentience which appears from difference is the "difference born of nature" (*nisargajo bheda*).

The sense is that because the word *sarga* (creation) preceded by the prefix *ni-* denotes an action whose counter-correlate is difference (*bheda*), difference is produced solely by action. The phrase "the consciousness (*cit*) opposed to insentience (*jāḍya*)" means that its essential nature is contrary to insentience, being non-different from the aforementioned *unmanī-nāda*. "You who shine"—that is, you who are such as this. Here, the particle *tu* serves to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and indicates the inherent nature of consciousness. The ellipsis is "you shine with a single effort" (*sakṛt*). The sense is that you shine through non-difference (*abheda*).

Just as the manifestation of insentience caused by difference is innate, so too the manifestation of consciousness caused by non-difference is likewise innate; this is the resultant meaning of the sentence.

Now, if the word *tu* (but) is intended to exclude the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), then why this "old woman's logic"? Just as the inertness of the world is natural when caused by difference (*bheda*), so too the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-bhāna*) must be equally natural when caused by non-difference (*abheda*). Or, why should the manifestation of the world's difference and inertness be considered natural while the manifestation of the non-difference of consciousness is not? Or, why should there not be a reversal of the relationship between the prompted and the prompter?

Just as the appearance of difference in the world, or the cognition of difference, is brought about by innate insentience (*jāḍya*), so too is the appearance of non-difference with the insentient brought about by consciousness (*cit*) that is not innate. Therefore, one might suspect that this would support the doctrine of difference (*bhedavāda*), wherein difference is ultimate (*pāramārthika*) while non-difference is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*). Yet, even so, the "old woman’s logic" (*arthajaratīya*) you have stated remains exactly as it was; this is not the form of the relationship between the instigator and the instigated.

Rather, it is the very presence or absence of the measurement of time—which is simultaneously illuminated by its own nature—that serves as the cause for the distinction or non-distinction between inertia (*jāḍya*) and consciousness (*cit*). Therefore, that you who shine within the circle of the Heart (*ārtamaṇḍapa*) as the Unstruck Sound (*unmanī-nāda*), whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and who are the adversary of inertia, you shine only once; thus you are remembered as such. As for the inertia of the world that appears through differentiation starting from the level of *parā*, that shines forth by its very nature.

The meaning is that [the world] shines forth repeatedly from the creation of time; since the repeated manifestation of duality is invariably concomitant with the mere existence of time, it is insentient by nature. With the intention that even beyond that [time], the experience of non-difference from the conscious witness (*sākṣin*) depends entirely upon memory, he provides the resolution by employing the word "remembered" (*smṛta*), saying: "It is said to be 'remembered'."

Otherwise, even though the existence of time has perished during meditative absorption and deep sleep, there would follow the impossibility of the recollection upon awakening that says: "I who was absorbed or asleep for such a long time now remember that state or that duration."

Furthermore, since both the difference of the world and the non-difference of consciousness are equally natural, even for those who maintain that difference and non-difference are mutually dependent—just like the relationship between a word and its meaning—it is merely an ornament for us, as we do not touch upon their foundational basis. Enough, then, with these digressions accessible only to the unwise. Moreover, the poet himself will later state in the fourth *Vimarśa* that memory and experience, in the form of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), possess this identity with one's own self; thus, I shall desist. (33–55)
That consciousness which moves eternally in the void where all sequences of activity have been cast away,
brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva.
Khecarī is the remover of all fatigue. || 34-56 ||

Although this verse—along with the two verses beginning with "O Mother, [the world] consisting of the ocean of the nectar of consciousness" and "Wherever the rays meet"—these three verses together are not found at all in the *Mūlacidgaganacandrikā* manuscript held by the Āgama Anusandhāna Samiti in Calcutta.

Nevertheless, although the venerable Svāmī Trivikrama Tīrtha—the compilers of that very work—have demonstrated [the inclusion of these verses] by recording them as authoritative citations by various teachers in the *Yoginīhṛdayasetubandha-ṭīkā*, the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*, and other texts following the completion of the root-text (*mūlakośa*), we have nonetheless included these three verses here according to our judgment and best understanding, despite their omission from the printing of his own root-text for reasons that remain unperceived.

Having already stated that [these points] were inserted at their respective places out of a desire for thematic consistency and have been explained accordingly, they are now explained here as well; thus, this introductory note should be understood.

In the preceding verse, having dispelled the consequences of the cessation of worldly activity and the blindness of the world by way of avoiding the transgression of the Person (puruṣa) in the form of insentience—establishing these as defects of the Person—the author now clarifies, through the phrase beginning with "in the void" (*khe nirasta*), how the means for attaining the state of Śiva consists in the removal of all exhaustion by means of the *khecarī* [mudrā], for the practitioner whose true nature has entered the fourth state of waking within the internal space (*daharākāśa*), wherein all sequences of action have been eliminated by means of the triad of sound, speech, and meaning, or the triad of the wheels of sound (*nādacakra*).

In the state where all sequences of ritual action have been cast aside: "O God! O handsome one, listen; I shall declare this sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*): [it consists of] emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), the Inexplicable (*anākhya*), and the nature of Light (*bhāsā*). [There is also] pure knowledge (*jñānamātra*) and the union (*melāpa*), which is both Śākta and Śāmbhava. One should know that knowledge is emanation, while maintenance is proclaimed to be mantra. Withdrawal is known as the supreme union with the Great Void (*mahākāśa*). The Inexplicable is the form of Power (*śakti*), while that called Light is the form of Śambhu. (1–3)

"This fivefold [process] is to be understood by those who perceive reality. Thus, according to the sequence stated in the *Śrīkramasiddhi* and other texts, even the entire sequence of ritual action (*sakalakriyākrama*) is set aside because consciousness alone is the sole refuge. In that "void" (*khe*), which is the internal space (*daharākāśa*) wherein the entire external sequence of creative acts such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth occurs, there is the consciousness whose arising is eternal; it is that very consciousness which brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva. For this reason, it is also the remover of all exhaustion (*sakalakhedahāriṇī*). By resting solely within the internal space, it is the destroyer of all weariness.

Thus, this is the definition of the essential nature of Khecarī, whether by way of her distinction as Vyomavāmeśvarī or through identity with her. For this very reason, it is said in the *Śrīkramasiddhi*: "Vyoma is known as Vāmeśvarī, and Nādabhūti is Khecarī; Ānanda is known as Dikcarī, and Gocarī is the ground of mantra. Because mantras take the form of substances, their series is considered Bhūcarī. (1)

Therefore, in the *Tantrāloka* as well, it is proclaimed in so many words that the manifestation of the power of His own universal wheel (*viśvacakra*) belongs to Śiva, the Lord of Knowledge (*vidyeśāna*), who governs the sequence of the universal wheels from one up to a thousand-spoked wheel. As it is said: "He is the Solitary Hero (*ekavīra*), He is the impurity, and here He is the fourfold Power; He is five-fold in form, six-fold in nature, adorned with seven and eight; He is nine-fold, the ten powers of the directions, and eleven-fold in His own essence. (1)

Bhairava stands as the leader of the great twelve-spoked wheel; thus, the all-pervading Great Lord, whose power is the universe, manifests within the universal wheel, whether it has a thousand spokes or even innumerable spokes. Because this has been stated, it should be understood that this very [manifestation] is the external unfolding of the preeminent hero among practitioners of the *āṇavavisarga*, who has attained the nature of the *śāktavisarga* while remaining within the womb of the *śāmbhavavisarga*. (Verses 34–56)

Thus, having first dispelled both the loss of worldly transaction and the resulting blindness of the world by means of the identity of word and meaning (*vāgartha-sāmarasya*) within the ninefold triad of *nāda*, he establishes therein— by virtue of the rule that what is non-different from one's own self is identical with one's own self— that the world, the individual soul, and the Supreme Self possess the nature of the three emissions (*visarga*) non-different from *nāda*, or else the nature of the three *bindu*s: "This entire universe is that which is determined as 'I am,' devoid of name and form."
O Mother!
You do not possess that radiance which belongs to yourself, because you are the Dharma of the Lord.

By the verse beginning with "viśvam" and so forth: O Amba! This [universe] consists of the playful manifestation of the sounds of speech—both conscious and unconscious, and both addressable and non-addressable by the gesture of the hand; or else, it consists of the collection of worlds beginning from Anāśrita down to Kālaśiva. That which is called the "universe" (viśvam) is Speech (vāk), which takes the form of sound as the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) within the Vaikharī stage of the playful manifestation of the Āṇava emission (*visarga*).

Regarding the reading "this universe," "I," and "that one": "this" refers to the universe of moving and non-moving beings, which consists of the play of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—the meaning of the *vaikharī* speech, the *āṇava* emission characterized by the repose of consciousness. Likewise, "I": "I" (*aham*) is "light" (*mahaḥ*). By this form, there is "I," which is characterized by the resonance of the meaning of the mantra "I," the play of the *śāmbhava* emission characterized by the dissolution of consciousness, and the resonance (*nāda*) of speech. Likewise, "that one who... [is that].

By the form *auṃ*, there is the reference to the play of the emission (*visarga*) of Śakti, which is the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇaspanda*) characterized by the awakening of consciousness; this is the individual soul (*jīva*), defined as speech and its object, and the power of the soul (*jīvaśakti*) is of that same nature—or it is called *mahaḥ*. "In the absence of name and form" means having abandoned name and form. That which is speech is its power of sound (*śabdaśakti*), and that which is sound is its denoted meaning (*abhidheyārtha*). This is determined to be the nature of the speech and meaning of such mantras as: "The one unborn, red, white, and black, giving birth to offspring of similar form."

Regarding the reading in the plural: one should understand that the meaning is that speech (*vāk*), which is its power of signification (*śabda-śakti*), and sound (*śabda*), which is its denoted, indicated, and other meanings—these combined are the "motes" (*trasareṇu*) of word and meaning consisting of the triad and tetrad of *bindus*, which are determined as the manifestations of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three: the individual (*āṇava*), the empowered (*śākta*), and the divine (*śāmbhava*) aspects of emission (*visarga*). The phrase "within the boundaries of word and meaning" implies "in the sections of the vowels of the Mātṛkā. You are she, the one whose form is the collective totality of such word, meaning, *Kāmakalā*, and the three *bindus*.

"You do not possess the nature of luminosity belonging to those things that shine. If the reading is *bhāsyatām*, the meaning is: "you do not possess the state of being illuminated. If one asks why this is so, it is because [you are] the Lord (*īśituḥ*), who is of the nature of light (*prakāśātman*), whose power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is inwardly absorbed, and who governs the fivefold cosmic functions (*kṛtyapañcaka*). As it is said in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa*: "May the Great Lord protect us—he whose body is pure light, whose self-reflective awareness is inwardly absorbed, and who is intent upon the playful manifestation of the sport consisting of the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of all worlds."

This means: "of the one who illuminates the play of the three emissions (visarga) previously mentioned. [He is] Paraśiva in the form of Kāla. "Dharma" means having the nature of the Nāda that mediates that [emission]. The connection with the preceding verse is: "You are not," meaning "you do not possess the state of being illuminated by this. Having thus explained it according to the tradition of the Āgamas, this very same verse is now explained again as referring to the emission of the meaning of Vedic speech: ... [The text continues with the Vedic interpretation] ... Thus, having explained it according to the tradition of the Āgamas, this very same verse is explained once more as having the purpose of the emission of the meaning of Vedic speech.

This is the cognition that this universe consists of the play of words and meanings indicated by the hands; or, according to the reading *yoham*, it is the conceit (*abhimāna*). Likewise, it is the cognition or the conceit expressed as "I" and "this one. Thus it has been stated by the Śruti, with reference to the various types of mental dispositions and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the sacrificer at the time of the sacrifice, within the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices: "The gods are the ancestors, the ancestors are the gods. Being who I am, I sacrifice. I do not neglect him from whom I am."

"My own highest sacrifice, my own gift, my own meritorious work, my own heaven, my own exhaustion; in my own heaven is the oblation offered. Over me as such, Agni is the witness, Vāyu is the listener, Āditya is the announcer, Heaven is the father, Earth is the mother, Prajāpati is the kinsman. Being who I am, I sacrifice"—with these words, which set forth the primary self-functioning that is devoid of name and form at the time of sacrifice, and which negates the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ego-identification.

Likewise, in the *Śārīrakabrahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya*, the venerable Śrī Śaṅkarabhagavatpūjyapāda, having raised the objection that the Self is not an object at all even for mental modification (*vṛtti*), established that it is indeed an object of the mental modification of the notion of "I" (*asmad-pratyaya-vṛtti*) according to the gradations of eligibility for knowledge, meditation, and so forth. As he says: "This [Self] is not entirely non-objective, because it is the content of the notion of 'I' (*asmad-pratyaya-vedyatvāt*), and because of its well-known nature as the inner self (*pratyagātmatva*). And likewise: "I who exist am Brahman; I am Brahman. "I am Brahman; I am Brahman."

Because, through such passages as "I alone am the Self; I offer myself, svāhā," there is the indication—based on the wording of the mantra—that the universe and the ego-sense (which are unreal and false due to their lack of substantiality), or the objects of the universe, constitute the oblation, while the Self is the agent of the offering; and because the aspects of name and form and the Self possess the unmanifested characteristics of the oblation and the sacrificer respectively; therefore, that aforementioned intellect—which follows any one of the three, four, or five modes previously mentioned—[is the subject].

The meaning is as follows: by being devoid of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), by the emptiness of name-and-form, and by having abandoned name-and-form—either as the triad of existence, manifestation, and bliss (*sattā-sphūrti-ānanda*) consisting of the fivefold parts described in the verse, "Existence, manifestation, and the beloved form, as well as name and consciousness: these are the five parts; the first three are the nature of Brahman, while the latter two are the nature of the world," or as the essential nature of the unity of the individual soul and Brahman (*jīva-brahma-ekya*) which is a mass of existence, consciousness, and bliss—you, who are characterized by both such cognition and the ego-identification with it, do not possess the state of being manifested (*bhāsyatā*).
