You do not shine forth [as an object].

The meaning is that Your own nature, being of the nature of both erroneous and non-erroneous cognition according to one's qualification, and being merely the witness (*sākṣin*) in both ways, does not bear the character of an external object to be illuminated, like a jar or a cloth. In the reading *bhāsvatām*, the meaning is "You do not bear the state of having illumination as Your sole essential nature"; the sense is that because You, whose primordial nature is consciousness (*cinmayaprakṛti*), consist of both illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ). This refers to the Lord (Īśvara), whose sole nature is light, who is the inner and outer controller. For [the following reason]: since you are a quality (dharma) of the substratum (dharmī) whose essential nature is light alone by virtue of having an inwardly latent reflective awareness (vimarśa), and since the quality possesses the inherent nature of an undissolved light and reflective awareness both internally and externally, there is no difference in the true nature of the reality; thus, it is one and the same reality, whose essence consists of supreme consciousness, existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccidānanda).

The literal meaning is that the universe—which consists of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), itself being composed of the categories of subject and object (*dharmin-dharma*) that are synonyms for *māyā* and *avidyā*—is merely designated through such distinctions as "this is the world," "I am this," or "that is I," but it is not actually experienced [as such]. For this very reason, the venerable Śrī Vidyāraṇya, the sovereign among teachers, has clearly demonstrated in his *Vedāntapañcadaśī*—preceded by citations from the *Vārttika*—the intention to express the internal differentiation within the nature of *māyā*.

Reality and unreality are as follows: "Māyā is known to be threefold—insubstantial (*tucchā*), indeterminable (*anirvacanīyā*), and real (*vāstavī*)—through its three distinctions. Having presented this threefold nature, it was determined through their respective perspectives: from the perspective of those qualified for the Vedic path, there is the insubstantiality of the forms of women, men, and so forth, appearing as men, women, and so on; from the perspective of logic, grammar, and reasoning, there is indeterminability; and from the perspective of ordinary people, there is the nature of being real, each according to its own distinction.

Furthermore, it has been shown that doctrines primarily based on reasoning—such as Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhāgavata, and others—are incomplete because they do not culminate in the true nature of the ultimate reality, which is the heart of the Vedas; as follows:

"Indeed, objections arise against those who maintain that the world is a real entity; however, no objection can be raised against *māyā*, because it is non-dual in nature. (1) If there were an objection even to an objection, then I would be objecting to your objection. Therefore, that objection must be resolved, and not further challenged with counter-objections. (2) What indeed is impossible for *māyā*, whose sole body is wonder? What marvel is there in *māyā*, which brings about the production of the utterly inconceivable? Liquidity in water, heat in fire, and hardness in stone [are its effects]. (3)

The inexplicability of illusion is established by itself, not from anything else. As long as the world does not know the nature of the magician, it experiences wonder; but once it realizes, "This is an illusion," that wonder subsides in the mind. Therefore, the wise should strive to investigate the resolution of this matter. If you say, "Illusion is indeed what you yourself have determined," then consider the definition of the illusion well-known in the world: that which cannot be defined yet appears with perfect clarity.

People have come to regard that [world] as "illusion" (māyā), such as in the case of a magician's trick (indrajāla) and the like. (7) Therefore, when the world was being examined by all scholars as being composed of illusion—due to its indifference toward both waking and sleeping states—the following occurred: (8) Ignorance appeared before them in certain stages, such as the body, the senses, and other such entities. [They asked: "How were these produced by the seed-syllable (vīrya)? (9) Or, when it was asked, "How is there consciousness therein?", what answer did they give? [If they say: "This is the inherent nature (svabhāva) of the seed-syllable," [then we ask: "How is that known by you? (10)

If positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) are broken because they lack efficacy, then at the end, when one thinks, "I do not know anything of this," you alone are my refuge. For this very reason, the great ones proclaim this to be a magical illusion (indrajāla). What else could this be but a magic trick, wherein semen deposited in the womb of a barren woman perceives itself and puts forth various sprouts from the feet, hands, and head?

"By turns, he is seen endowed with the various appearances of childhood, youth, and old age; he sees, eats, hears, smells, and likewise goes and returns. Through such passages, the Tīrthakaras—out of grace toward those of duller faculties who desire to know the true nature of reality—have clearly established that their doctrines are merely "prior discourses" (pūrvavāda) devised for the purpose of investigating the essential truth behind doctrines such as *māyā* and *avidyā*. Thus, the philosophical systems of Viśiṣṭādvaita, Bhāgavata, and others—which distinguish between the world, the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—result ultimately in nothing more than the practice of devotion as a means to that end.

Relying merely on the authority of traditional scripture (*āgama*), even those [practices] that do not conform to the ultimate intent of the Vedas have nonetheless been respected as Vedic—even by way of a partial perspective (*khaṇḍadṛṣṭi*)—by those devoted to Vedic *ahaṃgraha* meditations, because they are specific forms of meditation on attainments (*sampat*) and symbols (*pratīka*). Enough of this digression. (35–57)

Now, one might raise this objection: "Out of a desire for pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita), or out of a desire for the ultimate purport of the supreme Śruti, even if one were to adopt a 'partial' view (khaṇḍadṛṣṭi)—as in the systems of Vaidika, Rāmānuja, Pūrṇaprajña, and others—by not admitting a difference in the essential nature (svarūpa-bheda) between the insentient (jaḍa) and the sentient (ajaḍa), namely the world and the individual soul, the consequence would be the destruction of everything through the destruction of the world; thus, would not the Mādhyamika doctrine of emptiness or the Buddhist theory of momentary flux (kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda) be effectively endorsed? Anticipating this doubt, [the author proceeds] by means of both scriptural authority (āgama) and the language of the Upaniṣads, according to the distinction between the stages of the seeker of knowledge (bubhutsu) and the enlightened (prabuddha).

He offers a rebuttal— stating that there is never any entry into, nor imitation of, the systems of the Mādhyamikas and others within the traditions of Āgama and Upaniṣad— because it has been established as a settled doctrine that the theories of "unborn creation" (*ajāta-sṛṣṭi*) and so forth arise from the Lord who is the cause, standing apart [from the individual soul] as the very nature of *nāda* itself, whether in the ninefold *manonmanī*, or through the process of re-absorption (*pratisañcaraṇa*) into the Great Bindu at the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*),

which is the essence of both word and meaning: "Having taken hold of the jewel of the Void (*śūnya-ratna*) within the Lord, who is devoid of objective existence, vision, and memory, and who is the individual soul (*pudgala*)."
This world exists as something devoid of definitive explanation; because it does not abide on the upward path of consciousness, it is not truly so.

Regarding the phrase "bhāvadṛk" and so forth: the meaning is that [it refers] to the Lord (Īśvara), whose nature consists of the reflective awareness of "Īśana" included within the aforementioned group of six reflective awarenesses, and who is the regulator of the fourth speech and its objects. "Bhāvadṛk": "Bhāva" refers to this manifestation of Śiva—the creator of the phonemic series beginning with the letter 'A'—consisting of the fivefold cosmic acts such as the creation of speech and objects, the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and the rays [of consciousness]; the meaning is the Śiva-world. "Dṛk" means that which is seen; thus, "bhāvadṛk" is that in which this [world] is seen in the form of primordial attention (ādarūpa).

Likewise, "devoid of memory" (*smṛtiviyuktam*) means that here [in this state], the memory of the Self as consisting of the universe—as previously described in the preceding verse in such terms as "I am Caitra" or "I am Maitra"—is severed; it is "devoid of memory" because it is not joined with that [dualistic] memory due to its identity with the *Anāhata*. Likewise, the "jewel of emptiness" (*śūnyaratnam*): "Empty above, empty below, empty in the middle, and free from affliction."

"O Dear One, he who understands the three voids (triśūnya) is called a Guru. Thus it is stated in the section on recitation (*japa*). Among the ancillaries of mantra-recitation—such as the six paths (*adhvan*) taught in the Tantras, the seven equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), and the six voids (*śūnya*)—there exists that which is called the "Jewel of the Void" (*śūnyaratna*). This refers to that state whose nature consists of the ninefold resonance of the *unmanī* sound, wherein the voids to be contemplated as the essence of sound (*nāda*) exist like jewels. Likewise, there is *pudgala*, so called because from it the state of being a person (*puṃbhāva*) falls away (*galati*).

Relying upon such a group of nine sounds (*nāda*), this world—consisting of words and meanings that is perceived as being manifest through the witness-consciousness—is utterly defined as "beyond definition" (*nirniruktika*). This is because the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*) cannot be defined, nor can the reality of meaning (*arthatattva*); thus, through a distinction in etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), it remains as it is, "beyond definition."

Now, one might object: since the reality of the meaning of speech—the fourteen Māheśvara Sūtras beginning with *a i u ṇ*—or the reality of the meaning of speech as the fragment of vowels consisting of only four sūtras, is included within the Vairāja [level], which consists of the reality of *nāda* and *unmanī* (as stated: "Bindu, Artha, Candra, Rodhinī, Nāda, Nādānta, Śakti, Vyāpikā, Samanā, and Unmanā are proclaimed as the nine *nādas*"), then would the world not be devoid of etymological derivation (*nirniruktika*), being essentially nothing but the reality of the meaning of Vairāja-speech?

One might raise the objection that since the *tripuṭī* (the triad) is dissolved within the reality of *unmanī*, *nāda*, and the *mahābindu* at the *dvādaśānta*, and because of the traditional teaching (*āmnāna*) regarding the dissolution of the triad of word, meaning, and world into the state of the King of Kings (*vairāja*), the world of words and meanings must therefore possess the nature of emptiness as accepted by the Mādhyamikas; consequently, there would be a total destruction of everything. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] states that even in that state, because of the continuity of the Divine Current (*divyaugha-santati*) through the process of the contraction of the Guru’s Flower (*gurupuṣpa-saṅkoca*) to be described later—and because it is a "conducted lineage" (*nītasantati*) according to the method to be explained in the rays of the sequence of Gurus in the third *vimarśa* in the words "that lineage is again suddenly led"—[there is no such destruction].

He says "cillayā" (by the mind) to show that there is no room for the consequence of the Madhyamika doctrine of emptiness; [it refers] to the consciousness of mere external speech-sounds (*vaikharī*) and their objects, such as the thought "I am this mind."

*Laya* (absorption) is the attainment of identity with the *nāda*—which consists of the divine speech (*divyavāk*) that transcends the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the forms of *vyāpikā*, *samana*, and *unmanī*—by means of transcending the previously mentioned sixfold external *virāj-nāda* contained within the ninefold *nāda* beginning with *bindu* and ending with *śakti*; or it is the absorption of the *nāda* whose ordinary *virāj*-form is being dissolved, or which has attained a divine form. The meaning is: such an absorption into consciousness (*cillaya*), which is the absorption into the nature of the solar *nāda* consisting of the twelve-fold ordinary vital breath (*prāṇa*).

The "path ascending to consciousness" (*cillayordhvagapatha*) refers to that path which goes upward to the station of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) at the "twelfth end" (*dvādaśānta*), consisting of thirteen parts; it is, in other words, the path of the contemplation of the nature of the Sound (*nāda*) that ascends to the state of *unmanī*. From that path ascending to consciousness—wherein the ablative case is used in the sense of "attaining" (due to the elision of the suffix *lyap*)—that world which is to be attained is not "so," meaning it does not consist of a void as the Mādhyamikas assert, nor is it like the previously mentioned state of Vairāja.

However, the intended meaning is that even while consisting of the universe, one attains the innate nature of the Self which transcends the universe. For this very reason, in the Tantras, within the section concerning the recitation of mantras (*mantra-japa*), it is prescribed for the superior practitioner—who contemplates the essential nature of *nāda*—that they first intend the dissolution of the meaning of speech in its manifest (*vaikharī*) and unmanifest (*virāja*) forms, and then contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) within their own body.

And he will state the third reflection: "O Mother, the void is called 'I' by You," and "O Mother, the void is indeed the great sky," and so forth; thus, having explained this [verse] through the nature of the contemplation of the void according to the phonemes, traditional enumerations, speech, meaning, sound, and other verbal attributes of the scriptures, this very verse is also explained as far as possible as referring to the Upaniṣadic Puruṣa, who consists of the primary vital breath (prāṇa), which is the root of all words and the subject matter of the intent of all the Vedas.

"Bhāvadṛk" means one whose vision (*dṛk*) regarding the Lord as the object is that He is the cause of the world in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvapadārtha*), and not, on the other hand, a void (*śūnya*); the meaning is that He consists of consciousness beyond the senses (*parokṣacinmaya*). "Smṛtiviyuktam" means devoid of recollection (*smṛti*)—that is, devoid of the remembrance characterized by the statement to be explained in the *Turīyavimarśa*: "If there were no experience of the Lord, transmigratory existence would consist in the cognition of similar objects," and so forth; thus, [the world] is composed of insentient matter (*jaḍamaya*).

This world that is being perceived is a "jewel of emptiness" (*śūnyaratna*). Here, by the word "jewel," the knowledge of the Upaniṣads (*aupaniṣada-jñāna*) is intended. This is because in the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* passage beginning with "The blind man found the jewel" (*andho maṇim avindat*), the word "jewel" (*maṇi*) is used as a synonym for that very [knowledge]. Thus, "jewel of emptiness" means empty of the jewel of Upaniṣadic knowledge; the meaning is that it is empty of the knowledge of the reality that is the cause of the world. Such a person is a *pudgala*; [the term] *pudgala* is derived from the root *put*, meaning "to dissolve," as in "that from which the small creature (*puttikā*) dissolves."

By this etymology, the meaning is that the gross body—which is technical terminology within the Buddhist system (*bauddhasamaya*) characterized by a medium dimension—has dissolved. Relying upon such a sheath of the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇakośa*), one becomes "beyond etymological definition" (*nirniruktika*). This is because it cannot be defined as either existent or non-existent, due to contradiction with such scriptural passages and reasoning as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "In the beginning, this was indeed non-Being," and "For from non-Being, Being could not be born. Although this state remains even in other systems such as those of the Mādhyamikas, [it is here described in this manner].

Therefore, it is the form of the great abiding as the Self of the Lord; it is not empty like in the Mādhyamika and other systems, because the Lord is accepted through the doctrine of the reality of the three times—this is the intended meaning.

Now, one might object: "If you accept the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect in the cause (*satkāryavāda*) and the admission of creation and so forth due to an aversion to and dogmatic attachment toward other non-Vedic systems such as those of the Mādhyamikas, then alas, there arises for you—a proponent of the non-dual reality of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads as devoid of the threefold difference—both a contradiction of your own established tenet and an imitation of the doctrines of others according to the partial non-dualism of the Bhāgavatas and similar schools. Thus, a rope of double-bind has fallen upon you. To this objection, we reply by resorting to the established tenet of the *ajātavāda* (the doctrine of the unborn), which maintains that the world has the Lord as its cause.

And indicating that [the body] is fashioned by the Veda for the purpose of venerating word and meaning, he reveals the state of disembodied liberation (videhamukti) externally—by the words "cillaya" (dissolution into consciousness). Regarding the phrase "cillayordhvagapathāt," the ablative case here is used "in the sense of eliding the verbal suffix lyap" (lyablope pañcamī). This is because the path leading upward from the dissolution of the vital functions (prāṇavṛtti), which are denoted by the word *cit*, is the one described in the Śruti: "His prāṇas do not depart; they are absorbed right here. For it is heard in scripture that for the wise one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is no departure of the prāṇas, but rather their absorption right here.

Having reached the upward path of the heart—the path of dissolution for the vital functions of those liberated while living in Videha—that world does not exist in that manner; nor does it conform to the modes accepted in the systems of the Sāṃkhya proponents of *satkāryavāda*, the Bhāgavatas, and others. Why? Because other Śrutis negate the birth and so forth of the world, as well as any difference in its essential nature, through such passages as: "The wise one is neither born nor dies," and "All this is indeed Brahman; there is no diversity here whatsoever."

The intention here is as follows: for fear of contradicting the Śruti texts that teach the threefold activity (*kṛtyatraya*) and so forth—such as "from which indeed these beings are born"—which support the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), even within the established Vedāntic conclusion, just as in the systems of the Sāṃkhya and others, one might accept that during the state of the individual soul's departure (*jīvotkrānti*), the world has the individual soul as its substratum. Nevertheless, because the world—consisting of speech and meaning, which are composed of the *nāda* (the primordial sound) arising from the material cause of the upward path of consciousness—is non-different in nature from the Self of the Knower (*vidvadātman*), and because of such scriptural passages as "The wise one is neither born nor dies" and "There is no agent for this [world]," [it is concluded that the world is not distinct from Brahman].

Furthermore, because the doctrine of the uncreated creation (*ajāta-sṛṣṭi*) has been established as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by the force of other scriptural passages that negate the agent, the object, the action, the instrument, and other factors—such as "it does not exist" and "his vital breaths do not depart"—there can never be an entry into non-Vedic doctrines such as the Mādhyamika theory of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), nor is there any possibility of imitation of partial views held by the Sāṃkhyas, Bhāgavatas, and others.

An exposition of this established doctrine of the uncreated creation is to be found in the *Advaitaprakaraṇa* of Gauḍapāda’s *Kārikās*; it is not elaborated upon here for fear of excessive length. (Verses 35–57)

Now, in order to establish the firmness of the doctrine that creation is uncreated as previously stated, he explains that the collection of principles (tattvas) beginning with Anāśrita-Śiva and ending with Kālāgni-Rudra is indeed the true nature of the world as expressed by words:
"The state of Anāśrita, which partakes in tranquility and is the sole abode of the world consisting of pure Śakti..."
For the world has been submerged by you within that radiance, which is like a stainless, blazing, and pure fire.

By the words beginning with *śāntatama*, [the author explains]: that which is the "unsupported state" (*anāśrita-pada*)—derived from the verbal root *an* meaning "not to move"—is the first among the eighty-one states, being dependent on neither the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) nor its vibration (*spanda*). It is the Śiva-principle (*śivatattva*), which is the sole abode of the world consisting of mere power (*śaktimātra*). "Speech" (*vāk*) is indeed power; "mere power" (*śaktimātra*) is that which is the unique primary home of the world. Alternatively, "measures" (*mātrāḥ*) are those things measured, such as sound and so forth; or they are the durations of time (*kāla*) consisting of the components of *nāda* (sound), ranging from one, two, three, or four measures, up to the *raṅgu* and *pluta* prosodic lengths, or beginning with the "measure of meaning" (*arthamātrā*) and so on.

The powers of the *mātrās* are the *śaktimātrās*. They alone are the world, or rather, they are its single abode. Therein, within the great light called the *anāśrita-śivatattva*, the visible world—the entire multitude of living beings consisting of both the insentient and the sentient—is [present]. This is a poetic conceit (*phalotprekṣā*) suggesting that it is as if for the purpose of performing a purification by fire known as *saṅkarṣaṇa*, which removes impurities, like the purification by fire used for stainless flaming objects.

According to the method of poetic ornamentation (*alaṅkāraprakriyā*), it is just as in the world a goldsmith burns metals such as gold in fire for the purpose of purifying their impurities; that is to say, "as if for the sake of burning in the fire of universal dissolution" (*pralayāgni*). From the perspective of the actual reality (*vastu*), however, it is like the purity of a stainless flame. "Stainless" (*nirmala*) means that from which the threefold impurities, beginning with the *āṇava*, have departed. "Purity of a stainless flame" (*nirmalajvalanaśauca*) refers to the innate purity of the fire of consciousness (*cidagni*); because it possesses this, it is called "like a stainless flame," using the suffix *-vat* in the sense of possession (*matvarthe*). Indeed, [all things] have been conquered by you.

The sense is that although it consists of the six stainless paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), it has been immersed for the sake of attaining a luster equal to that of gold. The particle *hi* is a causal indeclinable; for (*hi*) because the world was immersed by you, therefore that very world, partaking in tranquility, becomes the unconditioned state (*anāśrita-pada*). The state of being fully tranquil is the direct realization of one's own self as non-different from Śiva—known as the principle of the Unconditioned (*anāśrita-śivatattva*)—which is the very state of the world’s transcendence while its body remains as mere power (*śaktimātra*).

The meaning is that [the nature of emptiness] is not a form of voidness called "total annihilation" as accepted by other systems such as the Madhyamaka; therefore, there is no opportunity for defects such as entering into or imitating other philosophical systems. || 37-59 ||

Since the triad consisting of the perceiver, the perceived, and the perception—described within the *anāśrita-śiva-tattva*—has as its very body mere manifestation (*bhānamātra*), there is not even the slightest room for the doubt that it contradicts the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita-siddhānta*). Thus he says:
"May that which is called the state of pervasion by the manifestation of the perceiver, who consists of the perfected power, shine forth."
O Mother, this collection of wealth which you extend toward your son is indeed [your gift]. (50)

By the words beginning with *siddhaśakti* and so forth: O Ambikā! In the reading *tvadantike*, it means "in your presence. This collection of objects (*arthanikara*) consists of the forms of speech such as sound and touch, as well as the forms of objects such as pots and cloths; it also includes the collection of the four aims of human life (*puruṣārtha*), beginning with dharma. It is the state of pervasion (*vyāptibhāva*) consisting of the manifestation of the subject (*bhātṛbhāsana*) which is composed of perfected power (*siddhaśaktimaya*). That state of pervasion of the manifestation of the subject is perfected as belonging to the Self (*ātman*), taking the form of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the powers of knowledge and action.

Even when separated by space, time, and so forth, he is one whose nature consists of the pervasive state of the subject characterized by unimpeded power of cognition; and being thus described as one whose nature consists of the pervasive manifestation [of objects] in the form of the accomplishment of such power of action, he becomes the means for his own self-luminosity by attaining the state of luminosity (*prakāśatā*). Alternatively, because he—having become manifest and illuminated through the pervasive manifestation of the subject consisting of accomplished powers—attains the state of luminosity, therefore [he is so called].

You are she whose form is the supreme mantra-speech consisting of a multitude of sounds, which is the manifestation of the Śākta emission (visarga) and primarily characterized by the awakening of the mind; yet you are also that which is imperceptible, the manifestation of the Śāmbhava emission, primarily characterized by the dissolution of the mind, whose form is the objects denoted by the supreme mantra—such as jars, cloths, and so forth—and who takes the form of the fourfold human goals, both perceptible and imperceptible.

The meaning is that you now expand the multitude of words and meanings—which previously existed as if directed toward a cognizer distinct from yourself—so that they become directed toward a cognizer non-different from yourself. The point here is that in this state, because the manifestation of the triad [of knower, known, and knowing] is of the nature of the self-luminous reality alone, there is no room for the suspicion that the non-dual nature is contradicted. (38–60)

With this much of the textual composition, having described the state of equilibrium between the nature of the Word and its Meaning—composed of Consciousness and Unconsciousness—as consisting of the Sound (Nāda) and Light (Jyotis) of Speech, [the author] now intends to expand, in due order, the worship of the three wheels (*cakras*) whose form is Light and Bliss through the sequence of the abodes (*dhāma*), consciousness (*saṃvit*), and phonemes (*varṇa*). To this end, by first demonstrating the two attributes of witnesshood (*sākṣitva*) and transmigratoriness (*saṃsāritva*) within the very nature of the Self which consists of that [equilibrium], and by effecting an exchange between the states of subject and object within the triad of Consciousness, Bliss, and the Three Worlds (*tripuṭī*), he first briefly indicates the Wheel of Light consisting of the Abodes (*dhāmamaya-prakāśacakra*) for the purpose of awakening to the reality of the nature of Bliss. He says: [The text follows].
In this world, that which is the state of being a seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) in the act of illumination,
and that which is the state of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtā*) in the process of ascertainment— that too, in the grasping of what is determined, is your own nature as the grasper (*grāhaka*).
He who is nourished by your livelihood knows that. || 61 ||

By the words "the state of being a seer," etc.: "jagat" means that which moves in the world (*jagati gacchati*). According to the etymology involving the transposition of letters as taught in the *Siṃhādi-gaṇa*—or by the etymology involving the addition of letters—the meaning is "in the living soul (*jīva*), which possesses motion and is of the nature of the primary vital breath (*prāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "in the manifestation": the meaning is "in the objective sphere consisting of the activity of the internal and external senses, which is characterized by engagement with and withdrawal from sense objects. "That which is the state of being a seer" (*draṣṭṛtā*) refers to the agency of seeing (*darśanakartṛtā*).

Thus, in the desire to provide a general indication of the nature of all the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), the neuter form "yat" is used. This should be understood similarly in what follows. Regarding the reading "dṛṣṭatā"—it means that which is the state of being an object of vision; that is, the state of being an object of the functions of both the internal and external organs. Furthermore, it refers to the operation of the intellect (*buddhi*) consisting in the determination of the reality of an object during the process of ascertainment (*niścaya-vidhi*), as well as to the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) consisting in the operation upon an object thus ascertained.

And that which is "the state of being a knower" (*pramātṛtā*)—consisting of the internal activity of the agent in the form of the substratum of a certain cognition characterized as "I am the knower"—is [the subject]. In the reading *pramātṛkā*, the meaning is either the excellent series of phonemes or the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) belonging to it. Likewise, in the case of the apprehension of the certain, there is the activity of the cognitive organs (*jñānendriya*) related to the nature of the certain object, as well as the activity of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) such as the grasping of objects, and with respect to the object itself, there is also the state of being the grasper (*grāhakatva*), which consists of both the cognitive and the active organs.

In the reading *prāhakam tvam*, the meaning is: "You alone are he," and "He alone is you. It means: "O Mother of the letters of excellent color (*prakṛṣṭavarṇamātṛkā*), toward whom do you speak? Being of the nature of the garland of letters consisting of the Śākta emission (*visarga*), toward whom—whether the individual soul (*jīva*) or the Lord (*īśvara*) situated between the Āṇava and Śāmbhava emissions—do you speak? All that [occurs] when your [sustenance] has been nourished—that is, when the nourishment has arisen through the internal and external activities such as speaking and listening belonging to you, the Goddess Parāvāk.

He—the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa), who is Śiva and the subject non-different from you as stated in the preceding verse—obtains through knowledge (*vidyā*). According to the meaning of the verbal root *vid* in the sense of "knowledge" and "attainment," by attaining [it] through the state of being the inverse subject (*viparītapramātṛbhāva*), he knows.

If one asks why, it is because—according to the analogy of the elephant and the bull painted on a wall—the sense organs, nourished first by the activity of your own mental modifications (*buddhi-vṛtti*), obtain the multitude of worldly objects consisting of action; subsequently, while transmigrating as one consisting of knowledge, nourished by the activity of the organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*) accompanied by mental modifications, one finally remains merely as a witness through the activity of *sāmarasya* (equipoise). This is the intended meaning.

This very Self, consisting of the ninefold *nāda*, should be understood as the sovereign ruler (*svarājya*)—a term synonymous with its own kingdom—by virtue of being composed of the eighteen vowels (the three groups, the six classes, and the six limbs), the sixteen-fold totality of the five triads, and the previously mentioned forms of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) such as the triad beginning with the first group (one, two, three, four, etc.), according to their respective possibilities; and because it consists of the wheel of rays of light in the form of self-luminous delight (*rañjana*), it is the author of its own sovereignty which consists of both activity (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*).

And the poet will state even further ahead: "O King, because of my sovereignty (*rājanāt*) and because of my people (*rañjanāt*), know me as 'Rāja' (*rājasaṃjñam*)," and so forth. By thus distinguishing between the two portions of sovereignty consisting of knowledge and action, he indicates the *prakāśacakra* (the wheel of light): the state of being a prince through the individual differentiation of the six wheels of the organs of knowledge and action, and the state of being the king himself through their collective totality as the Self. (Verses 39–61)

Now, having analyzed through a variation in the reading the relationship of part and whole— which serves as an aid to the predominance of the Wheel of the Light of Form (mūrtiprakāśacakra) to be described in the fourth contemplation (vimarśa), and which is occasioned by the state of being the subordinate and the principal within their own essential natures through their respective sovereignties— [the author] demonstrates this for the Wheel of Light of Consciousness (prakāśacakra), which consists of the totality of the ninefold resonance of the three triads indicated in the preceding verse, and which is the playful manifestation of the totality of the three emissions (visarga)— namely Śākta, Śāmbhava, and Anuttara— within the sphere of Word and Meaning (vāgarthamaṇḍala) comprising both the existent and the non-existent, [and for] the Goddess who is the smile of the body of the Intellect and the Unperishing (Dhīmanokṣavapuḥ):
"Abiding in the sphere of existent and non-existent objects, consisting of the Intellect, the Unperishing, and the Smile..."
Wherever that tenfold sovereignty exists, I am present there as well; I am that very portion of you (I am even more than you). || 62 ||

By the words "āsthita" (established) and so forth: this [subject] is the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), which consists of either the *śāmbhava* or *āṇava* emission (*visarga*) mentioned in the preceding verse; it is Śiva. The sense is that he is established in the "smile" (*asmitā*) whose form is the intellect (*dhīmat*) and the individual soul (*nokṣa*), and which is the root cause of the entire circle of existent and non-existent objects (*sadasadarthamaṇḍala*). Furthermore, he is established in the circle of existent and non-existent objects; that is, he presides over them by means of the nature of the play of the *āṇava* emission. Thus, he is the primary vital breath-Śiva who has attained the state of the play of the *āṇava* emission, both within that "smile" whose form is the intellect and the individual soul, and within the circle of existent and non-existent objects which are their effects.

The "tenfold" (*daśavidhi*) refers to that by which the ten organs of knowledge and action are established: five through the modes of intellect (*dhī*), mind (*manas*), the senses (*akṣa*), body (*vapuḥ*), and smile (*smitā*); and five through the modes of mind (*manaḥ*), giving (*pradāna*), knowledge (*jñāna*), the senses (*akṣa*), body (*vapuḥ*), and smile (*smitā*). Furthermore, if the reading here were *trayodaśavidha* ("thirteenfold"), it would be thirteenfold by means of the two—the mandalas of the existent and non-existent objects (*sadasadarthamaṇḍala*)—added to the [previous] eleven consisting of intellect, mind, the senses, body, and smile.

This *prāṇa-śiva*, which consists of the *āṇava-visarga*, is also suggested to be of thirteen kinds: by way of the ten-fold division described in the *Sadasadarthamaṇḍala*—namely, the three types of *asmitā* consisting of the body of intellect (*dhī-vapuḥ*), the body of mind (*manas-vapuḥ*), and the body of the senses (*akṣa-vapuḥ*)—and by way of the [remaining] three kinds of *asmitā* to be described later as non-different from the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) at the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*). This is because it will be stated later: "In this context, the sun of *prāṇa* consists of six *kalās* of consciousness," and so forth.

Alternatively, regarding the variant reading "the tenfold method" (*daśavidhi*) mentioned previously: in that sphere of existent and non-existent objects (*sadasadarthamaṇḍala*), that which is the tenfold method—though it is the smiling form of the Intellect (*dhīmanokṣavapuḥ*)—is independence (*svatantratā*). Even though it is non-dual (*ataddvaya*), it is independent by virtue of its own sovereignty (*ātmasvātantrya*), which consists of the nature of the Intellect, the Unmanifest (*anokṣa*), and the Smile (*asmitā*). Even though it is non-dual, it is independent through its own sovereignty consisting of the Intellect, the Unmanifest, and the Smile; and even though it is non-dual, it exists as the play of the Śāmbhava emission (*sarga*), which is the dissolution of the mind (*cittapralaya*).

Although [the Lord] is devoid of the two circles of existent and non-existent objects that are attached to the body and the smile, he is nevertheless the play of the unsurpassed emission (*visarga*) of Śakti, which consists of the awakening of consciousness; or rather, through the play of both—that which consists of the form of the Unsurpassed (A), which is the source-sound (*yonisvara*) of the ninefold resonance (*nāda*) expressed as "a i u ṇ"—and that which is the play of the two residing within the letter A, he is established in his absolute sovereignty (*svatantratāsiddha*) as the play of non-duality, according to the etymological derivation that this play of non-duality is "the play of that which is not those two."

"I am a portion (*aṃśaka*) of you" means: either by way of the manifestation of the *visarga* of Śambhu, which is primarily *nāda*, or by way of the expansion of the unsurpassed *visarga* of Śakti, which is primarily the *śabda-bindu*. You are a portion within that [reality] which consists of the ninefold *nāda*. Or, by way of *nāda*, because its nature consists of the unswerving play of the individual soul (*aṇu*)—whether in the form of speech, meaning, or sound—the sense is that it is indeed of the very form of your own portion.

Regarding the reading "tavādhikaḥ" (superior to you): [He is superior] either by virtue of the manifestation of the *śāmbhava* emission (*visarga*) in its formal aspect, or by virtue of being the essence of the identity (*sāmarasya*) between the Word and the Meaning through the manifestation of the *śākta* unsurpassed emission (*anuttara-visarga*). Whether it be "I am indeed He" or "He is I," having fallen away from the state of a limited individual (*aṇu*), he has attained the state of the Great Vibration of the Unstruck Sound (*unmanī-mahāprāṇana-nāda*). Thus, the meaning is that even for you, who consist of both Word and Meaning, he alone is truly worthy of worship. || 40-62 ||

Having spoken thus, [the text] illuminates the state of the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who consists of the wheel of bliss and whose form is non-dual, by means of the very nature of the wheel of light— which is the abode of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) and the manifestation of the Transmental (*unmanī*) at the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśānta*)— for one whose state of duality regarding the play of emission (*visarga*) as a limited individual (*āṇava*) has fallen away, and who has attained the state of non-duality regarding the play of the unsurpassed emission of Śakti and Śambhu.
This Supreme Person is the embodiment of bliss characterized by the objects of enjoyment consisting of this or that specific meaning.
Through the offering of the universe into the sky of consciousness,
that [reality] shines forth as the child consisting of withdrawal.

By the phrase "tattadartha... and so forth: this emission (*visarga*) of the *aṇu*, mentioned in the preceding verse, is the practitioner (*sādhaka*). It is the embodiment of bliss whose characteristic is the objects of enjoyment consisting of those respective meanings. Those words are "consisting of those respective meanings" (*tattadarthamaya*) because they go toward that meaning—which consists of the expressed, the indicated, the intended, and so forth—by means of the relationship of being the object to be communicated (*pratipādyatā-sambandha*). That very bliss, for which those [words] are the objects of enjoyment and which has them as its characteristic, is "the bliss whose characteristic is the objects of enjoyment consisting of those respective meanings" (*tattadarthamayabhogyalakṣaṇānanda*).

He alone is the embodiment (mūrti) of that [Supreme Reality] for one whose life-force (prāṇa) is immersed in the bliss of the primordial sound (nāda). Thus, he is the embodiment of bliss characterized by the objects of enjoyment consisting of various specific meanings. The sense is this: in the sovereign empire of the bliss of knowledge (vidyānanda), words that convey those various meanings serve as the cause of internal satisfaction according to one's qualification—just as food and other objects of enjoyment satisfy hunger for ordinary people—by acting as the causes of devotion, knowledge, and dispassion; therefore, they possess the characteristic of being the embodiment of bliss.

This has been stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata, in the eleventh skandha: "Devotion, the experience of the Supreme Lord, and detachment from everything else—these three occur simultaneously for one who takes refuge [in Him] according to his capacity; contentment and nourishment follow, just as the cessation of hunger follows the eating of food. The Śruti also says in the context of the Vājapeya sacrifice: "Speech was indeed the first food of the gods."

Regarding the reading *tattadarthamayabhogalakṣaṇa*: it "characterizes enjoyment (*bhoga*) consisting of those various objects of denotation (*tattadabhidheyārthamaya*) and consisting of the three or four aims of human life (*tricaturvargapuruṣārthamaya*)," thus it is *tattadarthamayabhogalakṣaṇa*. That which is both this [enjoyment] and bliss (*ānanda*) is its "form" (*mūrti*); or rather, he whose form is that very thing is *tattadarthamayabhogalakṣaṇānandamūrti*. This is the meaning. For this very reason, he is "supreme" (*uttama*), for by manifesting the imperishable (*akṣara*) which transcends both speech and meaning, he has risen above all else and is most exalted (*udgatatamaska*).

The intended meaning is that [He] consists of the *nāda* (the primordial sound) which transcends the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*). For this very reason, the Person (*pumān*) is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) precisely by virtue of His transcendence over the universe; such is the sense. This has also been stated by the Blessed One in the *Gītā*: "All beings are perishable (*kṣara*), while the Immutable (*akṣara*) is called the Unchanging (*kūṭastha*). But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. Since I transcend the perishable and am even higher than the Immutable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*)."

Thus [it is said]. By this, the piercing of the knot of ignorance (*āvidyaka-granthi-bheda*) is explained; for when the Self—characterized by the *manī*, *maha*, and *anāda* sounds, which are the causes of the words and meanings that awaken the bliss of the objects—is established as the very embodiment of bliss (*ānanda-mūrti*), its state as the witness (*sākṣitva*) to the ego-sense of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-ahaṃkāra*) is also effectively demonstrated. The method for this is found in the *Vedāntapañcapaśyā* and the *Pratyaktattvaviveka*: "Through non-discrimination, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and the conscious self (*cidātman*) are unified. Then, the desires denoted by the word 'kāma' arise in the form: 'This shall be mine,' 'That shall be mine,' 'This shall be mine.'"

"Without causing the conscious self (cidātman) to enter [the ego], one who perceives the ego as separate, even while desiring millions of objects, is not obstructed because of the piercing of the knot. O Śivā, you whose nature is contrary desire! O Mother! Therefore, from that cause—the enjoyment of objects characterized as previously described—for the sake of the world, namely the living being (jīva) characterized by the vital breath (prāṇa) possessing the aforementioned movement, through its offering into the sky of consciousness (cidambara), which is the space consisting of consciousness, it becomes "consisting of withdrawal" (saṃhatimaya); that is, it undergoes withdrawal (saṃhati)—meaning dissolution—or causes [it] to attain withdrawal. Thus, it is "consisting of withdrawal."

The meaning is this: he himself, consisting of the activity of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), becomes the withdrawer of his own self through the play of the *Śāmbhava* emission which is the dissolution of the mind, or he becomes the performer of the act of creation through the play of the *Śākta* emission which is the awakening of the mind. The point is that, just as there is a dissolution into the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) at the time of the dissolution of the winds—both the inert and non-inert elements of the world—there is a dissolution into the "small space" (*daharākāśa*) at the time of enjoyment for the objects of enjoyment of the wise; this is the secret of the science of the arising of the Sound (*nāda*).

In the reading "tava" (of you), the grammatical connection is as follows: in your sky of consciousness—that is, in the ether consisting of pure awareness which is non-different from you—you shine forth in one of two forms, being an embodiment of bliss composed of *sahṛta* (withdrawal). || 41-63 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "If the transmigratory cycle consisting of word and meaning—which is like a corpse—is dissolved for that noble person whose body is characterized by the attainment of the bliss of *nāda* through the power of such worship of *nāda*, and who no longer engages in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body, then what becomes of it? Anticipating this, [the author] demonstrates the linguistic usage of word and meaning as consisting of the eightfold *liṅga*-based impressions fashioned from the divisions of the eight groups of the Mother-phonemes (*mātṛkā*) according to the system of the Śaiva Tantras, such as the Kaula, Kāpālika, and Pāśupata; and he further shows the distinction between the states of the individual soul (*jīva*), the divine (*deva*), and the bound beast (*paśu*), which are both immanent in the universe and transcendent of it:
"O Śivā, she who shines forth eightfold in the City..."
Having attained a subtle state characterized by inference,
those whose mental fluctuations have been stilled do not perceive the sacrificial animal when it has entered your belly as you consume that which is offered through its consumption. || 64 ||

"Eightfold," it is said. *He śive* is the vocative case; or it may be the locative (*saptamī*), intended to express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the Śiva who is to be accomplished. The "lingistic subtle state" (*laiṅgikaṃ sūkṣmabhāvam*) is that which is conceived in one sense as the gross form of the five elements—earth and so forth—which constitute the *liṅga*, and as the gross state of the three spheres of fire, sun, and moon; and in another sense, it consists of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) such as smell belonging to those [elements], as well as the forms of consciousness (*cit*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the body. Elsewhere it is said: "Consciousness (*citi*), the mind (*citta*), the object of thought (*caitya*), and non-dual awareness (*cetana*) alone."

"The individual soul (jīva), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the body are declared to be the 'City of Eight' (puryaṣṭaka). Likewise, its definition is stated as follows: "Speech and the other four [organs of action], hearing and the other four [organs of perception], the five beginning with the vital breath (prāṇa), the five beginning with the face, the intellect (buddhi) and so forth, ignorance (avidyā), desire (kāma), and action (karman)—these they call the City of Eight, the subtle body. It is for this very reason that [it is said]: "The City of Eight Wheels, with nine gates, the primordial city of the gods; its inner chamber is a golden treasury, the heavenly world enveloped in light. He who knows that [city] of Brahman..."

"The city enveloped in nectar—to him, both Brahman and Brahmā bestowed longevity, fame, and progeny. Thus, that which is declared by Śruti to be the cause of the universe is also inferential (*laiṅgika*). It is called *liṅga* because the external primordial nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the universe, dissolves (*līyate*) therein, and the internal nature, consisting of word and meaning, is perceived (*gamyate*) therein.

Having attained its subtle state of being inferential, the City—which consists of meaning, sound, and the Brahman of resonance (*nāda-brahman*)—manifests eightfold as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the three limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the gross, the subtle, and the causal, respectively.

For this very reason, this same poet, in the introductory *nāndī* of the drama *Śākuntala*, has expressed through subtle suggestion the perceptibility of even the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) of Śiva: "He who is the first creation of the Creator; she who bears the oblation offered according to the rite; she who is the offerer; those two who ordain time; she who, possessing qualities that are the objects of the Vedas, stands pervading the universe; her whom they call the primordial nature of all beings; and by whom living creatures possess life—with these eight manifest and gracious bodies, may the Lord protect you."

*Tajjapauṣṭakṛtacittavṛttayaḥ* means those mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttayaḥ*) which, in the case of *tajjapa* (the recitation of that), are performed with the lips (*oṣṭhakṛta*)—that is, trained by the movement of the lips—in the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) belonging to the sacred sound (*śābda*). These refer to those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in which the recitation consists of the phonemes of the eight groups of the *Mātṛkā*, which signify the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*) [of Śiva]. However, in the case of the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) of the internal speech (*ārthikavāk*), it is that which is born from that (*tajja*), consisting of the threefold nature (*trivṛt*) and the three castes (*traivarṇika*) formed by the eightfold vibration of *prāṇa*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*, and produced within the subtle city (*sūkṣmapurī*). That which is *pauṣṭa* refers either to the state of nourishment (*puṣṭibhāva*) or to the action (*karma*) that nourishes only that much.

*Tajjapauṣṭam* means nourished by the recitation of that [mantra]. *Tatkṛtāḥ* refers to those mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttayaḥ*) which have been trained to such an extent; thus they are so described. Regarding the reading *tajjuṣoṣṭakṛtacittavṛttayaḥ*: they are *tajjuṣaḥ* because they cherish and delight in that eightfold group of Mātṛkās and the subtle city (*sūkṣmapurī*). They are *aṣṭa*, meaning numbering eight—the eight bonds (*pāśas*) whose characteristics are stated as: "Pity, doubt, fear, shame, disgust as the fifth, family, caste, and conduct—these are proclaimed as the eight bonds. These are the forms of the bonds of the bound souls (*paśu-pāśas*), and they constitute the mental fluctuations.

The meaning is that their mental dispositions have been cultivated since birth over many lifetimes. Regarding "impressions" (*vāsanā*): through different etymological derivations—namely, "that in which the inner self dwells" (*vasati*) and "that by which [the self] is perfumed" (*vāsyate*)—these refer to the impressions of the mind belonging to those holding office (*adhikārika*). "Upon his chest" means upon the chest of the aforementioned subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they exist while the bound soul (*paśu*) remains. The sense is that binding impressions belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) who consists of the universe, but not to one who has transcended the universe. "While the bound soul remains upon your chest" means while the bound soul resides within your belly.

Thus, in both readings, the meaning is as follows: for you, whose nature is that of the aforementioned stale matter (*paryuṣṭaka*), these [impurities] exist only in the sacrificial altar and pavilion consisting of speech within the chest, or in the belly consisting of meaning; they do not exist in the Supreme Śiva, whose essential nature transcends the universe. The established sense is that those whose mental fluctuations terminate merely in the nourishment of the body and senses become firmly rooted in the form of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of a bound soul (*paśu*).

Therefore, the definition of the bound soul (*paśu*) is stated in another Tantra: "He who has become an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), having his sovereign power eclipsed by *kalā*, is known as a *paśu*. Also, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "The *paśus* are said to be of three kinds: the *vijñānakevala*, the *pralayakevala*, and the *sakala*. Among them, the first is joined with *mala*; the second is joined with *mala* and *karman*; [the third] is joined with *mala*, *māyā*, and *karman*. Among these, the first [the *sakala*] is of two types."

"The first [category] has completed its impurity; the second is one whose impurity is not yet complete. (2) "Without bestowing grace upon the first, Śiva appoints eight as Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and creates other mantras; these are said to be seventy million in number. (3) By such passages, although the status of having the body of seventy million great mantras is established, it is shown in that very same place that the fivefold division pertaining to office (*adhikārika*) is likewise unavoidable.

With this very intention, even in the *Śruti*, it is stated that the fourteen worlds of knowledge (*vidyā-bhuvana*) and so forth—which are differentiated by the fourteen vowels—possess seven distinct species of animals each, totaling forty-nine, categorized by the distinctions of domestic and wild animal classes. This applies even to those born as gods (*ājāna-deva*), who possess bodies composed of unevolved speech and meaning (*apañcīkṛta-vāgartha-śarīrin*) and whose sound and touch are bound by the rules of meter, feet, syllables, and prosody; for they too, like those possessing bodies made of the five gross elements (*pañcīkṛta-pāñcabhautika-śarīra-abhimānin*), are subject to these classifications. Thus: "Seven... [and so on].

"There are seven domestic animals and seven wild animals, corresponding to the seven meters"—thus [it is said]. Likewise: "Those domestic animals which are of manifold forms; those wild animals which are of manifold forms. Furthermore, regarding the nature of the plant species, through such statements as "There are seven domestic plants and seven wild plants, corresponding to the seven meters," and so forth, [this is taught] in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, in the fourth anuvāka of the first pāṭhaka of the third kāṇḍa, and in the ninth anuvāka, as well as in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka under the guise of the narrative of Manu and Nābhānediṣṭha.

This is heard from various scriptural passages; therefore, beginning from the fifty-third verse of the nineteenth chapter of the fourth section of the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, even the Great Lord (Mahādhikārin) is explicitly proclaimed as being fit for slaughter as an animal. For instance, after establishing that even the Sacrificial Person (*Yajñapuruṣa*) possesses the status of an animal through such statements as, "He whose intellect is Brahmā, and he whose ego is Śiva," it continues: "By means of sacrifices involving violence, the Blessed One indeed attains satisfaction."

For [the scripture] describes even that [sacrificial animal] as attaining the state of Brahman through its being offered in the fire, beginning with the words: "If that sacrificial animal is fit for becoming Brahman... Thus, even for one who possesses such great qualification, there is the offering as a sacrificial animal by means of the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā*), which is synonymous with the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) residing in the form of the Teacher (*ācārya*). Likewise: "Birth, life, striking, awakening, consecration, then purification, nourishment, and again..."

"Satisfying (tarpaṇa), kindling (dīpana), and concealing (gupti)—these ten are the purificatory rites (saṃskriyā) of mantra. By such statements, the necessity of being purified through the Tantric purificatory rites of mantra as taught in the *Śāradātilaka* and other texts is established. And it is said in the *Śaivagama*: "He who, by the descent of the power that is the cause of eradication, conquers these souls whose impurities are fully ripened in the Supreme Reality—he, abiding in the form of the Preceptor (ācārya), [performs] initiation (dīkṣā). Likewise: "Initiation bestows perfection when it removes the web of bonds from the individual soul (aṇu) that was previously inverted, whether it pertains to the mantra or the practitioner (mantrin)."

"A mantra separate [from the Self] and a practitioner separate [from the mantra] never attain success. Those who merely recite mantras do not truly know them as mantras. The gods and Gandharvas are deluded and arrogant through false knowledge. Just as with the sugarcane of Puṇḍra, when the sweetness that touches the heart is present, the mere residue characterized by the utterance of syllables remains in the mouth. Thus, the detailed exposition of this matter is clearly found in the *Tantrāloka* and other works.

Now, regarding the Vedic perspective: in the *Vedāntapañcadaśī* and the *Citradīpa*, it is demonstrated through detailed analysis that the perception of difference—consisting of the states of subject (*dharmin*), attribute (*dharma*), and the bound soul (*paśu*) as distinct from one's own true nature—is precisely what leads to the attainment of lordship (*īśvaratva*). This occurs when the individual soul (*jīva*), existing as a reflection of consciousness within the modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*), is transformed by means of a body composed of consciousness reflected through latent impressions (*vāsanā*). In this process, the very manifestation of the distinction between subject and attribute within one’s own true nature—which is essentially a unity of the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*)—is brought about by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the reality of one’s own true nature. This is the summary [of the teaching]. (Verses 42–64)

In the manner thus described, through the ninefold resonance (*nāda*), the ninefold speech (*vāk*), the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), and the divisions of the way, within the cycles of transmigration consisting of the Śaiva, Jaina, and Pāśupata [traditions]—wherein there exist bodies composed of the activities of creation and dissolution characterized by the mutual relationship of eater and eaten—and wherein there exists either the state of identity with or non-difference from the empowered mantra consecrated by the previously mentioned initiations and purificatory rites; or else, between the two bodies composed of the effects of the Creator and the Obscurer, that which is experienced as either Śākta or Śāmbhava, manifest internally as the witness-consciousness or externally as an object of the senses.

He says: "To you alone, who are the embodiment of the Unmanī, Nāda, and Navaka-bliss, and who—though possessing a living body subject to saṃsāra—are a preeminent personage characterized by repose through the *āṇava* emission (*visarga*), [it is] in your own essential nature that the subtle body (composed of intellect, mind, and breath, as previously described), which is capable of the fivefold cosmic function (*kṛtyapañcaka*) and consists of the aforementioned *laiṅgika* [body], is graciously bestowed. Thus he says:
"[The union] of the two bodies, situated in the roles of the eater and the eaten..."
O Śivā! In the meantime, you have assumed a magnificent and auspicious form for the sake of liberation. || 65 ||

By the words "creation and withdrawal," etc., [it is meant as follows]. "O Śivā" is the vocative case. Alternatively, the locative case is used in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), with the intention of referring to the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva who abide in the state that is the abode of ignorance (*avidyā-niketapada*). Regarding the two bodies of creation and withdrawal: the body of creation consists of the *śākta-visarga*, characterized by the awakening of the mind (*citta-prabodha*); the body of the individual soul (*jīva-śarīra*). The body of withdrawal consists of the *śāmbhava-visarga*, characterized by the dissolution of the mind (*citta-pralaya*). In the reading "of the bodies of creation and concealment" (*sarga-saṃvṛti-śarīrayoḥ*), it refers to the body of the creation of both word and meaning by the Lord, consisting of either the awakening or the dissolution of the mind.

The conventional body (*saṃvṛti-śarīra*), however, consists of the emission of the *aṇu* characterized by the resting of the mind; it conceals its own true nature through the concealment of its essential form, characterized by abiding in either of the two abodes of nescience (*avidyā*)—either as identification with one or both of creation and withdrawal. This pertains to those two bodies of creation and withdrawal. Therefore, they abide in the state of the "eaten" and the "eater," meaning they abide in the state of the eightfold "eaten" and "eater" consisting of the bound soul (*paśu*) and the fetter (*pāśa*) mentioned in the previous verse, or in that very condition.

The sense is that, because of their equality, even within the boundaries of speech and meaning—wherein the *āṇava* emission has entered into the *śākta* and *śāmbhava* emissions, which consist of the nasalized vowel (*anusvāra*) representing the full state, and which abide in the relationship of eater and eaten—the same principle applies. All of this will be clearly established in the third *vimarśa* (contemplation) in the passage: "The sequence of the universe, beginning from its manifestation, resides in the four vowels of the Heart and the *Kuṇḍa*. Therefore, it is omitted here. [This occurs] between the two, namely, between those two forms of speech and meaning. *Antarā* means in the interval.

I have taken my stand upon this form of your thighs or this form of your belly mentioned in the preceding verse—a form consisting of the unsurpassed resonance (*nāda*), possessing the characteristics and dimensions to be described hereafter, the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*), the station of the state of *magā*, and the armor (*varma*). The sense is that I am established there through the state of being the Śuka-bheda, which is the differentiation between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśa*) as previously stated. Alternatively, the sense may be that I have taken my stand as a witness through non-dual identity, thinking "I myself am your chest or your belly," as stated in the previous verse.

O wise one, by you—through the nature of the six paths consisting of the *unmanī*, *nāda*, speech, and meaning—the body of the Indestructible (the Supreme Lord) has been offered. Since both the bound soul (*paśu*) and the Lord of Beasts (*paśupati*) reside equally within your chest and belly, they have been offered alike; thus, the sense is that there is no partiality on your part. || 43-65 ||

Thus, even according to the system of the *Pāśupata* and other Śaiva, Śākta, and Tantric Āgamas, there is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who transcends the universe consisting of the worlds of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as well as His own group of organs of action and cognition—which, being composed of ritual action and knowledge, serve the purpose of all sacrifices and rites—and which consist of the principles of the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*). This is established by first fulfilling the status of a Vedic-praised sacrificial animal (*paśu*) as stated in the Agnicayana section of the *Taittirīya Saṃhitā*, fifth book, second chapter, ninth section: "Other animals are indeed not animals compared to the cow and the horse. [The Supreme Person is thus the ultimate reality.]

Bearing the name *Cakrarāja* for himself as the Lord of Beings (*Paśupati*) and the name "Prince" for his retinue of the senses and so forth— just as a circle of twelve kings has a prince— he sows the seed for the description of the sovereign wheel (*cakrarāja*) as a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) consisting of the forms of Light and Bliss to be described hereafter, through the aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) of those two: "Because of ruling (*rājanāt*) and because of delighting (*rañjanāt*), know me as the one named 'King' (*rājasaṃjña*) in the acts of awakening and action."
O Śivā, these six have been established by you as distinct initiators [of the lineage], having been invested with the status of sons.

By the words "O King, O Āditya," and so forth: O Śive! This vocative is intended to refer to the conscious life-principle (*jīva*) consisting of the supreme emission (*anuttaravisarga*), which is the nature of consciousness (*cinmaya*) and power (*śakti*), characterized by the awakening of the mind. Alternatively, it is the locative case, intended to refer to the world as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) consisting of insentient life (*jaḍajīva*) born from the supreme emission of the individual soul (*āṇava-anuttaravisarga*), characterized by the repose of the mind; or else, it refers to the essential nature of Supreme Śiva (*paraśivasvarūpa*), the object of the supreme emission of Śambhu (*śāmbhava-anuttaravisarga*), characterized by the dissolution of the mind.

From the root *rāj* (in the sense of "pleasing" and "shining"), because it shines forth spontaneously in the form of the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), which is another synonym for the previously mentioned *unmanī-nāda*; and likewise, because it pleases primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—that is, because it delights the *prakṛti* consisting of sound and meaning, which is the source of *nāda*. The underlying sense is that this occurs through the *Māheśvara-mātṛkā-sūtra* in the creation of the worlds and the sound-meaning of the fourteen branches of knowledge, beginning with the three Vedas. It is called by the name "Rāja"—meaning that which has "Rāja" as its designation.

And thus it has been stated in the *Parimala*: "The King is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the manifest God, because he delights the world. Following (*anu*) me—myself, who am the triad of speech, meaning, and the threefold vital breath (*prāṇa*)—in the matter of knowledge and action, which consist of the previously mentioned paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, that is, of awakening and ritual activity.

"Acting separately" (*pṛthakpravartakāḥ*): the sense is that they act separately because they function through distinct paths—contradictory paths, as it were—by means of the previously mentioned division between the paths of engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*), which are otherwise known as superimposition (*adhyāropa*) and negation (*apavāda*), according to the specific distinctions of place and time, such that "whatever has come into being is said to be enjoined (or prohibited). These six, in order, consist of the six organs of knowledge together with the mind; they are the motivators and the desistors of the knowing self (*jñānātman*) regarding the knowledge of the form of the *nāda-svara*, and [the motivators] of the acting self (*kriyātman*).

Likewise, they consist of the six organs of action together with the intellect (*buddhi*). In the fivefold activity consisting of speech, acquisition of objects, procreation, and so forth—both in the performance of action and in its cessation—they are the impellers of the active self (*kriyātman*) and the restrainers of the cognitive self (*jñānātman*). Thus, acting as distinct impellers, the group of six organs of action together with the intellect has been established in the status of "sons" and in the status of "sons of the path of action. This is the meaning.

By the reading "api ropitāḥ," the meaning is that they have not only been made to attain the state of Unmanī and Nāda, which is non-different from the pair of Siddhas and Brahma-śaktis mentioned in the verse beginning with "From Brahmā onwards, the five Siddhas," nor even the state of the bound soul (paśu) and the Lord of Souls (paśupati) mentioned in the preceding verse, but rather they have been made to attain the state of a prince (rājaputra).

Just as in the world those installed in the position of crown prince protect the realm of a common empire, so too in the empire of the Self, you—whose nature consists of the Śākta, the Anuttara, the Visarga, Speech, Meaning, and Nāda—have raised [beings] out of the state of a "victim" (paśu) mentioned in the previous verse and brought them to the state of a "son" (putra), in order to protect the station of the Self by acting as its savior from the hell named Pums; this is the intended meaning. The phrase "by you alone" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

And in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*, having cited this very verse, it is stated: "The King is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) himself, because he delights the world; his sons are indeed the six sense-faculties (*indriya*), who are the princes. Among these, those with authority (*sādhikāra*) are the organs of action (*karmendriya*) together with the intellect (*buddhi*), while those without authority (*niradhikāra*) are the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) together with the mind (*manas*). The meaning of this is that "having authority" consists in being an agent of action, whereas "lacking authority" consists in non-agency.

Even in the treatises on worldly affairs (*arthaśāstra*) such as those by Kāmandaki, there is a specific hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisandhi*). For example: "The king whose territory is immediately adjacent is the enemy; beyond him is the friend. The friend of the enemy is the *ari-mitra*; the friend of that friend is the *mitra-mitra* beyond that. Then the friend of the enemy's friend and so forth are the [states] preceding the one desiring conquest (*vijigīṣu*). This and more should be seen in that very work. Also, in the *Śārīraka-brahmasūtra-bhāṣya*: "Excluding the activity of the world, because of the context."

In this context of the Sūtra-bhāṣya, by accepting the conventional meaning of the word *jagat* (the world), the connection of liberated souls with the fivefold external activities—such as the creation of the inert universe—is indeed refuted; however, their internal fivefold activities consisting of speech, objects, and knowledge are not. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the subsequent passage in that very same text: "By his mere volition, his ancestors appear," and so forth.

By this, it is shown that even those ancient [traditions] well-known as the Smārta and Sāṃkhya-Yoga paths—which, though originating from the sages, are auxiliary to the external sciences such as the Kāpila-Sāṃkhya and Haṭha-Yoga, and serve only to assist Vedic rituals—are intent upon the technical (yaugika) meanings [of the words]; whereas the more recent ones, fabricated by persons such as Dayānanda and others, which merely imitate the shadow of the Veda and are designated by different names such as the Ārya Samāj, do not rest even upon the mere external material nature consisting of the five elements.

It should be understood that they are refuted as being non-Vedic because they contradict the royal path of Vedic knowledge—which is also known by the name *Ādhyātmikarājavicārāja-guhyayoga*—insofar as [the latter] consists of: the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*) characterized by the relationship of teacher and disciple, whose object of knowledge is the three Vedas; the state of the Kṣatriya (*kṣatrabhāva*) characterized by the nature of royalty, whose object of knowledge is solely the six limbs and the six paths (*ṣaḍaṅga-ṣaḍadhvan*); and the state of the Vaiśya (*vaiśyabhāva*) characterized by the relationship of the bound soul and the Lord of Beasts (*paśu-paśupati*), whose object of knowledge consists of the various sciences such as the Tantras and Āgamas.

By means of the logic that even the fourfold objects of knowledge—consisting of the master and servant, the Śūdra-nature embodied in form, and the subject matter of compositions in vernacular speech—rests solely within the Self; and by means of the traditional worldly maxim that "conventional meaning (rūḍhi) is stronger than etymological derivation (yoga)," thereby accepting the conventional sense of Vedic words; and by means of the system which renders them helpful to the path of action, such as the Śūdra-nature mentioned in the statement, "One is born a Śūdra by birth, one is born a twice-born (dvija) by action."

This is because it is intended to show the establishment [of the Self] within the body of the *mahonmanī-bindu*—which is like the resonance (*nāda*) at the *dvādaśānta*—as that which expands the lineage of knowledge, being conceived for the sake of favoring the multitude of disciples, and with the desire to express its remote auxiliary function (*ārādupakārakatva*) extending up to the state of Brahman according to the Vedas. With this very intention, the learned, having in view the characteristics of worldly teachers and disciples, have said: "If they are capable of demonstrating [the truth], those who teach are indeed the true Gurus, the masters of the ritual of the resonance (*nāda*) as declared in the Vedas."

"Those very disciples serve their gurus in front; I consider them, moreover, to partake in the performance of both [the guru and the disciple]. This very point—the two lineages of gurus who initiate the two distinct traditions—is also described in the two subsequent verses above, following the indication of the sequence of the closing of the flower as stated in the *Jñānārṇava*. (44–66)

Thus, regarding the wheel (*vṛndacakra*) which consists of the Great Reality-Sequence (*mahārthakrama*) of five channels (*pañcavāha*), whose nature is the expansion and reabsorption of the two groups of six—the organs of knowledge and action accompanied by mind and intellect—which follow the path of Vedic, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga contemplation consisting of both natural (*prākṛta*) and supernatural (*aprākṛta*) vowels and consonants; and which, in the form of a pair of six types of gurus known as the Lineage of the Supreme (*paraugha*), the Great Current (*mahaugha*), the Divine (*divya*), the Siddha, and the Human (*mānava*), exists as the Self in the form of thirteen rays consisting of the pair of Kālī and Kāla-Paraśiva.

Having introduced that very seed-syllable (*bīja*), he intends to describe it as the root of the tree of Śiva’s worldly manifestation—which consists of both speech and meaning—by means of the aforementioned ninefold *nāda* (the "five perfected ones beginning with Brahman"). This is achieved through the repose in the Great Bindu at the *dvādaśānta*, which is utilized in the sequence of the "closing of the flower" (*puṣpasaṅkoca*) taught by the Guru in the *Jñānārṇava*. By being free from the defect of the "lost lineage" (*naṣṭasantati*) known as the forgetting of the internal wealth consisting of the twelve suns, he will establish it as such. In this regard, there occurs a reversal of the upward and downward flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, corresponding to the sun and the moon respectively.

Even within the wheel (*cakra*) whose form is the *nāda* consisting of the fire-bindu (*vahnibindu*), indicating the reversal of the digits of fire and moon (*agnīṣomakalā*), he reveals that the wheel of light consisting of the form of the *nāda* of fire and moon is essentially the assembly of the lineage of perfected gurus (*siddhaughagurumaṇḍala*):
"The sun of vital breath (*prāṇasūrya*), characterized by the bindu consisting of the upward-flowing [fire], is here the sixfold digit of consciousness."
In the lineage of the Guru, you are the body of light within the form of that Kālādhara, the circle of the Siddhas and their accomplishments.

By means of the two verses beginning with *aurdhvavāha*, [the text explains] the sequence of vowels, phonemes, and sounds characterized by the *aurdhvavāha* and *mayabindu*. First, there are the Bindus of Fire, Sun, and Moon, which are the root of the three *Māheśvara-sūtras* beginning with *a i u ṇ*—these sūtras being the source of the seven vowels and phonemes associated with the seven streams (*saptasrotas*) as indicated by the verse: "O Sovereign Goddess, you who exist in a sevenfold manner. Alternatively, they extend up to the invocation of the exertion (*udyoga*) of the Heart of Kāleya, which will be described at the end of the fourth *Vimarśa*.

The term "Aurdhvavāhamayabindulakṣaṇa" (characterized by the upward-flowing nectar-drops) refers to that which characterizes those drops consisting of the upward-flowing nectar (*ūrdhvavāha*). These drops are either designated by the phonetic series beginning with *ka* and ending with *pa*—the consonant class (*sparśavarga*)—as indicated by the syllable "kapay," or they are the root of the phonetic series consisting of the syllable at the "twelfth end" (*dvādaśānta*). The *praṇava* is the vowel; the wheel (*cakra*), which consists of the form of its resonance (*nāda*), is characterized by these drops consisting of the upward-flowing nectar.

Alternatively, as it is said: "The movement of the thighless charioteer [the sun] is horizontal, while that of the fire-eater [fire] is well-known to be upward-flaming"; thus, the three distinct movements of fire, sun, and moon—corresponding to the three functions of prāṇa, vyāna, and apāna—are comprised of the three streams of upward, horizontal, and downward flow. Consequently, the *vahni-bindu* (fire-drop) consists of the upward-flowing function of *prāṇa*.
