Or, it may be the *mūrticakra* (form-circle), which consists of the *nāda* (sound) characterized by that [bindu]. Here, the term refers to *rājane* (shining) or *rañjane* (coloring).

"Cidviṣaṭkala" refers to the "group of six consciousnesses," which consists of the two groups of six—the aforementioned sense organs (*jñānendriya*) and organs of action (*karmendriya*), both being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*). That which takes up or grasps this group of six consciousnesses is the "cidviṣaṭkala," namely the Sun of Breath (*prāṇasūrya*). The meaning is that the Sun of Breath itself is the wheel of the form of fire (*agnimūrticakra*), which is the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*), and which functions as the upward-flowing vital breath (*ūrdhvavāha-prāṇabindu*).

*Tatkalādharatanuḥ* means that [the body] which sustains (*dharati*) and sequentially expands (*tanoti*) the digits (*kalāḥ*) of those two, namely fire and the sun, until the full moon (*pūrṇimā*), and subsequently contracts (*kṣīṇayati*) them in reverse order during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "of that body which sustains its digits" (*tatkalādharatanuḥ*): previously, in the verse below beginning with "The digits of the moon, excluding the neuter vowels," the sixteen vowels were described as the digits of the moon; thus, the "full moon" here refers to that conventional moon which possesses a body sustaining those digits.

[This refers] to the conventional moon. Alternatively, it may mean: "O You, whose body (tanu) is that very moon which possesses those digits. In the lineage of the Gurus—by eliding the vowel 'a' in the compound *tatkalādharatanoh* (of her whose body possesses those digits)—it becomes *adharatanoh*. [The meaning is: "You hold down (*adharayasi*) the conventional moon by means of the solar self; on the new moon day, which is like the night of ignorance, You expand [the moon] and then cause it to wane, starting from the first day of the dark fortnight until the first day of the bright fortnight, according to the saying: 'Fire drinks the first digit, the Sun drinks the second.'"

The meaning is that this is because of such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as these. Furthermore, you expand [the light] from that point until the full moon within your lower body. And regarding the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*), the meaning is: in the context of the lineage of gurus who initiated the two previously mentioned paths of Sāṃkhya and Yoga belonging to you. "That digit" (*tatkalā*) means the digit of the form of those two, Agni and Sūrya; it is indeed that very digit. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Indeed, the Sun enters into the Fire at evening; or rather, the Fire ascends into the Sun at the end of the day."

In the *Raghuvamśa* poem, on the occasion of describing King Raghu’s accession to the throne, this very poet states: "Having received the kingdom bestowed by his father, he shone even more intensely, like the sacrificial fire when the light deposited at the close of day returns to the sun. Since the identity of the forms of Agni and Sūrya is established both by scripture and by experience, they possess but a single form and energy. Thus, [the subject] is one whose nature consists of that very form and energy.

The *prakāśatanusiddhamaṇḍala*—it shines forth by itself initially through the three non-different limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the three mandalas; it expands, that is, its own essential nature is extended, in the form of the six modifications of existence non-different from the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*); or else, it subsequently wanes and is perfected in due course of time as the *devīmānasiddhamaṇḍala*. Thus, the ellipsis is: "you become the *prakāśatanusiddhamaṇḍala*."

Regarding the reading *siddhimaṇḍalam*: the *siddhimaṇḍala* is the body of light (*prakāśatanu*), which is the nature of the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*). The meaning is that you yourself become the very reality that is to be worshipped first, because it is the wheel of light that constitutes the solar orb (*bhānumaṇḍala*) known as the "Enchanter of the Three Worlds" (*trailokyamohana*), which extends from the supernatural power (*siddhi*) of *aṇimā* up to the energy of the mudrā of the three sections (*trikhaṇḍā*). By this, [it is meant] here in the triple stream consisting of the three maṇḍalas, or in the stream characterized by the downward-flowing sound (*adhovahana-nāda*)—the sound of the downward breath (*apāna-nāda*)—which will be described below.

It is thus established that, according to one's inclination, the fire consisting of the threefold body has the nature of the *bindu*; the sun consisting of the threefold vital breath (*prāṇa*) has the nature of the *nāda* extending as far as the *dvādaśānta*; and the moon consisting of the light of the body is the possessor of the *kalās* of both of those.

Therefore, because the Puruṣa-moon, consisting of sixteen digits including the one called Sadā (Sadākhya), serves as the support for the entire celestial sphere—including the solar family and others composed of the seven previously mentioned streams—it possesses the nature of Kāla (Time), which is the referent of the term *Kālī* and the Mistress of the Left (*Vāmeśī*) among the seven principles previously mentioned in the phrase "You exist sevenfold," extending from Śiva and Śakti down to the digit Sadāśiva; and furthermore, by virtue of being the Sun of Time residing in the eighth sun named Kaśyapa, it possesses the nature of Paraśiva as Time (*Kāla*). This is also stated in the *Aruṇa-prapāṭhaka* within the *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka*.

It is thus recorded: "O Kaśyapa, that art of yours which is radiant, powerful, abundant, and multi-luminous, in which the seven suns are collectively established—to that [art] let us entrust this king. Thus, all of them receive light from Kaśyapa; Soma expels them from Kaśyapa like a failed artisan. In that very context, by means of the manifestation characterized by his emission of the individual soul (aṇu-visarga), [he acts] within the seven solar spheres, whose nature consists of the Moon, the individual soul (jīva), and Śiva.

The phrase "or like one who has fallen from ritual action" (*bhrastākarmakṛd iva*)—with the name *Soma* found in the supplementary portion of the text—indicates that, by abiding in the central point between the two triplets consisting of the seven streams, it possesses the nature of the *āṇava* emission (*visarga*) characterized primarily by repose. Likewise: "Since there is no other higher than he who was born; he who entered into all worlds, Prajāpati, in harmony with his progeny."

Furthermore, in the Soma sacrifice named *Ṣoḍaśī*, the preeminence of the sixteenth digit (*ṣoḍaśī-kalā*) is established by hundreds of scriptural passages through its identity with the cup (*graha*) bearing that name, as in the verse: "He is the three lights, and he is the sixteenth. Likewise, in the *Gītā* within the chapter on the Yoga of Manifestations (*Vibhūti-yoga*), it is stated: "Among the stars, I am the Moon," thereby declaring his nature as the *Abhijit* constellation belonging to Prajāpati.

Likewise, in the *Śāmbhavabindu* and other Āgamas, regarding the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the essential nature of the *Kāmakalā*, the two *bindus*—consisting of fire (*agni*) and moon (*soma*), and representing the two emissions (*visarga*)—are treated as the two breasts in the gross form of the Deity. Furthermore, in the *Paraśurāmakalpasūtra*, it is stated: "Having meditated upon the *Kāmakalā* according to the description 'the face by means of the *bindu*, the two breasts by means of the two *bindus*, and the rest by means of the [remaining] *bindu*," one employs the "moon of the face" (*mukhacandra*) which denotes the commencement of the consciousness-nature (*cinmaya*) of the Supreme Deity, who is the *Kāmakalā*. This is done through the application of the *mukhacandra* in the aforementioned gross form of the *Kāmakalā*.

In the worship of the triad of wheels consisting of the forms of Light (prakāśa), Bliss (ānanda), and Form (mūrti)—which are Speech (vāk) and Meaning (artha)—worship is perceived as being essentially the nature of the syllable *anusvāra* (the nasal bindu) which is full of both speech and meaning. Furthermore, even between the moon-bindu (*somabindu*) and the fire-bindu (*agnibindu*), which correspond respectively to the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*) and the wheel of form (*mūrticakra*) and consist of the emission (*visarga*) and the bindu of speech and meaning, the moon-bindu abides in the center by virtue of its non-difference from the wheel of bliss. This is because the fire-bindu, which consists of the wheel of form, burns away death—which is composed of the transmigratory world of duality and all fetters (*pāśa*).

Because it is the locus of dissolution, its ultimate inclusion as the playful manifestation (*vilāsa*) of the Śāmbhava emission (*visarga*) is established; thus, the revelation of the secret of the different modes of worship, which is the essential doctrine proven by all the Tantras, has been indicated.

Therefore, even the description of the nature of the *kāmakalā* as demonstrated by the sovereign Śrī Śaṅkaraguru in the *Saundaryalaharī*—namely, "Having made the face the *bindu*, and below that the pair of breasts, one should meditate below that on the *kāmakalā* which is the portion for Hara, O Consort of Hara"—refers to the worship of the nature of the *kāmakalā* consisting of the Soma of Apāna, characterized by the downward flow, wherein the twelve-fold number (the mind, the intellect, and the ten senses) finds its ultimate rest.

When the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the functions of either the self (*ātman*) or that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) are dissolved, there occurs—as if the continuity were destroyed—the cessation of the stream of the latent impressions of effects (*kāryavāsanā*). This applies even to the nature of external physical time, which consists of both the *kalī* and *kāla* [units], and to the number of months established by conventional time-measures such as the lunar and solar cycles; for instance, through Vedic statements such as, "They say there is a month consisting of ten [days]," when the latent impressions of the temporal parts—such as months, days, and lunar dates—are lost for the sake of accounting for omitted or intercalary months, [it is said]: "O Goddess whose eyes are the three paths, your face is composed of the three worlds."

This also indicates the state of one whose mental continuum has not been destroyed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the consciousness regarding the nature of the previously mentioned four triads manifested externally. Furthermore, even in the process of the contraction of the "flower" of the Guru—which consists of the abode, consciousness, and the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*), and which comprises the entire universe—Parashiva has explicitly stated in the *Jñānārṇava* that there is a prohibition [of the practice] once one rests solely upon the number twelve rays. As it is said in the sixteenth chapter of the *Jñānārṇava*: "The multitude of rays is joined with petals, but the Gurus possess more petals than those."

Therefore, one should contract the flower, for its expansion is the cause of the loss of infinite accomplishments. A flower that has withered should be known as destroying one's progeny, while a flower that is intact bestows all prosperity. If the flower is not contracted by the twelfth [day], the progeny is destroyed. Having lost his form through the destruction of his progeny, he would no longer be dear to the deity. For this very reason, O beloved, the flower was properly contracted by me.

Having thus prescribed the worship of the three lineages of gurus who initiated the tradition of the Vidyā known as Kāmarāja, he divides that very lineage of gurus into the higher (parā) and lower (aparā) categories. At the end of the Mānavaugha, [he says]: "O Supreme Goddess, these letters are fixed as the lower [lineage]. This triad is indeed fixed for the benefit of the teachers. Having extracted this, O Great Goddess, like a flower that has closed its petals, O Beloved."

Furthermore, by such passages as "one should subsequently worship the triad of one's own gurus at the limit of pride," the various methods of worship have also been analyzed and described. Therefore, according to the *Upāsanā-rahasya*, the phonemes (*akṣara-tattva*)—which consist of both word and meaning—are to be worshipped in the form of the lineage of gurus, until the attainment of non-difference with the nature of the *unmanī*, *prāṇa*, and *nāda*. This occurs through the division of the sequence known as the *vāma-saṃvit-varṇa* [tradition], and through the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the wheels (*cakra*) composed of the forms of light (*prakāśa*) and bliss (*ānanda*) within the spheres of the objective (*adhibhūta*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the subjective (*adhyātma*), in accordance with one's spiritual capacity.
The sequence of the closing of the lotus of the Guru is to be known solely from the mouth of the Guru according to the oral tradition. || 45–67 ||

Having thus described the primary Sun—the vital breath (*prāṇa*) consisting of the aggregate of the nine *nādas*, characterized by the upward-flowing *bindu* and composed of twelve *kalās*—as the Wheel of Light (*prakāśacakra*) together with the two forms and *kalās* of Agni and Soma; and having pointed out the lunar orb of the *apāna* consisting of mind (*manomaya*), characterized by the downward-flowing *nāda*, as its object of enjoyment (*bhogyavigraha*); he now demonstrates its nature as the Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*) by describing the sixteen previously mentioned vowels as being the very *kalās* of that [lunar orb]:
"That which is the lunar *apāna* here, characterized by the downward-flowing *nāda*, is the body of the object of enjoyment."
His sixteen digits have been made the bodies of the Nanda-circles in the lineage of the Guru.

Regarding the phrase "He who," and so forth: here, the meaning of the word *iha* (here) refers either to the previously mentioned path of Sāṃkhya or the path of Yoga (*yogamārga*) consisting of the state of aesthetic resonance (*sāmarasya*) in pleasing the king; or else, since the Wheel of Light (*prakāśacakra*) was the subject previously discussed, it refers to the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*)—comprising the Parā, Parāparā, and Divya lineages—which was intended in the preceding verse; or alternatively, it refers to the remaining triad of lineages of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), consisting of the three lineages of Siddhas, Mānavas, and Śiṣyas, within that lineage of gurus. This is the meaning of the word *iha*.

As for the word *tu*, it indicates a distinction from what precedes. Previously, in the wheel of manifestation (*prakāśacakre*), there was the solar *prāṇa* characterized by the upward-flowing bindu; here, however, there is the lunar *apāna* characterized by the downward-flowing nāda. According to the root *ana-*, meaning "to move," previously it consisted of a primary movement of the nature of the supreme self. The excellence of this movement is defined as resting solely within one's own essential nature, without deviating from that very form.

Now, because it has deviated from the essential nature of mere vibration (*spanda*), it is characterized by the absence of movement; thus, there is the distinction of the *apāna-soma*. For this very reason, it is defined by its downward flow, and being that *apāna-soma*, it is the embodiment of the object of enjoyment (*bhogya-vigraha*). First, within the inner self consisting of mind (*manomaya-antarātman*), according to the Vedic scripture, "The moon was born from the mind," it is a mental embodiment—distinct from the body composed of mind, devoid of [physical] characteristics, or rather, characterized as a specific planetary form.

The meaning is as follows: one whose power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) has transformed into the nature of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), or one whose power of action has transformed into the nature of the power of knowledge, possesses a body of enjoyment (*bhogya-śarīra*) consisting of action according to his respective qualification; subsequently, there arises a body of experience (*bhogya-vigraha*) consisting of the effect (*kārya-maya*), which is either of the nature of both [powers] together or of the nature of their equilibrium (*sāmarasya*).

Therefore, according to the Śruti: "It eats the beings today, and therefore it is called *anna* (food)," [the deity] exists in the form of the heart's exertion consisting of the seven currents (*saptasrotas*), which has evolved as the embodiment of the path of the six categories (*ṣaḍadhvan*)—predominantly mind and intellect—and characterized by the equilibrium of both action and its result. Thus: "He indeed is this sacrifice among men, the seven-fold invoker (*saptahotṛ*)."

"He carries the oblation to the six gods over there"—thus it is stated in the seventh section of the second chapter of the second book of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*. Having become the bestower of nectar even to the transcendent gods through the sacrificial body of the *Saptahotṛ-yajña*, and by means of a body consisting of the threefold and fivefold vehicles (*trivṛt-pañcavāha*) within either the vital breath (*prāṇa*) or time—such as fifteen, two, and so forth—predominantly characterized by the *anuttara-visarga* of the Śākta and Śāmbhava [powers] which are to be described hereafter, and having experienced both increase and decrease, he finally, through the nature of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of those two, becomes transcendent of the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*).

The meaning is that it becomes so because, through downward movement (*adhovahana*), the soma of the *apāna*—which is characterized by the absence of [ordinary] signs—attains the nature of an object of enjoyment (*bhogya-vigraha*). Thus, there exists this soma of the *apāna*, characterized by downward movement, which possesses a body of objects of enjoyment consisting of the five channels of the activity of the agent joined with knowledge and action.

The sixteen digits (*kalās*) that constitute the body of the Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*) expand it—or, as it were, attenuate it—by means of the form of *nāda*, which is either the meaning or the word consisting of the seven currents (*saptasrotas*). This is because it will be stated later: "O Mother, here the union [occurs] through those vowels of Yours which are differentiated and devoid of the neuter. The meaning is: by You—who are the very nature of *nāda* and the triad of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) consisting of word and meaning, and who are the equal embodiment of both knowledge and action—it has been made. How? "Then it made itself by itself."

"Therefore, that is called 'well-done' (sukṛta). Now, that which is "well-done" is indeed essence (rasa). For only by attaining essence does one become blissful. For who indeed could breathe, who could live, if this bliss did not exist in the ether? For it is he alone who causes bliss. Thus says the Śruti.

O You whose nature consists of the downward-flowing *nāda* characterized as *apāna*, the moon, the *dahara*-space, and the functioning of the elements, and who are composed of the play of the *śākta-visarga* through Your dual nature as both the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) regarding the phoneme, meaning, and their relationship—by You, the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarga* have first been sought after as non-different from the power of knowledge; these vowels signify the sixteen *kalās* (digits) named *prāṇa* and so forth, which denote the sequence of speech and meaning, and they indicate the temporal powers (*kāla-śakti*) such as the lunar days (*tithi*), starting from *Kāmeśvarī* up to the *Mahānityā*.

Subsequently, they are intended [to be taught]; thereafter, they are contemplated as the nature of the radiance of the deities of the lunar days (*tithi*) and rays (*raśmi*), beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Mahānityā; they are further conceptualized through the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) and fashioned [thereby]. Following that, according to their respective capacities and in due order, they are transformed into the sixteen-fold forms beginning with the previously mentioned *prāṇa* and ending with *nāma*, and are trained through the process of ascending and descending practice—how wonderful!

He clarifies—under the guise of an alternative reading—that [this bliss] is manifest in the fourth quarter (turyapāda) of the Creator, for the preeminent leader of contemplation (*vimarśaka*), within the wheel of bliss pertaining to the object of knowledge consisting of the lunar *apāna* [energy], which is characterized by the downward flow of your [power]; thus he says: "those whose bodies are the wheel of bliss beyond action" (*kṛtātyayānandacakratanavaḥ*).

The clear meaning is as follows: because of the rule that roots with the sense of "going" (gati) necessarily possess the sense of "attaining" (prāpti), the suffix *kṛta* signifies the Great Sequence of Five Paths (*pañcavāha-mahārthakrama*), which begins with the manifestation of the previously mentioned fourfold lost object and culminates in the attainment of one's own essential nature. Those whose bodies (*tanu*) are precisely this Wheel of Bliss (*ānandacakra*)—the sixteen digits (*ṣoḍaśakalā*)—are thus described.

The essential meaning of this is that all knowledge (*vidyā*), though consisting of ignorance (*avidyā*) as well, is entirely non-different from the wheel of bliss (*ānandacakra*) composed of the *kāmakalā*, which is the playful manifestation of the unsurpassed emission (*anuttaravisarga*) characterized by the awakening of consciousness (*cittaprabodha*). This very point has been stated in the *Mālinīvijayavārtika* through verses beginning with the forty-fourth and extending over more than a hundred subsequent verses, where it should be seen that even conventional distinctions are refuted. Furthermore, in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*: "Wherein even sufferings become happiness, even poison becomes nectar, and even worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) becomes liberation—that is the path of Śaṅkara. (46–68)

Having thus explained the nature and majesty of the Ānanda-cakra, [the text proceeds] for the purpose of the practice of meditating upon its nine constituent sounds: "The Brāhma, the Divya, the Pitrya, the Prājāpatya, and likewise that of the Guru..."

Having thus described the ninefold measures of time—saura, sāvana, ādara, and ārṣa—as belonging to Mahākālī, who is skilled in the fivefold cosmic acts such as creation, he now reveals the identity of the Sun and Moon—the aforementioned drivers of the Wheel of Light and Bliss (prakāśānanda-kālacakra)—as her two worldly eyes consisting of knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā), while establishing through a variant reading that she herself is the third eye composed of fire (vahni):
"The digit born of the Lord of Day belongs to the two Lords."

O Caṇḍī, as long as [the sun] is spread forth until its rising, so long indeed do the worlds endure; for the destruction of the day is truly brought about by you through your manifest and hidden form. (47–69)

In this passage, beginning with the word *vāsara*, the commentary is first explained according to the reading that uses the plural form *kalāḥ*. O *Caṇḍi*—the term *caṇḍi* being derived from the verbal root *caḍi* (meaning "to be angry")—this vocative is intended to signify that you are "wrathful" toward the person who creates differentiation within the three circles (*maṇḍala*) consisting of your own eyes or your essential nature, which encompass the states of the three social classes (*traivarṇika*). The phrase "of the Lord of Day and the Lord of Night" refers to your two eyes, which function as the regulators of time, cognition, and action. This is the underlying sense.

The digits (*kalā*), twelve in number, are the determinants of the white and black phases of the month and its half-months respectively; and the lunar portions (*śakalā*), sixteen in number, are the determinants of the white and black phases known as day and night within the lunar days (*tithis*). They extend until their rising—that is, for as long as they expand their respective risings. Alternatively, by intending the future sense according to the rule "the *laṭ* [present tense] is used with the particles *yāvat* and *purā*," the meaning is: "knowing that it will expand its rising."

"Right then, at that very time," means due to the absence of the twelve principles (tattvas) indicated by the previous verse, and due to the presence of the sixteen principles indicated by the preceding verse. [He is] the one whose form is both manifest and hidden.

In the cosmic cycle (*kalpa*) consisting of your fiery form, your body—manifest at the beginning of the month and hidden at the end of the month—is revealed through the nature of the twelve digits (*kalā*) associated with the wheel of light (*prakāśacakra*). Likewise, in the cosmic cycle of the day, your body, which primarily bestows the knowledge of time and possesses the form of the Moon-eyed Lord (*Somanetra*), is manifest at the beginning of the lunar day (*tithi*) and hidden at the end of the lunar day. As it is said: "The solar orb rises having reached whichever lunar day..."

"that lunar day is to be known as complete for rites pertaining to the Śruti and Smṛti," according to this scriptural authority; thus, he is described as such because he is skilled in the primary conventions of time-keeping according to your [tradition], and his body consists of the vital breath (prāṇa) and the sun.

The phrase *divasakṣayodayaḥ* means "the days and the waning [of the months]"; that is, the twelvefold cycle of day and night, consisting of either the lunar months ending with the new moon (*amānta*) as established by the common (*vyāvahārika*) lunar calendar, or those ending with the full moon (*pūrṇimānta*) as established by the Bārhaspatya calendar, each month being composed of either the new or the full moon. This is because of the Vedic scripture: "The twelve nights are indeed the image of the year. This is the intended meaning.

Likewise, according to the previously cited statement from the *Āstīkapurāṇa*, "The day belongs to the Bhūtas for their activity, while the night belongs to the Pitṛs for their deeds," and in accordance with the scriptural testimony regarding the measurement of time for the Pitṛs and Devas—namely, "Twenty-four half-months constitute a year"—there are twelve lunar days and nights (cāndra-ahorātras) in a year and a kalpa, which take the form of either the Pitṛ-night of the bright fortnight (the twelve Pitṛ-mānas established by the Pitṛs) or the Pitṛ-day of the dark fortnight.

Likewise, there are three hundred and sixty days consisting of civil (sāvana) ahorātras; these are the "losses of days. The word "occurrence" (*udaya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. And in the reading "the occurrence of the loss of the divine day" (*devadivasakṣayodaya*), it means following that occurrence. The "loss and occurrence of days" occurs for the two deities—the moon and sun of worldly convention—who are of the nature of the wheels of light and bliss (*prakāśānandacakra*). This is the case when the plural form "losses and occurrences of days" (*divasakṣayodayāḥ*) is used.

The construction is as follows: by resorting to the alternative reading *tvatkṛtaprakaṭaguptaviṣṭapāḥ* (the worlds made manifest and hidden by you), it is connected with the verb *bhavanti* (they exist). This is an interpretation following the plural form of the word *kalā*, namely *vāsareśarajanīśayoḥ kalāḥ* (the digits of the Lord of Day and the Lord of Night). Now, in the context of the third eye consisting of the form of Fire (*vahni-mūrti*), [it refers to] the digits of the Lord of Day and the Lord of Night: "From fear of him the wind blows... (*bhīṣāsmādvātaḥ pavate*).

This is because of scriptural authority (śruti) such as "From fear of Him the sun rises," and likewise, "The Creator fashioned the sun and moon as they were before," found in the *Taittirīya Upaniṣad* and the *Nārāyaṇī-pariśiṣṭa*. By being situated at the central point between those two [eyes], which consist of the right and left eyes respectively, she is the one who governs the fivefold cosmic functions beginning with creation for both; she is the form consisting of the third eye of fire (*agninetra*), that is to say, the *brāhmī* form. This is because she will be described later as "ascending the *kalā*s of the body of Brahmā. "Yāvat" means by whatever amount of time.

"Towards the arising," that is, towards the unfolding of the Self (*ātman*), "it is extended," meaning it is expanded. "By you alone"—this is the ellipsis—by means of your form as the wheel consisting of the fire-morphs (*agnimūrti*). "Just so," [are] those worlds in which both manifest and hidden realms exist, "for your sake"—that is, for the sake of your fivefold activity consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya*) during the Kṛta Age—or rather, "on account of you," meaning for the purpose of realizing your own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Those [worlds] in which the manifest and hidden realms exist are described as such.

Regarding the reading *tattvataḥ prakaṭaguptavigrahaḥ*—the sense is that in that [Lord] who is the day and night of the gods, there are manifest and hidden forms (*vigraha*) consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*). This refers either to the days and nights of Brahmā—the *kalpas*—as stated in the passage, "A thousand cycles of four ages (*caturyuga*) is called a day of Brahmā," or to the rise and fall of the series of worlds as stated in, "The succession of worlds is produced and destroyed by his opening and closing of the eyes. The point is that the entire series of worlds exists for a mere duration of your own opening and closing of the eyes.

The construction [of the sentence] is with the alternative reading *tādṛśadevadivasakṣayodayāḥ* (the days, nights, declines, and rises of such gods). Furthermore, the construction is: "And there occur the days, nights, declines, and rises of the gods—the five Brahmās who are the constituent parts of your throne. As it is also stated in the *Laghubṛṃhaṇī*: "The lifespan of Viṣṇu is said to be ten times that of Brahmā; the supreme lifespan of Rudra is indeed a thousand times that. The excellent lifespan of Īśvara is declared to be a hundred thousand times that."

"Therefore, the lifespan of Sadāśiva is said by the wise to be ten million times that [of Śiva], and from that, multiplied by the ocean [ten million], is the duration of the maintenance of the bodies of Śiva and Śivā. For this very reason, previously, during the commentary on the verse beginning with "That which is to be known by the mind is characterized as the leader," it was stated that the Moon—which consists of the sixteen digits (kalās) starting from Prāṇa and ending with the digit named Kalā, and which is the mind-made aggregate-vāsanā of Brahmā—remains in deep sleep along with the fifteen digits, just as the individual mind remains [with its parts] when only the imperishable digit named Sādākhya remains.

When [the mind] dissolves into the sun-like vital breath (*prāṇa*) that is of the nature of the universal consciousness (*samaṣṭi-cit*), then even for Brahman, the night of ignorance consisting of pure darkness arises, just as the new moon (*darśa*) appears when the moon of worldly activity has set. To the extent that the various parts (*kalā*) become distinct from the Self through the discernment of the sun-like universal consciousness and vital breath, to that same extent the moon of awakening (*bodha*) waxes.

That which is the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa is itself the Vidyā (knowledge) in the form of the absolute distinction between the sun and the moon; it constitutes the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), being endowed with the moon of the mind through the sixteen parts (*kalā*) or the sixteenth part.

Therefore, from the perspective of the wise, the auspicious wheel of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāracakra*)—which bears the fruit of the ritual action of *ṛta*—is [to be understood] according to the method stated in the *Sāmidhenī-brāhmaṇa*: "There are fifteen nights in a half-month; a year is obtained by [counting] half-months. There are three hundred and sixty syllables in them; there are that many nights in a year. Thus, one obtains the year syllable by syllable. In this way, because the days and nights—which are parts of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*)—consist of vowels, consonants, measures (*mātrā*), and syllables, [the wheel is likewise composed of these]. Furthermore, in that regard:

Because the opening and closing of the eyes consist of the primary sciences (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), which are represented by the sun and the moon, there is also the conceptualization of the months as consisting of the new moon (*amā*) and the full moon (*pūrṇimā*). Regarding this, it is said: "Which is that syllable, the *bṛhatī*, upon which all that is established? There are twelve full moons, twelve eighth-days (*aṣṭakā*), and twelve new moons. This indeed is that syllable, the *bṛhatī*."

"In that [wheel] it was established"—thus, in the final section of the fifth chapter of the first book of the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, within the discourse on the chariot of the meters (*chandoratha*), according to the manner described in the scriptural revelation of the *Prājāpatya Chandoratha*, the Wheel of Time (*kālacakra*)—which consists of the principles of the syllables that are the playful manifestations of the Self (*ātmavilāsākṣaratattva*) and which, as composed of the deities of the *Bṛhatī* meter and the nature of its syllables, is the intended object of the Vedic purport—is [revealed] out of compassion for the sake of awakening the wisdom of ignorant practitioners.

Within the stream of birth and death fashioned by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities, the Śrīcakra itself is the wheel of time (kālacakra), consisting of the cycle of saṃsāra through the fivefold functions (pañcakṛtya). Furthermore, for the world of demoniac living beings, there also exists the wheel of destruction known as Viṣṇu’s Sudarśana, called the "beautiful hub" (sunābha), in accordance with the respective latent impressions (vāsanā) of those individual souls.

By this, the meaning is as follows: within the celestial sphere (khagola) extending from the sun, moon, and stars—which set time in motion—up to the abodes of the gods in the world of Brahmā, there exist various measurements of time according to the specific duration of each respective world and its presiding deity. To fulfill their authority over the fivefold cosmic functions (pañcakṛtya)—creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace—of their own respective worlds and world-guardians, you, Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, possess a temporal power that measures a lifespan of hundreds of years for each. Thus, your status as the sole mother of all worlds is truly meaningful, given that you possess the three orbs of fire, sun, and moon as your very eyes.

Therefore, it should be understood that there is a state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with other *mātṛkās*: for while in the *nādamātṛkā* there is only the *nāda*, in the *varṇamātṛkā*—following the three *bindus* at the end of the fourteen vowels according to the repeated calculation of "agitations" (*prakṣobha*) mentioned in the *Mālinīvijaya*, and extending through the seventeen [consonants] up to the end of the *svāyambhuva* vowels—the realization of the reflective awareness of the phonemes (*varṇaparāmarśa*) is attained as far as the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) beginning with the three functions (*kṛtyatraya*). Thus, the state of identity with other *mātṛkās* is to be known.

Thus, this summary of the authority over the fivefold functions (pañcakṛtya) of all deities was stated by the author of the *Mantrarāmāyaṇa*: "Just as a palace is seen repeatedly within each individual mirror along with the interior spaces, so too is the world seen among the gods along with the internal spaces of the deities. Therefore, all deities are individually the sources of the universe, and they are also the sources of one another; for thus it has been declared by Yāska. This has been elaborated somewhat there through the citation from Yāska’s *Nirukta*; it should be examined in that very place. Enough of this prolixity. (Verses 47–69)

Now, indicating this secret meaning—that on the path of worship, Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī Mahākālī functions as the practical mistress of time through her third eye, which consists of the levels of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), by reversing the relationship between subject and object (*pramātṛ-prameya*) regarding the previously mentioned forms of the Lord of Day and the Lord of Night—he demonstrates that Agni is the nature of the wheel of Mahākālī’s form:
"O Goddess! That state which, through the intermingling of those two aspects, reaches the plane of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)."
For that form of yours here is indeed contained within the bindu, nāda, samavedya, and vedaka.

The meaning of the vocative is: "O Thou whose nature is Light, manifesting as the three mandalas consisting of speech (*vāk*), mind (*manas*), and breath (*prāṇa*)!
