Regarding the phrase "of the constellations," it refers either to the digits (kalās) in the form of the moon's phases—such as the digit known as Abhijit mentioned in the Śruti—when there is an intention to express their distinction; or to the digits in the form of the aggregate of thirty lunar days (tithis), which constitute the twelve months; or to the two digits of the two forms (mūrti-kalās) that bring about those [months]. By that aforementioned digit of Yours, the form of Fire, which is thus described as being mixed—that is, possessing a unique union—with those two digits, and together with that digit of Yours, the form of Fire.

The state situated within the Bindu and Nāda—which are the object and subject of experience, synonymous with knowledge and action—is the equilibrium of the object and subject through the nature of the non-duality of Bindu and Nāda. This is the state situated between the Sun and the Moon, which serve as the eyes for the worldly transaction of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) and the knower (*pramātṛ*). Your state of being situated in the middle is identical with that of the Fire-mandala, whose nature is consciousness and will, and which is synonymous with the means of knowledge (*pramā*), the act of knowing (*vedanā*), and the known (*veda*). Thus, your state of being situated in the middle is the ascent into one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*), just like a reflection.

The meaning is as follows: "Stability" (*sthiti*) is defined as the maintenance of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) in its respective form; or, it refers to the skill in maintaining the form of either the original image (*bimba*) or its reflection (*pratibimba*) by means of the digestive fire (*jāṭharavaiśvānara*). This stability, characterized as described above, attains—that is, reaches—the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), which is the neutrality between the two mandalas, or the state of being of one flavor (*samarasabhāva*), by means of the solar form of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the lunar form of the object (*prameya*).

Alternatively, even within the three mandalas of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*)—or within the triad of speech consisting of word, meaning, and sound, which are the embodiments of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas—the essence of the threefold form [of the Veda] is as follows: "The gods indeed milked Prajāpati as bright milk. That did not suffice for them. He made it manifest for Agni; those became the *Śukriya* Sāmans. From their essence, that which flowed forth... [is this very essence].

These became the *śukra-yajus* mantras. Thus, there is a state of *sāmarasya* (harmonious integration) consisting of the attainment of the aesthetic essence (*rasa-bhāva*) predominant in the meaning of the word "head," by virtue of the middle position occupied by the *ṛk* and *sāman*—which are the meanings and sounds of speech—between the right and left wings (*pakṣa*) described in the *Taittirīya Brahmavallī* as "His *yajus* is indeed the head; the *ṛk* is the right wing; the *sāman* is the left wing. This [state] is the embodiment of the person of the *Yajurveda*, who is non-different from the aesthetic essence of the sound of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu-nāda-rasa*), as declared in the *Śukriya-kāṇḍa* scripture: "Those [mantras] became the *śukra-yajus*. It is the *sāmarasya* characterized by the attainment of the aesthetic essence predominant in the meaning of the word "head," through the intermediate station of the *ṛk* and *sāman*—the meaning and sound of speech—situated between the right and left wings as stated in the *Taittirīya Brahmavallī*: "His *yajus* is indeed the head; the *ṛk* is the right wing; the *sāman* is the left wing."

In that very context, it says: "These are indeed the *śukriyas* of the *śukriyas*. One of these two is the milk of the *sāman*, and the other is the milk of the gods. That which is the milk of the cow—that is the milk of the *sāman*. That which is the milk of the goat—that is the milk of the gods. The meaning is that one attains (*eti*) the state of being characterized by the predominance of the essence of the word "cow" as mentioned in the supplementary passage (*vākyaśeṣa*), which consists of the milk of the *sāman* and the milk of the gods. In this very same way, the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) regarding the existence of the threefold form of the *nāda* (sound) within both mind (*manas*) and vital breath (*prāṇa*) should be applied.

For everywhere, the very state of the equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) of the couple consisting of sound and the object denoted—also known by the synonyms *vāk* (speech) and *artha* (meaning)—is the nature of the principle of form (*mūrti-tattva*). Regarding the reading "the blending of the two digits" (*tad-dvaya-kalā-vimiśraṇā*), it should be understood as a qualification of "that state" (*sthitih*); that state itself is what is meant here. In this context, within the central point of the triad beginning with the subject (*pramātṛ*), the particle *hi* (in *tava mūrtir hi*) is an indeclinable used to indicate what is well-known in all the Vedas and Śāstras.

The sense is that the entire collection of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such as the Vedas, the scriptures, speech, and the mind, is brought into harmony with the thought: "This very form of yours is of such a nature. Herein lies the secret of the *mūrticakra* (the wheel of forms): according to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad scripture—"For the mind, O gentle one, consists of food; the vital breaths consist of water; speech consists of fire"—one may, at will, establish for each of these—speech, breath, and mind—the state of being the threefold form (*tripuṭīmūrtitva*) or the triple-form (*mūrtitrapuṭītva*) by placing them respectively in the roles of the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the subject (*pramātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which are synonymous with the known, the knower, and the instrument of knowing. This is the summary. (48–70)

Thus, when the sun and moon— which are the inner essence of the wheel consisting of the object of knowledge, the knower, light, and bliss— have reached their internal state within the form of Unmanī, Nāda, Navaka, Mahākālī, and Vahni during the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and even while they dissolve into the form of Mahāsaṅkarṣaṇa-Agni, [the text] demonstrates through the lineage of the Gurus the persistence of the threefold wheel of forms (*mūrticakratripuṭī*) within the *khaṇḍacakra* of the aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) of the sounds, vowels, and letters of the nine *nādas*, by means of Yoga and Sāṃkhya:
"O You who have swallowed the orbs of the sun and moon, and who are embraced by the fire of universal dissolution!"
Within the abode of the vital breath, the form that exists as ten and sevenfold rests upon the lineage of gurus in Śiva.

By the verse beginning with *līḍhabhānu* and so forth: "O Śivā," [the word] *adhikaraṇabhūtasādhakaśive* (O Śivā who is the locus of the practitioner) is in the locative case; or [it means] by you, who are the fire of dissolution (*pralayavahni*), that is, by you who are the form of the fire of the vital breath (*prāṇāgni*) called Saṅkarṣaṇa at the time of cosmic dissolution.

Having licked the orbs of the sun and moon until the culmination of the full emergence of Vidyā, and having remained within the interval between the two drops (bindu) of Śāktavisarga—consisting of Agni and Soma, which are the states of the object and subject, and the Sun-orb itself—one remains in the interval between the Sun and Fire, which have attained the state of the object and subject, for the sake of consolidating the Vidyā that has emerged through the limit of the Māṇava-unmanī-visarga following the rise of Vidyā; and by means of the limit of Śāktavisarga, one remains as the nature of the Moon-orb called Sādākalā-Candra in the state of Abhijit. Following the attainment of the consolidation of Vidyā...

The meaning is as follows: by the desire to withdraw the three conventional maṇḍalas through the state of the Śāmbhava emission (*visarga*), having internalized the three conventional triadic maṇḍalas—namely the maṇḍala of fire (*vahni-maṇḍala*) which is the form of Saṅkarṣaṇa, the primary vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*), and its synonyms Apāṃvatsa and Nakṣatragola—one remains established in the form of the fourth consciousness-fire (*turīya-cid-agni-mūrti*), having consumed the solar and lunar maṇḍalas. In the alternative reading *līḍhamanuśaśimaṇḍalasthir lambita*, it serves as a qualifying attribute for the specific aspect of the previously mentioned third eye-form (*tṛtīya-netra-mūrti-kalā*).

"Līḍhā" means having been tasted, taken into oneself, and merged. It refers to the state of the orbs of the sun and the moon; or rather, it is that state in which the station of the fourth [turiya]—whose characteristic has been described as "the state of ascending to one's own essential nature like a reflection"—is unchangingly established within the formative power (*mūrtikalā*). Thus, she is "lambitā," meaning suspended or supported. Or, it may mean that very station itself is the formative power. She resides in the "abode of breath" (*prāṇadhāman*), the splendor of the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*), being tenfold and yet sevenfold.

It is tenfold when combined with the five primary functions of breath (*prāṇa*) beginning with *prāṇa* and *apāna*, along with the five secondary functions of breath beginning with *nāga* and *kūrma*. It is sevenfold when counted together with the five sense organs—either of knowledge or of action—conjoined with the mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*). Alternatively, it is sevenfold or tenfold through the union of the ten flames mentioned in the Tantras, such as Kālī and Karālī, or the tongues of fire such as Hiraṇyā and Kanakā; for this is seen in the descriptions of the wheels of the forms of Fire in works such as the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*.

In the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*, within the *Taittirīya-saṃhitā*, during the description of Agni as the form of Prajāpati in the eleventh section (*anuvāka*) of the sixth chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the first book (*kāṇḍa*), it is stated: "He who knows Prajāpati, the seventeenfold one, as inherent in the sacrifice," and so forth, continuing: "'Āśrāvaya' has four syllables; 'Astu śrauṣaṭ' has four syllables; 'Yaja' has two syllables; 'Ye yajāmahe' has five syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-call has two syllables. This indeed is Prajāpati, the seventeenfold one."

By means of the symbolic statement, "āśrāvaya" (cause to hear) consisting of four syllables, which refers to the nature of the wheel of the Prajāpati-fire-forms as previously described; by the phrase "astu śrauṣaṭ" consisting of four syllables, which refers to the reflective awareness of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) through the *visarga* joined with the triad of long vowels—representing the inward-turned *aṇava-visarga*, the inner self (*pratyagātman*) whose essence is the *pratyāhāra* "a i u ṇ" together with its meaning; by the phrase "yaj" consisting of two syllables, representing either of the two pairs of conjunct vowels; and by [the mantra] "ye yajāmahe"...

By the phrase "the five-syllabled," there is the reference to the four phonemes *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *lṛ*, and *lṝ*—which consist of the neutral vowels (*ṣaṇḍasvara*) and are endowed with the *āṇava* sense of the *bindu*. By the phrase "the two-syllabled *vaṣaṭ*," there is the reference to the pair of hexads consisting of the reflective awareness of the supreme *visarga*, which is the *anuttara* [state] characterized by the *śākta* and *śāmbhava* [powers] and comprising both expansion (*prasaraṇa*) and reabsorption (*pratisañcaraṇa*). Furthermore, by the supplementary statement "This indeed is the seventeenfold Prajāpati," there is the reference to the collection of phonemes of the *mātṛkā* composed of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), which is differentiated by the various rules for seeds (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*), or rather, to the segment of vowels (*svarakhaṇḍa*) that is the root of those [phonemes].

In the group of sixteen vowels, which constitute the essence of the Puruṣa of Speech as stated in the passage "The Puruṣa indeed consists of sixteen parts," there is—through the intention of joining the *anusvāra* (the point) which signifies the *āṇava-visarga*, or through the desire to express the differentiation between the *agni* and *soma* points that are components of the *anuttara-śākta-visarga*—the word "speech" (*vāk*), which is synonymous with the "vitality of the meter" (*chandovīrya*). This is because it is intended by the Śruti as a designation for the collective form of the Prajāpati-Puruṣa, who is the *śabdabrahman* itself.

The meaning is that within the abode of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), sound (*nāda*), word (*vāk*), and object (*artha*)—or rather, within the group of six consisting of *svara*, *nayana*, *dhana*, and *vaka*—your primary form as Fire (*vahni-mūrti*), which consists of the state of identity (*sāmarasya*) between word, object, vital breath, and sound, becomes the lineage of the Gurus (*gurukrama*) resting upon the letter *Ā* and so forth, even within all three sequences of phonemes (*varṇakrama*). This very [reality] exists as one, by way of being the first thread (*sūtra*) for the reflective awareness of the three mandalas whose nature is the identity of all words and objects.

The Wheel of the Form of the Fire of Consciousness, consisting of Pure Fourth-order Knowledge (*turīya-śuddhavidyā*), is indicated by the remainder of the verse, "The ninefold *Gama* is fourfold," as being composed of the fourfold division of the *Nādakārikā*—which teaches the ninefold musical scales—and as being composed of the collection of the fourteen *sūtras* of Maheśvara, which consist of the fourteen worlds.

Regarding the letter *ha* (the fourteenth consonant) mentioned in the word *hal*, although its meaning is already established by the fifth sūtra, if one were to rest solely upon the group of twelve sūtras, there would be a lack of continuity for the triad of sibilants (*ūṣman*)—namely *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ra*—as taught in the thirteenth sūtra. Consequently, because of this absence of continuity within the sequence of the Vidyā, there is the possibility of the destruction of the Vidyā’s lineage. For this reason as well, the aforementioned state of having a "lost lineage" occurs even in the Māheśvara Sūtra, just as in the case of the *praṇava*, by way of resting at the end of the twelfth *nāda* in the thirteenth [sūtra]: "yaḥ kilāse".

The secret is this: the previously mentioned sequence of the Guru’s closing of the flowers (*gurupuṣpasaṅkocakrama*)—which is illuminated by the accomplishment of the contraction (*pratyāhāra*) of the Śākta phonemes consisting of the *parā* mantra as stated in the verse of the first *vimarśa*—must be relied upon for both divisions, namely the vowels and the consonants. For this very reason, the sequence of phonemes in the vowel division is recited in the *Śikṣā*, an auxiliary of the Vedas, up to the twenty-first; that [sequence] will be analyzed further below.

Having thus analyzed the lineage of Gurus of the wheel whose form is the fire-consciousness of Kālasaṅkarṣiṇī, and by describing the manifestation of her *kāmakalā*, he also illuminates the specific division of that very *kāmakalā* as *Kālyā*. Then, through the non-difference between the three mandalas consisting of her three eyes and the triad of elements—fire, water, and earth—he describes the expansion of the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvitkrama*) within the three functions of withdrawal, maintenance, and emanation, and within the three states of deep sleep, dreaming, and waking—which are composed of knowledge and ignorance—according to the sequence of phonemes to be explained hereafter;
all this proceeds from the fourth station, which is one's own essential nature, as the unfolding of the sequence of consciousness consisting of will, knowledge, and action.

The powers that produce the states of desire and attainment have been withdrawn by You from the abodes of dissolution, maintenance, and emanation, and extended forth from the fearlessness of the state of the Fourth Consciousness.
From the state of deep sleep onwards, throughout the three abodes.

By the words "iṣṭa" and so forth: these are the *sadmāni* (abodes) because the perfected ones (*siddhas*) settle within them by their own will, according to the etymology "those in whom they sit. This means they are the offices of authority for the three activities beginning with withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Within those [abodes], there are those whose powers have been activated by the intended awakening. From the state of sleep onwards, in the three abodes—indicated by the word "triṣu" (in the three)—there is first the sequence of withdrawal of either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*). "Intended" (*iṣṭaḥ*) means made the object of the will; it refers to the volition to withdraw either knowledge or ignorance.

Awakening (*bodha*) is knowledge regarding each respective object; action (*kṛta*) is the performance of deeds conducive to those objects, consisting of the creation of external activity—thus there are three. Or, there are four, including their power (*śakti*), capacity (*sāmarthya*), unfailing will (*avandhyecchā*), and so forth, which take the form of spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*). By you—who, within the previously mentioned triad of wheels beginning with *Prakāśa*, exist as the tenth [digit] whose form is non-different from the ten digits predominant in the wheel of withdrawal, and who are the collective deity-form of the ninefold triads of the *Para-ogha*, *Mahā-ogha*, and *Divya-ogha* lineages of Gurus.

Likewise, in the lineage of the Gurus (*gurukrama*), the meaning is that [the state] belongs to you alone by means of the thirteenth [digit], which is the *mahābindu*—the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the fourfold currents consisting of the remaining human (*mānava*), perfected (*siddha*), and divine (*divya*) lineages—and which is non-different from the mass of light and bliss consisting of the twelve and sixteen digits primarily characterized by maintenance (*sthiti*) and emanation (*sṛṣṭi*). Regarding the "three abodes" (*dhāmasu*): they are called *dhāmas* because within them the functions of the vital breaths of inhalation and exhalation "blow" (*dhamanti*), or because the internal and external senses are "filled" (*dhamyante*) with the latent impressions of karma (*karmavāsanā*); these are the gross, subtle, and causal bodies.

Among those three, starting from the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and beginning with any one of the states consisting of the dullness born of birth, they are extended toward the state of the Fourth Consciousness (*turyacitpadamaya*). In the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), they are extended—that is, expanded—toward that state of the Fourth Consciousness which consists of the form of the nine powers of resonance (*nāda*) ending with *nādānta*. In the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), however, starting from the Great Bindu at the End of the Twelve (*dvādaśāntamahābindu*) and counting down to the Kāmakalā, the desired object—the Kāmakalā—is that which has as its domain the creation of the three letters inseparable from the three wheels.

The awakenings (*bodha*) consist of the three types of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the scripts; the "creations" (*kṛti*) consist of the withdrawal of internal latent impressions by relying on the power of their external activities; and the "powers" (*śakti*) are the powers for the manifestation of those [external] entities. These together make twelve. The thirteenth is the manifestation of the entity itself, which takes the form of the Great Bindu (*mahābindu*) at the end of the twelve. In this way, even in the sequence of abiding in the abodes to be described later, the [state] at the end of the sixteen should be inferred. Thus are the powers produced by the desired awakening, extended forth as the state of the Fourth Consciousness (*turyacit*), which is indeed Śiva.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of that" (*tanmaya*), according to the scripture, *maya* refers to the state of the fourth consciousness (*turyacitpadam*) itself, which is the bliss of one's own self-nature (*svātmānanda*). It is in that very form that they are projected forth. Likewise, even within the insentient universe (*jaḍaprapañca*), which consists of the fivefold flow of the Great Reality (*mahārtha*), first, by you who take the form of the Siddha lineage (*siddhaugha*), the desire for the previously experienced worldly pleasure of the insentient is generated—just as the desire for the previously experienced bliss of deep sleep (*sauṣuptānanda*) was [generated] by her who takes the form of the Sādhaka lineage. Following that, by her who takes the form of the Mānava lineage and whose nature is reflection (*manana*), the means to attain that [bliss] is understood, as in the state of dreaming.

Following that as well, it is established that even the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is made subordinate to that [lineage] by means of the multitude of disciples (*śiṣyaugha*) and the performance of actions conducive thereto; thus, the lineage of gurus known as the "multitude of human disciples" (*mānava-śiṣyaugha*) consists of a group of outward-looking practitioners. Standing at the central pivot between those two lineages is the venerable Kākalā Kālī, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, and whose form is the lineage of gurus for those who have taken refuge.

That very [tradition], consisting of the fourfold current beginning with the Divine Current (divyaugha) and ending with the Disciple Current (śiṣyaugha), is the form of the Great Current (mahaugha). When it comes to rest within the rays between the twelve [centers] of the Wheel of Illumination (prakāśacakra), it is also the form of the sequence of the wheel-gurus of both Light (prakāśa) and Bliss (ānanda). Therefore, because of the interruption of the lineage of the twelve gurus, its status as a *tati* (lineage) is lost; thus, everything is faultless. || 50–72 ||
The solitary *ekamuktā-kāmakalā* is indeed *Kālī*, the state of the Fourth (*turīyapada*); she is also *Anākhyakālī*, the state of the Fourth of Kāla. Thus he distinguishes [the levels]:
"Where the definition of the object (*meyam*), the subject (*mātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*mānam*)—that which is *Kula*—reaches its ultimate limit and finds rest."
O Mother, that fourth state of yours is the great ocean which is held to be beyond all description.

By the words "the object of knowledge" (*meyam*) and so forth: O Ambikā, the *kula*—meaning a collection of similar things—is characterized by the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the act of knowing (*miti*). Regarding the reading *mevamānamitilakṣaṇam*: according to the perspective of the alternative reading *prāptitaḥ*, the word *māna* (measure) is intended to convey the resting of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*). Thus, it is called *mevamānamitilakṣaṇam* because it characterizes the object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, and the act of knowing. As for *kula*, it refers to the group of six cakras beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending with the *ājñā-cakra*, which are named after the three knots of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra together with their respective powers (*śakti*).

The characteristic of that [state] has already been analyzed in this very investigation, during the commentary on the verse beginning with "O Mother, whose body consists of the fivefold functions. This is because, ultimately—that is, near the end—due to the proximity of the initial consonants (*pra-*) in the words *meyam*, *mātṛ*, *māna*, and *iti*, they are produced in the form of the words *prameya*, *pramātṛ*, *pramāṇa*, and *pramiti*. "Ultimately" (*prāntataḥ*) means "at the end" (*prakārāntataḥ*), that is, at the point where [the sequence ends]. According to the order of the variant readings, the meaning is: "it comes to rest either in the place of *pramāṇa* or in the place of *pramātṛ*. It attains repose.

The meaning is that it comes to rest in the station of repose known as the *divya*, *mahāpara*, *ogha*, *kāraṇa*, *guru*, and *ogha*. In the reading "it goes by means of attainment" (*prāptito vrajati*), it means that by means of attaining the modes of the *kula* characterized as the object of knowledge (*meyamātṛ*) [and the means of knowledge], one reaches the station of the supreme subject (*paramapramātṛ*). "It goes to repose" remains the same; for that which is the form of the supreme subject is the station of repose for the *kula*.

By the great ones—those known as the "Great Flood" (mahaugha), who are heavy with weight, such as Ādisiddha, Nātha, and others belonging to the lineage of the succession of gurus mentioned in the *Hṛdayacandrikā* and other texts—the Nameless (*anupākhya*) is desired; that is, by means of the root *anu* meaning "to move," it is designated by the mere vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spanda*), and is made an object through the forms of will, speech, and meaning. That is your fourth state (*turya-pada*). Your own fourth station is precisely that. In the reading "whom [is] the great ocean" (*yaṃ mahābdhiḥ*), the meaning is: whom [is] the repose of the supreme subject (*paramapramātṛ-viśrama*), or the egoity of the knower (*pramātṛ-ahambhāva*).

The "great ocean" is the previously mentioned waveless ocean of consciousness (cit) which is Śiva; it is held to—meaning it is desired by you—to be that very fourth state (turya-pada), which is inexpressible, designated merely by the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇaspanda), or whose nature consists of name and form as the mere vibration of the inseparable word and its meaning. This is the syntactical connection. || 51-73 ||

Thus addressed, he said: "The lineage of the Guru tradition worships Your very fourth state (*turiyapada*), which—though consisting of name and form through the mere vibration of speech whose meaning is never-failing—is itself nameless due to the vibration of Your vital breath (*prāṇa*). This worship is performed through the divisions of the *sāṃkhya*, *yoga*, and the triad of emanation (*sarga*), as well as through the various distinctions of the triad of mudrās, by means of the two visions of the three-quarters and the one-quarter manifestation.
He continues: "The worship of You, which is differentiated by the movements, the offerings (*caru*), and the mudrā..."
Under its influence, your lineage— having attained a stable form— follows that succession, manifesting in a clearly defined shape.

By the words *cārarāva* and so forth: "distinguished" means characterized by specific divisions, either through the division of the lineage (*guru-sampradāya*) consisting of the upper stream (*ūrdhva-srotas*), which comprises the names of the Guru, the scripture, and the disciple (beginning with the supreme, *para*, etc.); or else through the division of the succession of the flood of Gurus (*gurv-ogha-krama-sampradāya*) consisting of the horizontal stream (*tiryak-srotas*), which is synonymous with the state of being the remainder of the contemplation of perfection (*siddhi-manana-śeṣatā*). Regarding the term *cārarāvarubhiḥ*: here, by the three words beginning with *cāra*, the primary triad of subject and so forth (*pramātṛ-ādi-mukhya-tripuṭī*) is intended according to the maxim of the secret spy (*gūḍha-cāra-nyāya*). Alternatively, from the verbal root *car* meaning "to eat," *cāra* refers to the state of being the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ-bhāva*).

From the verbal root *ruśabdane* (to sound), *rāva* refers to the activity of the speaker’s speech and so forth. *Caru*—derived from the sense that "the collection of ritual acts (*carati*) is performed here"—is synonymous with the category of the "agent of action" (*kāryakartṛbhāva*), which refers to the external display of ritual activities. Alternatively, *cāra* is conventional practice (*samayācāra*), *rāva* is the deliberation of speech (*vāgvimarśa*), and *caru* is the collection of substances consisting of the five categories of objects established by the tradition of the various Tantras, such as the first and second [Tantras].

Alternatively, *cāra* refers to the triad of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and the conduct with fear (*sabhayācāra*) found in the systems of Rāmānuja, Pūrṇaprajña, Nakulīśa, Pāśupata, and others; *rāva* refers to the internal alchemical practice (*rāsāyanika*) which is the object of the triad of systems beginning with Śaiva, Pratyabhijñā, and Rasēśvara; and *caru* refers to the agent who is conscious and of the nature of the self, as established by the systems of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, Jaimini, and others.

The meanings of the words *cāru*, *āvacara*, and *caru* consist of the external and other tri-varṇika family duties (*kuladharma*), which are non-different from name and form, and are composed of the threefold empirical reality (*tripuṭī*) of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*)—which itself consists of the performance of actions, the verbal expression of the experience of the nature of the embodied self (*śārīrakasvarūpa*), and that very experience itself. By means of those various such *cāru-āvacara-carus*, [the term] *mudrā* refers to a specific form at the time of experiencing those respective blisses; it is called *mudrā* because it "bestows" (*rāti*) or "grasps" (*gṛhṇāti*) joy (*mudaṃ*), which is a particular kind of bliss differentiated by the various levels of mental impressions (*vāsanā-bhūmikā*).

It is another name for *sphoṭa*, which reveals the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛbhāva*)—the object of knowledge (*prameya*) according to the triad of systems beginning with Pāṇini, Sāṃkhya, and Pātañjala; or it is a mere external sign (*liṅga*). By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood that the connection [of this term] occurs through a change of gender (*liṅgavipariṇāma*) due to its being differentiated. The resultant meaning is: by means of a fourth [factor], which merely reveals the knowledge and action of the three castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, and which consists of an external mark resting solely upon the aggregate of body and senses.

And by means of such a mudrā, your worship—by virtue of which [the result] depends on that alone—insofar as it is dependent (*vaśa*), meaning "dependent" (*āyattatā*) and "lineage" (*vaṃśa*), according to the rule "the word *vaśa* denotes dependence, lineage, desire, and mastery," [it occurs] either by her will or by her mastery, up to the very limit of the hair.

*Tāvakakramagatā* means "having entered Your Krama": *tāvaka* means "Your," referring to the Great Krama of Fivefold Meaning (*pañcārtha-mahākrama*), which consists of the expansion of the five cosmic acts beginning with emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and ending with concealment (*saṃhāra*); the Great Krama of Fourfold Meaning (*caturartha-mahākrama*), which begins with emission and ends with the Unnameable (*anākhyā*), a synonym for concealment; and the Great Krama of Threefold Meaning (*tryartha-mahākrama*), which begins with the creation of either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*)—synonyms for consciousness (*cit*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*)—and ends with their dissolution. She is so called because she enters that [Krama]. *Sthirīkṛtiḥ* means "the act of stabilization": it is the act (*kṛti*) of becoming stable (*sthirā*) from being unstable (*asthirā*). It is the state of having been made firm.

The meaning is that "creation" (kṛti) refers to that which is accomplished through immobility, which takes the form of the heart's exertion known as the natural vibration of the vital breath, and which takes the form of the heart's exertion of Niṣādas, Pañcajanas, and Mānavas, as well as of the four castes, the three [upper] castes, and so forth.

One should worship the lineage, which consists of the tradition of the *ūrdhvasrotas* gurus, beginning from Paraugha and extending up to Divyaugha; thus is established the determination of the succession of the sequence of worship, starting with *cāra*, *rāva*, and so forth, belonging to the Mother of Lower Knowledge (*aparā-vidyā-mātṛkā*), including all the Smārta Tantras and Āgamas such as the Ṛgveda. Now, therefore, regarding the Mother of Higher Knowledge (*parā-vidyā-mātṛkā*), first, within the tradition of the *Anuttara-tantra-āgama*, that Mātṛkā is briefly threefold according to the divisions of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi*.

Therein, each being twofold through the distinction of the *hādi* and *kādi* systems of phonetics (*vidyā*), there are six varieties. Furthermore, when combined with the Brāhmī Mātṛkā—which is designated by the terms "vital breath," "vowel," and "consonant," which will be described in the third *Vimarśa*, which is characterized as stated in the Vedic auxiliary *Śikṣā*, and which is distinct from the wheel of the multitude of rays of time belonging to Svāyambhuva—there are seven varieties. These very same [six or seven] are also the Vedic understanding that there are six or seven Kṛttikās, as mentioned in the *Kṛttikeṣṭakā-mantra* beginning with "Ambādule."

Even there, although there are infinite varieties according to different schools—whether it be through the lineage transmission of the *Kāmakalā* starting from the *Vidyā* of Lopāmudrā and others well-known in the *Anuttara-āmnāya*, or the nature of the *Kāmakalā* beginning with *Ha* and ending with *Kṣa*—the sequence of the lineage transmission for the respective supreme (*anuttara*) modes of worship, known as the sequence of manifestation, withdrawal, the unnameable, and light, or that which is termed the fivefold action (the reverse of the five acts) beginning with the manifestation of the four lost objects and ending with the manifestation of the non-conceptual object of knowledge, is of one and the same kind; thus, there is no difference in the sequence of the lineage transmission therein.

And likewise, scripture also states: "Two knowledges are to be known: the higher and the lower. The lower is characterized by the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; now, the higher is that by which that Imperishable (*akṣara*) is attained," and so on. Therein too, according to the order of dissolution, the lineage of disciples and the sixfold lineage of gurus—characterized in brief as the venerable form of the disciple-lineage consisting of speech and meaning, which emerges externally as if through the differentiation of one's own self—is the first [knowledge], primarily characterized by either the order of emanation or dissolution of the lower knowledge (*aparā vidyā*).

When that very [consciousness] ascends into its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the application of *dhāraṇā* (concentration) as each respective form is the "form consisting of stability" (*sthitimayī mūrti*). This is precisely what is called "stability"—the maintenance of the essential nature in its various forms—as stated in other Tantras: "Stability is the ascent into one's own essential nature, which occurs just like a reflection. If this consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the principle of stability (*sthititattva*), it is said to be "of the nature of the human current" (*mānavaugharūpiṇī*).

If the *dvamarśa* (the reflective awareness of the two) is established in its full form through the process of internal withdrawal (*upasaṃhāra*) within one's own self, then Gaurī—whose primary nature is that sequence of withdrawal, who consists of the *mātṛkā* of Sound (*nāda*) or the *mātṛkā* for that purpose, who is the *paśyantī* speech consisting of the six paths of word and meaning, and whose primary nature is the *śāmbhava* emission—is also capable of being the embodiment of the *siddha-ogha*.

Immediately following that state, this very [consciousness], primarily characterized by the attainment of the internal *nimeṣa* (momentary flash) of Sādāśiva, consists of the emission (*visarga*) of Śambhu; yet, through the manifestation of the fourfold objects—whether lost or attained—and the subsequent appearance of conceptualizable objects as will be described, it proceeds by way of the sequence of the five acts, whether those of knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*). According to its specific capacity, under the guise of the process of the manifestation of the Unnameable (*anākhyā*), which is synonymous with concealment (*tirodhāna*) or grace (*anugraha*), it assumes the form of the Divine Current (*divyaugha*) and the Couple (*mithuna*), even while revolving through the cycles of the Krama.

And by means of the Great Abiding (mahāsthiti), which is also known by the name "the state of being the self-nature of all beings," the Great Form itself—the triad of the assembly of great disciples—manifests as the triad of Word and Meaning consisting of the *sphoṭa*, sound, and speech, sharpened by the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the Bindu. This manifestation occurs through the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*) of one's own form, wherein the unity of the reflective awareness of the Supreme Speech (*parā-vāk*) and its Meaning is shattered along with the light of one's own Self. This is, in brief, the determination of the essential nature of the lineage of Gurus (*gurvaugha*) according to the sequence of the six paths, or the sequence of the five vehicles of the couple Kālī and Kāla.

Thus, the inclusion of the sequence of the three-fold triad (*tripuṭī*) and the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), or the sequence of the great meaning (*mahārtha*) consisting of three, four, or five flows, within the sequence of the three meanings, should be inferred by those who move freely within the stream of the unsurpassed great consciousness (*anuttara-mahāsaṃvit*); this is the direction [of the argument]. Regarding the reading "manifested as your own sequence" (*tāvakakramatayā sphuṭākṛti*), worship itself is the agent. That very worship which belongs to your fourth state (*turīyapada*), mentioned in the preceding verse, is what exists through the chewing of the flow of differentiated movement and so forth.

It is manifest in form either by virtue of being under your control—that is, being dependent upon your fourth state (turiya-pada), by your will, or through your sovereignty; or by virtue of being your own lineage (krama)—that is, as the lineage of the Middle Guru (madhyauva-guru-krama) which is another name for the state where all things culminate in the realization of *siddhi*, extending from your own Great Krama of the Five Principles (*pañcārtha-mahākrama*) up to the Great Krama of the Three Principles (*tryartha-mahākrama*).

In whatever manner—whether as the form of the meaning of the words for Your feet, from the cowherds down to the shepherds, or as the manifest forms of the sequence of classes, individuals, qualities, and actions pertaining to the body and senses known through the eye of flesh—they worship You, the Supreme, who is the nature of Kāla and Śiva, and You, the Supreme, whose form is the ultimate Speech (Parāvāk) and its meaning; they indeed serve You by means of observing their respective family duties (*kuladharma*). And it was said by the Blessed Lord in the *Gītā*: "I am the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not know Me in truth, and therefore they fall. (52–74)

Thus, within the Great Sequence (*mahākrama*) of the Guru’s tradition consisting of the Great Sound (*mahānāda*) of the four and five meanings, specifically in the sequence of the Guru of the four meanings, first—by means of removing the defect of the lost lineage (*naṣṭasantati*) as taught in the twelfth [chapter] regarding the sequence of the "closing of the flower" (*puṣpasaṅkoca*)—and for the sake of attaining the state of the "established lineage" (*nītasantati*) through the form of the meaning of speech culminating in the "bursting of touch" (*sparśasphoṭa*) which is about to be described, [one should contemplate] by the logic of the middle measure (*madhyamamāna*), the primordial nature of meaning (*arthaprakṛti*) consisting of the triad of speech, meaning, and sound (*vāgarthanādatripuṭī*), which is the supreme object of knowledge in the form of the three aims of the Veda (*trivarga*). [As it is said: "Reflection (*vimarśa*), the point (*bindu*), and the sound (*nāda*)."

And [he describes] the verbal *prakṛti*, which consists of the five channels mentioned in the verse, "The *sphoṭa*, the sound, and the sequence of speech," and which constitutes the supreme subject (*paramapramātṛ*): "Speech is measured in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not stir."

The digit (kalā) consisting of the forms of the letters *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi*—which is the eightfold form of the authoritative embodiment (*pramāṇapadamūrti*) comprising both the Vedic embodiment whose purpose is the sacrificial rite mentioned in the Śruti as "men speak of the fourth [state] of speech," and the Tantric embodiment of the human goals of life (the three aims and liberation) taught in the Kāmaśāstra beginning with the *Padminī* and ending with the *Hastinī*—exists within the embodied Nature (*mūrtaprakṛti*). This digit consists of the assembly of the circle (*vṛndacakra*) whose essence is the Light and Bliss to be described through the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*), the abodes (*dhāma*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*), by way of the integration (*sāmarasya*) of the Vedic and Tantric knowledge, action, messenger (*dūtī*), sacrifice (*yāga*), and yoga.
Describing the fitness for worship through its fourfold nature, he concludes the investigation:
"In the auspicious quartet of speech, you are she who flashes forth as the supreme form within the circle [of the mandala]."
She, whose form is the letters, the bindu, and the resonance (nāda), and who possesses a radiant circle of beautiful faces, is to be worshipped. || 75 ||
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Cidgaganacandrikā*, composed by the great poet Kālidāsa.

Regarding the passage beginning with *maṅgale*: the term *maṅgale*—interpreted according to the "lamp on the threshold" (*dehalīdīpanyāya*) or by intending both the vocative and locative cases—should be applied as an adjective qualifying both the embodiment of the Goddess of Speech (*vāgdevatāmūrti*) and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). O Mahākālī, who are the essence of all auspiciousness through your body of reflective awareness (*vimarśaśarīra*), you are the golden auspicious one (*hemaṅgale*). You are the fourfold speech (*vākcatuṣṭaya*) consisting of Parā, Paśyantī, and the others; likewise, you are the pavilion of that very form. You are composed of reflective awareness (*vimarśamayī*).

The meaning is that you are the auspicious one in one place as sound (*śabda*), in another as object (*artha*), and in both as the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in a state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*). Regarding the reading "in the circle of forms" (*mūrtimaṇḍale*): the meaning is in the collection of forms existing in the form of a mandala. This refers to the fourfold speech consisting of *parā*, *paśyantī*, and so forth, as well as the circle of forms consisting of the *padminī*, *citriṇī*, and other types. Alternatively, *parā*—the speech named *parā*—is the form belonging to the *padminī* class; or else, the speech named *vaikharī* is the form belonging to the *hastinī* class.

Among the various types of heroines described in the *Kāmaśāstra*—such as the *svīyā* (one's own), *parakīyā* (another's), and *sāmānyā* (common)—the *parakīyā* is also suggested here. Although she manifests through a threefold differentiation, at the time of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), she shines forth as non-different from one's own self (*svābheda*). For instance, even *vaikharī* speech is "one's own" (*svīyā*); yet, because she is the mother of the eight groups of phonemes (*varga-aṣṭaka*), she is perceivable by the ears of others and is her own object of experience, thus she shines as the supreme (*parā*) and most excellent. Even in the context of the *mūrtimaṇḍala*, the supreme lotus-lady (*parā-padminī*) shines as the most eminent.

And the female elephant (*hastinī*), being useful to a man of noble lineage (*rasvajāti*), shines as supreme and most excellent. Even though she belongs to another, by accepting—on the basis of the Pāṇinian-Vedic linguistic rule "even when there is an intervention" (*chandasi vyavāye 'pi*)—the fact that she serves as the cause for great purposes such as the establishment of one's lineage (*vaṃśa*) through the transference of meaning (*arthātideśa*) in Vedic injunctions (*niyoga*) and so forth, which is agreed upon by both [parties] and by Manu and others, it is shown that even a woman belonging to another may be the object of a *niyoga*; thus, the female form, as the cause for the stability of the thread of the lineage, shines as the most preeminent of all.

She is like the supreme *padminī*. By the etymological derivation that she possesses the lotuses described in such Vedic passages as "eight-wheeled, nine-gated," she is indeed a *padminī*. The same applies to *vaikharī* as well; she is either the supreme *vaikharī* or Speech itself.

She whose radiance (*bhā*) is the assembly of circles (*vṛndacakra*) that has light as its opening (*prakāśamukha*). That is to say, she is the one whose radiance is the assembly of circles—the multitude of circles consisting of the form of the bliss of light (*prakāśānanda*)—at the beginning (*mukha*), which is the commencement; such is *prakāśamukhavṛndacakrabhā*. Alternatively, regarding the variant reading *prakāśasukhavṛndacakragā*, the meaning is: she who moves within the assembly of circles of bliss that is of the nature of light, which is a collection of the joys of objects conceived in the form of a circle.

She goes to the circle of the *bṛndacakra*, which consists of fivefold rays (*raśmiskandha*) as elucidated in the *Mahārthamañjarīparimala*; thus, she is "one who goes to the circle of the *bṛndacakra* of light and bliss. The detailed nature of this circle of the *bṛndacakra* consisting of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*)—composed of rays made of the five aggregates whose characteristics will be described hereafter as the Jñāna, Mantra, Yoga, Śākta, and Śāmbhava—and composed of the multitude of letters of the *mātṛkā* numbering sixty-four, will be expanded upon later. Furthermore, in the context of the embodied form (*mūrtipakṣa*), she is the female form belonging to the classes such as the *padminī*.

The "multitude of light-faced bliss" (*prakāśamukha-sukha-vṛnda*) is so called because it brings together or centralizes light-faced bliss in one place. The Guru—whether in the form of a husband or otherwise—who teaches or bestows either the bliss of the self-luminous Self-bliss (*svayaṃprakāśātmananda-sukha*) or the bliss of sensory objects (*viṣayānanda-sukha*), is also that very multitude of light-faced bliss. That wheel (*cakra*), which has the alternative name "the wheel of living beings" (*jīvacakra*) and consists of the sacrificial seats (*pīṭha*) for the sacrifice of the messengers of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-dūtī-yāga*), will be described in the third *vimarśa*.

Its *bhā*—meaning its splendor (*kānti*) or its form (*rūpinī*)—goes toward or attains that [Light]. It is the wheel of the multitude of faces of light (*prakāśa*). It is the form of *nāda*, *bindu*, and *lipi*. By the etymology "it resounds, thus it is *nāda*," the *bindu*—which is the unmanifest form of the *bindu* corresponding to the *nāda* of the extroverted subject as described in the verse, "Vimarśa, *bindu*, *nāda*, *sphoṭa*, *śabda*, and the sequence of speech"—is another name for *vimarśa*. This *bindu* has reached the state of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-pada*), and is another name for the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) once it has entered that state.

[She] is of the nature of sound, manifest or unmanifest, as either *paśyantī* or *madhyamā*. *Lipi* (the written script) consists of the *kalā* (aspects) produced by the forms of the objects of cognition; its essence is *sphoṭa*. The aggregate of these three is the form of the fourth *mūrti* (embodiment). "You are worshipped"—this is the ellipsis, meaning "by practitioners. In the reading *iṣyase*, the meaning is that you are made the object of the term *iṣṭi* (sacrifice/desire), either through the vocalization (*samprasāraṇa*) of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) or from the root *iṣ* (to desire), which respectively signify sacrifice and the act of desiring.

It is understood that [the Lord] is made the object of desire and made the object of worship. This very point constitutes the meaning: that the Vedas and the gods prefer the indirect (parokṣa) and dislike the direct (pratyakṣa), according to the sequence of the fivefold creative acts such as emission (*sṛṣṭi*) and the established order of the expansion of the universe as expressed in secret speech. Thus, in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*, in the third book, within the section on the "Vision of the Gateway to Heaven" (*svargadvāra-darśana-prakaraṇa*) starting from the second anuvāka of the twelfth prapāṭhaka, the text states: "The heavenly world was indeed hidden from the gods."

They said to Prajāpati: "O Prajāpati, our world has indeed become dark; seek it out for us. He sought it by means of the sacrificial rites (*yajña-kratu*). He did not find it by means of the sacrificial rites. He sought it by means of the *iṣṭi* offerings. He found it by means of the *iṣṭi* offerings. That is why they are called *iṣṭi*; for they are truly *eṣṭayaḥ* (seeks), though they are spoken of as *iṣṭayaḥ* cryptically. For the gods, it is said, are fond of the cryptic. This is made clear by the passage beginning with, "He said to Āśā," and so forth.

By this very [explanation], the meaning that you are also being sought after for the sake of realizing the nature of your own Reality (*satya*)—by virtue of the distinction between verbal roots and nominal stems such as *eṣa* (to seek), *satya* (reality), and *anveṣaṇa* (searching)—is indeed obtained. For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kāmakalāvilāsa* that the pair of white and red dots (*bindu*), consisting of Śiva and Śakti, serves as the cause for the creation of the Word and its Meaning (*vāgartha*) in the form of Sound (*nāda*), precisely through the state of the Śākta emission (*visarga*) which is the essence of the *kāmakalā*: "The pair of white and red dots, representing the distinct contraction and expansion of Śiva and Śakti..."

The unmanifest sound (*rāva*)—the sprout of the *Nāda-Brahman* arising from the root of the tree of pride and the rest, which has burst open, and in which word and meaning are clearly interpenetrated—is the cause of the creation of word and meaning. Through such passages as "Desire (*kāma*) by virtue of its desirability, and the two points (*bindu*) whose forms are fire and moon, and the digit (*kalā*)" and so forth, the fact that Maṅgalādevī—the essence of inseparable luminosity and reflective awareness—is the cause of the creation of word and meaning, is clearly described.

The sequence of the yoga of the *dūtī-yāga* is also found in the *Jñānārṇava*. Having described the sequence of the *kriyā-dūtī* in the twenty-second chapter, the method for the sequence of the *jñāna-dūtī* is shown in the twenty-third chapter, beginning with: "O Goddess worshipped by the gods, I shall now explain another type of *dūtī*, by means of which one enters the eternal Brahman—the sacrificial abode known as the *praṇava*. And continuing: "The distinction of the classes of *dūtīs* is proclaimed to be fourfold: the *hastinī*, the *śaṅkhinī*, the *citriṇī*, and the *padminī*, O Dear One."

There are four kinds of messengers (dūtīs), whose eyes are beautiful and steady. Vaikharī should be known as Hastinī, because she is gross (*sthūlā*) and supports this entire, variegated cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), O Goddess of the gods; and since she gives birth to the collection of the world-elephants within the eight groups of consonants (*vargāṣṭaka*), she is called Karinī. Madhyamā becomes Śaṅkhinī. Just as Śaṅkhinī, O auspicious one, is pure and free from sin, so indeed is she beloved by all the gods, adorned with peace and good fortune.

Likewise, O fair-faced one, the middle speech resides in the *dhanaspati*; she is the goddess Citriṇī Ballarī, the destroyer of great defects. Her fruit, O lady of excellent hips, is eternally composed of Śiva and Śakti. O Goddess, the three worlds and every living being are composed of Śiva and Śakti. Within all those living beings, the Supreme Goddess Parā Vāk is the ultimate refuge; she is merged within the Supreme Brahman. Having purified oneself, one should worship that messenger there with fragrant flowers.

"The *padminī* is to be known as *parā*, moving at will like a swan (*haṃsa*). O daughter of the Mountain, the swan, having abandoned the lotus through non-duality, causes its contraction to blossom; thus, through the manifestation of the reality, grace (*saubhāgya*) arises. *Parā* attains illumination, and from this she becomes the *padminī*.

O lady of beautiful hips, the sixteen *kalās* are to be worshipped within her body. By such passages, one should observe therein the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the state of aesthetic equilibrium (*sāmarasya*), which is non-dual in nature, through the identity of the limited levels of speech beginning with *parā* and the distinct forms of the heroines beginning with the *padminī*. This is the general direction. (Verses 53–75)
Although this verse is not found in the manuscript of the *Mūlacidgaganacandrikā* held by the Research Society in Calcutta, it is nevertheless included here for explanation as it is found elsewhere.
It is that self-manifestation known as "I," which consists of the collection of phonemes grasped from beginning to end.
"O Mother, you are that very Guru who has realized the potency of mantra through the established scriptures. || 76 ||

This is the introduction: having thus established with authoritative evidence the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) consisting of the union of knowledge and action (*jñānakriyā*), [the author now addresses] the non-difference between the Śiva-power (*kauśivaśakti*) and that which is called the "vitality of mantra" (*mantravīrya*), which consists of the form of Gaurī established through the sequence of the respective *pratyāhāra*s, and which is common to both the nine-syllable Mātṛkā—employed through the traditional enumeration of the syllables of the Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Māheśvarī, and other [scriptures]—and the two-fold [reality] of "I" (*ahaṃ*) and the digit of Ramā (*ramākalā*), within the manifestation of the sequence of the nature of the phonemes belonging to the previously mentioned groups such as the three clusters (*tripuṭī*), the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), and the seven currents (*saptasrotas*).

He establishes this with the words beginning "the first and the last," etc.: O Ambikā! The first is [the Absolute] (anuttara), beginning with the letter A; the last is the effect of the Śāmbhava emission (*visarga*) and terminates in the letter A. For this very reason, it is "seized" (*gṛhīta*). It is "attained" (*prāpta*) by way of the form of a house (*gṛha*); it is "obtained" through identity with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the nature of the house, speech, and meaning. The meaning is that it is perceived at the beginning as the self of the *amākalā*. Likewise, the first is any one of the forms of the letters within the class of vowels starting from the Absolute form; the last consists of the two points (*bindu*) of the Śākta emission.

It is the effect of that [consciousness]. Alternatively, it takes the form of any one of the letters belonging to the groups of *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ra* (the sibilants). Or, being endowed with the emission (*visarga*) of Śambhu, it consists of the letter *ha*, which is the final consonant in the sūtra concerning the effects of that [emission]. Furthermore, the meaning is that this [consciousness] is subsequently perceived as the nature of the *aham-kalā*. And by those [two], the collection of letters—from *a* to *m*—is sequentially grasped and the act of apprehension is performed.

The meaning is that the collection of phonemes (*varṇarāśi*)—whether manifesting as vowels or manifesting as the *nāda*—is perceived through the various divisions of *pratyāhāra*, which consist of mutual states of being the womb and the embryo, according to their respective functions from the beginning [the letter *a*] up to the final *visarga*. That [collection] is her essence. The sense is that the self-manifestation "I" (*aham*), which consists of the digit *amā*, is the state of expansion whose ultimate nature is name and form (*nāmarūpa*) and the "I-sense" (*ahaṃkāra*). The feminine gender in the phrase "that very one" (*saiva*) is intended to emphasize the status of the predicate. [She is known] by the *āgamas*, that is, the scriptures.

The nature [of the mantra] is both "mantric power" (*mantravīrya*) and "essential form" (*svarūpa*). This has been established by the statement: "He, being unknown, resides in the self and in his own [belongings] within the three. Thus, through the distinction of perspectives based on the hidden intention (*gūḍhābhisandhi*) regarding the three genders conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the proof has been rendered both accomplished and yet to be accomplished. That very [nature] is the Guru; the Guru is also identical with the form of Gaurī. You alone are that. Just as the perception of time occurs through the nominal stem in the beginning of a kalā (unit of time), so too, through the specific distinctions of Your vision, there is the conceptualization of differences such as sacrifice and yoga even within the essential form.
However, from the perspective of the essential form itself, there is nothing at all—this is the intended meaning. (vv. 54–76)

In this second [chapter], which touches upon the pair consisting of linguistic usage and the single cognizer, the *Bhāṣya* and other works—whose face is the moonlight of consciousness—are like *cakorika* birds; they have been composed by Dhanadānandanātha to bestow the attainment of all goals. Therefore, the wise should discern here the pervasive dyad of the cognizer (*mātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*māna*). May those who, having attained the state of limited individuality (*aṇutā*) from the nature of power, and having approached and honored the venerable form, desire to behold this [work] so as to unveil the vision of the divine state shining intensely within, [attain their goal].

3. || This work, which delights the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), is free from many other [faults] and is measured [in its length]; indeed, everyone constantly enjoys it together. 4. || Just as the *Guruprasāda* is [esteemed] for the *Śabdenduśekhara*, so too is this divine commentary on the works of Kālidāsa, the *Cakorikā*. 5. || ...In order to incline [the reader] toward engaging with it, I have composed this [work] beyond compare; may the discerning critics here be pleased that my words are [spoken] with such clarity. 6. ||

"Āgamas, vikāras, and pratyayas are expressed by means of roots and suffixes; therefore, these [categories], such as *kalā* and the rest, do not apply here. Likewise, the statement of the Great ... [Mahā-...yakāra] is also an illustration in this regard, concerning the act of reciting āgamas and so forth when they are devoid of conceptual construction (*kalanā*)."
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Divyacakorikā*, a commentary on the *Cidgaganacandrikā* composed by Śrī Dhanadānandanātha.
This has been offered as a gift at the lotus feet of the venerable Sadguru Kāmākṣyambānandanātha; may there be auspiciousness.
